title: Keep It Offline
pitch: A file workbench that doesn't upload your content. WebMCP lets an AI agent edit your PDFs, photos, video and audio through 29 tools. More upcoming!
about_excerpt: A file workbench that doesn't upload your content. WebMCP lets an AI agent edit your PDFs, photos, video and audio through 29 tools. More upcoming! Like Comment Story Updates empty bench photos loaded pdf pages redaction agent rotated audio video I got the inspiration from one of the many online tools that, unfortunately, force you to upload your documents in order to work on them. What it does This is file workbench for PDFs, photos, video and audio that runs entirely in the browser tab. It registers 29 WebMCP tools (more coming!) so an agent can drive all of it, but the tools return facts about your files, never their contents. You can ask it to black out every bank account and it gets back { matches: 10, pages: [4] }, never the numbers. Every tool also has a button, so you can use it without an agent as well. How we built it Vanilla JS, no framework and no build step, so the repo is what runs. Tools go through document.modelContext.registerTool(). The registered set tracks page state (2 tools on an empty bench, 29 with every file kind loaded), the agent and the UI share one state object, and Web Workers keep heavy work off the main thread. Every dependency is vendored, and a CSP with connect-src 'self' makes the browser itself block an upload. Challenges we ran into Redacting for real, since black rectangles leave the text extractable underneath, so pages are flattened to images. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent that redacts a document it is never allowed to read. The page runs the search locally and strips the matches out of the return value, so they never enter the model's context. What we learned That there are way too many things that could go wrong for such a "simple" app! What's next for Keep It Offline More type of files and more tools! title: LostLoop  Human  Companion
pitch: LostLoop uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT read live, bounded evidence and stage the next recovery step, while every physical fact remains reserved for explicit human confirmation.
about_excerpt: LostLoop uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT read live, bounded evidence and stage the next recovery step, while every physical fact remains reserved for explicit human confirmation. Like Comment Story Updates 1 2 3 4 5 6 Inspiration Misplacing an everyday object is often part of a larger continuity problem. A plan changes, someone leaves without updating what they need, and later a Search begins under stress. Hardware trackers solve one object at a time. Generic assistants can be helpful, but they may also sound more certain than the available evidence allows. LostLoop explores a different idea: an AI recovery companion that can reason about the next useful step without ever pretending to know what physically happened. ChatGPT plans the next move. You own reality. What it does LostLoop is a private, local-first Human- Companion built around a strict separation between AI planning and human-confirmed reality. The complete loop is: Remember a human-confirmed place. Prepare reusable Foresight Moments and Ready Journeys. Adapt a journey through a reviewable Plan Shift. Recover through explainable Search, Rewind, and the Living Home Canvas. Confirm every physical report and possession state separately. Learn personal place language only after explicit human approval. For example, ChatGPT can read the current LostLoop state through WebMCP and stage a change to a saved journey. LostLoop shows the exact Kept / Added / Removed diff, but staging the proposal changes no physical fact. The person alone can apply or discard it. During Search, LostLoop keeps three things separate: what the evidence recommends, which room the person has selected, and which exact place is eligible for a report. A statement such as “I checked the bathroom” is not automatically converted into a physical fact. LostLoop first asks for an exact visible landmark and any missing outcome, then presents the normal confirmation boundary. The system also supports natural personal language such as “my little table”, but teaching that phrase changes language only — never memory evidence or physical truth. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the core interaction layer rather than an add-on. LostLoop exposes exactly 27 closed-schema WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . ChatGPT can read the live browser-local workspace, understand which actions are structurally possible, and stage bounded proposals against exact revisions. The tools are intentionally asymmetric: read tools are pure; proposal tools are revision-bound and inert; physical facts require explicit human confirmation; there is no agent-side approval path. LostLoop exposes a versioned Action Graph describing allowed and blocked operations, their revision bindings, human gates, and truth effects. Every WebMCP call also passes through a common Verified Effect runtime contract. The result includes a bounded receipt showing the before/after revision, observed changes, human gate, replay status, and next legal read. The in-app Judge Inspector displays actual session receipts while explicitly describing them as application-level verification rather than a cryptographic audit. Natural Recovery without invented certainty The Living Home Canvas provides a familiar room-and-landmark interface for recovery. It is intentionally not a tracking system. It does not use GPS, indoor positioning, cameras, Bluetooth, or inferred person/object locations. The WebMCP projection makes this boundary machine-readable: tracking: false currentPersonLocation: null currentItemLocation: null Natural language is resolved only against bounded visible candidates. Exact spatial relations such as under, inside, or behind require a visible anchor. Ambiguous near / next-to / beside language becomes a visible choice rather than invented geometry. The interface exposes Heard → Understood → Selected , making language interpretation inspectable instead of silently guessing. Human Truth One of the most important LostLoop rules is: Found ≠ possession. Finding an item does not automatically mean the person has it with them. Search completion and possession are separate human-confirmed states. This prevents the assistant from collapsing a real-world observation into a stronger claim than the person actually made. The same principle applies throughout the product: AI can suggest, organize, rank, explain, and stage — but the human owns the facts. Privacy and safety LostLoop is local-first. There is no account system, analytics backend, automatic cloud sync, GPS tracking, stored microphone recording, stored transcript, or user-data backend. Personal place phrases and custom home layouts remain local and exportable. Private text is redacted from collaboration receipts and inspection summaries. The Personal Home Canvas is a bounded schematic editor, not architectural CAD or an AI-generated location model. It is explicitly marked as not to scale and never claims where a person or object currently is. How im built it LostLoop 14.0 uses: React 19 TypeScript Vite / Vinext Cloudflare Workers browser-native PWA capabilities local browser storage Web Speech input/output WebMCP The application uses a deterministic state-transition engine with strict schema validation, revision-checked writes, bounded inputs, explicit migrations, and fail-closed WebMCP contracts. The final competition release contains exactly 27 WebMCP tools . Challenges The hardest problem was not adding more AI capability. It was deciding what the AI must not be allowed to claim. Natural language is messy. People say things like “I checked there”, “go back to the table”, or “try beside the bed”. A normal conversational system may resolve these confidently, but LostLoop has to preserve uncertainty whenever the evidence is incomplete. That required closed candidate sets, revision binding, explicit confirmation gates, deterministic semantic framing, and careful separation between navigation, suggestions, observations, and physical facts. Another challenge was keeping the same interaction useful through voice, typing, touch, WebMCP, desktop, and mobile without creating hidden state transitions. Accomplishments The final 14.0 release passed the complete release gate with: 355 tests passed 0 failed 0 skipped zero production runtime audit vulnerabilities a verified 27-tool WebMCP contract deterministic language and dialogue regression suites clean fresh-extraction build verification The public competition build is deployed independently and can be tested without access to the development workspace. What I have learned The most valuable lesson was that useful agentic software does not require giving an agent unlimited authority. A system can become more capable by making its boundaries clearer. WebMCP made it possible to give ChatGPT structured access to the live application while preserving a strict distinction between: what the agent can understand, what it can propose, and what only the human can make true. What's next The competition version intentionally focuses on one complete and inspectable recovery contract. Future directions could include household sharing, optional cloud synchronization, broader multilingual voice support, additional accessibility modes, and richer personal home presentation — while preserving the same human-confirmed truth boundary. title: Signal Timing Workbench
pitch: A San Francisco intersection that a human and an AI agent retime together. The simulation lives only in the tab, eight WebMCP tools let an agent search hundreds of signal timings while you supervise.
about_excerpt: A San Francisco intersection that a human and an AI agent retime together. The simulation lives only in the tab, eight WebMCP tools let an agent search hundreds of signal timings while you supervise. Like Comment Story Updates Interface What it is A four-arm signalised junction that a human and an agent operate together. The traffic simulation runs entirely in the tab — no backend, no API, nothing meaningful to scrape off a canvas. The state exists only in the page. That is the point. A conventional browser agent could screenshot this and learn nothing: it cannot read mean_wait_s out of pixels, and evaluating a candidate timing would cost it a slider drag, a button click and a screenshot round trip. It would manage perhaps five experiments while an agent with site tools runs two hundred. Not faster — categorically different. The junction exposes seven WebMCP tools. An agent arrives cold, reads the model specification, searches the timing space off the main thread while the traffic keeps flowing on screen, and hands back a scrubbable explanation of what it found. The operator watches, locks parameters mid-search, and decides. The design argument The interesting part is not the simulation. It is the shape of the tool surface, and three decisions in particular. run_batch reports physics. apply_config enforces policy. run_batch evaluates any timing, including ones that are illegal to deploy, and reports honestly what would happen. It checks nothing. apply_config is the only tool that can commit a timing to the junction, and the only one that enforces the constraints. Keeping those separate means the agent can discover that the fastest timing is inadmissible rather than being silently steered away from it. Under school-run demand the best-scoring timing is a permissive-left plan at 27.4 s mean wait; it is prohibited, because opposing volume × left-turn volume exceeds the phasing threshold. The best legal timing costs 45.8 s. An agent that only ever saw filtered results would never understand what admissibility cost. The refusal says so explicitly: a refusal is a fact about what may be deployed, not a scoring signal — a refused timing may well be the fastest one. Constraints ship with their derivations, and it changed agent behaviour describe_model publishes every constraint with the arithmetic behind it. Yellow and all-red are not tuning parameters; they are safety intervals derived from the ITE change-interval formulae: approach speed v = 15 m/s (54 km/h) yellow y = t + v/(2a) → 3.50 s → floor 4 s all-red r = (W + L)/v → 1.33 s → floor 2 s Two measured effects on a real agent run: Unprompted, it used 5 seeds and 60-minute runs. run_batch's description warns about ±2 s of simulation noise and recommends averaging at least 3 seeds; the agent went further on its own. It never hit the phasing refusal. Its 50-config refine batch was entirely left_protected: true — it read the cross-product rule, worked out that school-run demand mandates protected phasing, and pre-filtered its search space. Publishing constraints in full meant a careful agent self-checked instead of learning by rejection. Locks are a permission boundary with no unlock tool The operator can pin any parameter. read_state reports which are locked; apply_config refuses to change one and says so. There is deliberately no tool that unlocks a parameter. The agent can read the lock, reason about it, and re-optimise around it — only a human clicking the button releases it. A permission model expressed through the shape of the surface rather than a confirmation dialog. Tools Tool Kind Purpose describe_model read Parameters, metrics, constraints with derivations, scenarios read_state read Committed timing, phase, per-arm queues, locks, live metrics run_batch read Evaluate ≤50 timings in a Web Worker apply_config write Commit; enforces constraints and locks set_scenario write Switch demand profile; re-checks the committed plan pin_result write Surface a candidate to the operator with a rationale play_sequence write Narrated, scrubbable explanation Other choices worth naming: Tool results are budgeted. run_batch returns full per-arm detail for the top 3 rows and summary metrics for the rest, and does not duplicate the payload into structuredContent. Measured on a 36-config batch: 53,558 → 11,284 characters, a 79% reduction. Context bloat is what degrades an agent over a long session. run_batch runs in a Web Worker. A 50-config batch is ~500 ms; on the main thread that freezes the junction every time the agent thinks, and the premise is that the human watches a live workspace while the agent works. apply_config restarts the live run and says so, along with the ~4 simulated minutes before metrics settle. Otherwise the agent commits, re-reads two seconds later, and reasons about a transient. set_scenario re-checks the committed timing. Switching demand can make the deployed plan illegal. It reports that and leaves the plan committed — the agent asked to change the demand, not to redeploy the signal plan. pin_result re-measures over 3 seeds regardless of what produced the original figure, so two pins are always comparable. The agent's search is drawn in the domain's own notation. Evaluated candidates appear as miniature ring-and-barrier phase diagrams — the diagram a traffic engineer actually reads — with bar width encoding cycle length. A scatter plot would show convergence more precisely and say nothing about what was tried. Verification npm run agentsim mocks document.modelContext, registers the real tool surface, and drives the exact sequence a competent agent follows: cold discovery, coarse sweep, the constraint refusal, recovery inside the legal region, a lock refusal, malformed input, two pins, a scenario round-trip, a narrated replay, and AbortSignal cleanup. It runs in about four seconds and caught several schema bugs before any browser was involved. The simulation itself was validated before any UI existed: metric spread of 162 s against 1.6 s of seed noise, an interior optimum in cycle length that moves with demand (57 s under morning rush, 87 s under event egress), and four scenarios with four distinct optima. Notes on the model A stochastic cellular automaton (Nagel–Schreckenberg). Arrival rates are representative of a mid-size German town, not measured. Two modelling details matter for the decisions the agent faces: Opposing traffic is platooned. Gap acceptance uses the opposing flow concentrated into its green window, not the hourly average — the platoon is released by the same green in which a permissive left-turner is trying to cross. Without this, permissive lefts are far too easy and left_protected becomes a parameter with one always-correct answer. The left-turn bay is 60 m. When it fills, left-turners spill back and block the through lane behind them. That is why protected phasing is ever worth its cycle time, and why sizing the protected phase wrong is worse than not having one: at school-run demand, protected at 8 s scores 214 s against permissive's 74 s, while protected at 16 s is the best timing available. Running it bash npm install npm run agentsim # headless tool-surface harness npm run dev # then open in a WebMCP-capable browser Node 22+. WebMCP is secure-context only; localhost qualifies. Try: "Optimise this junction for mean wait under the school run scenario, then pin the two options you think I should choose between." title: Infinite Awareness Agent Lab
pitch: A human-led WebMCP experiment where AI prepares awareness protocols, structures reflections, protects blinded scoring, and compares privacy-conscious personal and collective signals.
about_excerpt: A human-led WebMCP experiment where AI prepares awareness protocols, structures reflections, protects blinded scoring, and compares privacy-conscious personal and collective signals. Like Comment Story Updates A fictional participant records a direct observation before the agent structures it for review. Blinded scoring protects the hidden condition while the person reviews usefulness, novelty and testability. The agent separates observation, interpretation and uncertainty; saving requires visible human confirmation. Read-only personal and cohort signals show aggregate patterns without exposing raw reflections or claiming efficacy. The prepared three-minute session updates the same visible page state shared by participant and agent. The initial session: a fixed three-minute protocol ready for WebMCP preparation, with later stages still locked. Judge Sandbox overview: eight registered WebMCP tools, fictional data and a protected hidden condition. The main Infinite Awareness experience—the human-facing 33-day programme that inspired the isolated Agent Lab. Inspiration: Infinite Awareness began with a simple problem: people can collect ideas about meditation, consciousness and self-awareness for years without turning those ideas into a repeatable practice they can examine for themselves. The existing Infinite Awareness application addresses that gap through a structured 33-day programme combining progressive awareness sessions, journaling, forecasting, blinded outcome scoring and personal analysis. The programme is designed as structured educational self-observation rather than treatment or proof of efficacy. The WebMCP Challenge presented a new question: 'What should an AI agent be allowed to do inside this experience—and what must remain human?' An agent cannot meditate, experience awareness or decide what an observation means for somebody. It can, however, organise the experiment, retrieve the correct protocol, structure an observation, protect the scoring method and analyse privacy-conscious trends. That division of responsibility became the foundation of the Infinite Awareness Agent Lab. What it does: The Agent Lab is an isolated, fiction-only WebMCP demonstration. A participant can open the live page in a compatible browser and ask an agent to help run an awareness experiment using natural language. The page exposes eight structured WebMCP tools: Read-only tools: 1 get_today_protocol retrieves the fictional participant’s current day, purpose, instructions and safety guidance. 2 analyse_personal_signal returns aggregated fictional personal trends without exposing raw reflections. 3 compare_collective_signal compares the participant’s aggregates with a fictional cohort after checking a fixed minimum sample threshold. 4 explain_safety_boundary explains the educational scope, consent rules, privacy boundary and stop guidance. Guarded tools: 5 prepare_session prepares the correct shortened demonstration session but cannot complete the human practice. 6 draft_observation turns a fictional participant’s words into a structured draft without saving it. 7 save_confirmed_observation saves the reviewed draft only after a visible human confirmation. 8 score_blinded_outcome records usefulness, novelty and testability scores without revealing whether the session was an intention or control condition. Every tool call creates a visible, structured update on the page so the participant can verify what the agent did. Why WebMCP?: A normal chatbot would need the participant to paste information into a conversation or depend on fragile screen interpretation. WebMCP allows the website to expose narrow, typed actions directly from the live page. The agent can discover the available tools, understand their input schemas and work with the same visible application state as the participant. No separate plugin or remote MCP server is required for the demonstration. This makes the experience both easier and safer. The agent receives only the information needed for the current task, while the website continues enforcing progression, validation, privacy and consent. Human and agent collaboration: The agent provides structure, consistency and analysis. The person retains experience, consent and interpretation. The agent can: Retrieve and explain the protocol. Prepare the correct session. Structure an observation for review. Preserve the blinded scoring sequence. Calculate and compare fictional aggregate signals. The person must: Decide whether to practise. Have the actual experience. Review the agent’s proposed draft. Explicitly confirm anything being saved. Review and confirm outcome scores. Decide what the resulting information means. The central principle is: 'An agent can organise the experiment. Only a person can have the experience.' Existing project and new challenge work: Infinite Awareness existed before the challenge as a 33-day commercial awareness-training application built over a month and a half with AI and human collaboration. The work added during the challenge is the WebMCP-powered Agent Lab, including: Eight registered WebMCP tools. An isolated /agent-lab experience. Fictional participant and cohort data. Structured tool results displayed in the interface. One-time visible human confirmations. Privacy-conscious personal and collective analysis. Blinded scoring protections. Safety and educational-scope boundaries. WebMCP discovery, execution and confirmation tests. Judge instructions, submission documentation and demonstration materials. The challenge extension is intentionally isolated from the existing production application. It does not connect to production customers, journals, payments, course records or private data. How we built it: The tools are registered from the top-level page using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool has a narrow JSON input schema, a clear description and an explicit read-only or guarded behaviour. The execution handlers reuse one shared page state so tool results and human interactions remain synchronised. The confirmation bridge was especially important. Saving and scoring initially required a confirmation identifier in the public tool input. Testing in ChatGPT’s browser showed that this identifier was held inside the page and was not available to the agent. We redesigned the bridge so the public tools accept only their genuine task inputs. Their execution closures independently validate the current page-held confirmation. Each confirmation is consumed after one successful use and cannot be replayed. Challenges: The largest challenge was making the agent useful without allowing it to overstep. We needed to ensure that: An agent could not save an unreviewed reflection. A confirmation could not be reused. Scoring could not happen before the observation was saved. The intention or control condition remained blinded. No raw reflections appeared in personal or cohort analysis. The demonstration made no medical, psychological or efficacy claims. The pre-existing application remained clearly separated from the new challenge work. Accomplishments: The public challenge repository passes all eight bundled tests, TypeScript validation, the production build and GitHub CI. The live sandbox was also verified for clean non-WebMCP fallback behaviour and native WebMCP discovery in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. ChatGPT successfully discovered all eight tools. Direct save and scoring calls failed before confirmation, succeeded exactly once after visible confirmation and failed when confirmation reuse was attempted. The blinded condition remained hidden throughout. What we learned: WebMCP tool design is not simply about exposing functions. Tool descriptions, input schemas, visible page state, confirmation handling and verifiable results are all part of the user experience. We also learned that human control works best when it is enforced by the application rather than left to an instruction in a prompt. The agent can request an action, but the page itself determines whether the required human review has happened. Human-led, AI-assisted creation: Like the experience it enables, this project was built through human-agent collaboration. I defined the purpose, methodology, safety boundaries and final decisions, while AI tools helped implement, test and refine the WebMCP extension. That process reinforced the principle at the heart of the project: AI should expand human capability without quietly taking away human agency. What’s next: The Agent Lab now has a stable public home, a reviewed MIT-licensed repository and a compliant 2:55 demonstration video. After the challenge, I want to make the Agent Lab freely available so more people can explore structured awareness, reflection and self-observation without surrendering their privacy, judgement or control to an algorithm. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: CiteApply
pitch: A scholarship portal where the website, not the model, owns the evidence rules. An agent cites answers via six WebMCP tools; conflicts are refused; every decision stays with the applicant.
about_excerpt: A scholarship portal where the website, not the model, owns the evidence rules. An agent cites answers via six WebMCP tools; conflicts are refused; every decision stays with the applicant. Like Comment Story Updates The agent cites. You decide. I built CiteApply because I kept seeing the same thing in every agent demo: the agent fills the form, and the website has no idea where any of it came from. For a scholarship application that's not good enough. The hard part was never typing. It's knowing which document proves each answer, what to do when two documents disagree, and whether what you submit is what you actually checked. So I flipped it. CiteApply is a fictional scholarship portal that publishes six WebMCP tools of its own. An agent can read the rules, see the applicant's parsed records as citable evidence, and bind answers to specific quoted lines in one atomic call. It cannot declare the applicant's email, pick between two records that disagree, confirm, or submit. The website enforces that on the server. The model is never asked to behave. The moment I care about most is the refusal. Two income records disagree. The agent asks to bind income. The site says conflict_requires_human and writes nothing. Then it's the person's turn. Try it: open the live site in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, choose the record set that disagrees, and press Watch an assistant fill this in . A scripted client makes nine real tool calls and you watch it get refused. Or ask your own agent to fill it in; I verified that in the ChatGPT in-app browser, where the agent binds the cited answers and is refused on the conflict. Then finish the three decisions yourself and download the receipt. Why WebMCP This only works because the site is a participating website . WebMCP lets it publish a site-owned evidence contract: six small operations (state, requirements, evidence index, evidence-backed mutation, validation, review preparation) that an external agent uses to collaborate with the visible application instead of around it. Requirements are live. Binding the dependency field makes guardian name and household size required; the agent is told to re-read the rules mid-session (6 questions become 8). Contradictions are structured refusals. Two accepted income records disagree (INR 540,000 vs 480,000). apply_evidence_backed_answers returns conflict_requires_human and writes nothing. Readiness is the server's answer. prepare_submission_review freezes a draft only when the server says it is ready, and returns opaque metadata, never the review itself. Authority never travels in tool arguments. The page injects its page and consent capabilities as headers from page memory; an agent with a valid cookie but no live page capability gets stale_page from all six tools. What changes for the person filling it in By hand, you open each record, type the value exactly as written, and pick the line that says so; a wrong line or value is refused. With an assistant, the same eight answers are cited in one call and only three decisions remain: choose between the disagreeing records (with a reason), declare your email, and submit. A Feel the difference panel shows your real by-hand tally next to the assistant's counts from the same session. I don't claim a time saving because I didn't measure one. What people and agents do together The agent does the reading and the citing; the site validates every binding. The applicant keeps every act of judgement. The frozen review carries the chosen source, the reason given, and both excerpts. The receipt carries the same content hash whether the review was prepared by hand or by the agent. How I built it Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Zod 4, PostgreSQL (Neon) on Vercel. The six tool descriptors are generated from the same Zod schemas the server re-validates against, with closed input schemas and correct readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint annotations. Record PDFs are parsed at runtime with pdfjs-dist after an allowlisted SHA-256 check; every excerpt is reconstructed from stored page/span anchors, so the UI cannot show a quote the source doesn't contain. Idempotency is keyed on an HMAC of the canonicalised change set. Verifiers prove the production code contains no hardcoded answers and imports no test goldens. Proven, not claimed 61 node tests (contract, unit, security, real-Postgres integration) and 45 real-browser Playwright specs, including the full 13-step journey for both record sets in Chrome 152 with the WebMCP flag, all passing against the live deployment. Verified by hand in the ChatGPT in-app browser. Axe accessibility clean on every screen. Every tool request and response from those runs is logged verbatim in the repo. What went wrong along the way Chrome's real document.modelContext differs from the draft spec: getTools() returns a Promise, executeTool takes the tool object and a JSON string, and no options object is passed. My first callback threw before doing any work. Other hosts differ again, so the in-page client now bounds every host call, accepts both calling conventions, and falls back to the page's own registered tools mid-run, saying so on screen. A second bug only showed up on the deployed site: two quick human actions could share the same expected revision, so the server correctly refused the second as stale. Localhost never showed it because the round trip was too fast. It's fixed with an action queue and a regression test that injects latency. Honest limits Everything is synthetic. The parser handles only the six committed records. The in-page demonstration client is scripted (real calls, no model choosing them) and says so on screen. WebMCP is a Community Group draft; support varies by browser build. Try it Live: https://citeapply.vercel.app (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) Code: https://github.com/amithrh/citeapply (MIT) Judge walkthrough: docs/JUDGE-TESTING.md in the repo Built With next.js playwright postgresql react typescript vercel webmcp Try it out citeapply.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by amit mishra Like Share this project: Updates amit mishra started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:24 PM EDT

video_transcript_excerpt: This is a website refusing an AI agent and being right to. I'm Emmet and this is Site Apply, my entry for the Web MCP challenge. Filling a scholarship form isn't hard because of typing. It's hard because of judgment. Which record proves each answer and what if two records disagree? Site Apply publishes six Web MCP tools so an agent can cite answers and the site, not the model, decides what's allowed. These are synthetic records that disagree with each other. The page registers six tools when it loads and everything the agent does goes through those six. Consent is a real disclosure. What the tools may receive, what they never receive, what they cannot do. And the capability it creates is never handed to the agent. The page holds it. It reads the rules, then the evidence index, then binds four answers in a single atomic call. All of them or none. Answering one question changed which questions apply. Guardian name and household size just became required. So the agent has to read the requirements again. Here's the moment. The agent asks to fill in income. Two accepted records disagree. 540,000 and 480,000. The website answers conflict requires human and writes nothing. The agent can read exactly why it is blocked. It cannot clear the block itself. So I decide and I read both records first. The buttons stay dead until I say why. The site will not write a reason on my behalf. I choose a source and I declare my own address. No tool can do either. The agent can ask the site to freeze the application, but the review appears only here and assisted access closes when it does. Every answer sits beside the exact text it came from. Same hash, same warning. The record I chose and the reason I gave. Synthetic records, a fictional program, and Web MCP is still a draft standard. But the contract is real and the website is the one enforcing it.

 IntentCart 🛒🤖 

 AI researches. You decide. 

 IntentCart is an agent-native collaborative shopping experience built with WebMCP . 

 Instead of endlessly searching through products, users can simply describe what they want. For example: 

 
 “Build me a coding setup for college under ₹70,000.” 
 

 The AI agent can then research products, compare options, create a shopping plan, and calculate the total budget — while keeping the human in control of the final decision. 

 💡 Inspiration 

 Online shopping can involve searching through dozens of products, comparing specifications, checking prices, and trying to stay within a budget. 

 I wanted to explore a different experience where an AI agent could actually interact with the shopping website and help with the research and planning, instead of just acting like a chatbot. 

 🚀 What IntentCart Does 

 IntentCart provides 8 native WebMCP tools : 

 
 🔎 Search products 
 📋 Get product details 
 ⚖️ Compare products 
 🛒 Add products to cart 
 ❌ Remove products from cart 
 🛍️ View the cart 
 💰 Calculate the budget 
 🧠 Create a shopping plan 
 

 For example, the agent can create a complete college coding setup while staying within a ₹70,000 budget. 

 Each recommended product includes a “Why Selected” explanation so the human can understand the recommendation. 

 👤 Human Approval 

 The AI does not automatically make the final shopping decision. 

 The agent creates a proposal first. The human reviews the products, reasons, and budget, then explicitly clicks: 

 “Approve & Add to Cart” 

 Only after approval are the products added to the collaborative cart. 

 This creates a simple principle: 

 
 AI handles the research and planning. Humans make the final decision. 
 

 🔧 How It Was Built 

 IntentCart was built using: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 WebMCP 
 Native browser WebMCP APIs 
 HTML5 
 CSS3 
 

 The application uses a shared cart state so that changes made through the website and WebMCP tools remain synchronized. 

 An Agent Activity timeline also shows tool activity as the agent interacts with the application. 

 🧩 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing a shared state that could work consistently between the normal UI and agent tool calls. 

 Another important challenge was creating a safe approval flow where the AI can propose actions without automatically making purchasing decisions . 

 I also had to handle WebMCP tool registration carefully to avoid duplicate registrations during React development and remounts. 

 🏆 What I'm Proud Of 

 
 Native WebMCP tool integration 
 Agent-accessible shopping capabilities 
 Human approval before cart changes 
 Real-time shared cart state 
 Product comparison and budget planning 
 Clear visibility into agent activity 
 

 📚 What I Learned 

 This project helped me understand how to build for the agent-native web . 

 Instead of designing only for humans clicking buttons, I learned how to expose meaningful application capabilities as structured tools that AI agents can use. 

 I also learned that good agent experiences need a balance between automation and human control . 

 🔮 What's Next 

 Future versions could include: 

 
 More personalized shopping preferences 
 Larger and real-world product catalogs 
 Smarter recommendations 
 More advanced comparison features 
 More granular human approval controls 
 Multi-user collaborative shopping

title: MC Beats
pitch: Think OP-1 but to jam live (with agents).
about_excerpt: Think OP-1 but to jam live (with agents). Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration MC Beats began as an investigation into human-agent interaction. As a musician, one of the most interesting forms of interaction I experience is playing music with other people. When I perform with someone, I am always listening, reacting, and looking for small cues that help me understand what they are doing. I wanted to explore what that relationship could look like with an AI agent. Could I build an instrument where I could play with an agent, respond to its ideas, and let it respond to mine? What it does MC Beats is a browser-based live synthesizer and two-deck performance tool. I can play drums, bass, chords, and lead; record loops; shape each sound; and move between two four-bar decks. At the same time, a WebMCP agent can read the musical state, follow what I am playing, prepare new material, arrange patterns, schedule transfers, and perform solos. This lets me play while the agent works in the background, then respond when it brings a new idea into the performance. Everything runs on one shared musical clock. The agent queues its actions to beats and bars, so its changes fit the timing of the music. The interface shows what is on each deck, what is playing, and what the agent is doing, which helps me understand the performance at a glance. Every sound is generated in the browser using oscillators, filters, envelopes, effects, and procedural noise. There are no recorded samples or backend music services. How I built it I built MC Beats in three main stages. I started with the synthesizer. I set myself the challenge of generating every sound from basic waveforms, such as sine and saw waves, along with random noise. It took a couple of days to get the synth sounding good. I spent much of that time adjusting the values for each instrument until the drums, bass, chords, and lead sounded the way I wanted. Next, I designed the interface. I first sketched it by hand, drawing some inspiration from instruments such as the OP-1. I wanted it to feel like a physical music tool while still making sense as a web app. I then gave it my own visual style, with two decks, clear instrument colours, playable controls, and a compact layout. The third stage was the WebMCP integration. I connected the interface and synthesizer to tools that let an agent understand the current performance and take musical actions. This was the point when the separate parts came together and began to feel like one instrument. Challenges The hardest problem was timing. Agents work across two conflicting time scales. Once an agent makes a tool call, the action can happen almost instantly. However, listening to the music, processing the available information, and deciding what to do can take longer than it takes me to reach the next bar. In my first implementation, the agent queued every action at an exact musical time. Calls sometimes failed because they were formatted incorrectly. Other calls arrived after their requested time had already passed. Each failure meant another tool call, more thinking, and another delay in the music. I worked on this from both sides. I built higher-level WebMCP tools that give the agent more context and let it complete useful musical tasks in fewer calls. I also gave it clearer information about the current bar and the earliest safe time for its next action. One experiment was to tell the agent how many tokens it could use during each bar, encouraging it to make faster decisions. I also let the agent schedule actions across several bars. A single tool call can prepare a phrase, arrange a deck, or plan a transfer that unfolds over time. This helps the agent’s actions fit the pace of a live performance. The second challenge was communication. When I play with other musicians, I use eye contact, movement, and other small signals to understand what they are about to do. Those cues do not naturally exist when I play with an agent. I tried to recreate some of that awareness through the interface. My actions and the agent’s actions use a similar visual language. A control bar shows what the agent is doing, and the deck displays let me see the current state of the music. In the other direction, WebMCP tools give the agent structured information about the key, transport, deck contents, and what I have recently played. What I learned Building MC Beats taught me how much good collaboration depends on timing and shared information. Giving an agent control is easy compared with helping it understand when to act, what I am doing, and how to show me what it plans to do. I found that an agent works best as a musical partner when it can listen, prepare ideas in the background, enter at a useful moment, and leave enough space for me to respond. title: WebHUD
pitch: Smart glasses without the vendor OS — a WebMCP surface for your agent, your inputs, and any display.
about_excerpt: Smart glasses without the vendor OS — a WebMCP surface for your agent, your inputs, and any display. Like Comment Story Updates How WebHUD connects your agent, WebMCP, and any heads-up display. The compare intent renders as a full table on desktop The compare intent renders as a swipe-able cards on glasses Tool registration is dynamic. For example, `map_show_route` exists only while a compatible map is active. Not every pair of glasses has a camera, so WebHUD pairs a navigation input to whatever the hardware offers. Inspiration Smart glasses usually come bundled with a vendor-specific operating system, assistant, and app ecosystem. That creates a strange mismatch: the assistant on the glasses often knows less about the user than the agent they already use every day. WebHUD flips that model. The glasses become a display, the web page becomes the adaptive interface, and the user keeps their preferred agent, memory, apps, and language. What it does WebHUD is an interactive WebMCP-enabled heads-up display. A WebMCP-capable agent supplies structured data and the user's purpose; WebHUD chooses the interface that fits the current context. The same venue comparison becomes: a wide comparison table on desktop; focused, swipeable cards in a simulated glasses lens. That reflow happens locally without another agent call. People and agents co-drive the same surface: voice expresses intent; keyboard, touch, a Bluetooth ring, or a locally processed palm gesture changes focus; surface_get_view_state tells the agent what the user is currently looking at, enabling references such as “this one.” WebHUD can present calendars, email decks, documents, images, people, choices, comparisons, triage queues, maps, and walking routes. Why WebMCP WebMCP is central to the product rather than an added integration. The page registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback. The main smart-responsive contract is surface_present . The agent declares one of six purposes— glance , browse , inspect , compare , choose , or triage —and provides semantic items. WebHUD maps that request to an appropriate renderer for desktop, phone, or glasses. Tool registration is dynamic. For example, map_show_route exists only while a compatible map is active. The page emits tool changes as capabilities appear and disappear, reducing irrelevant or unusable actions. Every presentation call returns a receipt describing what was rendered, giving the agent reliable feedback instead of forcing it to guess what appeared. Better human-agent collaboration Without WebHUD, the user must repeatedly describe which item they mean or ask the agent to navigate one step at a time. With WebHUD, the human can swipe to an email or venue and then speak naturally. Gesture supplies context; voice supplies intent. This makes small displays practical without forcing every interaction through speech. Privacy and safety Camera frames stay inside the browser tab and are processed locally. View-state responses expose identifiers and titles rather than email bodies or image pixels. Map location is supplied explicitly by the user; the page does not read device GPS. Sensitive actions remain agent-controlled and human-confirmed. WebHUD has no application backend. How it was built WebHUD is a static TypeScript and Vite application deployed using Cloudflare Workers static assets. Key components include: WebMCP registration and dynamic re-registration; centralized surface and focus state; desktop, phone, and glasses renderers; keyboard, ring/controller, touch, and palm-input adapters; Leaflet maps with walking routes and fallback estimates; vendored MediaPipe assets for local hand tracking; automated tests and GitHub Actions verification. Testing Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in a compatible Chrome build with WebMCP testing enabled. Confirm the page displays WebMCP ✓ . Ask the agent to compare three venues with shared price, capacity, distance, and AV facts. Confirm the desktop table appears. Press G and confirm the same state reflows into glasses cards without another presentation call. Navigate with Left or Right, then ask about “this one.” Ask for nearby cafés and a route to number one to see the map-only route tool register dynamically. The public repository includes source code, tests, setup instructions, screenshots, the WebHUD specification, an MIT license, and third-party notices. Built with TypeScript, Vite, WebMCP, Cloudflare Workers, Leaflet, MediaPipe, Vitest, and GitHub Actions. title: OutcomeMesh
pitch: Ask once, approve once: dinner and a ride booked via WebMCP
about_excerpt: Ask once, approve once: dinner and a ride booked via WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates The booking runs a second origin's WebMCP tool, called only after the human pressed Confirm. Six WebMCP tools become eight live, no reload: the page lists every tool call with its origin. One combined receipt: exact prices, cancellation windows, and only the ride was retried. Inspiration Jordan uses a wheelchair. Booking dinner and a ride tonight means two websites, and the restaurant's site gives an AI assistant nothing to call. Agents can navigate many websites, but navigation is not a safe, inspectable action contract. Cross-site tasks still break when a capability is missing, a route violates a human constraint, consent is vague, or one provider fails after another action already succeeded. OutcomeMesh explores a different layer: a neutral control plane between web capabilities and human outcomes. The open web needs both a way to create missing agent-native supply and a way to route that supply under visible human control. What it does Deterministic, fixture-driven demo: two bundled sample connector packages stand in for community submissions; all providers are synthetic. The demo begins with one synthetic intent: dinner tonight at 7 for two people, wheelchair accessible, with a ride included and a total budget under $80. The page registers six WebMCP tools when it loads; the header shows the live count ( 6 WebMCP tools live for your AI assistant ). Restaurant booking is not one of them, so the outcome cannot complete. Community Foundry reviews a sample restaurant connector package, submitted the way a community package would be. The risky version is rejected; the safe version passes an executable 18-check validator and is published with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The header count changes from 6 to 8 without a reload, and the Step 2 screen lists every WebMCP call as it runs: publish_connector twice, plan_outcome , then the brand-new restaurant_search_accessible_slots . Router rejects a cheaper restaurant because its entrance has three steps, and shows the exact plan: $44 restaurant + $26 ride = $70 , who receives what data, and the cancellation boundary. Nothing is booked until the person presses Confirm on the page. An agent that calls execute_outcome earlier receives a structured consent_required result, and the page shows that call as Needs your OK . After Confirm, Step 4 lists the booking calls: execute_outcome , restaurant_hold_slot , and then stepway_book_accessible_ride , which runs on a second origin ( https://outcomemesh-provider.pages.dev ). The first ride fails deterministically, the table stays held, and only the ride is retried. Done shows one confirmation, RCPT-OM-0007 , with exact prices and cancellation windows. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP is the lifecycle being demonstrated, not an add-on. The restaurant tools genuinely do not exist at startup. Community Foundry publishes them with the imperative API; a WebMCP-aware browser then discovers and calls them as structured, page-origin tools. Chrome DevTools' Application → WebMCP pane shows the same eight tools plus the provider tool, with live invocation status. If WebMCP is unavailable, the demo blocks instead of pretending that a badge or browser macro created native tool supply. The provider ride is a real cross-origin WebMCP call: the synthetic Stepway page registers stepway_book_accessible_ride with exposedTo limited to the OutcomeMesh origin, and OutcomeMesh discovers it with getTools({ fromOrigins }) and runs it with executeTool only after the page-owned consent grant. How it creates a better user experience The human and agent share one visible state. The agent receives structured tool schemas instead of guessing at page controls. The human sees why one route was rejected, exactly what data will be shared, who receives it, what will change, what costs $70, and which boundary is irreversible before anything consequential executes. Every tool call is visible on the page as it happens, with its origin, so trust does not depend on a hidden log. Accessibility needs change which tools are called: the route with three entrance steps is rejected even though it is cheaper. This is a fixture-driven demonstration, not validated accessibility evidence. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can inspect the page's current capabilities, publish the missing sample connector package, create the route, and attempt execution. The page stops it at a human-only approval boundary, then exposes the approved state so the agent can resume and retrieve the same receipt the person sees. Together they complete a multi-provider task while preserving provenance, constraints, consent, failure, recovery, and outcome evidence across the full loop. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite, using WebMCP's imperative API. Six platform tools register when the page initializes: inspect_capabilities publish_connector plan_outcome approve_outcome execute_outcome get_outcome_receipt Foundry publication dynamically registers two domain tools: restaurant_search_accessible_slots restaurant_hold_slot A second static origin hosts the synthetic Stepway provider page, which registers stepway_book_accessible_ride for the OutcomeMesh origin only. Every registered tool is wrapped so each call (from the page or from a browser agent's executeTool ) is recorded with its origin and result and rendered on the Find and Book screens. Tool callbacks, Router, the consent checkpoint, execution, recovery, event ledger, and receipt all read and mutate one deterministic runtime store. A Playwright verifier uses native getTools() and executeTool() to prove the 6 → 8 lifecycle, the cross-origin provider call, receipt integrity, and recovery. Hosting is two static Cloudflare Pages projects; there is no backend, login, or API key. Challenges we ran into Keeping one system instead of two: a visual workflow plus a nominal WebMCP layer would have been easy and dishonest. Every visible phase and every tool callback share one state machine. Modeling failure honestly: a pre-consent stop resets to a safe six-tool state because nothing mutated; after a consequential mutation the UI starts a fresh proof and does not claim provider rollback. Browser differences: Chrome's WebMCP testing surface parses executeTool input as a JSON string, so the runtime tries the object form first and falls back to a string. Accomplishments we are proud of The page-origin registry really changes from six to eight tools without a reload, and the page shows the count live. A second website's WebMCP tool is discovered and executed cross-origin, only after visible human consent, and the call is shown with its origin. Exact rejection, least-privilege consent, deterministic failure recovery, and one combined receipt stay synchronized. Zero-key, deterministic, responsive, keyboard-operable, runnable without accounts or services. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experience is not "an agent can click less." It is that a website can expose a precise capability contract while the human stays inside the same visible state and consent boundary. Dynamic availability matters as much as schema quality, and a receipt is credible only when it is derived from the same actions the tool callbacks actually performed. What's next Validate one agent builder who wants the Action Contract／connector workflow and one website owner who wants to provide it. The prototype does not claim that demand, adoption, payment, or production integration evidence exists. pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. about_excerpt:
Be Capable. 
BeCapa is the marketplace for agent capabilities. Discover and install trusted tools, skills, and workflows in the public marketplace, or private BeCapa's to secure share your companies.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Have you tried to find new capabilities for your agent? Have you tried installing skills, tools, or new workflows for your agent? Have you tried to share a skill you developed with your work colleagues? If you have you'll know why BeCapa is a must for you and your team. If you haven't, then you are missing out on the power of agents. 

 What it does 

 Becapa makes capability discovery easy. BeCapa makes secure sharing of enterprise developed skills secure and easy. It's your private app store for the enterprise. 

 How we built it 

 BeCapa was built with Codex. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Speed. Once the problem was identified. It was running into speed boundaries at which point we've moved to parallel agent execution. Beyond development challenges, it's the cold start problem with starting a capabilities marketplace. You have none to start with, so where do we start? Then it's a marketing and acquisition problem. How do we get users? You can build something amazing, but if people don't know it exists, you have provided value to nobody but yourself. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 It's incredible to experience how easy tools, skills, and workflows are to install on any machine across all of your agents. I don't even use a companies docs for MCP tool installs anymore. I tell my agent to publish X in BeCapa and then I install the new capability using BeCapa. The workflow is insanely smooth. Not a single config file or text edit required by the user. 

 What we learned 

 Third party MCP servers, skills, and Ai capabilities should be a thing. If a company is too slow to develop for AI, why can't third parties do it on their behalf? To close the gap the way software hackers closed the gap decades ago until vendors caught up with their own tools. One reason is Apache licensing. Another is "reselling" of API laws that need clarity around is an MCP wrapper or business wrapper around an existing companies API's actually a violation of the API license? TBD...Nobody has challenged these yet. 

 What's next for BeCapa 

 We are growing our capabilities. We want more users, but we see the largest opportunity within the enteprrise to deploy their own private capabilities stores. We also see a great opportunity for third party publishers to run ahead of companies that aren't developing for Ai and monetize their agent capabilities. BeCapa will push the "Earn" portion of our offering to attract those third party developers.

title: Day Canvas
pitch: Day Canvas is a visual planner where you and AI shape your day together—adding, moving, and organizing tasks live on one shared canvas.
about_excerpt:
Day Canvas is a visual planner where you and AI shape your day together—adding, moving, and organizing tasks live on one shared canvas.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Day Canvas: Building a Planner Shared with AI 

 What inspired it 

 Day Canvas began with a simple frustration: planning tools and AI assistants often live in separate places. You might describe a change in a chat, then manually reproduce it in a calendar or task list. I wanted to make that handoff disappear. 

 The idea was to create a shared workspace where a person and an AI can plan the same day together. Instead of receiving a text-only confirmation, the user can watch the canvas change as the AI adds, moves, prioritizes, or removes work. The result is a planning experience that feels collaborative, visible, and grounded in the actual schedule. 

 What I built 

 Day Canvas is a visual daily planner with a timed calendar, a task inbox, priority controls, and day/week/month/year views. Users can add blocks, drag them to reschedule, manage unscheduled tasks, and see overlapping events arranged clearly in separate lanes. 

 The defining feature is browser-native WebMCP integration. An AI agent can use tools to inspect the schedule, find open time, add or move calendar events, triage inbox tasks, and delete items. Those tool calls operate on the exact same actions as the user interface, so the canvas stays in sync and changes animate live. AI actions also have their own feedback, including activity toasts, a moving cursor for reschedules, and a deletion animation. 

 How I built it 

 I built the interface with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and a custom client-side store. The planner canvas renders a vertical time grid, while reusable components handle event cards, calendar views, inbox tasks, theme controls, and agent activity. 

 The core architectural decision was a single source of truth for task and calendar mutations. Both drag-and-drop interactions and WebMCP tool handlers call the shared functions in lib/taskActions.ts . This keeps UI actions and AI actions consistent: there is one set of validation rules, one state update path, and one way to announce changes. 

 WebMCP tools are registered in the browser after the app mounts through document.modelContext.registerTool . The AI can therefore reason about the open day using functions such as calendar summary and free-time search, then make a targeted update without a separate MCP server. 

 For scheduling, the free-time logic treats each event as an occupied interval. If an event begins at (s_i) and lasts (d_i) minutes, its occupied range is 

 [
[s_i,\; s_i + d_i).
] 

 After sorting events by start time, the app finds gaps between these ranges and returns the first gap that can fit a requested duration. That makes suggestions practical rather than merely descriptive. 

 Challenges I faced 

 The hardest challenge was ensuring that AI edits felt trustworthy. An AI must not be a separate, hidden layer that happens to modify data; its changes need to be understandable to the person looking at the plan. I addressed this by routing agent actions through the same shared action layer as user interactions and by giving those actions visible motion and feedback. 

 Calendar layout was another challenge. Events can overlap, have very short durations, recur across dates, or belong in different views. I added collision-aware lanes for simultaneous events and compact card layouts for 15- and 30-minute blocks so the calendar remains readable instead of becoming visually crowded. 

 Finally, browser-native AI integration required careful boundaries. Tool inputs are defined with schemas, calendar updates validate time formats and durations, recurring events require an end date, and free-time calculations distinguish scheduled calendar events from independent inbox tasks. These constraints help the agent make useful changes without creating impossible or ambiguous schedules. 

 What I learned 

 This project taught me that AI features are strongest when they are embedded directly in a familiar workflow. The most valuable interaction is not simply asking an AI for advice; it is seeing that advice become an understandable, reversible action in the tool already being used. 

 I also learned the value of designing state and interaction models before adding intelligence. Because Day Canvas has shared task actions and explicit scheduling rules, the UI and the AI can work together without drifting into separate versions of the truth. Good AI UX depends as much on clear product feedback and reliable state management as it does on the model itself. 

 Where it can go next 

 The current project lays the groundwork for authenticated, persistent planning with Clerk and Supabase. Next steps include resilient offline syncing, per-user timezones, production deployment, and richer scheduling assistance that respects priorities, deadlines, and personal working patterns.
