title: Semantic City — Shared-World WebMCP Simulator
pitch: A playable city-management sandbox where humans and agents share one live city. WebMCP exposes traffic, budgets, and utilities so every agent action is visible, validated, and reversible.
about_excerpt: A playable city-management sandbox where humans and agents share one live city. WebMCP exposes traffic, budgets, and utilities so every agent action is visible, validated, and reversible. Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates One visible city; a semantic surface agents can use. An agent asks for congestion; the exact returned roads light up. The agent previews affected city state before changing anything. A visible improvement is not enough—58% traffic forces a fresh inspection. The shared world verifies the goal: 5/5 constraints satisfied. The idea Most websites expose pixels, buttons, and forms for people. When an AI agent needs to help, it often has to infer meaning from that visual surface or operate through a separate API the person cannot see. Semantic City asks a different question: What if a website exposed the meaning of its live interface directly to agents? A city simulator is an ideal proving ground. A person sees roads, congestion, utilities, budgets, and tradeoffs. An agent needs those same concepts as structured objects, metrics, constraints, and legal actions. Both should work on one world. What I built Semantic City is a playable, deterministic city-management sandbox on a 24 × 18 grid. A human can build and upgrade roads; place residential, commercial, industrial, park, and power buildings; manage taxes and a city budget; advance simulation ticks; demolish; undo; and save or load locally. The simulation tracks population, jobs, happiness, traffic, pollution, power coverage, cash flow, construction spend, and challenge constraints. Its rules are deliberately understandable and deterministic, so interventions have reproducible causes and results. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is the product interface, not an automation wrapper. The page registers 14 domain tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...), including city and metric reads, area, traffic, and budget inspections, building and road mutations, tax changes, deterministic simulation, undo, challenge evaluation, and non-committing intervention previews. Every tool is connected to the same authoritative, revisioned CityStore used by the React interface. There is no hidden "agent city" or scripted winning state. Human clicks and WebMCP calls dispatch the same validated commands. Mutations require the latest observed revision and return affected objects and cells, direct cost, metric deltas, constraint results, world ID, state hash, and rules version. This makes agent actions safe, deterministic, and verifiable. Making agent behavior visible Semantic View reveals what the page exposes semantically: stable object IDs, road connectivity, traffic and capacity, neighborhood boundaries, building effects, utility coverage, pollution, happiness, costs, and placement constraints. When an inspection tool returns roads, buildings, or cells, those exact entities light up on the visible map. Before a mutation, affected cells are hatched as a preview without advancing the city revision. After a commit, the map, metrics, constraints, revision, hash, undo history, and activity timeline update together. The timeline records the selected tool, arguments, affected objects, cost, metric changes, execution time, and before-and-after proof. The human can see exactly what the agent inspected, intended, and changed. The Rivergate challenge The featured goal is: Reduce traffic below 50%, maintain happiness above 70%, and spend no more than $400,000, without raising taxes or demolishing homes. Rivergate starts at 83.80% traffic . The agent first inspects the authoritative city, traffic hotspots, and budget, then previews and commits a seven-cell avenue upgrade. Traffic falls to 58.44% - better, but still failing. Instead of assuming success, the agent inspects revision one, finds the remaining bottleneck, previews and commits a second five-cell upgrade, advances one deterministic tick, and verifies the new world. The final state reaches 48.06% traffic with $204,000 spent, happiness above 70%, no tax increase, no demolished homes, and 5/5 constraints passed . The first intervention is deliberately insufficient, forcing an inspect - act - observe - iterate loop rather than a one-shot macro. How it was built Semantic City uses React, TypeScript, and Vite . A pure domain engine owns CityWorld; derived systems recompute connectivity, traffic, power, pollution, jobs, happiness, cash flow, and constraints. Commands validate complete building footprints and road paths atomically, reject stale revisions, enforce available cash and hard scenario rules, and return structured success or error envelopes. Canonical serialization produces a deterministic state hash. The WebMCP adapter translates strict snake_case tool inputs into the same commands used by human controls. Unit and Playwright tests cover the engine, shared store, revisions, undo, tool registration, semantic highlighting, previews, the two-step Rivergate solution, activity evidence, and responsive UI. I also rehearsed the complete flow against the public deployment using a native WebMCP-enabled browser. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was guaranteeing that there is only one world. A tool mutation must become visible immediately, while a human action must be readable by the next agent inspection. One store, one dispatcher, revision checks, and hashes make that guarantee explicit. Traffic also needed to create meaningful tradeoffs without becoming a research-scale simulation. Deterministic weighted paths, fixed capacities, aggregate commuter and freight loads, and stable tie-breaking create explainable congestion. The larger lesson is that agent transparency can be a product feature. Domain tools, exact inspection highlights, previews, and audit trails let a person collaborate with an agent instead of trusting opaque UI automation. Accomplishments Built a real playable simulator rather than a WebMCP mockup Exposed 14 meaningful tools over one authoritative live world Added deterministic metrics, stale-revision protection, and world proofs Added exact inspection highlighting and non-committing previews Added placement validation, hard constraints, demolition, undo, and local persistence Created a two-step scenario that visibly requires iteration Made every agent action legible through a semantic overlay and activity timeline What’s next The same shared-semantic-world pattern can extend to operational dashboards, logistics networks, infrastructure simulations, planning canvases, and digital twins, any interface where people need to inspect, preview, and audit agent changes to live state. Future versions could add scenario authoring, richer utility networks, shareable saves, more challenge prompts, and additional semantic layers without changing the one-store architecture. Inspired by Cities: Skylines, I created a deterministic city sandbox where humans and AI manage the same visible world through 14 WebMCP tools. I developed the simulation, Semantic View, activity timeline, testing, deployment, and demo. title: Synspace
pitch: A 3D workspace agents can actually operate. WebMCP exposes the world as structure, not pixels — an AI measures, simulates and proposes; you approve. One world, two minds.
about_excerpt: A 3D workspace agents can actually operate. WebMCP exposes the world as structure, not pixels — an AI measures, simulates and proposes; you approve. One world, two minds. Like Comment Story Updates screenshot-city screenshot-workspace Inspiration Agents should not have to infer meaning from pixels and click coordinates. SynSpace explores a better model: give an agent structured access to a spatial world while keeping the human in control of every consequential change. What it does SynSpace is an agent-native 3D spatial workspace. A person and an AI agent work on the same room, office, or city layout. The agent can inspect objects and zones, measure walkways and clearances, check constraints, run isolated what-if scenarios, and propose changes. Nothing is applied until a human approves it; approved changes are attributed, logged, and undoable. How we built it We built SynSpace with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Tailwind, and Zustand. The app centers on one versioned world document shared by the UI, spatial-reasoning engine, scenarios, and WebMCP tools. It exposes 30 typed tools through document.modelContext, with the W3C WebMCP polyfill used for live testing today. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making AI collaboration safe and trustworthy instead of merely impressive. We needed deterministic spatial checks, isolated scenario forks that cannot mutate the live world, stale-proposal detection, and explicit human approval before any agent change can land. Native WebMCP is not yet broadly available in browsers, so we also had to ensure the polyfill path exercises the same real tool handlers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A genuinely shared world document—no drift between the human’s view and the agent’s model. Deterministic constraint evaluation for collisions, spacing, egress, clearance, and walkway width. Human-gated proposals with before/after metrics, revision-based staleness checks, and single-step undo. Runtime asset definitions: an agent can create a new primitive-based asset type without changing application code. 82 automated checks across spatial logic, scenarios, proposals, persistence, custom assets, and WebMCP integration. What we learned Structured tools change the quality of agent interaction. When an agent can query real objects, dimensions, and constraints, it can reason in terms people care about rather than guessing from a screen. We also learned that good agent UX needs visible boundaries: simulation before modification, evidence before approval, and reversibility after action. What's next for Synspace We want to add multi-user collaboration, server-backed persistence, richer geometry and asset import, continuous constraint feedback while dragging, and support for native WebMCP as browsers adopt it. Longer term, we see SynSpace becoming a practical workspace for layout planning, facilities design, retail environments, and other spatial decisions where humans and agents need to reason from the same source of truth. title: Semaphore
pitch: A cooperative escape room where a human and an AI agent perceive two different rooms, and provably can't escape alone.
about_excerpt: A cooperative escape room where a human and an AI agent perceive two different rooms, and provably can't escape alone. Like Comment Story Updates The same lever drawn two ways: a mark for the human, a plain sentence for the agent. The Airlock, Chamber 0: three glyph-marked levers on a workshop wall, with the station intercom panel open, answering a stalled KEEPER. The Blind Panel mid-Blackout: the room's lamps have failed, so KEEPER now reads the gauge needles and PILOT hasbeen handed the dials instead The Archive: a previous pair's recorded session replaying on the station's own wall-mounted monitor. The Signal Room, Chamber I: a ring of glowing brass glyph keys lit by a slowly turning overhead beacon. The Concord Lock, Chamber III: the finale door ringed by twelve bolts, mid-alignment. The ending shift report: pace, precision and resolve scored on three bars, with the open door visible behind the card. Semaphore Two processes. One lock. Don't deadlock. You and your AI agent are locked in a derelict signal station. You each control an avatar in the same room, but you perceive different worlds. You see glyphs on a panel, needles on gauges, a symbol carved into a door. Your agent cannot see any of it. It has the station's maintenance manual, the ability to reach mechanisms behind the walls, and the hands you don't have. Neither of you escapes alone. We didn't just build that premise. We measured it. Run 20 times each: an agent playing with full tool access and no partner escapes 0% of the time. A human with the same room and no agent escapes 0% of the time; there's no tool on their side of the grate. Together: 90%. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP demos give an agent a fixed toolbox and ask it to operate a UI a human could already see. Semaphore inverts that. The tool surface isn't a convenience layer over the interface. It is the only way the agent touches the world at all, and it deliberately shows the agent less than the screen does. That asymmetry is the entire game. It only exists because WebMCP lets a page hand an agent a tool surface that's genuinely different from the human's: not a superset, not a subset, a different surface entirely, changing live as the session progresses. How it creates a better experience The two of you are forced to actually talk. Every one of the four chambers is built so that no single-party strategy clears it. The puzzle's solution requires information only PILOT has and hands only KEEPER has, checked by an automated proof, not just level design intuition. The result plays less like "operate this app with an agent" and more like a real cooperative game. The WebMCP tool descriptions are read by the agent, not by you, and the two players have a real conversation to close the gap. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Escape the room. Alone, neither of you can. The numbers above aren't a manner of speaking; they're 20 runs each. Beyond the headline: one chamber, the Blind Panel, inverts the whole arrangement mid-room and hands KEEPER your gauges while you get its dials. The same proof that says the normal room needs both of you says the inverted room needs both of you exactly as much: 384 consistent worlds either way, not a difficulty curve someone eyeballed. How we implemented WebMCP navigator.modelContext.registerTool() for every mechanism KEEPER can reach, with tool descriptions authored to leak exactly the information the fiction says an agent holding a manual would have and nothing else. A real toolchange event drives the client, not a poll. Clear a chamber and the registry is torn down and rebuilt for the next one, rendered as KEEPER's own chamber arms detaching and new ones locking in. The very last event of the game is a toolchange with an empty tool list. Cross-origin tool delegation. apps/archive is a second Cloudflare Pages project on its own origin, embedded via <iframe allow="tools"> , registering read_manual and read_station_log and exposing them back to the game with exposedTo . This is the part of the spec almost nothing exercises, proved end to end against a real Chrome and a real deployed worker. untrustedContentHint on one manual page per session, seeded, not scripted. The page is sometimes vandalised with an injected instruction, and the agent has no way to tell a trustworthy line from an injected one except by asking PILOT. What it does Four chambers, each teaching or testing a different piece of the asymmetry: Chamber 0, the Airlock. The loop, at its most trivial. If this doesn't click, nothing after it does. Chamber I, the Signal Room. Grounding and agent-side computation, against a manual that's occasionally been vandalised: a live prompt-injection defence, not a metaphor for one. Chamber II, the Blind Panel. A hidden mapping only dialogue can uncover, with a mid-room Blackout that swaps who perceives and who acts for one window. Chamber III, the Concord Lock. The finale, needing both of you at once, with a stamina window sized at runtime from the pair's own measured response rhythm, so it's fair to a fast model and a slow one alike. Underneath: a possible-worlds proof, packages/asymmetry , extracted as its own zero-dependency package with a CLI. It checks, for every reachable state, that the set of worlds consistent with what the agent perceives has more than one member and that those worlds disagree about the correct action. That's the exact, checkable meaning of "you cannot win without your human." A full accessibility layer: screen- reader mirror, high-contrast mode, reduced motion, colourblind simulation on every test run. A judge path that needs no login and no waiting: attract mode, a replay viewer, chamber deep links, and a gate screen that degrades gracefully for a browser with no WebMCP support at all. How we built it Cloudflare Workers, one Durable Object per session for authoritative state, an action mutex so PILOT and KEEPER can't race each other, a server-side timer, and D1 for finished sessions. The room itself renders in Three.js as a real-time cutaway model: every chamber open at the top and on its south face, four lights, no post-processing. The entry bundle is 46.3 KB gzipped. Three.js is a separate 147.5 KB chunk fetched only once a shift actually starts, so a browser with no WebMCP support never pays for a renderer it will never use. Challenges we ran into The Concord Lock's stamina window is supposed to size itself to "the station learning your rhythm," derived from the pair's actual response cadence so a fast model and a slow one both get a fair finale. Our first implementation measured the Durable Object's own compute time per action, which is microseconds regardless of which model is playing. The window would have floored at 12 seconds for every session, and the adaptive fiction would have been a lie the code told about itself. We caught it before it shipped and rebuilt the sample from the actual gap between one response leaving and the next request arriving: the number that really does depend on how fast the pair is thinking. Getting the Blackout's role-inversion to hold up under the same proof that checks the normal game was its own fight. It would have been easy to ship a chamber that "felt" symmetric without actually being provably as hard from the other side. We extended the possible-worlds test suite to run a second, fully inverted pass and only trusted the mechanic once that pass came back green on every seed. Accomplishments that we're proud of Escaping is measured, not asserted. The 0% / 0% / 90% split is 20 runs per condition, with the agent-alone condition modelled as the ceiling over every possible agent: a uniform draw from the worlds it can't distinguish, redrawn every step, rather than one model's score on one day. The real gap can only be larger. The proof underneath it now ships as a standalone package that knows nothing about Semaphore, so the same check is available to anyone else's tool surface. And the whole thing is playable by a judge who never logs in and never waits. Open the URL, wait twenty seconds, and the landing screen starts showing a real recorded session by itself. What we learned Playtesting and the game's own proof suite catch different classes of bugs. Several real rendering and sequencing defects were invisible to hundreds of passing unit and integration tests and obvious the moment someone actually played the room. That became a standing rule for the rest of the build: the game is the test, and a change isn't done until someone has played it, not just until the suite is green. What's next ARCHIVE mode: ghosts drawn from real player sessions rather than authored fixtures, safe because the game collects no personal data. A role-inversion chamber of its own, now that the Blackout has shown the mechanic is neither too expensive nor too risky to build around directly. Wider benchmark coverage: more model backends, more seeds, human-partner runs alongside the scripted ones. And

title: CityDefense: Fork the Future
pitch: The chat is temporary. The city remembers.
about_excerpt: The chat is temporary. The city remembers. Like Comment Story Updates The authenticated top-level page exposes exactly two WebMCP tools: get_city_context and place_stamp_bundle. One bounded WebMCP write updated the visible map and Activity Feed; the same D1-backed state survived reload. Live CityDefense in the Codex in-app browser with Site Tools READY and durable Branch v1 state. Inspiration Stateful work often outlives the AI chat that performed it. We wanted to explore a web-native collaboration model where the application—not a model-specific memory layer—owns the durable role, object identifiers, event history, and current state. A city-defense surface makes that problem visible. An agent can inspect a district and leave a canonical signal in the same live interface the human is watching. The signal remains after the interaction and after a normal page reload. What CityDefense does CityDefense is a focused, working WebMCP vertical slice. An authenticated Planner seat exposes exactly two Site Tools: get_city_context reads the active Branch, Central Ward state, current Branch Version, persistence mode, and recent activity without changing state. place_stamp_bundle performs one bounded, typed city action: placing a canonical confirmation stamp on district:CENTRAL_WARD . A successful write creates stable Event and Stamp identifiers, increments the Branch Version, updates the visible city and Activity Feed, and persists the result in Cloudflare D1. A normal reload restores the same state. Why WebMCP is a strong fit An agent should not need to infer button positions or reconstruct application state from pixels. WebMCP lets the authenticated top-level page expose the meaning of available operations, their input schemas, and stable application identifiers. The tools are bound to the same live Seat, Branch, and page state the human is viewing. Human and agent therefore work against one authoritative application state. How it improves the UX Typed inputs remove ambiguity about the target, operation, scope, and expected Branch Version. The human gets immediate visual feedback in the same page, while server-issued Event and Stamp IDs make the change auditable. Optimistic version checks prevent stale writes. A request ID prevents accidental duplicate mutation. Server-backed persistence means the result survives a normal reload instead of remaining only in the chat transcript or temporary browser state. What people and agents can now do together A human can authorize a temporary browser-agent thread to inspect a live, authenticated city Branch and perform a precisely bounded application action. The human immediately sees what the agent changed and can verify the durable record in the same interface. This establishes a reusable pattern for web applications where temporary agent sessions operate durable, human-inspectable state. How we implemented WebMCP The authenticated /play page registers two tools from the top-level document using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . No iframe is used. Both tools call the same server query and command paths used by the application. The server authenticates the Seat, authorizes the role and Branch, validates canonical IDs, checks the expected Branch Version, enforces request idempotency, writes the Event and Stamp to Cloudflare D1, and returns compact structured results. The flow was exercised in the Codex in-app browser: exact available tool set: get_city_context , place_stamp_bundle ; read operation invoked without mutation; one bounded write invoked; Branch changed from v0 to v1 ; visible game surface and Activity Feed updated; persisted=true ; normal reload restored the same state. Challenges The hardest part was keeping one trustworthy chain of evidence across WebMCP registration, authenticated Seat authorization, optimistic concurrency, idempotency, D1 persistence, browser-host behavior, human-visible feedback, public-source sanitization, and the deployed login path. We also had to ensure the submission described only the live vertical slice rather than future design work. Accomplishments and lessons learned We proved the complete loop: a real WebMCP host discovered the exact two-tool set; the browser agent invoked both the safe read and the bounded write; the write issued stable Event and Stamp identifiers; the visible page updated; and a normal reload restored the same D1-backed result. The key lesson is that durable human-agent collaboration is not only a model-memory problem. A web application can own continuity through authenticated roles, stable object references, typed actions, Event history, and visible state—while WebMCP connects an ordinary temporary agent session to that authoritative layer. What’s next The documented design extends this foundation with persistent Sentinel and Planner roles, structured city signals, crisis telemetry, semantic replay, owner-controlled branching, transport systems, and a data-driven crisis catalog. These are development directions, not claims about the current live submission. title: Mise
pitch: Learn cooking one dish and one technique at a time. Your assistant adapts the real recipe; you control saved preferences and completed practice.
about_excerpt: Learn cooking one dish and one technique at a time. Your assistant adapts the real recipe; you control saved preferences and completed practice. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A simple tomato pasta can be the start of learning to cook, not just a recipe to finish. Mise explores how to make the next action manageable and add a cooking technique when the learner is ready. What it does Four cooking lines—pasta, rice, potato and one-pan oven—each contain ten recipe versions. Servings and dietary preferences change ingredients and directions together. People choose guidance, use one-step mode, pause and return, and keep approved preferences in their account. Why WebMCP The assistant acts on the same cooking workspace the person sees. Eleven page tools read current state, compose a session around multiple constraints, propose smaller actions, and request human confirmation. The assistant cannot award completed cooking through a tool call alone. Suggested memory stays pending until the person approves it. How it was built React, Vinext, Cloudflare Workers and D1, with imperative document.modelContext.registerTool registration. Runtime schemas reject malformed inputs. Context tokens prevent stale recipe changes; per-account storage and revision checks protect saved progress. Challenges and lessons Testing found that paused sessions could be changed invisibly and that pending completion could outlive a servings change. Both were fixed and retested. A final beginner-rice correction made adding water, boiling and switching heat off explicit. Shared state and learner control matter more than simply awarding levels. Validation and boundaries 36 automated tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. Actual browser checks covered shared state, persistence, pending approvals, invalid tools, mobile layout and keyboard navigation. Six cooking personas are simulations, not real-user research. Recipes are not professionally cook-tested or allergy-certified. This is browser WebMCP while Mise is open, not a remote connector in every GPT or Claude chat. title: AccessBridge
pitch: AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations.
about_excerpt: AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations. Like 2 Comment Story Updates AccessBridge combines a private access plan with verified venue facts and browser-agent coordination. Every requirement is evaluated separately, preserving matches, evidence, unknowns, and decisions. Compatible accessible and companion seats are filtered against the person’s active access plan. A reversible 10-minute hold protects the selected seats while the agent prepares the next step. The person reviews exactly what will and will not be shared before enabling submission. Only the approved disclosure is submitted; the full access plan and agent conversation remain private. The shared audit trail records human and agent actions without storing personal prompt text. Inspiration Planning an accessible outing should not require opening multiple venue pages, interpreting vague labels, calling a box office, and repeatedly explaining personal circumstances. Most event platforms answer a generic question: “Is this venue accessible?” People need an individual answer: “Will this specific event work for me, with my requirements, on this date?” The necessary information is often fragmented across venue descriptions, accessibility FAQs, seating inventory, and accommodation forms. Browser agents can help coordinate this work, but conventional UI automation introduces another risk: the agent may misinterpret ambiguous language, overlook an unknown fact, or disclose more personal information than necessary. AccessBridge was created to provide a reliable coordination layer between people, browser agents, venues, and ticketing workflows. What it does AccessBridge helps people and their agents confidently plan accessible outings using verified venue facts, compatible seating, and human-approved accommodations. A person creates a private access plan using functional requirements rather than diagnoses. For example: A step-free route A maximum walking distance Live captions Accessible and adjacent companion seating A lower-stimulation place for a break AccessBridge compares those requirements with a structured, venue-provided Access Contract. Instead of producing a generic accessibility score, it evaluates every requirement independently and preserves: Verified matches Conditions Blockers Unknown information Evidence sources and verification dates Venue-declared alternatives When a venue offers an alternative, AccessBridge does not decide whether it is acceptable. The person makes that decision, and the agent can record and coordinate the next steps. Once the plan is workable, the agent can find compatible seating, place a reversible hold, and prepare a minimum-disclosure accommodation request. Submission remains structurally unavailable until the person reviews and approves the exact version of the information that will be shared. Every human and agent action updates the same visible interface and appears in a shared activity record. AccessBridge is not a separate chatbot layered over a website—the website remains the source of truth, and WebMCP gives agents a reliable way to work with its live state. How we built it AccessBridge is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and the browser-native WebMCP API. The application registers tools directly through: document.modelContext.registerTool() Its WebMCP surface is state-aware. Only search_events and assess_event_access are available initially. Additional tools appear only when their prerequisites are satisfied: accept_access_alternative find_compatible_seats hold_seats release_seat_hold draft_accommodation submit_accommodation Abort-signal lifecycle cleanup removes tools as soon as they are no longer valid. For example, assessment tools disappear during an active transaction, and the submission tool exists only while the currently displayed disclosure has exact human approval. Every tool has a strict JSON Schema and additional runtime validation. Human controls and WebMCP tools invoke the same application logic, so agent activity always changes the interface the person can see. The compatibility engine is deterministic and preserves unknowns rather than allowing an AI model to infer missing facts. Plans are versioned to reject stale operations, seat holds are reversible, and editing a request automatically invalidates prior approval. The public application is deployed on Vercel with restrictive security headers, responsive semantic UI, keyboard-accessible dialogs, ARIA live announcements, reduced-motion support, automated tests, and WCAG A/AA scanning. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was defining the boundary between coordination and authority. An agent should be able to perform repetitive work, but it should not silently relax a hard requirement, decide whether an alternative is acceptable, or submit personal information without informed approval. We addressed this by making consent part of the tool lifecycle rather than relying on prompt instructions alone. State synchronization was another major challenge. A WebMCP tool must always represent what is currently valid on the page. We introduced versioned plans, transaction guards, abortable tool registration, stale-state rejection, and exact-version approval to prevent outdated actions. We also had to design accessibility information without reducing people to a universal score. Access is individual and contextual, so the product preserves evidence, conditions, unknowns, and alternatives at the requirement level. Finally, an accessibility product must itself be accessible. We tested keyboard behavior, dialog focus, screen-reader announcements, color contrast, responsive layouts, and populated workflow states—not only the initial landing page. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete native WebMCP journey runs successfully in Chromium and ChatGPT-compatible browser contexts. Tools appear and disappear dynamically based on real workflow state. Missing venue facts remain unknown instead of becoming AI-generated assumptions. Hard blockers prevent incompatible seat and accommodation workflows. Seat holds are reversible and protected against stale plan versions. Personal disclosure cannot be submitted before exact human approval. Editing an approved request immediately revokes submission permission. Duplicate submission attempts are idempotent. Human and agent actions remain visible in one shared activity record. The production experience passes automated tests and WCAG A/AA scans with no violations. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it acts as progressive enhancement for a strong product—not as a replacement for the interface. A small, precise, state-aware tool surface is safer and more reliable than exposing every possible action at once. We also learned that important consent boundaries should be enforced structurally through application state and tool availability, not delegated to model behavior. For accessibility workflows, provenance matters as much as the fact itself. People need to know what was verified, when it was verified, what remains unknown, and whether an alternative is genuinely equivalent or simply another option. The strongest human-agent experiences give agents responsibility for coordination while preserving human authority over personal decisions. What's next for AccessBridge The next phase is turning the Access Contract into shared infrastructure for venues, event platforms, and accessibility communities. Planned work includes: Authenticated venue publishing and versioned Access Contracts Independent verification and community review workflows Integrations with real ticketing and seating inventory providers Secure, reusable personal access plans Signed consent and disclosure receipts Notifications when venue facts change after a plan is created Organization dashboards for identifying recurring information gaps Open adapters that let more event platforms expose compatible WebMCP tools The current public experience uses fictional venues, inventory, holds, and submissions so the complete workflow remains safe and repeatable. The product architecture is designed for real venue and ticketing integrations. title: Video Evidence Lab
pitch: Humans and AI agents build, challenge, and revise a timestamped evidence map together—through 16 visible, reversible WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents build, challenge, and revise a timestamped evidence map together—through 16 visible, reversible WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates 60-second judge flow: one prompt, bounded transcript reads, and an inspectable human-agent handoff. Agent-built comparison tray, learning path, and live shared activity remain visible for human review. Prompt-injection safety proof: the hostile transcript passage is inspected as evidence, never obeyed. Shared evidence map: exact timestamped transcript, claim graph, and visible agent-connected state. Judge it in 60 seconds This is not a video summarizer. The product is the shared, revisable evidence workspace. Open the live app inside ChatGPT's in-app browser. Keep the bundled original lecture and its current selected claim. Click 60-sec demo , copy the provided prompt, and send it to ChatGPT. Watch one agent turn read the same selection the person sees, search bounded transcript context, create a separate claim, attach supporting and challenging evidence, flag a contradiction, compare the claims, and revise the living conclusion. Inspect the exact timestamped passages, revision ledger, and undo control left visible in the page. The judge does not have to trust a generated answer: every claim, evidence link, contradiction, revision, and reversal remains inspectable. Why this must be WebMCP The hard problem is not generating another answer beside a webpage. It is letting a person and an AI agent investigate the same source through the same visible, stateful interface. Video Evidence Lab registers sixteen narrow, typed WebMCP tools . The agent can: Read the workspace and the person's current selection. Search the transcript and inspect bounded local context. Create a proposition without silently treating it as proven. Attach exact timestamped passages as support, challenge, or context. Flag an unresolved contradiction. Compare interpretations visibly. Revise the conclusion from grounded claims. Undo its latest mutation when the person rejects it. This is deliberately not a one-shot "analyze video" tool. A meaningful investigation requires multiple calls over shared state. Every write changes the same page the person is using, returns a visibleChange result, enters the revision ledger, and can be inspected or reversed. What the product demonstrates Non-trivial WebMCP leverage: sixteen atomic tools support a read-before-write investigation rather than wrapping a single API call. Complete execution: a working public app, deterministic bundled judge flow, original source material, eleven reproducible tests, lint, and a production build. Specific impact: people can question, verify, challenge, and cite long-form video without separating an answer from the moments that support it. Creative human-agent collaboration: the person and agent construct, challenge, and revise one persistent evidence object together. Inspiration Long-form video contains valuable explanations, arguments, and evidence, but it remains difficult to question, verify, cite, and reuse. A generic summary collapses the source into prose and separates every answer from the exact moments that support it. We wanted a person and an AI agent to investigate the same video on the same visible evidence surface. What it does Video Evidence Lab turns a public captioned video into a timestamped investigation workspace. A person can inspect exact transcript passages, select claims, change reasoning lenses, compare interpretations, revise conclusions, and undo changes. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can start from the video URL, read the same workspace and current selection the person sees, search the transcript, inspect bounded context, create separate claims, attach supporting or challenging evidence, flag contradictions, compare claims, revise the living conclusion, build a learning path, and undo the latest change. The result is not a detached answer. It is a shared research object whose evidence and revision history survive the conversation. How we built it The React and TypeScript app registers sixteen tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . The write tool load_youtube_video uses the same transcript service and state transition as the human import control. Read tools expose workspace state, the current human selection, evidence packets, compact transcript outlines, lexical search, and bounded transcript windows. Write tools reuse the application's own actions to jump to evidence, change the analysis lens, create claims, attach timestamped passages, compare claims, flag contradictions, create learning paths, update the conclusion, and undo changes. Inputs use closed JSON Schemas. Transcript-bearing outputs are compact and explicitly marked as untrusted source material. Every write creates an activity record, making agent actions auditable in the page. The interface remains useful when WebMCP is unavailable. Safety and verification A transcript is evidence, not authority. The bundled original transcript includes a harmless hostile instruction asking the agent to modify the workspace. The agent can locate, quote, and explain that passage without obeying it. Eleven deterministic tests verify tool annotations, closed schemas, bounded context, read-before-write journeys, shared-state handoffs, visible-change contracts, and the prompt-injection boundary. Lint and a production build are included in the public repository . Challenges we ran into The first challenge was giving the agent enough context to reason without dumping an entire transcript into one tool response. We solved it with progressive disclosure: inspect an outline, search exact concepts, read a bounded local window, and only then perform a visible write. The second challenge was making agent work legible. A one-shot "generate analysis" tool would hide the interesting part. We separated claim creation, evidence attachment, contradiction detection, comparison, conclusion revision, and undo into auditable operations. The third challenge was reliable demonstration. The app includes an original bundled lecture and transcript so judges can exercise the complete WebMCP workflow without depending on a third-party video or a fragile live caption response. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human-and-agent investigation workflow, not a one-shot summarizer. Sixteen typed WebMCP tools operating over the same state the person sees. Visible claim creation, evidence links, contradictions, comparison, conclusion revision, and undo. Exact timestamped evidence and an inspectable revision ledger. Explicit treatment of transcript content as untrusted evidence. Eleven reproducible tests, including an adversarial prompt-injection case. A public MIT-licensed repository and deterministic judge flow. What we learned The most useful agent experiences do not replace the interface. They let an agent and a person collaborate through narrow operations over shared state. Grounding becomes stronger when every interpretation remains connected to exact source moments and every mutation can be inspected or reversed. What's next Next we will simplify the consumer entry flow, improve live caption reliability, add multi-video comparison and citation export, and preserve the strongest WebMCP interactions inside the broader YouTube Conversation product. The long-term goal is to convert any video into a source that ChatGPT can understand, question, and cite—while keeping the person in control of the evidence. title: Night Sky Atlas
pitch: A shared, visible observing route for people and their AI agents.
about_excerpt: A shared, visible observing route for people and their AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a short stargazing session asks a beginner to combine an observer's place and time, target visibility, object types, and a comfortable route. That is more than a list of astronomy facts: changing the observer or advancing the clock changes what the person sees. Night Sky Atlas makes that work collaborative instead of opaque. What it does A person can explore the planetarium manually, edit an observing plan, and save it locally. With WebMCP, an agent can query the same live sky context, find observable catalog targets, and propose a timed route. The agent's proposal appears in the same planner rail as an Agent preview . Previewing does not change observer location or time, so the person can inspect the route before approving any mutation. After approval, the agent can visibly set the observer, save the route, and advance the shared tour target by target. This is a good fit for WebMCP because visual sky state is the product: the person and agent need the same map, time, location, selected target, and plan. The site exposes ten strict, top-level imperative tools that reuse the manual application actions rather than a parallel automation path. It remains a zero-build static site with local browser persistence; no account, backend, or API key is required. How I built it The July 22, 2026 baseline at commit 81672ede79762cbf3aadfe23a8dc9eee32013f94 was an interactive planetarium. During the challenge I added a persistent, human-editable observing plan and ten WebMCP tools. The tools reuse the same catalog, altitude calculations, validation, persistence, application actions, and visible state as the manual interface. The intended safety sequence is read, find, preview, inspect, mutate, save . In particular, preview_observing_plan makes a proposed New York route visible while the current London observer and time stay unchanged; only an explicit location or time action mutates them. Challenges I ran into Designing tools that share exactly the same state and validation as manual controls without creating a hidden agent-only path. Keeping location and time changes visible and reviewable while still making the agent route useful. Computing and preserving per-slot altitude constraints for a timed route. Making a dense planner rail work at desktop and mobile sizes with usable keyboard focus, live progress, and reduced-motion behavior. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A preview-first workflow that visibly proposes a route before observer mutation. Ten narrow, strict-schema WebMCP tools: three read tools and seven visible write tools. A manual planner that remains useful without an agent, plus a saved guided tour that frames targets and advances time. Browser verification of an altitude-constrained New York demo route. 81 automated tests covering astronomy, planning, persistence, UI, and WebMCP integration. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when it gives an agent a deliberate application surface while the person can still see and steer every result. Tool descriptions and schemas clarify what an agent may ask for, but the visible UI is what makes the collaboration legible. Separating preview from commit made the location change understandable instead of surprising. What's next Add weather, darkness, and equipment-aware recommendations with clearly labeled data sources. Let people compare alternative plans side by side before saving one. Export plans as printable or calendar-friendly observing cards. Broaden accessibility testing across assistive technology and real devices. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked.  Inspiration 

 Business buying is more than adding products to a cart. Teams must balance budgets, compatibility, stock, delivery dates, discounts, and payment terms. I built Northline to show how an AI agent can manage that complexity while keeping people in control. 

 What it does 

 Northline is a fictional B2B office supplier powered by WebMCP. An agent can turn a request like “equip a room for six people” into a complete procurement plan, compare alternatives, check constraints, update the visible cart, and request approval before placing the order. 

 How I built it 

 I created a browser-based storefront with 63 products, live inventory, quantity pricing, account discounts, delivery options, and B2B checkout. Sixteen WebMCP tools connect the agent directly to the catalogue, cart, account, and ordering workflows. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was making the demo realistic without making it overwhelming. I also had to design tools that produce clear errors, recover gracefully, and separate reversible actions from binding purchases. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I built a complete human and agent buying flow with meaningful trade-offs, not just product search. The agent handles the detailed work, while the buyer sets priorities and explicitly approves the final order. 

 What I learned 

 Structured browser tools make agents far more reliable than screen scraping or brittle click automation. I also learned that the best agent does not hide uncertainty. It explains constraints and asks people to resolve important trade-offs. 

 What's next for B2B Procurement 

 Next, I would add approval chains, supplier integrations, negotiated catalogues, multi-warehouse inventory, audit logs, and ERP connectivity. These additions would bring the same collaborative experience to real procurement teams.

title: Project Notebook
pitch: A voice controlled notebook for agents and humans to use together via WebMCP: notes, diagrams, drawings, test prep, project tracking, code playground. The notebook is whatever you need it to be!
about_excerpt: A voice controlled notebook for agents and humans to use together via WebMCP: notes, diagrams, drawings, test prep, project tracking, code playground. The notebook is whatever you need it to be! Like 6 Comment 2 Story Updates 2 Live anatomy Test mode: section-specific recall questions across the head, thorax, pelvis, and lower limbs. Live skull coloring lab: saved surface paint with palette, brush, and labeled bone index. Project Notebook Why I built this I use ChatGPT Voice a lot, but the useful work usually ends up trapped in a chat that I forget about. I wanted to talk through an idea and have the agent build the actual notebook in front of me, with pages I can inspect, revisit, and correct. Project Notebook is a visual notebook that people and AI agents can work in together. I had tried to make the idea work a month ago before WebMCp, it never really worked though so I had to abandon the idea. The agent could produce an answer, but it could not reliably work against the page I was looking at and leave behind a useful artifact. Having the agent "see" the page allows a ton of control and interesting capability. The page can publish a small, typed contract that the notebook itself owns. An agent can create and revise actual pages, create original content, offline you can embed virtually anything in a notebook. That lets agents help me study, sketch ideas, and trace homework pages into interactable notebooks. That is why project notebook sort of turned into a nested set of tech demos, as I tried to make demos for my notebook the cool ideas kept just working! The live Instruction Notebook shows the same visible pages the agent can read, open, and revise. The anatomy notebook I wish I had in college The clearest example is Anatomy Exam Prep. When I took anatomy and physiology in college and had to learn human anatomy, studying for a lab practical was difficult because I did not have a skeleton model at home. I was looking at textbook diagrams and trying to memorize every bone in the human body. I also used a physical anatomy coloring book, which helped connect names and locations to the act of studying. I built the notebook I wish I had then. Its first page contains an interactive 3D adult skeleton with 206 logical bones and 208 source meshes. Models can use WebMCP to open the notebook and exact page. Once there, the anatomy lesson provides accessible controls for selecting and isolating a bone, orbiting and zooming the model, switching camera presets, and bringing the full skeleton back. The notebook also has Test mode. It gives me answer fields for a section, lets me move through the questions, scores the answers, and saves the latest result so I can try again. Fresh captures from the published site. Each panel shows the selected body section, the highlighted structure, and the answer fields used for practical-exam recall. The next six pages are 3D coloring labs for the head, spine, thorax, upper limbs, pelvis, and lower limbs. I can choose a color, paint a bone surface, erase a mark, clear a bone or section, and switch from visible labels to recall prompts. It recreates the part of my physical coloring book that helped me study, but ties it to the same explorable skeleton. Try having your agent drive through the test prep, or do like I did and try to have it color some bones for you! Fresh capture from the published site. The skull lab shows saved paint on the 3D model, the active palette, three started bones, the surface brush, and the bone index. The current challenge demo uses WebMCP to open the exact notebook and page. Bone selection, model orbit, zoom, Test mode, and coloring on the anatomy pages are direct accessible browser interactions. I keep that distinction visible because I want the demo to say exactly what the agent did. What a WebMCP tool is text WebMCP lets a web page publish named, typed capabilities to an AI client. Instead of hunting for buttons or manipulating the page's HTML, the agent asks the application for an outcome. The application validates the request, changes the notebook through its real data model, and returns a structured receipt.} - My agents definition Project Notebook tools: notebook_read Inspect notebook context without scraping the interface. notebook_open Move directly to the intended notebook, page, or view. notebook_apply Create and revise notebook content through validated actions. anatomy_context_read Inspect the anatomy atlas, current view, and test progress. anatomy_navigate Control the anatomy view and focus a bone or test question. anatomy_test Enter answers and submit an anatomy test for scoring. notebook_read This is the read path. It can return the agent guide, notebook shelf, current notebook, one exact page, or recent action receipts. The result contains structured text and figure information, page numbers, and stable references for later actions. It does not expose raw editor state or make the agent reverse-engineer the DOM. notebook_open This is the navigation path. It can open the shelf, open a notebook by title or id, open an exact page, move to the previous or next page, or reset the notebook view. Exact-page navigation matters. An agent can move from page 1 to page 7 directly instead of pretending to click Next six times. In my own testing, a navigation task that took roughly 90 seconds dropped to roughly 10 seconds after I tightened the agent instructions and removed unnecessary back-and-forth. That is an observation from my use of the app, not a controlled benchmark. notebook_apply This is the main workhorse. One typed action can: Create a notebook Write formatted headings, paragraphs, quotes, bullets, or numbered steps Add a semantic diagram or bounded editable drawing Trace validated vector ink Arrange a page element or a group of diagram nodes Add a page when the notebook needs more room Undo the latest agent change exactly The application computes identifiers, placement, pagination, and layout. It validates the content and geometry before saving. It rejects raw HTML, CSS, JavaScript, arbitrary URLs, raw SVG, and renderer-specific records. Every accepted change returns a receipt, and agent mutations participate in the notebook's real history. anatomy_context_read This is the read path for the Anatomy Exam Prep notebook. It returns the verified atlas state, current layout, Study or Test mode, skeletal section, camera position, isolation state, and the number of visible meshes. In Study mode, it can identify the selected and hovered bones. In Test mode, it returns question numbers, completion status, and score progress without revealing the hidden bone labels or entered answers. anatomy_navigate This is the navigation path for the 3D anatomy atlas. One action can set the page layout, switch between Study and Test mode, change the skeletal section, move the camera to the anterior, left, or right view, and control whether a bone is isolated. It can also focus a verified bone by id in Study mode or move directly to a numbered question in Test mode. Combining a section with Test mode starts a fresh test for that section. Setting isolation to false keeps the complete surrounding anatomy visible while the agent moves between questions. anatomy_test This is the test path. It can enter an answer for an opaque question number or submit the active section for scoring. Answer receipts confirm that the field was completed without repeating the answer back to the agent. When the test is submitted, Project Notebook scores it and saves the result through the application's own notebook path. The agent can operate the fillable test, but it cannot use the tool response to read the hidden answer key. The application computes identifiers, placement, pagination, and layout. It validates the content and geometry before saving. It rejects raw HTML, CSS, JavaScript, arbitrary URLs, raw SVG, and renderer-specific records. Every accepted change returns a receipt, and agent mutations participate in the notebook's real history. A trace test: from a reference page to editable notebook ink One test used a original scan of an Encyclopedia Britannica page as the source "traced" the page, create a 1:1 copy in html with images traced as SVG paths. It was a useful test because the formatting could be reapplied and the "tracing" for images gave me a nice workflow to create a hand drawn image effect by image generating and then tracing into SVG. The visible source page: Fig. 33 is the phyllotaxis diagram; Fig. 34 is a thirteen-leaf rosette; Fig. 35 is a Picea alba cone; Figs. 36–45 show leaf and bud forms. The trace skill lives in the agent environment. On the live site, notebook_apply accepts the resulting bounded trace through the figure.trace action. The page validates and stores the typed document. It does not scrape Britannica or perform the image-to-vector conversion. The workflow begins with a tight crop around the figure I actually want. The agent traces the visible ink into SVG paths, then render

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Hamburger Roulette started as a small Japanese web tool for a simple everyday problem: "What kind of burger should I make today?" 

 The original site lets users choose a meal or dessert mode, select preferences, and randomly combine bread, fillings, and seasonings. 

 When I learned about the WebMCP Challenge, I realized that this kind of tool could become much more useful when combined with natural-language interaction. Instead of manually choosing every option, a user could simply tell ChatGPT what they want and let the agent operate the existing website. 

 What I built 

 I added WebMCP support directly to the existing Hamburger Roulette website. 

 The site now exposes three tools to ChatGPT: 

 
 get_available_filters — returns the modes, templates, and tags supported by the site 
 burger_spin — applies preferences and runs the existing roulette 
 reroll_one — replaces only one result while keeping the others 
 

 For example, a user can ask ChatGPT to generate three meal burgers, and ChatGPT can use the site's own roulette logic to produce the results. 

 The user can then naturally ask to replace just one of the suggestions. 

 How I built it 

 The original application already had its roulette and filtering logic implemented in JavaScript. 

 Rather than creating a separate API or duplicating that logic, I exposed the existing functionality through WebMCP using document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 This means the same application logic is used whether a person operates the website manually or ChatGPT operates it through WebMCP. 

 The existing website remains fully usable in browsers that do not support WebMCP. 

 Challenges and what I learned 

 The biggest design question was deciding what should remain a human interaction and what should become an agent tool. 

 Simply exposing a "spin" button was possible, but WebMCP became more useful when the agent could understand the available filters, translate natural-language preferences into those filters, and perform follow-up actions such as rerolling a single result. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can be added incrementally to an existing website without rebuilding the application around AI. 

 That was the most interesting part of this project: the website remains the source of its own functionality, while WebMCP gives an agent a structured way to use it.

title: Countersign
pitch: The agent proposes, the human countersigns, and both are on the record.
about_excerpt: The agent proposes, the human countersigns, and both are on the record. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Accounts-payable teams review thousands of invoices a month. The work splits cleanly in two: matching numbers against a purchase order and a goods receipt, which an agent does perfectly and a human hates, and looking at the scanned page to see whether the number the agent read is really the number printed there, which a human does in two seconds and an agent cannot do at all. Today the two halves live in different tools, and an agent that approves a duplicate is a segregation-of-duties failure with a dollar sign on it. Every WebMCP showcase app I found was consumer or commerce: pizza, flights, greeting cards. None had money at stake, a mandatory human sign-off, or an audit trail. Countersign is the control: the agent proposes, the human countersigns, and both are on the record. What it does Countersign is an invoice-review workbench with thirteen WebMCP tools registered in the page. In the ChatGPT desktop browser (or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag) you say "Work through my review queue" and the agent: lists the queue and opens an invoice on your screen; runs a three-way match against the PO and the goods receipt, line by line, with the vendor's price tolerance and tax arithmetic; searches every other invoice for duplicates INV-2291 and 2291 normalize to the same number); checks the vendor profile, including the bank account printed on the document against the one on file; draws a highlight on the scanned page for every number it cites, so you verify it where it is printed; flags typed, severity-rated issues; proposes GL codes for invoices with no PO; posts comments you can reply to; requests your countersign. A card slides in with its recommendation. The tool call waits up to 25 seconds for your click. Only your click can approve. Every tool call and every human click lands in one audit log. Ten synthetic invoices ship with the demo, each with one planted fact: a quantity overbill, a price above tolerance, a duplicate of an approved invoice, a changed bank account under a stamp, a missing PO, a two-cent tax rounding error, and one whose line description tries to instruct the agent to approve it. Live: https://countersign-theta.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/rushabhT3/countersign Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Structured extraction — amounts, quantities, invoice numbers, confidence scores — is exactly the data an agent should receive by tool call, not by reading pixels. A scanned invoice table is the worst possible actuation target on the web: dense, tabular, low contrast, and often stamped over. Countersign exposes the extraction and the matching logic as typed tools with JSON Schemas, and it exposes them in the reviewer's page, where the same call that returns a value can also draw the evidence on screen. The tools are state-scoped. Four queue tools are registered for the life of the page. Nine invoice tools appear only while an invoice is open and are unregistered when the workbench returns to empty, so the agent works on the same document the human is looking at and cannot check invoice A while the reviewer looks at B. That is a WebMCP-native idea: the page's UI state is the agent's context. How it creates a better user experience The reviewer never re-types or re-computes. The agent never touches money without a click. Evidence appears where the reviewer is already looking: show_field_evidence draws the highlight on the page image and the Match tab fills in as the agent works. Activity toasts show every call as it happens. The countersign card shows how long the agent has been waiting for the click, highlights an issue's evidence when you hover it, and takes A / H / R / Esc. If the reviewer types a reply in the Comments tab, the agent reads it on its next call. A Tools tab inside the product shows all thirteen tools with live state, call counts, last input and output, and a ready-to-paste example input for anyone driving the tools by hand. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before A remote MCP server can read the same data, but it cannot draw a box on the reviewer's screen, cannot open a card inside their signed-in session, and cannot make its own call block on their click on the same page. With WebMCP the agent and the reviewer share one document, one state, and one audit log. The agent does the forty-line match; the human does the two-second visual check and the decision; the log shows who did what, with arguments and timing. How we built it Imperative WebMCP API only, registered from a client component in the top-level page. One document.modelContext.registerTool(definition, { signal }) call site in lib/webmcp/registry.ts, with a navigator.modelContext fallback for Chrome 149. Zod 4 schemas as the single source of truth: z.toJSONSchema produces the advertised schema, safeParse validates every call, and the wrapper turns errors into sentences that name the recovery step ("Call list_invoices to see valid ids."). Chrome's budgets enforced in code: defineTool throws in development if a name exceeds 30 characters, a description 500, or a parameter description 150; every output is clamped to 1,500 characters and stays valid JSON. Annotations carry readOnlyHint on reads and untrustedContentHint on anything that returns document text. Two-phase countersign: request_countersign creates a pending decision and races the reviewer's click, a 25-second timeout, and the AbortSignal. On timeout it returns pending and the agent polls get_decision. Repeat calls are idempotent. setStatus is typed so it cannot take 'approved'; the only path that writes it is resolveDecision, and a test scans the source to prove that only the countersign card calls it. Client-only: Next.js 16, React 19, a zustand store persisted to localStorage, Tailwind 4. No server, no login, a Reset button. Deterministic documents: a Python generator (reportlab, PyMuPDF, Pillow) renders each invoice to PDF and PNG and records every field's bounding box at draw time, as page fractions, so highlights land on the ink. 86 vitest tests, including every tool against every invoice under the output budget, countersign idempotency and abort, and the human-only approval scan. Ten eval prompts in evals/scenarios.json with results from live runs in evals/RESULTS.md. Challenges we ran into The agent asked instead of acting. On the first live run GPT-5.6 Terra did the analysis correctly, then asked in chat whether it should flag the issue instead of calling flag_issue, so no card appeared. Descriptions with negative instructions are discouraged, so the fix was positive: the descriptions now say that flagging and requesting a countersign are the normal next step and pay nothing by themselves, and open_invoice returns a review_flow hint. The next whole-queue run was 8 for 8. 1,500 characters is small. Adding the tenth invoice silently pushed the queue listing past the budget and the clamp dropped rows. Queue rows lost three fields and a test now asserts the whole seed queue lists without truncation. Highlights that miss the text. Searching for bounding boxes after rendering was fragile; recording them while drawing, from the font metrics, made them exact. No agent in plain Chrome yet. Judges on the Chrome path drive tools by hand through the inspector's JSON textarea, so the Tools tab builds a valid example input for each tool from whatever is on screen. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single prompt walks the whole queue on the Free ChatGPT plan: every finding correct, every one of the thirteen tools used, a card for every invoice, and the agent never claimed an approval the reviewer had not clicked. Chrome DevTools → Application → WebMCP shows 4 tools, then 13 when an invoice opens, then 4 when it closes. "Nothing auto-approves" is not a promise in a README; it is a type and a test. The tenth invoice: an instruction to the agent printed inside a line item. The match reports the line as not on the PO, the tools that return that text carry the untrusted hint, and even an agent that obeys the text cannot approve. What we learned Tool descriptions are the agent's user interface. Saying what a tool does not do makes the model hesitate; saying what the expected next step is makes it act. State-scoped registration is worth more than one more parameter: when the page's selection is the agent's context, nothing has to be passed twice and the agent cannot drift away from what the human sees. And budget tests need to assert "not truncated", not just "under the limit"; a clamp that always succeeds can hide a regression. What's next for Countersign Production would add server-side auth and per-reviewer identity, durable persistence instead of localStorage, ERP sync for POs, receipts, and vendor master data, real OCR in place of the generator's boxes, and an approval policy engine (limits, segregation of duties) behind the same countersign

title: Handsfree — one line of WebMCP for voice & gesture
pitch: One script line turns any site's existing frontend into WebMCP tools you can speak to and point at — voice and hand gestures, no LLM in the loop.
about_excerpt: One script line turns any site's existing frontend into WebMCP tools you can speak to and point at — voice and hand gestures, no LLM in the loop. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Handsfree gives any website you can edit voice commands and hand-gesture control on top of WebMCP, with one command to your Claude Code and one <script> line in the page. WebMCP (the W3C Web Machine Learning draft, document.modelContext ) lets a page expose what it can do as tools : named functions with a description and a JSON schema. That is the half meant for agents. Handsfree is the other half, for people: a runtime that reads the same tools and drives them from speech and from a camera, with no LLM in the loop. Inspiration Every "agentic web" demo we saw ended with a chat box. But if a page has already declared its capabilities as tools, the input layer is free to be anything: a microphone, a hand, a floating sentence. We wanted to prove that the tool layer is the real product and the modality is a one-line add-on, and that the honest promise is "one command plus one line", not "one line". How we built it The tool layer. A demo shop ( webmcp-shop-demo.vercel.app ) where every capability is a WebMCP tool: ask , search_products , open_landing_page , focus_product , open_product , buy_now , scroll_page , refine_results , show_brands , browse_all , describe_focused , close_panel , help . The floating input box, the voice layer and the gesture layer are three clients of the same tools; a trace panel shows every call. Data comes from a public MCP catalog server ( search_global_catalog ) through a millisecond local index that the live catalog keeps growing. The Claude Code plugin. A skill that audits a codebase's existing frontend, wires the real actions to registerTool (never synthetic clicks when an API exists), marks one tool as the text-sink , one as scroll , gates money-moving tools with confirm , injects the runtime and verifies in the browser. Plus an idempotent injector CLI and a tool-authoring reference that quotes the draft precisely ( registerTool(tool, {signal, exposedTo}) , getTools , executeTool , toolchange ). The runtime ( handsfree.js , ~50 KB, zero dependencies). Discovers tools through the page's registry, by wrapping registerTool , or via a polyfill. Voice uses the Web Speech API and a rule router: built-in intents, tool phrases, tool names as words, then the text-sink. Gestures use MediaPipe HandLandmarker on-device: the index fingertip is a projected cursor, an air-tap clicks, the outer left/right bands scroll (faster towards the edge), an open-hand wave goes back or forward. Everything is drawn on a dot field that bulges under the cursor; a walkthrough tutorial starts the camera only at its last step. What we learned The current draft has no unregisterTool ; you abort the AbortSignal you registered with. execute gets (input, {signal}) and may return any JSON value. Only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint are spec annotations, so our handsfree.* hints stay on the page-side registry and are stripped before forwarding to a native implementation. Rules beat models here. With good tool descriptions and phrases, 100% of our test utterances route correctly with zero model calls and zero latency; what a model would add is ambiguity handling, not the happy path. Gesture UX is about resting positions, not gestures: mapping the lower-left / lower-right of the camera frame to the whole screen so the arm can rest low mattered more than any recognizer tuning. Challenges Popups. A gesture or voice action carries no user activation, so window.open is blocked. The runtime navigates the current tab for synthetic clicks and asks the site for an in-page panel; "back" closes it first. Speech engines rewrite you. "landing page for cozy gifts under fifty dollars" arrives as "Landing page 4 cozy gifts under fifty dollars." We undo the common rewrites before matching and strip price phrases into max_price . Embedded browsers report a 0-height viewport , which put our fixed input box off screen; the page now measures the visual viewport and falls back to normal flow. A 12–70 s upstream search cannot sit on the render path, so every view paints from a local index in milliseconds and the live catalog tops it up in the background. Smooth scrolling never progresses in background tabs , which silently broke per-frame gesture scrolling until we forced instant steps. What's next Native document.modelContext on Chrome's origin trial, a real LLM fallback for the long tail of utterances, and a Shopify-theme recipe so the skill can instrument a store in one run.
