 Event Growth OS 

 Event Growth OS helps event teams find the people who would genuinely benefit from an event—without turning outreach into spam. 

 Inspiration 

 Event promotion often rewards volume over relevance: organizers broadcast broadly, while potential attendees get generic messages that do not reflect what they actually need. We wanted to explore a better relationship between people and agents: let an agent do the patient research and first-draft work, while people retain the judgment and responsibility to decide whether to reach out. 

 That question became Event Growth OS: an agent console for finding genuine audience fit, explaining the evidence, and keeping a human approval checkpoint before any response could be used. 

 What it does 

 The centerpiece is an Agent Console that starts with a plain-language goal such as: 

 
 Find people who would genuinely benefit from my event. 
 

 It then makes a transparent, human-supervised tool sequence: 

 
 get_campaign loads the event context. 
 find_relevant_conversations surfaces discussion signals. 
 analyze_conversation explains intent, context, and audience fit. 
 draft_response prepares a useful, transparent reply. 
 request_human_approval stops for a person before outreach. 
 record_outcome closes the learning loop. 
 

 The interface exposes the reasoning rather than hiding it: opportunity scores, the signal behind each recommendation, the proposed draft, AI-assistance disclosure, and an explicit approval gate. Low-relevance conversations are intentionally rejected. 

 How we built it 

 We built Event Growth OS with Next.js , React , and TypeScript as a focused, responsive operator console. 

 For WebMCP, the app defines six purposeful tools and registers them through navigator.modelContext.registerTool when a compatible browser host exposes the API. Each tool has a name, a clear description, an input schema, and an execution result designed to be discoverable by an agent. The same definitions power the visible console timeline, so a person can understand exactly which capability is being requested at every stage. 

 The demo data is deliberately realistic but clearly simulated. It lets the product demonstrate the decision flow without pretending that it is scraping conversations or automatically posting to external networks. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The main challenge was resisting the temptation to make the experience look autonomous at the expense of trust. A fast draft is useful; an unreviewed message is not always appropriate. We designed the system around a hard human checkpoint and clear disclosure instead of an auto-posting loop. 

 A second challenge was making WebMCP legible to both audiences. Agents need tools with concrete, discoverable contracts; people need to see why each call matters. The tool timeline and opportunity inspector were designed to bridge that gap. 

 Finally, native WebMCP support depends on the browser host. We made the integration progressively enhanced: compatible hosts can register the tools natively, while the product still presents an interactive, inspectable demo flow where that API is unavailable. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that a strong WebMCP experience is not just a list of functions. The tools need to map to meaningful moments in a real workflow, communicate their purpose clearly, and preserve a person’s ability to intervene. 

 We also learned that the most compelling agent experiences pair automation with context. In Event Growth OS, the agent does not merely return a score—it shows the source signal, explains the fit, and asks for approval. That makes the system feel less like a black box and more like a thoughtful collaborator. 

 Built with 

 Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP APIs. 

 Running locally 

 Install dependencies, then run: 
 pnpm install
pnpm dev
 
 Open http://localhost:3000 . Enter an agent request, run the toolchain, select a conversation, and approve a high-confidence draft to see an outcome recorded. 

 AI and Codex usage 

 AI and Codex were used to help implement and refine the product experience. All product claims, simulated conversation signals, and outreach drafts are explicitly presented as demonstration data; the app does not automatically post to external social networks.

title: Threadline — Debug the Argument
pitch: Your agent researches. You decide what becomes canonical.
about_excerpt: Your agent researches. You decide what becomes canonical. Like Comment Story Updates A contested claim becomes an inspectable graph; three agent proposals wait for human review. Nine dated source records preserve provenance before synthesis. Two proposed groups and one atomic verdict stay staged—not canonical—until reviewed. What Threadline is Threadline is a provenance-preserving argument debugger for contested online claims. A browser agent reads the same investigation a person is reviewing and uses eight in-page WebMCP tools to stage sources, atomic claims, typed relations, non-destructive groups, and a bounded verdict. Agent-authored proposals are visibly noncanonical until a person accepts them. If a person rejects a proposal with a reason, that rationale returns through get_workspace so a later agent call can revise its approach. The result is not another feed summary. It is an inspectable collaboration in which the agent does the expensive work of researching and structuring an argument, while the person retains authority over what becomes durable truth. The problem Fast-moving technical discussion on X and the wider web flattens primary evidence, repetition, interpretation, prediction, and contradiction into one stream. A claim can look independently corroborated simply because many posts repeat the same underlying source. An autonomous summary hides those dependencies and can quietly become the next person's “fact.” Threadline makes the evidence lineage visible. It separates what a source directly establishes from what people infer, predict, amplify, or dispute. What people and agents do together The agent can: inspect bounded canonical workspace state and deterministic structural analysis; inspect full source evidence inside explicit untrusted-data boundaries; research and stage public sources it actually accessed; propose atomic claims and typed supports , contradicts , qualifies , or amplifies relations; propose non-destructive groups for repeated claims; propose one bounded verdict and its evidence relations as an atomic patch; and focus the visible graph on unresolved or primary-evidence work. The person can: inspect every source trail and staged graph entity; accept a defensible proposal; reject a weak proposal with a recorded rationale; decide which verdict becomes canonical; reopen saved investigations after reload; and export portable JSON or a Markdown evidence brief with the decision receipt. Why WebMCP is essential Threadline registers eight imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Tool Purpose Authority get_workspace Compact canonical state, structural analysis, recent human decisions, and rejection rationale Read only inspect_sources Full evidence records inside explicit untrusted-data delimiters Read only stage_sources Propose public evidence the agent actually accessed Review queue only stage_claims Propose small evidence-grounded claims Review queue only stage_relations Propose typed claim-to-claim relations Review queue only stage_merge Propose non-destructive repeated-claim groups Review queue only stage_verdict Propose one verdict and its relations atomically Review queue only set_focus Change reversible presentation focus Presentation only This is more than “chat with my site”: The registered tool surface enforces proposal-only authority. There is no registered accept, reject, reset, import, delete, rename, or case-switch tool. Acceptance is available only through the person-facing UI. This is a capability boundary, not authenticated proof of personhood. The agent and person share one live object. Stable source, claim, relation, group, proposal, and case IDs refer to the exact graph on screen. The agent does not reconstruct graph meaning from pixels. Optimistic concurrency prevents silent cross-talk. Every non-discovery call requires expectedCaseId ; every staging call also requires expectedRevision . A stale staging call or cross-case call returns structured recovery output before any proposal or canonical mutation. Rejection becomes protocol feedback. get_workspace exposes up to eight recent human decisions, including rationale, for later agent calls. Schemas and trust boundaries are explicit. Inputs are closed and bounded. Read tools carry read-only and untrusted-content hints, and full third-party evidence is returned only inside named untrusted-data delimiters. Staging is idempotent. Equivalent proposals reuse a stable ID, and pending entity IDs are reserved so competing proposals cannot present different content under one identity. Because the tools live in the page, Threadline needs no backend, database, account, API key, or bundled AI runtime. A complete product, not a proof of concept The primary interface is a responsive, keyboard-accessible provenance graph and review queue—not a chatbot. Pending graph entities are visibly marked STAGED — NOT CANONICAL and open their owning proposal. Amplification is first-class: repeated claims can be grouped without deleting original wording, relations, or sources. A verdict is an atomic patch. Its conclusion and evidence relations enter canonical state together, while only direct claim-to-verdict edges become its basis receipt. Up to eight investigations can be created, opened, renamed, reset, removed, imported, and exported. When exclusive Web Locks are available, cases labeled Saved survive reload. Otherwise they remain clearly labeled Memory only and exportable before reload. Screenshot transcriptions are explicitly labeled human-supplied evidence; Threadline never fabricates a public URL or treats an attributed statement as proof of its underlying claim. The deterministic preview is visibly labeled as a checked-in fixture replay, never as a live model response. Threadline uses dependency-free browser ES modules, semantic HTML, CSS, functional SVG, and Node's built-in test runner. It is hosted on ChatGPT Sites and released under the MIT License. The bundled challenge case The main investigation asks: Will WebMCP replace browser automation? Nine dated public records include Chrome documentation, the WebMCP explainer, a pinned WindTunnel benchmark result, and WebKit and Mozilla standards-position records. The graph separates a large demonstrated efficiency advantage on instrumented sites from task-level parity, explicit fallback guidance, and unresolved cross-browser implementation. The evidence supports a narrower verdict than the feed does: WebMCP is a semantic fast lane on instrumented sites, not a replacement for browser automation. The walkthrough deliberately stages one defensible group, one weak group, and one atomic verdict. The person accepts the first, rejects “Adoption and fallback” with the rationale “Same topic, different claim,” inspects the verdict evidence, and accepts the verdict. The unresolved standards claim remains visible after resolution. Verification npm test : 226 passing tests covering all eight registrations, phase prompts, prompt-boundary injection, case and revision guards, screenshot provenance, proposal identity, human review, atomic verdicts, reload-safe storage behavior, import/export, evidence briefs, and registered-callback/preview parity. npm run evals : 3 passing deterministic workflow evaluations . Seven live-agent journey definitions are checked in and deliberately marked not-run until observed in a compatible live session. npm run smoke : deployable static entrypoint, 2 local assets , 25 JavaScript modules , metadata, accessible landmarks, interaction sizing, responsive guards, and module syntax. Judge testing instructions No credentials are required. Open https://threadline.jameswirths.chatgpt.site in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. Open Investigations , select or load the bundled WebMCP example, and choose Reset case . Confirm 8/8 Site tools ready , Saved , Unresolved , 0 pending , and 09 sources. If the case says Memory only , do not rely on the reload check. Paste the Exact live fixture prompt from docs/demo-runbook.md into Site tools. It reads both guidance pages, verifies the case and revision, calls stage_merge once and stage_verdict once, then stops. Expect exactly three pending proposals while canonical state remains unchanged. Accept Performance amplification . Reject Adoption and fallback with Same topic, different claim. Inspect the verdict evidence, then accept the verdict. Confirm Resolved · human accepted , 0 pending , four installed verdict relations, and three direct basis-receipt relations. The Ask card now advances to Investigate what remains . Use Focus unresolved and confirm the cross-browser standards claim remains unresolved. Reload the saved case, then export the Markdown evidence brief. If Site tools are unavailable, Preview example pass provides the same checked-in three-proposal fixture through the production store. It is clearly disclosed in the UI as a deterministic preview and must not be described as a live agent call. Built With chatg

title: WebMCP Guard
pitch: WebMCP Guard is a security control plane between your app's WebMCP tools and the agent, providing data protection and other security policies for agents accessing data through your WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Guard is a security control plane between your app's WebMCP tools and the agent, providing data protection and other security policies for agents accessing data through your WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Organizations often run their own internal apps that have access to sensitive data. They often have tools to enforce data protection and security policies on these apps, but an improperly implemented WebMCP tool may circumvent them. I wanted to create something that would allow them to have these same kind of policies for their WebMCP tools without forcing them to code it themselves. But it needed to do more than block data for the agent. I wanted it to control data access in a way that preserved the agent's ability to reason about the data. What it does WebMCP Guard is an SDK that wraps WebMCP functions written with the Imperative API and injects controls. It has a corresponding management console that allows the organization to define policies. It has the following types of policies Data Protection This gives the company control over what data the agent can see. It classifies sensitive data, including names, SSN, credit cards, and more, and transforms them before the agent sees it. It can replace this data with a unique token. If the same piece of data appears across multiple records, it will use the same token identifier, which allows the agent to reason about the data without actually knowing what it is. In some cases, it can contextualize the data while removing the specificity. For example, it can replace a DOB from a patient health record with an age range. Human confirmation To prevent errant destructive actions polices can be created that require the user to approve (via an on-page modal) an action before it can be completed. This is most often used before an agent takes an irreversible action, such as deleting a record. Posture Assessment It can restrict what types of agents can access the tools. For example, you can block unidentified agents or restrict it to agents from one provider, such as OpenAI. Justification Policies can require the agent to provide a written justification before a sensitive action runs — bulk export, for example. The requirement is injected directly into the tool's input schema, so the agent learns about it from the tool definition rather than from a refusal. The agent is instructed to stop and ask its user for the reason and relay it verbatim, and the justification is evaluated and stored on the audit record as the human's stated reason. How we built it TypeScript end to end, in a pnpm monorepo. The SDK splits into a browser half and a server half: the client package wraps document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback) and runs every call through a gate → execute → transform pipeline, while everything secret — the policy engine, the data classifier, the deterministic tokenizer, the encrypted token vault, and the audit writer — lives in a Node package the host app mounts as ordinary API routes. Tokens are deterministic by construction: HMAC-SHA256 over a canonicalized value under an org secret, so the same SSN or name yields the same token in every tool, every turn, even inside the free text of a clinical note. The vault encrypts originals with AES-256-GCM, using the token itself as authenticated data so a tampered row fails closed instead of decrypting to the wrong person. Storage is a small adapter interface (SQLite for the demo, in-memory for tests, both run against one shared conformance suite) so an organization brings its own database. This way the organization isn't reliant on SaaS infrastructure to protect their audit logs, etc. We also built an example medical app for the demo. It existing in the same repo. We used AI coding assistance for this project. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new, and building against it seriously means finding the edges. Three real ones: tools' execute is invoked with no second options argument despite the typings declaring one (every tool crashed on its first real call); registering a live tool name again silently keeps the old tool, so policy-driven schema changes must abort-then-re-register; and feature detection has to cover both document.modelContext and the older navigator.modelContext surface. Tokenizing a structured name field is easy. A clinical note that says "Reached Tricia by phone" is not, and an agent can de-anonymize the token if information like that leaks. We fixed this by resolving bare name fragments to the same token as the full name (never hashed independently, which would split one person into two tokens), replaced only when the fragment maps unambiguously to one known person. Early on, the justification refusal told the agent what a justification should contain, so agents composed plausible ones themselves, defeating the control. The message now instructs the agent to stop, ask its human for the reason, and relay it verbatim. The denial text turned out to be as much a part of the security design as the policy engine. In the future, we will probably replace it with a modal like the approval workflow. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tokenization loop working end to end was a big win. An agent searches, gets tokens instead of names, reasons about them, passes one back into another tool, and the real value is swapped in server-side. The agent is actually able to reason about the data without access to the cleartext value. Getting the justification flow to work correctly was also a big win. Like I said earlier, a lot of agents just wrote the justification themselves, which isn't exactly what is intended. It's not foolproof, but this tool isn't supposed to be silver bullet for security; it is meant to complement other security measures for organizations that want to implement WebMCP. What we learned We'll still need some kind of control surface for the DOM. Agents that cannot accomplish their task via the WebMCP tool may fall back to DOM inspection. Currently, this requires a separate security tool to address, like an enterprise browser. But I think we could come up with some kind of native solution. Alternatively, this tool might be better as a browser extension, and then the SDK would merely enforce the use of the extension before serving the page. This would give us more control over what the agent can access, but it is also a bigger deployment than the current state. But when it comes to security, perfect can't be the enemy of good. Easily deploying controls on a WebMCP tool still greatly improves security and compliance, especially if it eliminates it as a path to circumventing other security controls. What's next for WebMCP Guard Smarter classification: NER-based name detection beyond the host-supplied dictionary, and free-text detectors for addresses and insurance ids. Structured export rows so bulk export gets the full transform treatment instead of leaning on the justification gate. Richer policy: combined confirmation-plus-justification actions, per-class control over inbound detokenization, and the pluggable LLM justification evaluator the interface already supports. Real identity: SSO/OIDC session resolution in place of the demo's mock personas. This allows the user to attach policies to specific people or user groups. LLM-as-a-judge: For justifications, I want the admin to be able to define what an acceptable justification is and use an LLM to determine if the justification given is adequate. Better agent posture controls: I want to determine a better way to identify agents so our posture controls are more reliable. End user notifications: Alert end users during WebMCP activity to prevent adversarial attempts to hijack the users session while hiding their activity. An optional browser extension: A stretch goal is to use a browser extension to better lock down the DOM so agents can't circumvent controls through DOM inspection. This will have to be optional since it significantly increases the deployment complexity, but it will close a major gap. Demo The live demo has two sites: Example EHR app: https://webmcp-guard-portal.onrender.com/patients Admin console: https://webmcp-guard-console.vercel.app/login?token=Nit52TvyXZWpgzot1UIqMV4ktAB3oCdFbrk5M5AFSYg%3D Built With chatgpt claude codex nextjs render sqlite vercel Try it out github.com webmcp-guard-portal.onrender.com webmcp-guard-console.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Andrew Akers Like Share this project: Updates Andrew Akers started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:49 PM EDT

title: Ordering an Endotoxin Assay from My Lab Notebook
pitch: Allowing agents to order and interpret the results of a routine biochemical assay.
about_excerpt: Allowing agents to order and interpret the results of a routine biochemical assay. Like Comment Story Updates "Notebook paired". This means a session exists between the lab notebook and chatGPT browser ClearSignal. The price from the website is quickly found and quoted via webMCP `quote_endotoxin_tests`. The lab notebook can receive status updates. Order ID available for confirmation. Results page shows actionable data and the standard curve. All in the lab notebook. Inspiration Life sciences labs sell services to other labs. One of those services is the endotoxin detection assay. An assay is a test. Endotoxin is a molecule from bacteria that can cause fevers in humans and other animals. Labs producing a product like a vaccine or a protein want to ensure their product is free of endotoxin. Detecting endotoxin is a routine, well-known biochemical assay that uses horseshoe crab blood or a protein from horseshoe crab blood. The problem is that this simple test is encumbered with difficulty. 1) A researcher who wishes an endotoxin test must search online for a provider. 2) The researcher "reaches out" through a site request form or by email or by phone calling another human. 3) The researcher and provider discuss terms: how many samples, how often, customization, etc. 4) The providers gets back in a few days with a quote. 5) The researcher agrees to the quote, signs it, sends it back. 6) The researcher prepares the samples and mails them 7) Samples are received and processed, usually 3-5 business days. 8) Provider sends email saying samples have arrived and are being processed. 9) Results are sent, usually by email, in a pdf. Fancy provider labs have the researchers create an account and sign in to download a pdf. 10) Researcher combs through 5-8 pages of lot numbers and temperature settings to find the 3 or 5 datapoints that are actionable, i.e. "Endotoxin < 0.05 EU/mL". I want to condense the above steps to one step: A researcher uses their lab notebook to order an endotoxin test. And then I want every lab in the world to join us. Every lab selling their specialized assay order-able, update-able and interpretable with webMCP-enabled sites. This is the Federated Cloud Laboratory Network. Materials Needed 1) chatGPT desktop with browser and webMCP enabled. 2) Obsidian, https://obsidian.md/ 3) Obisidian plugin, "ClearSignal Lab Assistant", https://github.com/har1eyk/clearsignal-lab-assistant 4) Lab notebook page for testing (any markdown file will do!) 5) ClearSignal access, https://clearsignal-gray.vercel.app/ 1) user: endo@toxin.com 2) pass: horseshoe What it does A researcher keeps a lab notebook in a markdown file. A markdown viewer like Obsidian is used. Obsidian can use plugins for beyond-markdown functionality. I created a plugin that allows a researcher to call for an endotoxin assay test from their lab notebook using three backticks. After the backticks, "clearsignal" is typed and a researcher can request: Order an endotoxin assay on two samples if the price is less than <$500. The sample IDs are: "ID-0001 and ID-0002". Then, the plugin begins a session with chatGPT's browser and the ClearSignal site. The webMCP-enabled site can easily find the endotoxin-per-sample-cost and report it. The quote is provided to the lab researcher in their notebook! Additionally, the researcher can also ask questions in their original prompt like: Can I send in plasmid samples? (Plasmids are circular pieces of DNA purified from bacteria.) The webMCP-enabled site answers it directly from the FAQ. No hunting and clicking for the page and the question. Save those tokens with webMCP. Lastly, the researcher's samples are loaded and the price is visible. The final "submit" creates the order. Order information is transmitted to the lab notebook. Status updates are also provided. In this demo version, status updates occur every few seconds. In real testing conditions, the status updates occur every few days. I like that when the testing is "complete", that endotoxin concentration and standard curve data is sent to the lab notebook so the researcher can take actionable next steps. Table 1: Time Savings with WebMCP-enabled ClearSignal Site With WebMCP Without WebMCP Calls quote_endotoxin_tests with two sample IDs Has to navigate forms, locate fields, type IDs, submit, and inspect the rendered result Receives exact fields such as unit_price: 375 and total: 750 Extracts prices from page text and infers which numbers represent unit price and total Automatically returns structured events to the Obsidian note Require a separate copy/paste or integration workflow How we built it 1) Building landing page. Paper and ChatGPT desktop 2) Build backend (postgres, Supabase) 3) Create login page 1) successful via chatGPT sites 2) successful via localhost 4) Create user dashboard or login landing page 5) Create order page, make it webMCP enabled 1) Human successfully order via chatGPT site? 2) Human successfully order via localhost? 3) Bot successfully order via chatGPT site? 1. Logged in (success) 2. Not Logged in (success) 4) Bot successfully order via localhost? 1) Logged in (can't get chatgpt plugin to use webmcp; uses navigation.) 2) Not Logged in 6) Build Obsidian plugin 7) Publish website (Vercel) 8) Use Obsidian plugin chatbot to order via published clearsignal site 1) get status updates from backend 2) Upon status update "Complete", Obsidian plugin connection automatically closes. 9) Generate supabase cronjob to process all the order sequences steps for demo purposes. Real testing takes days/weeks. 10) Next Steps: Use Benchling plugin to order via published clearsignal site Challenges we ran into Lots of hard parts here. Some we overcame, some we patched, and some we're leaving for later. Overcame 1) How do we get markdown to chat with a website? Answer: The Obsidian plugin routes with chatGPT desktop session which connects to the webMCP-enabled site. 2) How do we get so much sci-knowledge into webMCP? Even a simple test like the endotoxin assay can have dozens of questions from researchers, e.g. Do samples need to be aqueous? Do you perform dilution series? What about inhibition? Answer: this one was easier to solve than expected. Having a FAQ list and then loading the questions and answers into get_endotoxin_faqs was a nice, quick way to help find answers. I imagine an entire page of FAQs with every question a researcher has every asked easily navigable with webMCP. 3) How do we show a quote, order updates and results? Answer: we instantiate a session between Obsidian plugin and chatGPT desktop. Quotes, results and updates are added to the lab notebook. Patch 1) Chrome chatGPT extension with sites-enabled still did not invoke some of webMCP items on ClearSignal. For isntance, sometimes I would ask "What is the cost per sample?" and the extension would show a pointer and click around until it found a price. Lots of troubleshooting later, I realized that chatGPT desktop web interface behaves different than Chrome websites with chatGPT extension enabled. So, I continued to use chatGPT desktop. Future Work 1) The site still relies on chatGPT desktop. Can we make an Obsidian Plugin chatGPT API and bypass chatGPT desktop? Still, how do we sign off on the ordering step. 2) Right now the order status come in a few seconds after each other, e.g. "in_preparation", "in_testing", etc. These updates typically occur every couple of days. How do I keep a Obsidian-plugin-chatGPT session going that long? I probably can't. I need to build out the plugin to do periodic polling probably via REST API or webhook. 3) I would love to see this in popular Lab notebook like Benchling and Notion. Custom plugin for each? Chrome extension? 4) What would it take to let every biotech lab sell and describe their assays to researchers and their agents so that they can be ordered from a lab notebook? Accomplishments that we're proud of Two that I'm proud of: 1) Quotes, ordering, questions, updates and results are all incorporated into the lab notebook. Having all these timestamped updates and results in one place with a collapsible menu is so fun! 2) Using webMCP on a science site as a way to quickly arrive at answers like cost and sample criteria will save days of back-and-forth clarification and negotiation. What we learned 1) The FAQ lives on. 2) All scientists should be keeping a lab notebook in mardown. 3) Obsidian is a fabulous markdown viewer. 4) There are important webMCP differences between chatGPT desktop browser and Chrome chatGPT extension. What's next for Endotoxin Let's help all researchers order all assays via their lab notebooks! title: Automata - a WebMCP co-creation playground
pitch: You and your agent, one universe. A cellular automata playground where a human and an AI agent build, run, and study Game of Life worlds together through WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: You and your agent, one universe. A cellular automata playground where a human and an AI agent build, run, and study Game of Life worlds together through WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Automata is an interactive cellular automata canvas where a human and an AI agent share one Game of Life universe. The human draws, erases, and stamps patterns by hand. The agent drives the same universe through 10 WebMCP tools: spawning catalog patterns, inventing new ones from RLE, switching rule systems, fast-forwarding up to 5,000 generations, and analyzing what emerged. Every agent action lights up on the canvas and lands in an on-screen activity feed, so the human always sees what their collaborator did. Why it's a strong fit for WebMCP Cellular automata are a natural human + agent collaboration. The work splits cleanly: humans sketch curiosity (a squiggle, a stamped pulsar, a splash of soup), and agents run the experiment (hundreds of generations in a blink, then a classified report of the outcome). That only works if the agent can operate the app itself, not a parallel API - which is exactly what WebMCP provides. Each of the app's 10 tools is registered through the WebMCP Imperative API with document.modelContext.registerTool, mixing read-only tools (get_state, analyze, list_patterns) with mutating ones (spawn_pattern, load_rle, set_rules, run_steps, add_noise, clear, set_running). What people and agents can do together that was hard before Say "add a glider gun and some chaos, run 400 generations, tell me what emerges." The agent stamps the gun, sprinkles noise, fast-forwards 400 generations, and returns a named census of the wreckage: "12 blocks, 5 blinkers, a beehive, 3 escaped gliders, stable since generation 212." The analyze tool is non-destructive - it clones the universe, simulates ahead, detects extinction, stabilization (with period), or ongoing activity, and names the objects that emerge. Then the volley continues: the human stamps a pulsar into the agent's world, the agent weaves gliders around it with load_rle, or flips the physics to HighLife or a custom B../S.. rulestring and reports what the same world does under new laws. Before WebMCP, an agent could advise about Game of Life; it couldn't sit at the same table. How WebMCP was implemented All 10 tools are registered via the WebMCP Imperative API (document.modelContext.registerTool), with JSON tool results. The page ships a WebMCP origin trial token so Chrome 149+ gets native WebMCP (also testable via chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing); without either, a built-in shim provides the same registerTool/getTools/executeTool surface and an in-page Agent console lets you call every tool by hand. The automata engine is pure dependency-free JavaScript (grid, Life-like rule parser, pattern catalog, RLE round-trips, cycle detection, object classification) with 16 Node tests, so tool behavior is verifiable outside the browser. Challenges and learnings Making analyze non-destructive: it had to clone the universe and simulate ahead without touching the live world the human is watching. Naming what emerges: classifying the settled state into named objects took cycle detection plus object classification, not just a population count. Keeping the human in the loop: every tool call highlights the canvas and posts to the activity feed. Dual registration path: native WebMCP via origin trial/flag, with a shim exposing the identical surface. title: WhenToProfit
pitch: Know when your small business makes money.
about_excerpt: Know when your small business makes money. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page - What If Scenario For Tech Business Home Page - What If Scenario For Retail/FnB Business Home Page - "Reach The Goal" Recommendation Inspiration Recently, I spent a lot of time learning Finance, especially financial modeling. Building a financial model was much harder than I expected. It requires you to think about assumptions, scenarios, how metrics (COGS, Cash Conversion Cycle, Liabilities, etc.) relate to each others, and many other things at the same time. But I realized something: I was learning this because I had the time and motivation to study finance. Many builders and small business owners around me don't. They often have much simpler questions: How much money do I need to survive if I quit my job? How much cash do I need to sustain my business before it becomes profitable? When will my business break even? If I increase my price by 20%, will it actually help? What happens if I hire someone next month? What can I change to improve my profit? These are financial questions, but they shouldn't require everyone to become a financial analyst first. That became the inspiration for WhenToProfit . My ambition is to eventually build a financial guide and decision-support tool for builders and small business owners — something that helps them understand their business financially and make better decisions without needing a finance background. What it does WhenToProfit is a simple financial planning and decision-support tool for builders and small business owners. I built it around a few questions that I think many entrepreneurs have but often struggle to answer: How much money do I need to survive if I quit my job? How much cash do I need to sustain the business before it becomes profitable? When will the business break even? What happens if I increase my price? What happens if I hire someone? What can I change to improve my profit? How much could the business be worth under a simple valuation approach? The goal is not to replace accounting software or build a complete financial system. Instead, WhenToProfit focuses on turning financial modeling into something more understandable and actionable for people who don't have a finance background. The tool supports two common business types: Tech / Solo businesses , such as SaaS and mobile apps Retail / F&B businesses , where revenue can be estimated from visitors, conversion rate, operating days, customers, and average order value At the core, the model connects simple assumptions to practical financial outcomes: $$ Revenue = Volume \times Price $$ $$ Gross\ Profit = Revenue - Variable\ Costs $$ $$ Operating\ Profit = Gross\ Profit - Fixed\ Operating\ Expenses $$ $$ Cash\ Flow = Operating\ Cash\ Flow - CapEx + Financing $$ From these inputs, WhenToProfit estimates monthly revenue, gross profit, operating profit, cash flow, cash balance, break-even timing, cash-flow-positive timing, runway, and a simplified valuation. The other important part is scenario planning . Instead of forcing users to build a complicated 24-month financial spreadsheet, they can describe business changes as events. For example: Increase the price by 20% in July Hire 5 engineers in January Improve monthly churn from 5% to 3% Raise $2M in March The user can then compare different scenarios and see how those decisions change the financial outcome. I also built WebMCP into the product so an AI agent can interact with the financial model instead of only talking about it. The agent can read assumptions and results, analyze the business, simulate decisions, compare scenarios, and perform structured actions such as creating scenarios or adding and moving scenario events. This creates an experience where the agent can help the user explore financial decisions while the user remains in control of the actual business plan. How I built it I built WhenToProfit in about two days , from the initial idea to the final submission. The project uses Next.js, TypeScript, a client-side financial calculation engine, local project storage, and WebMCP . I deliberately kept the architecture simple because the goal was to build a useful prototype quickly rather than create a large backend system. The financial model is separated from the UI so that the same calculation logic can be used by the dashboard, scenario simulations, and WebMCP tools. The project uses a scenario-based approach. A base case contains the original assumptions, while other scenarios describe changes to those assumptions over time. For WebMCP, I designed the tools around three stages: Read → Analyze → Act The agent can first understand the current project and financial model, then analyze or simulate possible decisions, and finally make structured changes to scenarios when the user wants to act. I also wanted WebMCP actions to use the same mutation paths as the normal application UI whenever possible. This means an action performed by an agent updates the same application state and persistence layer rather than creating a separate system just for AI. One important design decision was keeping the Base Case immutable . Agents can create and modify other scenarios, but they cannot directly modify the original base assumptions. I also added persistence for the active scenario so that the user's current planning context remains after switching projects or reloading the application. For development, I used AI heavily and treated it as a coding partner. I broke the work into small steps, gave it detailed product requirements, reviewed the generated implementation, ran builds and tests, and corrected the direction when something didn't match the intended product. Challenges we ran into 1. Building a financial model without making the product too complicated Financial modeling can become extremely complex very quickly. I deliberately avoided trying to build: Full accounting Tax calculations Double-entry bookkeeping Complex debt models Detailed cap tables Banking integrations Instead, I focused on the financial questions that are most useful for an early-stage builder. That constraint helped me keep the product understandable and practical. 2. Making WebMCP actually useful I didn't want to add WebMCP just because the hackathon required it. I had to think carefully about which parts of the product an agent should actually be able to interact with. This led me to think about the experience in three stages: Read → Analyze → Act The agent should first understand the business, then help analyze possible decisions, and finally be able to take structured actions when appropriate. This was an important design challenge because I wanted WebMCP to feel like a natural extension of the product rather than a separate feature added for the hackathon. 3. Controlling AI while working under a very short deadline My biggest development challenge was probably not writing code. It was controlling the scope . I had only two days, so I had to continuously ask: "Is this feature actually necessary?" "Does this help the core financial question?" "Will this make the user experience better?" "Is WebMCP actually useful here?" I had to guide the AI step by step instead of letting it build too much at once. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The biggest accomplishment is going from an idea to a working financial planning product in about two days . Building it helped me revisit my financial knowledge in a much more practical way, while also learning how to use AI to build a real product under a very tight deadline. I'm especially proud of seeing a possible future of work where people can collaborate with AI without being technical . I see WebMCP as a smooth bridge toward a more AI-native web, where existing websites can become tools that AI can understand and interact with. More importantly, I see this as a way for small entrepreneurs to leverage AI more naturally — not by learning how to code, but by simply working with AI through the tools they already use. What we learned This project gave me two very different kinds of learning: financial modeling and building with AI . Financial modeling Before this project, I mostly understood financial modeling as something you study. Building WhenToProfit made me understand it as a way to support decisions. The important flow became: Assumptions → Model → Scenarios → Financial Results → Decisions A financial model becomes much more useful when the numbers help someone decide what to do next. I also learned how difficult it is to simplify a financial model without making it meaningless. Every metric and assumption needs to have a reason to exist. Building with AI I also learned a lot about vibe-coding. AI can make implementation incredibly fast, but it doesn't remove the need for product thinking. title: DAG Studio: Agent-Ready Causal Modeling with WebMCP
pitch: DAG Studio lets researchers and AI build and analyze causal diagrams through WebMCP, with transparent assumptions and analysis-ready R or Python code.
about_excerpt: DAG Studio lets researchers and AI build and analyze causal diagrams through WebMCP, with transparent assumptions and analysis-ready R or Python code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I'm a trained epidemiologist with about 10 years in pharma supporting drug development. When we approach the development of a study we begin with a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In a causal DAG, every node and arrow expresses a scientific assumption. Those assumptions determine which biases may be present, which variables should or should not be adjusted for, and whether a causal effect is identifiable. We created DAG Studio to give epidemiologists and other researchers an approachable, browser-based environment for constructing and examining those assumptions. However, an AI assistant interacting with a conventional web application still has to interpret what it 'sees' on the canvas. It cannot reliably distinguish a parts of a graph from a decorative line or know whether its internal description of the graph still matches what the researcher sees. WebMCP suggested a better model: give the agent structured access to the same scientific object the researcher is editing. That inspired DAG Studio WebMCP, a shared causal-modeling workspace for researchers. What it does DAG Studio WebMCP allows a researcher and an AI agent to collaborate on the same live causal DAG. The researcher sees and edits the visual canvas, while the agent uses nine structured WebMCP tools connected to the exact same client-side state: get_current_dag add_node remove_node add_edge remove_edge analyze_current_dag check_adjustment_set generate_analysis_code simulate_current_dag An agent can read the current graph, propose changes, inspect open backdoor paths, identify minimal sufficient adjustment sets, verify a researcher-proposed adjustment set, and generate R or Python analysis code. The simulation tool uses DAG Studio's existing linear Gaussian structural equation model to generate synthetic data from the live graph. For each node (X_j), the illustrative model follows [ X_j = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{pa}(j)} \beta_{ij}X_i + \epsilon_j. ] The tool returns bounded summaries, correlations, a small data preview, model-implied total effects, and crude and minimally adjusted ordinary least squares estimates. In our demo, a researcher can ask the agent to retain results from two different DAG hypotheses in the conversation and compare their implications using the same sample size, random seed, and coefficients. These simulations do not determine which DAG is scientifically correct. They reveal what follows from the assumptions encoded in each model. How we built it DAG Studio WebMCP extends the existing React and Vite DAG Studio application. We deliberately reused the established causal and simulation functions in dag-engine.js and its dag-engine.d.ts declarations rather than rewriting the algorithms for the Challenge. The WebMCP layer registers tools through the current document.modelContext API. It also includes a compatibility fallback for hosts implementing the earlier navigator.modelContext location. The WebMCP tools receive dependency-injected access to the same synchronous state references and React mutation functions used by the visual canvas. Therefore: an agent mutation immediately appears on the canvas; a human canvas mutation is immediately visible to the next tool call; agent and human graph edits share the same undo history; and analysis and simulation always operate on the graph currently visible to the researcher. Agent changes receive visible attribution. The simulation tool also opens DAG Studio's existing simulation interface, so the result is reflected in both the conversation and the application. Everything remains browser-side. The Challenge version is an isolated static HTTPS deployment on Cloudflare Pages, separate from the production DAG Studio website. The source is published under the MIT license, and GitHub Actions runs the original engine-parity suite together with the new WebMCP shared-state tests. Challenges we ran into The most important challenge was not tool registration, rather it was guaranteeing that the agent and researcher were truly modifying the same graph. React state updates are asynchronous, while a sequence of agent tool calls may need to observe each mutation immediately. We addressed this by wiring the tools to the canvas's synchronous references and existing mutation wrappers rather than creating a second “agent graph.” WebMCP is also an emerging standard, and browser implementations differed during development. The API appeared under different objects across environments, some Chrome testing calls required JSON-serialized arguments, and not every ChatGPT or Codex browser session exposed site tools. Clear connection diagnostics and compatibility support were essential. We also had to preserve the scientific boundary between assistance and authority. A variable being associated with an outcome does not automatically make it a confounder, and simulated data cannot validate a biological hypothesis. Tool descriptions, responses, and visible language therefore characterize graph changes as assumptions or proposals for researcher review. Finally, simulation results can become too large for a useful agent interaction. We bounded sample-size options, limited row previews, summarized variables and correlations, validated coefficient overrides, and made every run reproducible with a recorded random seed. Accomplishments that we're proud of Nine WebMCP tools operate on the exact graph visible in DAG Studio. Human and agent mutations remain synchronized and undoable. The original DAG Studio causal algorithms were reused rather than approximated by the language model. The agent can analyze competing hypotheses and retain reproducible simulation results for comparison. Simulation outputs explicitly separate model-implied effects from crude and adjusted estimates. The integration includes current and earlier WebMCP API compatibility and visible connection diagnostics. Thirteen automated tests cover engine parity, tool registration, shared state, mutations, cycle rejection, adjustment analysis, code generation, simulation reproducibility, input validation, bounded results, visible simulation state, and a two-hypothesis comparison. The project is available as an open-source repository and a static public HTTPS application. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful domain operations rather than reproducing every button in an interface. analyze_current_dag is more reliable and scientifically legible than asking an agent to visually inspect a set of arrows. simulate_current_dag is more useful than teaching an agent how to navigate a simulation panel one control at a time. We also learned that shared state changes the nature of human–AI interaction. The canvas is no longer just something the agent can see; it becomes a common scientific object that both participants can inspect and revise. The conversation can retain multiple hypotheses and their results even though the visual editor displays the current model. Most importantly, greater agent capability makes explicit epistemic boundaries more important. The engine can verify the graphical and statistical consequences of a DAG, but neither the engine nor the agent can decide whether its assumptions are scientifically true. What's next for DAG Studio: Agent-Ready Causal Modeling with WebMCP Next, we want to deepen hypothesis-centered workflows: named DAG versions, persistent side-by-side comparisons, researcher approval checkpoints, and exportable analysis reports that preserve the connection between assumptions, adjustment decisions, simulations, and generated code. We also see opportunities for collaborative provenance, where every proposed node or edge can carry a rationale, citation, reviewer comment, and acceptance status. Additional simulation families could support binary, count, survival, longitudinal, and nonlinear outcomes while preserving transparent assumptions about the data-generating process. The long-term goal is not an autonomous system that declares causal truth. It is an agent-ready scientific workspace that helps researchers articulate alternatives, expose disagreements, test implications, and document why a final model was chosen. Ideally this workspace can be called upon in a multi-agent orchestration that runs a research workflow from end to end. title: Redactly
pitch: WebMCP tools let AI agents view redacted documents, verify fields without exposing them, and request human approved, one time reveals with a full audit trail for every action.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tools let AI agents view redacted documents, verify fields without exposing them, and request human approved, one time reveals with a full audit trail for every action. Like Comment Story Updates arhitecture Inspiration WebMCP lets browser-based AI agents call tools directly on the page a user is looking at — which is powerful, but also a little terrifying when that page contains sensitive documents. Redaction tools today assume a human is the only reader. The moment an agent can call verify_field or read_document , redaction stops being a UI concern and becomes a security boundary problem: what happens when the "user" reading your masked document is an LLM that can be prompted, jailbroken, or simply mistaken? We built Redactly to answer that question directly: can a document viewer expose real WebMCP tools to an agent — verify, request-unmask, challenge a redaction — without ever letting a raw sensitive value leak into the DOM, browser storage, logs, or an agent's context by accident? What it does Redactly is a document viewer that exposes five WebMCP tools bound to the currently open document: request_document_view — returns the masked document, paginated by cursor. verify_without_reveal — lets an agent check whether a guessed value matches a redacted field without ever returning the field itself (rate-limited, so it can't be used as a brute-force oracle). request_field_unmask — asks a human owner to approve revealing a specific field. Approval creates a grant that can be consumed exactly once ; a second attempt returns already_consumed , not the value. challenge_redaction — lets an agent argue a field was mis-classified (e.g., a false-positive PII detection). A human approval flips the field to non-sensitive for that session only — it never rewrites the underlying model's global output. get_redaction_audit_log — a read-only, cursor-paginated trail of every view, verification, unmask, and challenge event. Every reveal is a server-side, at-most-once event : once a value is returned to a tool call, Redactly has no way to un-send it, so the whole system is designed around never handing it out casually. A same-page approval modal drives the human side of the demo; in a production deployment that approval channel would move out-of-band, since a browser agent could otherwise observe the same page the human is approving on. How we built it Frontend: Next.js App Router, with the document viewer as the sole route the WebMCP tools are registered against — tools are torn down on unmount, and pending fetches are aborted rather than left running. Backend: A FastAPI policy service that owns all raw text, ONNX-based PII detection, and the state machines for reveals and challenges. The detector's raw-inference route is internal-only and deliberately never exposed as a tool. Data model: Documents are stored AES-GCM encrypted. Redacted fields are referenced by random per-session public_ref values, never a real placeholder-to-value map — so nothing outside the trusted API process can resolve a field back to its text. Equality checks for verify_without_reveal go through a canonical, domain-separated HMAC compared in constant time, so the endpoint can't be turned into a brute-force oracle. Reveal consumption: Grants are consumed inside a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction with a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE state = 'READY' , so under concurrent requests exactly one caller gets the value and every other caller gets already_consumed — verified with a 50-way concurrency test against a synthetic sentinel value. Audit trail: Every state mutation and its audit event commit in the same transaction, so there's no window where an action succeeds but goes unlogged. Audit metadata is allowlisted so raw values, verification guesses, and session tokens structurally cannot end up there. Challenges we ran into The core challenge was designing for an adversarial reader that isn't a browser — it's a language model that might be prompted (by us, by a compromised page, or by the document text itself) to try to exfiltrate a value. That reshaped almost every decision: Treating document text itself as untrusted input, since it can contain adversarial instructions aimed at the agent reading it. Making sure a "read-only" tool actually is read-only — verify_without_reveal looks harmless but is a textbook equality oracle if not rate-limited and constant-time. Deciding that unmask has to be at-most-once , not just access-controlled — because once an agent has a value in its context, revocation is meaningless. Keeping model confidence scores out of the normal masked view entirely, while still surfacing them during a challenge review, so the classifier's internals aren't leaking through the "harmless" viewing path. What we learned Building for an AI-agent caller changes the security model even when the underlying stack (Next.js, FastAPI, SQLite) is completely ordinary. The interesting design work isn't the CRUD — it's things like proving a reveal grant is consumed exactly once under concurrency, or writing an invariant test that greps every non-reveal response, log line, and audit row for a leaked sentinel value. WebMCP makes it trivially easy to hand an agent real capabilities on your page; it does not make it easy to reason about what an agent will do with them, and that gap is where most of our design time went. What's next for Redactly Move human approval to a genuinely out-of-band channel (push notification / separate authenticated device) so a browser-resident agent can't observe or race the approval UI. Add real user authentication and document ownership, replacing the session-cookie isolation used for the hackathon demo. Expand the canonicalization rules for verify_without_reveal to more field types (dates, phone formats, addresses) beyond the current type-aware set. Publish the concurrency and no-raw-leak invariant tests as a reusable test suite other WebMCP tool builders can adapt. title: Feather Engine
pitch: Give browser AI agents direct control over a live 3D engine. Build scenes, configure physics, and test gameplay through natural language using the W3C WebMCP standard.
about_excerpt: Give browser AI agents direct control over a live 3D engine. Build scenes, configure physics, and test gameplay through natural language using the W3C WebMCP standard. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The hackathon prompt pointed me toward WebMCP, and I wanted to know the performance rate of agents when giving MCP tools to create games in a 3D engine. I am a Unity game developer, so I know firsthand how much manual work goes into coordinates, physics, and object placement. I wanted to see how much of that an agent could just take over. What It Does Feather Engine WebMCP connects browser-native AI agents directly to Feather Engine (React 18, Three.js, Rapier physics) using the W3C WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext ). Browser-native agent control: Agents auto-discover engine tools through document.modelContext . Zero plugins, zero CLI setup. Full 3D world building: Agents can spawn objects, sculpt terrain, generate wind, create water volumes, set lighting presets (cyberpunk, sunset), and tune rigid-body physics. Gameplay and controllers: Third-person character controllers, vehicle handling, and live Play mode to test games in place. Live agent HUD: A floating status bar shows real-time agent activity so you always know what it is doing. Tool inspector: A WebMCP modal lets developers explore tools, view input schemas, and copy executable snippets to test directly in DevTools. Human-in-the-loop: Every agent action goes through the engine's undo/redo history. You can tweak or roll back anything the agent does. How I Built It I registered tools onto document.modelContext.registerTool with fallback emulation and a global window.__featherWebMcp debug handle. The architecture runs on two tiers: 14 direct core tools covering high-leverage actions: create_new_project , create_object , set_physics , create_meadow , set_character_controller , set_vehicle , and more. 2 gateway tools ( search_engine_tools and execute_engine_tool ) that give agents on-demand access to the full 200+ tool catalog without loading it upfront. All tool parameters run through a Zod validation pipeline compiled to JSON Schema, preventing runtime crashes. Tool calls mutate the Zustand store directly, which triggers Three.js rendering and Rapier physics updates at 60 FPS. Challenges I did not plan the two-tier architecture upfront. I registered the full 200+ tool catalog and ChatGPT's browser agent rejected it outright. The schema payload came in over 150 KB and hit an undocumented size limit. I had to step back and redesign on the fly: strip the initial payload down to 14 core tools (about 7 KB), then build the gateway layer so agents could still reach the full catalog on demand. It worked, but it was not the plan going in. Everything else, including physics sync and history integration, held up through the demo without major issues. Accomplishments I Am Proud Of A visiting browser agent can take a high-level prompt, query the scene, build an environment, add physics, and start gameplay without human intervention. A web app with 200+ tools can operate within browser agent constraints using a dynamic gateway. That is a real architectural pattern other projects can use. What I Learned Browser agents have hard payload constraints most web apps are not designed around. If your application has a large tool catalog, dynamic gateway discovery is not optional. It is the only way to scale within browser limits. Exposing your app's core logic through WebMCP also changes how the tool feels to use. The engine stopped feeling like something you operate and started feeling like something you collaborate with. What's Next Visual blueprint generation: Agents inspect and wire visual scripting node graphs to create custom game logic. Multi-agent co-creation: Specialized agents (level designer, environment artist, gameplay scripter) working the same scene at the same time. WebRTC multiplayer + AI: Remote human teams and agents building 3D worlds together, live. title: Taste Gate
pitch: An explainable WebMCP preview gate where agents plan queues and people choose what to reveal.
about_excerpt: An explainable WebMCP preview gate where agents plan queues and people choose what to reveal. Like Comment Story Updates Four narrow WebMCP tools expose previews and proposals — never full post content. The agent proposes an order; the person independently selects and reveals stories. Judge's 45-second path Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask for a preview-only two-card queue. Inspect the four discovered Site tools and the visible proposed queue. Select cards yourself and press Reveal my selected stories . The agent can propose and explain; only the person can choose a reveal. Inspiration Project .taste already proves that a social card can begin as a compact, deterministic 16-byte preview packet. Taste Gate asks a different question: when an agent and a person share the same live page, can the agent help plan attention without silently deciding what the person must open? What it does Taste Gate exposes a preview-only view of a live feed through WebMCP. The agent can inspect media shape, text geometry, engagement heat, visual seed, and existing interaction flags; it can then explain and write a proposed queue. The user sees that proposal in the same page but must select cards and press Reveal my selected stories themselves. The gate filters muted or blocked cards before they reach the agent-facing preview list. It does not infer author identity, topic, timestamp, or full text from a packet. How I built it I reused the existing zero-dependency TypeScript .taste decoder and built a small static JavaScript app around it. The top-level page conditionally registers four WebMCP site tools: get_gate_state list_previews explain_preview set_proposed_queue The normal UI remains fully usable without WebMCP. Full sample content is fetched only when the user uses the ordinary Reveal action. The app labels this honestly as a coordination contract for the demo, not server-enforced privacy. The demo video voiceover is generated with macOS text-to-speech (Samantha). Challenges I ran into The hard part was defining a useful agent boundary without inventing meaning that the 16-byte protocol does not contain. A packet gives layout, media, coarse heat, and social-state signals; it does not justify a claim about a post's topic, author, or relevance. The tools therefore return field-level reasons and explicit non-inferences instead of a hidden recommendation score. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A shared-page agent workflow that stays inspectable by the person using it. Four narrow tools, including a state-changing proposal tool that cannot reveal content or alter the human selection. Tests that reject gated, unknown, and repeated cards and verify that the agent-facing list contains no author, topic, timestamp, or full text. A normal UI fallback and a live ChatGPT desktop-browser check that discovers all four tools. What I learned WebMCP becomes most compelling when it exposes application state that a person can see and review immediately. Narrow, verifiable operations are more useful than a broad agent action that obscures how a decision was made. What's next for Taste Gate Replace the demo content source with an application-controlled hydration endpoint, retain the same packet-only agent contract, and evaluate whether users find proposed queues more understandable than automatic ranking. title: Resume Match
pitch: Tailor your resume to the job with an agent that proposes, and a human who decides.
about_excerpt: Tailor your resume to the job with an agent that proposes, and a human who decides. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept seeing resume tools that either rewrite everything behind your back or leave you hunting for keywords at 1 a.m. Neither felt honest. If an AI is going to touch something as personal as a resume, I want to see the before and after on the actual bullet — and I want a button that says no. WebMCP clicked because the agent and I share the same page. It can read the job I pasted and the bullets already on screen, then propose a change. It cannot quietly replace my experience with something I never agreed to. What it does Upload a PDF or Word resume, paste a job posting. The agent can pull out the role and required skills, point out gaps, score ATS coverage, pull in a public GitHub or Medium profile, and suggest a rewritten bullet or a cover-letter opener. Every suggestion shows up as a diff. I accept or reject it myself. Review and Export only include what I accepted. I recorded the demo with ChatGPT desktop . It found the page tools, ran the flow, and the diffs showed up the way they should — that’s the video I’m uploading. Live demo: https://resumematch-617103164879.us-central1.run.app How I built it Python on the server (FastAPI, Jinja2, SQLite). One small JavaScript file registers the WebMCP tools and updates the page. The real work stays in Python so I can sanitize and length-cap it. Intake forms use WebMCP’s declarative form tools, without auto-submit. Analysis and rewrites use document.modelContext.registerTool() . Because the tools live on the page, ChatGPT desktop could drive them the same way Chrome’s inspector can — I didn’t have to build a custom ChatGPT plugin. Only three tools call a model: analyze the job, propose a bullet rewrite, draft a cover opener. Gap finding and ATS scoring are plain skill matching: $$\text{coverage} = \frac{|\text{JD skills} \cap \text{resume skills}|}{|\text{JD skills}|} \times 100$$ Original bullet text is never overwritten. A proposal sits as its own row until I accept it. Running on Google Cloud Run. Session secret and the server Gemini key are in Secret Manager. What I learned The agent in the desktop app and the Gemini/Vertex key on the server are not the same job. ChatGPT picks which tool to call. Our server is what actually writes a proposal. That split is why the demo could look “agentic” without letting ChatGPT silently rewrite the resume. Tools belong to the current page. Stay on Edit for matching and diffs. analyze_job_description taking {} is fine — the job text is already in the session. Challenges Session cookies once split so submit saved a job and analyze couldn’t see it. A prompt on the Upload page also looks like nothing works until you actually click Upload & Parse. I hit both while testing, including with ChatGPT desktop, and had to fix the session path and the copy on the page before the recording was worth keeping. Cloud Run with SQLite wipes sessions on a new deploy, so I recorded against a stable revision. Job descriptions are still untrusted text I treat them as data and never commit a generation without a click. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation.
