title: No Seat Without a Route
pitch: The seat was available. The journey was not. WebMCP plans the route, lift, companion seat and assistance as one revalidated bundle.
about_excerpt: The seat was available. The journey was not. WebMCP plans the route, lift, companion seat and assistance as one revalidated bundle. Like Comment Story Updates The venue knew. The booking didn't. A wheelchair space can be available even when the journey to it is not usable. A route can contain steps. A lift can go out of service. The adjacent companion seat or entrance-assistance capacity can change before the booking is confirmed. That mismatch became the design question behind this prototype: what if the unit of booking were not the seat alone, but the accessible journey that makes the seat usable? No Seat Without a Route links the route, lift status, wheelchair space, adjacent companion seat and entrance assistance in one plan. At confirmation, the server evaluates that plan again against the current venue state. It either commits the wheelchair space, companion seat and assistance together, or reserves none of them. Federal ADA ticketing regulations require covered public entities and public accommodations that sell tickets for a single event or series of events to give individuals with disabilities an equal opportunity to purchase accessible seating, including during the same hours and through the same distribution methods used for other seating. Upon inquiry, entities that sell or distribute those tickets must identify and describe available accessible seating in enough detail for an individual with a disability to assess whether a particular seating location meets their accessibility needs ( DOJ ticket-sales guidance , 28 CFR § 35.138 and 28 CFR § 36.302(f) ). This prototype explores a product opportunity in that context. It does not claim that the ADA requires this route-and-booking model, or that the prototype establishes legal compliance. The failure is the demo A visitor asks their browser agent for a step-free route for a 72 cm wheelchair, under 80 metres, with one companion, a quieter entrance and somebody waiting at the door. The page exposes structured WebMCP tools. The agent reads the current synthetic venue state and stages a complete plan through East Entrance and East Lift L2. The route and its named dependencies appear on the page for review. Planning reserves nothing. The demo then introduces a race condition between review and confirmation. A visible control arms a deterministic fault on East Lift L2, but the lift remains operational until the next valid confirmation attempt. When the visible confirmation control is pressed, the server applies the outage, advances the venue revision and refuses the now-stale plan with STALE_RESOURCE_VERSION . The result shows 0 partial reservations : no wheelchair space, companion seat or assistance slot was held on its own. The agent calls explain_access_refusal . It receives the failed LIFT_OPERATIONAL rule, the old and current venue revisions, the zero-partial-reservation result and the Garden route that remains available. It replans through Garden Entrance and Garden Lift L4 without requiring the six inputs again. The replacement is reviewed and confirmed through the visible page. The server checks the current venue state once more, then commits wheelchair space W12, companion seat W13 and entrance assistance in one transition. A happy path would show only that a plan can become a booking. The demonstrated failure path shows the harder part: stale state books nothing, the refusal explains what changed, and the agent has a structured way to recover. Why WebMCP fits The booking page is both the human-facing interface and the agent surface. WebMCP gives the browser agent structured, site-authored tools. In the demonstrated stale-plan flow, the staged plan, refusal and replacement are rendered in that same page for review. Tool availability follows the booking state. Search and staging are removed when they no longer apply. After the demonstrated stale-plan refusal, explanation and replanning become available. Once a booking exists, the visitor tool surface is read-only. No registered WebMCP tool can prepare or commit a booking confirmation. In the intended page flow, confirmation is a visible page action. This is a tool-surface boundary, not an identity guarantee: the prototype has no user or operator identity authentication and does not prove who pressed a control. The ordinary form and buttons complete the same visitor flow when WebMCP is unavailable. This shared page state is why I built the project with WebMCP instead of placing an agent beside a separate booking API. The structured actions, map, failure explanation and confirmation control stay in one interface instead of becoming two experiences that need to be kept in sync. How I built it The client is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A zero-dependency Node.js service holds synthetic venue state in memory and runs on Render. The visitor code defines nine imperative tools and registers only the subset valid in the current state. A separate operator demo page defines three facility tools over the same synthetic venue state. It has no operator identity authentication and is not an authorization boundary. In the Chromium hosts I tested that exposed the declarative contract, the visible requirements form also appeared as a tool, deliberately without automatic submission. Planning, explanation and final revalidation use the same route-evaluation implementation. Every plan records the venue revision against which it was built. Confirmation checks that revision again and moves every reservable resource in one synchronous in-memory state transition. For expected browser-facing domain refusals, the first-party pages request a typed ok: false envelope. The result keeps its error code and original domain status, while the expected safety decision does not appear as a failed network request. Raw API clients still receive conventional 4xx responses, and unexpected failures remain 5xx. What broke, and what I learned During earlier testing in Chrome 151, I observed that unregistering a tool while its own call was returning could cancel the in-flight call. I fixed that by delaying the tool-surface update until the execution had settled. Across the hosts I tested, I also observed different enforcement of required fields at the host boundary. The tool wrapper, visible form and server therefore each validate the input that reaches them. While auditing the regression suite, I found a test that removed the very counterexample it was meant to detect before asserting that the list was empty. The test passed while its claim was false. Since then, for release-critical repairs, I have restored the defect deliberately, confirmed that the regression test fails, and only then put the fix back. I manually exercised the deployed app in ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser on 2 September 2026. The automated browser run used Chrome 152.0.7977.66 and also exercised Edge 152.0.4191.53. Firefox 155 was checked only as a manual, non-WebMCP fallback. These are observations from those specific versions, not a claim of compatibility with every browser or agent. The current release gate passed 740/740 Node tests and 389/389 browser checks . Current scope This is a focused synthetic prototype: two routes, one event, in-memory inventory, no payment, no real ticket and no user or operator identity authentication. The visitor and operator labels describe demo roles, not authenticated identities. The operator page is an open demo control surface, not a production authorization boundary. Production would need durable storage, real authentication and authorization, live ticketing and facility feeds, outbound notifications, and testing with wheelchair users and venue access teams. The same transaction pattern may be worth testing in other journeys where one missing dependency can make the rest of a reservation unusable, such as rail transfers, airports, hotels or hospitals. A seat is only accessible when the whole route works. video_transcript_excerpt: The venue knew. The venue knew. The booking didn't. No seat without a route. One request. A real browser agent calls the live page through WebMCP. The request combines the route, a wheelchair space, a companion seat, and entrance assistance in one complete plan. The agent rechecks and stages the East route. It can prepare the journey, but it cannot confirm the booking. Nothing is reserved yet. The complete proposal waits for the visitor's decision. Now the venue changes after review, but before commit. East lift L2 will fail during confirmation. I confirm. Before writing anything, the server rechecks the route, lift, seats, and assistance against the live venue. The prepared plan is stale, so the booking stops. Revision one no longer matches revision two. Zero partial reservations. I ask what changed. WebMCP returns the failed lift rule, both revisions, and the route that still works. The agent replans against the live venue through garden entrance and garden lift L4, keeping the chair space, companion seat, and assistance together. The changed route is visible before commitment. I review the replacement, then make the final decision myself. Only now does one atomic commit create one booking and reserve three connected resources. Nothing was ever left half booked. Synthetic data, no real ticket or payment. A seat is accessible only when the route works.

title: StreamBot | Agent Edition
pitch: A streamer dashboard with a built-in AI teammate: it proposes themed setups, teaches the UI with guided tours, and edits vertical clips you approve everything
about_excerpt: A streamer dashboard with a built-in AI teammate: it proposes themed setups, teaches the UI with guided tours, and edits vertical clips you approve everything Like Comment Story Updates Home Clipit Studio Custom Command Chat Alert Overlay Builder StreamBot — Agent Edition Project Story Inspiration Streamers run a one-person production studio. Before they ever go live, they may have to manage chat commands, alerts, timed promotions, overlays, clipping highlights for TikTok, and countless other pieces of production across a dozen different tabs. Meanwhile, AI agents are still largely stuck outside the product. They screen-scrape interfaces, guess which buttons to click, and operate without a real understanding of the application's state. We wanted to change that. StreamBot is a real streamer dashboard already in production use. The WebMCP Challenge gave us the missing piece: instead of bolting an AI chatbot onto the side of the product, we gave the agent a first-class seat inside the application . The agent uses the same tools as the streamer, operates against the same state, and leaves the same audit trail. That led to the question driving this project: What does setup feel like when a streamer and their AI agent share one workspace, while the human remains in control of anything that matters? What It Does Three experiences define StreamBot Agent Edition. 1. Propose, Don't Just Do The agent isn't simply given unrestricted control. A streamer can say: "Set up my horror night." Instead of immediately changing their dashboard, the agent creates a complete themed proposal: !scary and !brave commands 👻 Follow alerts Timed promotional messages A JUMPSCARE channel-point reward A follower goal bar Other relevant stream configuration The entire setup appears as a review card . The streamer can inspect the proposal, remove anything they don't want, and then hit Approve . Only after approval does the agent execute the changes. Proposal → Review → Approval → Execution It's collaboration with a veto, rather than blind automation. 2. Guides That Teach on the Live UI Agents shouldn't teach users from outdated screenshots or hallucinated interfaces. If a streamer asks: "How do chat alerts work?" The agent first uses discover_targets to inspect the actual DOM and identify the elements currently available on the page. It then uses compose_tour to build a spotlight walkthrough directly against those discovered elements. The result is a guide that operates on the real product, in its current state . No stale screenshots. No guessed buttons. No hallucinated UI. The agent discovers the interface first, then teaches from reality. 3. Skilled Hands, Not Chat The agent isn't limited to answering questions. Inside StreamBot's ClipIt editor, it can stage vertical social edits directly against the mounted editor state. That includes: Vertical layouts Facecam resizing Caption placement Real transcribed captions Designer-created caption presets Editor configuration The agent isn't pretending to edit a clip through text. It's operating the actual editor. How We Built It with WebMCP Route-Scoped Tool Suites Each StreamBot dashboard route registers the tools relevant to the feature currently being viewed. Examples include: Commands Alerts Timed Messages Rewards Canvas ClipIt This is implemented through src/webmcp/suites.ts . The agent only sees tools that are valid for the current context and available to its seat. The Agent Uses the Same API as the UI We didn't create a separate "AI version" of StreamBot's functionality. Every agent tool calls the same endpoints used by the human interface . That means the resulting state is identical regardless of who performed the action. For example: Agent creates !scary → the command immediately appears in the streamer's command list. There is no synchronization layer or second source of truth. Agent actions and human actions operate on the same application state. Tool executions are also written to the account's audit log, just like actions performed by other members of the team. A Bridge into Live Editors For ClipIt, we needed the agent to interact with a mounted editor rather than a traditional API. We built mountClipItEditorCommands , which connects the WebMCP suite directly to the ClipIt store. The bridge dispatches real reducer actions and waits for state convergence before reporting success. That distinction matters. We don't report success because an action was dispatched. We report success when the editor has actually reached the requested state. Human-in-the-Loop Primitives Human approval is built into the tool architecture itself. propose_stream_setup opens a PrepProposalCard and blocks execution until the streamer makes a decision. Our guide tools work similarly: they compose tours from curated block types that can only be placed on targets discovered from the current page. The agent therefore has useful autonomy without having unlimited authority. Permissions The agent is treated as a real seat within StreamBot. Its permissions are governed through: Settings → Your Team Tool suites are only registered in areas where the agent has permission to operate. Challenges 1. Timeouts That Lied Our first ClipIt bridge used pixel changes as proof that an operation had succeeded. That seemed reasonable until we encountered a simple case: A facecam was already in the requested position. The operation succeeded, but because the pixels didn't change, the bridge waited 12 seconds and eventually reported a timeout. We rewrote the system around state convergence instead. A no-op move is now considered a successful operation if the editor is already in the requested state. We also added fail-fast validation using valid-ID lists. 2. Making the Demo Deterministic Transcription and streaming are inherently live, variable, and slow. A two-minute demo can't wait around for production systems to finish processing. We built a simulated backend using: An in-browser API shim A simulated stream engine Deterministic application state This gives us a world that behaves like the real product without depending on unpredictable external timing. For captions, we went further. The demo pipeline uses real ASR transcripts generated with the same model and segmentation approach as production , then bakes those transcripts into the demo environment. The result is deterministic while still containing genuine transcribed speech , rather than lorem ipsum pretending to be captions. 3. Spotlight Honesty Our earliest tours referenced UI elements that didn't actually exist on the current page. That exposed a fundamental problem with agent-generated walkthroughs: The agent was assuming what the interface looked like. We turned the fix into a core design principle: Discover before you teach. Every walkthrough begins with discover_targets . The tour is then composed against what actually exists. What We Learned The biggest lesson was simple: Agents Don't Need More Autonomy. They Need Better Seats. Once the agent shared the human's: Tools Application state Permissions Audit trail Context the interaction fundamentally changed. It stopped feeling like: "Prompt and pray." And started feeling like genuine teamwork: Proposal → Review → Approval → Execution The guardrails aren't friction. Scoped tool suites, approval cards, permission boundaries, and discover-before-teach aren't there to make the agent weaker. They're what make the agent trustworthy enough to delegate to . That's the direction we believe the agent-native web should move toward: AI agents shouldn't sit outside applications, guessing how to use them. They should have a real seat inside the product with the right tools, the right context, and a human who stays in control. title: MarketPane
pitch: Bring your AI agent along to explore financial products and test your screener ideas.
about_excerpt: Bring your AI agent along to explore financial products and test your screener ideas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 This is our design goal for a grid and widget based editable UX Inspiration MarketPane, is an AI assisted research workbench for doing stock price analysis. Our goal is to build a tool that removes the barriers between an AI and the research canvas, so that a user can spend more time developing their hypothesis, and less time copying charts data back and forth. By putting the tools directly into the hands of an AI, we are basically shortening the iteration loop, allowing you to get to your goal faster. What it does MarketPane is a WebMCP-powered stock screener and research workbench shared between a human and an agent. Either one can define a screener over a universe of instruments (asset class, exchanges, sectors), build a filter tree of typed conditions, set a ranking, and run it to get a pinned, stable set of results. Results land in a panel grid: a results table the agent or the human can inspect, and — via drag-and-drop or a tool call — individual rows become live price charts on the same canvas. Every panel, chart, and result the agent creates is visible and rearrangeable by the human in real time, and vice versa. How we built it The frontend is SvelteKit 5 (SPA) with a browser-side panel/grid system and a workspace document that both the UI and the WebMCP tool layer read and write. WebMCP tools ( define_screener , run_screener , get_screener_results , create_panel , resolve_ticker , search_catalog , get_canvas_state ) operate on that same document, so an agent's actions show up as first-class panel changes instead of hidden side effects. The backend is a FastAPI service (Python, pandas) that evaluates screeners against an OHLCV panel of real market data (EODHD-sourced, object-store backed) and exposes a stateless /api/screener/run endpoint. A typed catalog of fields, operators, and universes keeps every filter condition validated rather than arbitrary code — the agent composes screeners out of known building blocks, it doesn't write expressions the backend has to trust blindly. Challenges we ran into There was a series of challenges that we ran into along the way. Firstly, we ran out of coffee half way through development and had to make an emergency trip to Costco. There were also a number of WebMCP specific challenges that we resolved: The browser was not aware of any WebMCP tools being available and kept trying to use UI elements. The agent has to query a document schema to know that the tools exist, and if it does not suspect them to be there it does not do this. We had to add specific UI elements to notify the agent. The browser did not support the number of tools that we initially created, and blocked them entirely. We had to minimize our implementation. It was very difficult to debug issues with the tools, especially in prod where we don't have all the BE logs handy. This is because issues are not just "bugs" in the app code, but problems with the sequence of actions that the agents take over time. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got a late start on the hackathon and had to build everything very quickly. Our AI enabled development platform has allowed us to achieve the capacity necessary to deliver a POC in time. We managed to add some not-so-simple features, and will continue to expand the feature palette. What we learned Building agentic tools is more than just developing the right workflow and backend scalability. It is also very much about giving the agent the proper awareness and context for the tools that you build. Without clean, self-explainable interfaces, agents will spend extra tokens going on detours or producing errors. What's next for MarketPane Next, we want to widen the live tool surface back toward the fuller design we already built and tested: similarity search ("find setups like this one"), chart annotation and capture, computed fields and custom studies, watchlists, alerts, and backtesting are all implemented behind feature flags today and just need to be wired back into the live composition root. We also want richer chart controls (timeframes, overlays, multi-ticker comparison) and stronger measurement tools so a user can move from spotting a pattern to testing it across cohorts, outcomes, and market regimes.  Inspiration 

 Archbro started as a living system architecture map for understanding components, dependencies, tasks, and project changes. 

 With WebMCP, we realized that map could also become a structured interface for external AI agents — without embedding agents or model-specific APIs inside Archbro. 

 What it does 

 Archbro turns a living system architecture map into a semantic WebMCP workspace. 

 Understand architecture → inspect dependencies → manage tasks → collect evidence → compare reality → recommend changes → human review 
 External AI Agent
 ↓ WebMCP
 Archbro
 ├─ Living Architecture
 │ └─ Dependencies · Tasks · Evidence
 │
 └─ Authorized MCP Bridge
 └─ Connected MCP Services
 (e.g. GitHub)
 
 The Living Architecture provides the shared project context , while connected MCP services extend what the agent can inspect and use. 

 How we built it 

 We mapped Archbro's core concepts into native WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . 

 Instead of exposing clicks and UI actions, we expose semantic engineering operations for architecture, dependencies, tasks, evidence, recommendations, and connected MCP capabilities. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was designing the right WebMCP tool surface . 

 Too few tools force agents to guess. Too many low-level tools simply recreate the UI as an API. 

 We also had to keep the frontend, backend, authentication, persistence, MCP connections, and WebMCP contracts aligned while building quickly as a team. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We turned Archbro's architecture map into a WebMCP-native engineering workspace covering a meaningful end-to-end workflow. 

 External agents can work from the same Living Architecture while important architecture changes still require human review . 

 We also extended WebMCP beyond Archbro itself by allowing agents to use MCP services already authorized by the user . 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when it exposes product meaning instead of UI behavior . 

 We also learned that AI does not always need to live inside the product — the product can provide shared context and capabilities while external agents provide the reasoning. 

 What's next for Archbro-WebMCP 

 We want to expand Archbro's WebMCP surface across more engineering workflows and connect more MCP services — including Miro, Figma, Notion, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Drive, and more . 

 This will let the Living Architecture bring together more of the tools and project context teams already use every day. 

 One living architecture, accessible to humans, agents, and the tools they already use.

pitch: Agent Theater is a WebMCP-powered playground where humans and agents build, perform, and share screenplays together.
about_excerpt: Agent Theater is a WebMCP-powered playground where humans and agents build, perform, and share screenplays together. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Theater – a hilarious agent-human coop Hundreds of characters, props, animations and sounds Dynamic camera controllable by the agent Subtitle system with Gibberish Engine™ Fairytale stories Inbetweens that show the cast One of the many extra tools, a Motion Lab for animating characters One of the many extra tools, the Gibberish Engine Lab Inspiration Hey, we're Marcel and Felix, from Needle. Most of our professional time we build tools for web and 3D. As many others, by now we are heavy agent users. So when WebMCP arrived, we were quite excited! We wanted to see how it could improve workflows between humans and websites, and how we could build tools that get the best of both worlds – the creative touch of a human, paired with the speed and accuracy of an agent. For this hackathon, we first started building a human-agent collage tool. It worked! But also, it wasn't very exciting… Then, with a small twist, it suddenly became fun: We teached the agent to move things around on the stage on its own, and enabled voice mode on the ChatGPT side. And from there, things escalated rather quickly... what started as productivity tool ended up being a full-blown theater stage setup with cast, sound effects, dialogues (yes, with a custom gibberish engine), hand-crafted motion and more. And honestly, that ended up being way cooler! So the unnamed collage tool became Agent Theater, a WebMCP-powered playground where humans and agents build, perform, and share screenplays together. What it does Agent Theater gives the human and the agent access to the stage. Both can place and manipulate characters and props. The agent can actually do more – it can write scripts, set up acts, come up with dialogues on the fly and even perform things in parallel. It can also watch the human, and act accordingly by making adjustments or narrating. Here's what you can do: Build a set from hundreds of stage pieces – or ask ChatGPT to create completely new sets (as efficient spritesheets). Let the agent design and play a show that you can share with the world. Take things into your own hands, and let the agent narrate fantastical stories based on what you're doing. Come up with a story or a draft, and let the agent play it out on stage . Underneath that, there’s quite a lot of interesting tech going on: stages, acts, motion, music, sounds and special effects are driven by the agent in a sort of sequencer there's built-in WebMCP skills for spritesheet generation, storytelling and narration, so you can simply say "ask the page what images it needs" and get perfect spritesheets out. screenplays can be shared by link , or by sharing an image with embedded metadata there's 600+ generated stickers , 100+ generated sounds and infinite combinations to manage this, stickers are created in 5x5 sheets, and sounds are generated locally. Technical specialties save the entire play inside a screenshot, then load it back up later we even made a custom gibberish engine for wonderfully ridiculous dialogue a custom Houdini CSS effect for the stop-motion look even more tools for creating custom motion, effects, and tuning parameters you can find them under /talk and /record How we built it Conceptually, the core idea is simple: We expose functions on the stage and scene through WebMCP, so an agent can interact with the same creative world as its human: placing things, moving characters, triggering actions, narrating scenes and building stories. Around that we built a number of systems, pretty much entirely with Codex and Claude (Felix likes to use Codex, while Marcel is a Claude poem enjoyer). a library of reusable stage pieces generated sprites, audio and custom data per sprite (where it looks, what it is) screenplay and storytelling tools motion, audio and visual-effect systems the gibberish dialogue engine the Houdini-powered handmade animation style screenshot-based save/load for complete plays Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was the somewhat flaky integration of WebMCP into ChatGPT. Some things work with Voice, some not, sometimes the agent forgets what WebMCP is or how to connect. We believe these are mostly side effects of the early days of WebMCP and are excited to see that stabilize. And also, we wanted the agent interactions to feel like play, not like an automation happening. We also had a wonderfully dangerous problem: every time we added one capability, we immediately wanted to ship five silly new things. As evident from the result, the scope was… flexible. Accomplishments that we're proud of We’re especially happy that Agent Theater became something we actually want to play with, and build upon! But there's other things we're proud of: finding interactions that actually feel like doing something together getting the agent to, at the same time, narrate the scene and let characters talk and move the agent reacts to what the user does, so spontaneous changes can turn out quite hilarious all the state is saved with each screenshot, so you can just drop that image later to continue – hidden metadata is always fun the quickly made storytelling and gibberish engines have turned out to be quite nice, and likely very usable for future projects And we’re very glad we made the pivot from the collage tool :). What we learned It was fun to learn how the agents and us interacted, and responded to each other's sometimes rather silly and random ideas. At times, it really felt like two collaborators inside the stage, which was the goal, so it's really cool that we could reach it! We also learned that giving an agent more autonomy doesn’t necessarily mean giving the human less control. The back-and-forth is interesting, and it feels quite different from asking AI to simply generate the finished result. And technically, it was very fun to work on this kind of fast-paced project, and to see new systems – and fun! – emerge from literally nothing in such a short time, is still amazing. What's next for Agent Theater There’s a lot we’d like to keep pushing: more storytelling and performance skills easier sharing and remixing of other people’s plays (a gallery?!) screenplay editing for humans, potentially better motion, music, sound and special effects (though the gibberish engine is already perfect) increasingly strange ways for humans and agents to improvise together win at the Hackathon Built With chatgpt claude codex css houdinipaint html javascript svelte webaudio webmcp Try it out theater.needle.tools github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I made the gibberish engine! title: NetSpectre — Human-Led Cyber Investigation
pitch: A review-first WebMCP workspace where people and AI agents investigate the same evidence while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A review-first WebMCP workspace where people and AI agents investigate the same evidence while humans retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates 1. Human-led investigation workspace with five WebMCP tools ready 2. Step 1: The agent retrieves a structured case briefing 3. Step 2: The agent returns explainable signals from preserved evidence 4. Step 3: The agent creates a reviewable draft finding 5. Step 4: Only the investigator can approve or return the draft 6. Human-approved finding with evidence provenance and agent activity preserved Inspiration Cyber investigations are fragmented across evidence folders, specialist tools, notes, and reports. AI can organise this work, but an investigator still needs to understand what the agent used, why it reached a conclusion, and who authorised the final decision. NetSpectre Challenge Edition explores a safer collaboration model: the person and agent share one visible investigation workspace. The agent can read structured case facts, explain signals, and prepare a finding, while the investigator retains final approval. What it does The demonstration follows a fictional supplier-impersonation and payment-diversion case. NetSpectre exposes five focused WebMCP tools that let an agent: obtain a structured case briefing; list safe metadata for preserved synthetic evidence; retrieve explainable signals above a chosen confidence level; create a reviewable draft finding; and generate an incident summary reflecting the current human-review state. The agent cannot approve its own output. Approval happens through the visible interface, and the activity record identifies whether each action came from the agent or the investigator. Why WebMCP A conventional browser agent must infer meaning from cards, labels, and buttons. WebMCP gives the agent narrow, typed operations tied directly to the live case. Evidence references, confidence thresholds, and review state become explicit instead of depending on visual guesswork. Before this workflow, an investigator might manually copy evidence details into an AI conversation and then copy the response back into a separate case system. That loses provenance and blurs the line between an AI suggestion and an authorised finding. NetSpectre keeps context, evidence, recommendations, and approval state together. How we built it The challenge edition is a standalone TypeScript and React application. It feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool and registers five tools with narrow JSON schemas. Read-only operations are annotated accordingly; the drafting operation declares its side effect and returns an awaiting_human_review state. The WebMCP tools and interface share the same application state, so agent actions are immediately visible to the person. The site also remains usable as a normal web application when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making agent assistance genuinely useful without allowing it to become the decision-maker. We designed a strict draft-and-review boundary, preserved evidence provenance, kept the public challenge edition separate from private NetSpectre code, and used synthetic data throughout. Accomplishments we're proud of A working human-agent investigation rather than a scripted chatbot demo Five discoverable, narrowly scoped WebMCP tools Visible agent activity and preserved evidence references Mandatory human approval for consequential findings A public, reproducible, MIT-licensed challenge repository What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes domain actions, not generic UI automation. Typed tools make the agent more reliable, while shared visible state keeps the person informed and in control. What's next Next we would extend the pattern to multi-case queues, configurable investigation playbooks, exportable audit records, and integrations with authorised security-data sources—without weakening the human approval boundary. Safety and privacy All organisations and evidence are synthetic. The demo opens no arbitrary files, scans no networks or devices, and contains no customer data, production credentials, or private commercial NetSpectre engine code. Challenge work NetSpectre existed previously as a private Windows-first product. This separate browser-based WebMCP edition, its five tools, synthetic case, approval workflow, activity record, deployment, and submission materials were created during the challenge period. The public repository contains only this new challenge work. Built With chatgpt javascript openai-sites react typescript vinext vite webmcp Try it out netspectre-webmcp.stuhall44.chatgpt.site github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived and led NetSpectre’s human-led cyber-investigation workflow, product direction, safety boundaries, interface, and submission. During the challenge, I created and tested the separate browser-based WebMCP edition with five typed tools, synthetic evidence, shared human-agent state, mandatory investigator approval, and a visible activity record. I also prepared the public repository, deployment, documentation, demonstration video, and submission materials with assistance from OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT. title: ForgeMCP-Multi-Agent Research & Game Studio
pitch: Humans and AI agents use real WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test Cube Chess 512 AI, create 3D systems, verify evidence, and keep final decisions human-controlled.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents use real WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test Cube Chess 512 AI, create 3D systems, verify evidence, and keep final decisions human-controlled. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ForgeMCP — Multi-Agent Research & Game Studio ForgeMCP is an agent-native web platform where people and AI agents use real browser-native WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test a deterministic 8×8×8 chess engine, create verifiable 3D systems, and keep consequential decisions under human control. Core workflow HUMAN → COORDINATOR → SPECIALIST AGENTS → WEBMCP TOOLS → REAL DATA / ENGINE → VERIFICATION → HUMAN DECISION What it does ForgeMCP brings three working systems into one visible, auditable workflow: OBSERVE — Terra Observation System A user can select or search for an area of interest and investigate environmental change using public Earth-observation sources. Terra can retrieve location context, bounded research areas, representative satellite imagery, terrain/elevation context, hydrology signals and public hazard observations. Results return structured provenance, timestamps, confidence, uncertainty and a verification state. Terra never presents an AI-generated picture as satellite evidence. Missing or failed provider responses remain INSUFFICIENT_DATA or NOT_CONNECTED . Observations, anomalies, hypotheses, preliminary risk alerts and verified findings are kept separate. A hypothesis is not promoted to a fact without supporting evidence and, where required, field or in-situ verification. LEARN & COMPETE — Cube Chess 512 AI Cube Chess 512 is a deterministic three-dimensional chess laboratory with an 8×8×8 board and 512 addressable fields. ForgeMCP uses a pinned rules engine to execute a small candidate-versus-baseline benchmark with paired seeds and side swaps. The records contain replayable legal moves, results, termination state, legality checks, a deterministic material proxy and engine provenance. The application does not invent Elo ratings, game counts or training results. A candidate cannot be promoted merely because an agent recommends it: legality and regression gates must pass, a recorded result must exist, and literal human approval is required. CREATE — Game and 3D Creation Studio The Game Studio lets a person and agents configure procedural station concepts, generate deterministic low-poly glTF assets and PNG textures, inspect the exact generated geometry, compare visible results, run QA and export a manifest. It also includes a deterministic basic Capture Chess blueprint and a separate link to the playable Cube Chess 512 deployment. Concept artwork is labelled as concept artwork. A generated prototype is not described as manufactured hardware, an original satellite product or a production-ready model. How we built it The public application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and browser-based 3D rendering. Real tools are registered through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a focused responsibility, a validated input schema, structured output, explicit error states and a traceable source or engine boundary. The coordinator is deterministic and does not claim that an LLM ran when it did not. The live tool inventory covers system status, place and AOI handling, Terra observation and verification workflows, the pinned Cube benchmark and promotion gates, visual QA, reversible actions and guarded commerce drafts. Chrome 149+ smoke tests discover and execute the native WebMCP tools in a real browser session instead of mocking document.modelContext . The dashboard exposes the human request, coordinator decision, active specialist, WebMCP tool, validated input, real source or engine, structured output, provenance, confidence, uncertainty, verification result, proposed action and human approval state. The hardest challenges The hardest problem was not adding more AI. It was defining where AI must stop. For Terra, the authority must be the original observation, provider metadata, measurement method and verification record. For Cube, the authority must be the deterministic rules engine, legal execution and saved game result. For mutations, the authority remains the human. A second challenge was integrating two projects that existed before the competition without presenting older work as new. The public repository therefore separates: PRE-CHALLENGE WORK: earlier Terra data integrations, Earth-observation research, Cube rules engine, self-play experiments, 3D models and game UI. NEW WEBMCP CHALLENGE WORK: ForgeMCP coordinator, browser-native tool registration, integrated Terra/Cube/Create workflows, structured provenance, verification timeline, approval gates, public dashboard, judge path and demo. A third challenge was making failures honest and visible. A provider timeout, missing image, unconnected service or unsupported browser must not quietly become a fabricated answer. Accomplishments we are proud of A public working web application with real document.modelContext.registerTool(...) handlers. Fifty registered central tools discoverable through the live capability inventory. Terra workflows grounded in public providers with provenance, uncertainty and strict evidence classes. A pinned deterministic Cube engine that executes the current-run benchmark and rejects illegal promotion paths. Real-browser Chrome 149+ WebMCP smoke testing. Visible PASS / WARNING / FAIL states, audit history, human approval and rollback boundaries. A free judge path with public source code, an open-source license, run instructions and a short demonstration video. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it lets a person and an agent operate a real application together, not when it merely adds another chat box. Small, single-purpose tools are easier to validate and audit than one oversized agent action. Structured results are safer than persuasive prose. Provenance and uncertainty must be visible at the same time as the result. Most importantly, an agent can coordinate and propose, but evidence, deterministic engines and human judgment must remain the final authorities. Why it matters My long-term goal is to use technology to help people and protect the environment. Terra approaches that goal through earlier investigation of water loss, rivers, lakes, terrain and environmental hazards. Cube Chess 512 approaches it through logic, spatial reasoning, competition and learning. The Creation Studio provides a practical space for turning ideas into testable visual systems. ForgeMCP connects those directions around one principle: AI should help humans observe, learn, create and verify — while real evidence and human decisions stay in control. What is next The next steps are to expand the audited Terra tool coverage, strengthen browser and regression testing, connect additional verified data adapters, run larger reproducible Cube candidate evaluations, improve accessibility and mobile performance, and keep every new mutation behind explicit approval, audit logging and rollback. The project will continue separating observations from hypotheses and challenge-period work from earlier research. The aim is not to claim certainty where it does not exist, but to help people reach better, faster and more transparent decisions with real tools. title: Archflow
pitch: A collaborative educational tool to learn system design
about_excerpt: A collaborative educational tool to learn system design Like Comment Story Updates The studio The simulation with the result Agent modifying the canvas on the web app using web MCP end points Testing whether a specific system design solution scales with the help of the agent and websit And finally the fix Finding bottleneck Inspiration System design interviews still happen on a whiteboard. You draw boxes, a senior engineer pokes holes, and you learn by defending the sketch under load. We wanted that loop in a tab . Archflow is the whiteboard. The agent is the senior — or the teacher — who can read the same diagram, ask about the box you just clicked, suggest a cache, and say “run it again.” Web MCP becomes a perfect fit here because the agent with its vast knowledge can view the whiteboard that you are using and guide you when needed. By exposing the whiteboard along with the capability to edit it, you have the perfect sparring partner while learning system design. Not a chatbot next to a picture. A practice studio for the interview: you sketch, they guide, the SLO keeps score. What it does You pick a use case (URL shortener, news feed, realtime chat, video streaming). Each one drops you into a naive first sketch that misses its SLO — the same kind of incomplete design an interviewer might start you from. Drag blocks like a whiteboard: clients, CDNs, APIs, caches, queues, databases. Hit Run . Traffic walks the graph. Overflow becomes errors; p99 is the hottest sync path; robustness is $0$–$100$. Ask the agent to play senior: “What’s wrong with this shortener?” or “Help me pass the SLO without exploding cost.” It uses WebMCP tools on the live canvas ( get_architecture , get_selected_node , connect , run_simulation , …) so guidance shows up as rewires and a second run — not a paragraph of advice you have to copy by hand. Change the graph, run again. The inspector tells you if the design got better or worse — the same feedback a good interviewer gives, with numbers. How we built it Next.js, React Flow, Zustand, usewebmcp . No backend: the tab is the session , like a physical whiteboard that happens to simulate. Archflow registers 16 WebMCP tools on the page. Read • get_architecture — Current graph: challenge, node ids, edges, call trees, last simulation. • get_catalog — Block types you can add, default capacity, and connection rules. • get_selected_node — The block the human has selected, what it means, neighbors, and last-run stats. • get_robustness — Last run’s robustness score (0–100) and whether the latest change helped or hurt. • get_simulation — Last run: utilization, p99, errors, bottlenecks, SLO, robustness, and delta. • list_challenges — The four system-design use cases. Change the board • load_challenge — Reset the canvas to a starter sketch (url-shortener, news-feed, realtime-chat, video-streaming). • add_node — Add a block; optional id, label, and nearId for placement. • connect — Connect two blocks left-to-right (queue inbound defaults to async). • disconnect — Remove the edge between two blocks. • set_node_props — Change replicas, RPS capacity, cache hit rate, or lock a node. • annotate_node — Pin a finding on a block so it shows on the graph. • remove_node — Remove a block and its edges (asks the human to confirm). • repair_graph — Drop dangling edges and broken/unknown blocks so the graph can run. • run_simulation — Push traffic through the graph, animate packets, and score the SLO. Batch • apply_plan — Apply a list of ops in order (add_node, connect, disconnect, set_node_props, remove_node) after one confirmation. What we learned The agent is useful as a teacher only if it shares the board. Taking a screenshot and pasting every time you want to show the agent that something has changed is painful. Web MCP becomes a perfect fit in such situations since the agent gets first hand view of what is happening without the user having to intervene. Challenges Identifying what are the key capabilities to be exposed as web MCP end points required some serious thinking. title: EasyFloww
pitch: Drag and drop flow chart builder with built in WebMCP support.
about_excerpt:
Drag and drop flow chart builder with built in WebMCP support.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP powered flow chart builder 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP powered flow chart builder 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP powered flow chart builder 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I was thinking about a practical useful tool that makes someones life a little better with WebMCP and that is when I decided to build this flowchart builder app (EasyFloww). It demonstrate WebMCP capabilities in a practical and visually engaging way so more people can understand it and explore. 

 What it does 

 EasyFloww is a drag and drop flowchart builder, it lets users create diagrams easily and share and editable as well as non editable version with anyone easily. With built in WebMCP support and no vendor lock in, any ai model with tool calling capabilities will be able to create flowchart seamlessly. 

 What makes this app special is that an AI agent and a user can work on the canvas together to create diagrams and collaborate in real time. 

 The data is stored in localstorage and never leaves your system, which tighten the security. 

 How we built it 

 I used AI as a companion to plan and develop the application. React and TypeScript is the technologies along with the npm package xyflow which power this application. 

 The app exposes actions as tools using webmcp. We have built and registered 10 tools.
get_flow_state: returns the current nodes and edges (with type, label, config, position, and connected handles) for the active flow
add_node: adds a new node of a given type, label, and optional position
connect_nodes: connects two nodes by ID, with an optional sourceHandle for decision branches.
move_node: repositions an existing node by ID
update_node_config: updates a node's label/condition/description/borderColor
delete_node: removes a node (and its connected edges)
insert_node_between: splits an existing edge to insert a new node directly between two connected nodes
remove_edge: disconnects two nodes by removing a specific edge
clone_flow: duplicates a flow (active or specified) into a new independent tab
import_flow: creates an entire new flow in one call from a complete node/edge JSON graph, with validation 

 Every tool calls the exact same Zustand store functions that the UI itself uses, addNode, moveNode, addEdge, updateNodeConfig etc. There's no separate path for the AI agent through the code, a tool call and a mouse drag both end up mutating the same store the same way. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was to design the architecture of the project in a way that makes the agent-human collaboration foolproof - meaning a human and an agent editing the same live canvas should never produce corruption, silently divergent data, lost work, or ambiguity about who changed what. 

 The design decisions that highlight the actions an agent is performing in the canvas was another challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The end product came out really well and useful, anyone who is looking for an AI support flowchart builder can use this product. 

 I am proud about the fact that I got a deeper understanding about the latest features of the web and got hands on experience in it. I am really proud of it. 

 What we learned 

 I got a pretty solid understanding about the WebMCP protocol and got really confident in implementing it in my future projects. 

 What's next for EasyFloww 

 Most diagram tools lock you into their own built in AI assistant. If you want AI help, you use their model, in their chat box, on their terms. EasyFlow is here to change that, to provide a better experience for the end user to use the AI models they are comfortable with and to create complex diagrams seamlessly. 

 We want to provide the user at most security and privacy possible so that their data belongs to them and not any servers.

title: Holy tool for uni students
pitch: WebMCP-powered course planning: build a conflict-free schedule, balance your workload, and track graduation requirements all through conversation, with enrollment always under your control.
about_excerpt: WebMCP-powered course planning: build a conflict-free schedule, balance your workload, and track graduation requirements all through conversation, with enrollment always under your control. Like Comment Story Updates Check your degree audit Plan schedule for semester Adjust your schedule with ease Inspiration Let's be honest, we all have gone through the time of choosing courses for school. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of courses available in my school - Bucknell University. Scrolling through tabs just to find 4-5 courses that suit us must feel like hell. Therefore, I created this holy tool to assist us in choosing the best courses for us. What it does Imagine you're a robot that can actually click buttons on a student's screen instead of just yapping about what buttons they should click. That's basically what this is. You type something like: "Plan my next semester: max 15 credits, nothing before 10am, prioritize AI and cybersecurity" and the AI reads your actual transcript, cross-checks prerequisites, confirms there are seats open, and builds you a conflict-free draft schedule. No tabs, no spreadsheets, no prayers to the registration gods. And because professors matter (let's be real), you can tell it "I hate CS320, it's brutal" and instead of rebuilding the whole thing from scratch like some kind of masochist, it just swaps that one course for alternatives and tells you the trade-offs. The whole app is visible as you talk: a course catalog you can filter, a weekly timetable that shows both your actual schedule (solid blocks) and proposed courses, a transcript, and a degree audit that tells you exactly what you're missing before graduation. Draft courses wear a big blue banner that screams no seats held, you haven't committed to anything so you never accidentally think you're registered when you're not. How I built it JavaScript. All of it. HTML for the page, CSS so it doesn't look like a 1997 geocities site, and the brain of the thing lives in a standalone file so it could be tested without mocking the entire DOM. Then I wired up 13 tools via WebMCP: search courses, check if you're eligible, build a schedule, swap one course, explain what a course does to your graduation timeline, handle registrations, join waitlists. The AI calls these tools; the tools update the page you're looking at; you see the results instantly and decide whether to confirm or bail. It all runs in the browser. No backend. No database. Just sample student data and a 22-course Bucknell catalog baked into the JavaScript, so the demo works anywhere without authentication headaches. I use Vercel to upload it and push my project on Github. Challenges I ran into The Draft vs. Registered blurry line : A timetable showing five proposed courses looks exactly like a registered schedule if you're not careful. I solved this by slapping a warning banner on drafts ("no seats held"), color-coding the timetable blocks differently (solid orange = real, dashed blue = proposed), and keeping separate credit counters ("6 of 15 registered · 9 in draft"). Students should never have to guess. Small changes breaking the whole plan : Traditional schedulers rebuild everything when you tweak one thing. That's sucks .So I built a "replace one course" tool that keeps the other four courses exactly as they are, shows you alternatives ranked by how well they fit your goals, and explains the specific trade-offs. "This swap is 8 hours lighter per week but drops a team project from the term." That's useful. Credits lie : "15 credits" sounds light until you realize it's 52 hours a week of work if you hit CS320 (the hardest course I seeded). So every course now carries a weekly workload estimate, a project count, and a workload band (light / moderate / heavy). Proposing a schedule without showing this is just being mean to the student. Accomplishments that I am proud of I built an end-to-end workflow where a student and an AI do something neither could alone: review degree progress, propose a schedule that respects constraints and interests, explore alternatives, swap one course intelligently, then register after the student clicks a confirmation button. The AI doesn't fake-click anything. Instead, it calls structured tools that update the real page. I also made recommendations actually useful by connecting three things that usually live in separate tabs: scheduling, workload, and graduation requirements. When the AI suggests a course, it tells you why (elective vs. required), how much time it costs, and what graduation requirement it closes. And I made the invisible visible. There's an activity log timestamping every action and crediting it to either the student or the advisor. You always know who did what and when. What I learned Academic advice is complicated : Just matching a student's interests to course descriptions is useless. You need to fold in prerequisites, seat availability, time conflicts, workload, degree requirements, and what happens downstream if you defer a course. A good recommendation juggles all of these at once. State must be bulletproof : Students hate ambiguity. "Is this registered or just a proposal?" "Does deferring this course block me next term?" These questions need crystal-clear answers, baked into the UI, not buried in a chatbot transcript. I learned this the hard way when I first tested with the page. Structured tools > vague chat : A chatbot can describe what a student should do. WebMCP tools let an AI actually do it —and because the tools are typed and validate input, the AI is less likely to hallucinate or contradict itself. Honesty about limits : Workload estimates are imperfect. Graduation timelines are projections. Our UI shows these as estimates and projections, not guarantees. If you're going to let an AI influence a student's academic path, you have to be clear about what you actually know. What's next Ideally, I'd swap a course and lock in its replacement as a single transaction, so you're never in limbo holding a draft. I'd also validate workload estimates against historical student feedback (if a university had that data). Multi-semester planning would help students see the full path to graduation, not just the next term. Longer term, real integration with a university's enrollment system (with proper auth, privacy safeguards, and audit trails) would make this a genuine advising tool instead of a demo. Right now, this is a prototype with sample data. title: DiscountHub WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP-powered deal discovery layer that lets AI agents search live discounts, promo codes, and store offers directly from DiscountHub.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered deal discovery layer that lets AI agents search live discounts, promo codes, and store offers directly from DiscountHub. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP in action: a browser agent finds offers and displays the same results for the shopper. DiscountHub brings product deals, promo codes, and store offers into one place. Browse product deals with filters for country, store, category, and minimum discount. Find store promotions and coupon codes, review their conditions, and copy a code. DiscountHub's own AI Finder: laptop search results with prices and links to the stores. Inspiration Finding a useful deal should take less effort than comparing dozens of browser tabs. I built DiscountHub to bring product discounts, promo codes, and store offers into one place. For this challenge, I wanted browser agents to use that catalogue directly, while keeping shoppers involved in every decision. What it does DiscountHub WebMCP gives compatible browser agents four tools: search_deals — search product discounts with optional filters. find_promo_codes — find coupon codes and their available conditions. get_store_offers — retrieve a store's product discounts and promotions. get_best_deals — find the largest percentage discounts. Agents receive structured results, and the same offers appear on the website using DiscountHub's existing cards. A shopper can review prices, compare offers, copy a coupon, and choose which store link to open. The tools support relevant filters such as keywords, country, store, price, and minimum discount. Prices and budgets are in USD. Coupon codes come from the catalogue; they are not verified at checkout. Why WebMCP Shopping requests combine several constraints: what someone wants, their budget, and the market they are shopping in. WebMCP gives the browser agent explicit tools and input schemas for these requests. The agent can retrieve structured offer data without extracting it from page layouts. The visible result matters just as much: people can inspect the offers returned by the agent and continue browsing from the same page. Tool calls search the catalogue; shoppers decide whether to visit a store. How I built it Existing foundation: DiscountHub already had a public website, a Flutter application, a Python/FastAPI backend, a SQLite catalogue, automated offer processing, and its own AI Finder. New work for this challenge: I added native WebMCP registration, four tool definitions, validated inputs, structured responses, and shared on-page results. The implementation uses document.modelContext where available, with support for the earlier navigator.modelContext API. The JavaScript adapter reuses the existing public deals and promotions endpoints. It handles pagination, timeouts, cancellation, and partial failures. It excludes expired or future-dated offers and coupons without codes. Older requests cannot overwrite newer visible results. The website and WebMCP integration live in a separate repository from the backend and mobile application. Both repositories include MIT licenses. The WebMCP implementation and dated commit history document the challenge addition. Challenges The main challenge was making tool results dependable across browser API differences and changing catalogue data. Testing required both native tool execution in Chrome and checks against the live API. I also needed to preserve the familiar browsing experience while making agent results visible and understandable. Accomplishments All four tools were exercised through native browser execution. In the recorded live demo, Gemini uses Chrome's Model Context Tool Inspector to call search_deals for three headphone offers in the United States, under fifty dollars, with at least twenty percent off. Three offers appear on the page, giving the shopper and the agent a shared view of the results. What I learned A useful agent integration needs clear tool boundaries and visible outcomes. Structured data helps the agent act reliably; shared results help the person understand and evaluate what happened. What's next I plan to improve multilingual catalogue search, add clearer country and availability information, and make it easier to refine and compare an agent's results. For this challenge, I added four native WebMCP tools that connect browser agents to the live catalogue and display their results on the website. I handled deployment, browser testing, and demo recording and editing. I used AI assistance for coding, debugging, documentation, and English narration. pitch: An AI-agent-ready study planner where students and AI work together.

An AI-agent-ready study planner where students and AI work together.

 Inspiration 

 As students, managing assignments, revision, practice, and deadlines can quickly become overwhelming. Most study planners are designed primarily for humans to interact with through buttons and forms, but we wanted to explore a different approach: what if an AI agent could work with the same study planner alongside the student? 

 This idea led us to build StudyPilot, a study planner designed from the beginning to support both human users and AI agents. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave us the opportunity to explore how websites can expose structured capabilities to AI agents instead of forcing agents to rely only on traditional UI interaction. 

 What it does 

 StudyPilot is an AI-agent-ready study planner that lets students organize and manage their academic tasks. 

 Through the normal web interface, students can: 

 Add study tasks with subjects, priorities, dates, and estimated time
View their study tasks
Mark tasks as completed
Delete tasks
Generate a prioritized study plan 

 The same functionality is also exposed through WebMCP tools, allowing compatible AI agents to interact with the application programmatically. 

 StudyPilot currently provides five WebMCP tools: 

 add_study_task
get_study_tasks
complete_study_task
delete_study_task
generate_study_plan 

 This creates a simple human + AI collaboration model where the student can use the interface directly while an AI agent can use structured tools to help manage their study workflow. 

 How we built it 

 We built StudyPilot as a lightweight web application using: 

 HTML — application structure
CSS — responsive interface and visual design
JavaScript — application logic and task management
WebMCP — exposing StudyPilot functionality to AI agents
LocalStorage — persistent task data in the browser 

 The application uses WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool API to register the five tools. 

 We designed each tool with clear inputs and outputs so that an AI agent can understand what the tool does and interact with StudyPilot without needing to manually navigate the UI. 

 We also deployed the application publicly so the project can be tested as a live web application. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was understanding how to design a normal web application while also making its functionality accessible to AI agents. 

 We had to think beyond traditional button-based interactions and define structured tools, parameters, and tool responses that an agent could reliably understand. 

 Another challenge was making sure that actions performed through WebMCP stayed synchronized with the user interface and persisted correctly using LocalStorage. 

 We also had to test each WebMCP tool individually and fix issues such as parameter naming and ensuring the tools were correctly registered and discoverable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that we turned a simple study planner into an application that can be used by both humans and AI agents. 

 Some accomplishments we're particularly proud of: 

 Built and deployed a complete working study planner
Implemented five functional WebMCP tools
Made the same underlying study data accessible through both the UI and WebMCP
Added persistent task storage using LocalStorage
Implemented automatic prioritized study-plan generation
Tested all WebMCP tools successfully
Created a public live demo and open-source repository 

 Most importantly, StudyPilot helped us move from simply building a website to thinking about how websites can become usable interfaces for AI agents. 

 What we learned 

 This project taught us that building for AI agents requires a different way of thinking about web applications. 

 Instead of only asking "What buttons should the user click?", we also had to ask: 

 "What capabilities should an AI agent be able to discover and use?" 

 We learned how WebMCP tools can expose specific application capabilities in a structured way and how human interfaces and agent interfaces can coexist within the same application. 

 We also gained practical experience with JavaScript, browser storage, tool registration, debugging, deployment, and testing an AI-agent-ready web application. 

 What's next for StudyPilot 

 StudyPilot is currently a lightweight prototype, but we see several possibilities for expanding it. 

 Future versions could include: 

 AI-powered personalized study recommendations
Automatic task creation from assignments or syllabi
Calendar and reminder integration
Progress tracking and analytics
Cloud synchronization across devices
More advanced AI-agent workflows
Collaboration between students and AI agents for long-term study planning 

 Our long-term goal is to make StudyPilot more than just a task manager — a study companion where students stay in control while AI helps them plan, organize, and execute their learning goals.

title: CO Draft WebMCP
pitch: A shared board where humans and AI agents collaborate using WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A shared board where humans and AI agents collaborate using WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 The future of human-AI collaboration doesn't require separate APIs, authentication layers or complex backend services. WebMCP proves that when an agent and a human interact with the same code on the same page, magic happens, they see each other's changes in real-time, build together and trust is transparent. 

 What it does 

 Co-Draft is a shared task board where humans and AI agents collaborate in real-time. You add notes via a form (like a human), and at the exact same time, an AI agent can add, remove or list notes using WebMCP tools. Same functions. Same state. Same page. No API keys, no backend complexity, no session management, just a webpage that exposes JS functions as tools that both humans and agents can call. 

 How I built it 

 
 Core app: Plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, deployed to Vercel 
 State management: Single array (cards) held in browser memory 
 WebMCP registration: document.modelContext.registerTool() wraps the four functions (addCard, removeCard, listCards, clearBoard) 
 UI binding: The same addCard() that the form button calls is what the agent tool invokes, one function, two callers 
 Styling: Gradient design, responsive layout, CSS pseudo-classes for live agent-interaction feedback 
 Deployment: Vercel for instant hosting, GitHub for version control 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 WebMCP browser support: Chrome 149+ has native support; older browsers need the extension. I added feature detection so the app degrades gracefully. 
 State persistence: Browser memory clears on refresh. I decided to keep it simple for the MVP, but documented how to add Firebase/Supabase for real persistence. 
 Testing without desktop: Building on a tablet meant we couldn't easily test the full WebMCP inspector. I solved this by verifying tools register correctly in the console, then tested the human UI thoroughly. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 
 Excellent documentation: Comprehensive README with API docs, extension ideas, troubleshooting and examples so others can fork and build on this. 
 Mobile-first: Built entirely on a Samsung tablet, responsive design works on any screen size. 
 Proof of concept: I proved that WebMCP isn't just theory, a human and an agent can truly collaborate on the same live interface with zero backend. 
 

 What I learned 

 
 WebMCP is a paradigm shift: Traditional APIs separate human UI from agent access. WebMCP unifies them, the same page, same code, one state. 
 Transparency builds trust: When an agent action updates the UI you're looking at, you don't need to check logs or JSON responses. You see it happen. 
 Simplicity scales: I started with one function (addCard). By the end, I had four tools, beautiful styling, error handling and input validation, all because I kept the core idea simple. 
 

 What's next for CO Draft WebMCP 

 
 Persistent backend: Integrate Firebase or Supabase so notes survive page refreshes and sync across devices. 
 Rich media: Extend cards to support images, links, embeds, agents can describe what to add, humans review.
