title: Verb - Sight off. Voice on
pitch: Chat by intent, not by sight
about_excerpt: Chat by intent, not by sight Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Close your eyes and try to catch up on your messages. A screen reader gets you there, but it turns a ten-second task into a navigation exercise: find the unread thread, find the right control, react to the right message, figure out what's in the photo everyone is laughing about. Browser agents were supposed to help, but they still look at the screen and guess where to click — fragile, slow, and easily misled by page content. WebMCP flips that: the page names its own actions. And messaging is the perfect fit, because messaging is made of verbs — send, react, reply, summarize. Name the verbs, and nobody needs sight to use them. Nouns need eyes. Verbs need a voice. What it does Verb is a complete real-time messenger — 1:1 and group chats, reactions, stickers, image and file attachments, editing, unsend, drafts, search, typing and seen states — where every meaningful action is also a typed WebMCP tool: 22 in a signed-in session . So a blind or low-vision user can simply say what they want: "What did I miss?" → the agent lists, reads, and summarizes the conversation "Reply that Friday works." → draft_message saves it, the user reviews, send_message sends "What's in the photo?" → describe_image runs a vision model on the authorized file "Start a group with Maya and Tony." → people resolved, group created in one request The human chooses the goal, the agent composes tools, and the app stays the authority. Destructive actions (unsend, leave a group) require a second call with confirm: true . There's even a public sign_up tool that creates a passkey-only account : the agent collects a name and email, but the human completes the browser's own WebAuthn prompt. No password ever exists. How we implemented WebMCP Verb talks to the browser's document.modelContext API directly — no wrapper library. The lifecycle is session-aware. A connection provider owns registration end to end. Signed out, the page exposes just two public tools: get_connection_status and sign_up . The moment a Supabase session appears, it registers the 21-tool authenticated catalog; the moment the session changes or ends, an AbortController tears everything down — an agent can never call tools that belong to a previous user. const controller = new AbortController(); await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "get_connection_status", description: "Report whether the page is signed in and agent tools are connected.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: false }, execute: async () => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(connectionState) }], }), }, { signal: controller.signal } // sign-out → abort → tool gone ); Every call flows through the same pipeline: Human voice or text → agent chooses a registered tool → Verb validates the input in the page → the signed-in user's Supabase session executes it → Postgres row-level security authorizes the operation → a small structured result returns to the agent and the activity panel The catalog: 22 tools in an authenticated session , one file per tool, each with a focused description, a strict JSON schema ( additionalProperties: false ), and behavioral annotations so agents know what is safe to call: Discover — list_conversations , read_conversation , search_messages , search_people , get_my_profile Navigate — open_conversation , start_conversation Compose — draft_message , send_message , edit_message , delete_message , react_to_message , send_sticker Organize — create_group , delete_conversation Understand — summarize_conversation , describe_image , read_file , read_link Connection & account — get_connection_status , setup_passkey , sign_out (+ public sign_up , signed-out only) Rules enforced across the whole catalog: Reads are honest: read-only tools carry readOnlyHint: true , so agents can explore freely Writes are deliberate: composing and sending are separate tools; unsend and leave-group require a second call with confirm: true Other people's words are untrusted: message bodies are wrapped as labeled untrusted content before they reach the agent, so injected text stays data Results are bounded: a shared clamp keeps every tool response within a 1,500-character budget How we built it App: Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS WebMCP: document.modelContext directly. A connection provider registers two public tools while signed out, swaps in the 21-tool authenticated catalog on sign-in, and tears everything down with an AbortSignal when the session changes. One file per tool: focused description, JSON schema, behavioral annotations, execute . Authority: Supabase Postgres with row-level security. Tools run on the signed-in user's browser session — the database decides what's allowed, never the agent. Realtime: database-triggered broadcasts on conversation and per-user topics Files: private storage buckets with signed URLs AI: configurable Anthropic / Gemini / OpenAI provider for summaries and image descriptions Testing: Vitest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end accessibility specs Challenges we ran into Building on a brand-new spec. WebMCP lives behind a Chrome flag with thin documentation, so every design decision was tested against real agents, not just the docs. Tool lifecycle. Tools from a signed-out session must not survive. Abort-based cleanup on every session change took real care to get right. Prompt injection. Message bodies are written by other people — attacker-controlled by definition. We wrap them as labeled untrusted content and clamp every tool result to a 1,500-character budget so injected text stays data, not instructions. Safe without being annoying. Agents that confirm everything are useless; agents that confirm nothing are dangerous. The draft-then-send split and two-call confirmation pattern was our answer: composition is cheap, execution is deliberate. Passkeys are picky. Origin and RP ID must agree exactly, so we made the production build verify its own WebAuthn config and refuse to ship a broken one. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real messenger , not a demo — realtime, groups, files, reactions — fully drivable by voice through an agent Account creation where the agent never touches a secret : passkey-only sign-up completed by the human A trust model where the agent holds no keys: session-scoped tools, RLS as the enforcement layer, untrusted content labeled at the boundary Accessibility on both paths: the visual UI is keyboard- and screen-reader-conscious, and the agent path removes the need for sight entirely What we learned Tool descriptions are UX. Agents read schemas the way users read buttons — a vague description produces a wrong click, just invisibly. The page should be the authority. Once the app validates everything and the database enforces access, you can hand an agent real power without handing it trust. Separating composition from execution preserves human control — the draft-then-send pattern felt like a workaround and turned out to be the design. Accessibility and agent-readiness are the same work. Semantic actions help a screen-reader user and an AI agent for the same reason: both need meaning, not pixels. What's next for Verb - Sight off. Voice on More verbs: scheduled send, pinning, cross-conversation search, a "morning digest" tool that recaps every unread thread at once Voice-first onboarding so the very first session never needs a screen Adopting elicitation and richer annotations as the WebMCP spec evolves Extracting our lifecycle + safety patterns (abort-scoped registration, untrusted-content wrapping, confirm-twice writes) into a small open-source library, so any web app can add its verbs Built With chatgpt css liveperson-agent typescript webmcp Try it out github.com verb-webmcp.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Tony Nguyen Tony Nguyen A figuring-it-out person Hung Truong Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Hung Truong started this project — Sep 03, 2026 10:47 PM EDT

title: TheraFlow: Ethical Clinical & Behavioral WebMCP Agent
pitch: An ethical, browser-native clinical workspace empowering AI agents to dynamically generate interactive CBT exercises, grounding tools, and deterministic crisis guardrails via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
An ethical, browser-native clinical workspace empowering AI agents to dynamically generate interactive CBT exercises, grounding tools, and deterministic crisis guardrails via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Inspiration 

 In clinical mental health practice, interactive tools like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) thought records, pacing routines, and behavioral activation logs are essential for patient engagement. However, browser AI agents typically rely on brittle DOM scraping or simulated mouse clicks. We built TheraFlow / MindBridge to explore how the new WebMCP client-side standard enables AI agents to dynamically generate, scaffold, and adapt interactive clinical interventions with zero DOM scraping, backed by deterministic crisis circuit breakers. 

 What It Does 

 TheraFlow turns a web workspace into an agent-executable clinical environment: 

 
 Interactive Tool Registration: Registers structured tools ( generate_cbt_thought_record , build_pacing_grounding_exercise , trigger_crisis_containment ) directly via document.modelContext.registerTool . 
 Dynamic DOM Scaffolding: Agents pass structured clinical parameters to render interactive tables and visual grounding animations. 
 Deterministic Safety Overrides: If acute distress signals are evaluated, the agent triggers an immediate client-side containment sequence that locks the active workspace and presents verified support lifelines. 
 Non-Repudiable Audit Telemetry: Every tool invocation and safety state transition writes to an on-screen runtime telemetry log. 
 

 How We Built It 

 
 Client-Side Architecture: Pure JavaScript, semantic HTML5, and CSS3 designed for zero-latency execution. 
 WebMCP Standard: Implements document.modelContext tool declarations with input validation, schema descriptions, and client-side sanitization. 
 Deployment: Hosted directly on GitHub Pages with MIT licensing. 
 

 Challenges We Overcame 

 Balancing open agent interaction with strict ethical boundaries required implementing deterministic safety containment. We ensured that clinical safety overrides always take precedence over generative outputs. 

 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 Fully functional WebMCP registration working natively in Chrome. 
 Smooth 4-7-8 visual pacing animation that adjusts pacing dynamically. 
 A clear telemetry logging interface that makes agent tool calls visible in real time.
*Assisting clinicians provide easier and safer assignments and instructions to clients. 
 

 What We Learned 

 WebMCP makes human-agent collaboration in web apps far more robust and predictable than traditional screen-reading and UI simulation. Dynamic AI helps clinicians like me use AI more ethically and safely. 

 What's next for TheraFlow: Ethical Clinical WebMCP Agent 

 The future is open, and hopefully we can provide more resources and support both for clients and management for the private practice clinician or organization.

title: Weople
pitch: Weople is relationship intelligence. It connects context, commitments, and opportunities to surface the right person at the right moment. Human judgment stays in control.
about_excerpt: Weople is relationship intelligence. It connects context, commitments, and opportunities to surface the right person at the right moment. Human judgment stays in control. Like Comment Story Updates Weople started from a simple problem: relationships rarely weaken because people stop caring. They weaken because people, commitments, context, and opportunities fall out of working attention. I wanted something different from a CRM. A CRM manages contacts and records activity. Weople is built for relationship intelligence: helping someone notice the right person at the right moment. The broader idea predates the WebMCP Challenge, but the challenge gave me a reason to turn it into a focused, working vertical slice. The question I wanted to answer: What changes when an agent can reason over the same relationship context a person is using, instead of merely looking at a webpage? That became the challenge version of Weople. What Weople does Weople maintains structured relationship context: people, commitments, upcoming moments, evidence, hypotheses, and relationship policies. In the demo, the user asks ChatGPT: What am I missing today? If something is genuinely worth my attention, add it to my Weople Today view. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT reads the structured context and notices a connection Weople had not precomputed: Maya has an upcoming working session. I still have an unresolved promise to introduce her to someone with relevant experience. Maya's company announced an expansion. That expansion may create scaling pressure, but that's an inference, not a confirmed fact. Carlos recently worked through a similar scaling problem. ChatGPT connects those pieces and creates a timely intervention directly inside the live Weople workspace. The point isn't remembering information. It's surfacing a connection that would otherwise go unnoticed. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit for Weople because the important information isn't always what's visible on the screen. Relationship intelligence depends on structured concepts such as: people commitments evidence upcoming interactions hypotheses timing authority and relationship policies Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer meaning from the rendered interface or navigate through multiple pages to reconstruct that state. Instead, Weople exposes semantic tools that let ChatGPT work directly with the application's underlying relationship context. The challenge version exposes six WebMCP tools: Read get_today_context get_person_context get_relationship_context Write create_intervention snooze_intervention update_relationship_policy The human interface and the agent operate on the same Weople state. The agent doesn't need a separate, agent-only version of the application. That creates a collaboration neither side has alone: Weople maintains relationship continuity, ChatGPT notices connections across that context, and the person supplies judgment and authority. The agent can surface a possibility without taking over the relationship. Human judgment stays in the loop I didn't want Weople to become an autonomous agent that contacts people on someone's behalf. Noticing an opportunity and being authorized to act on it are different things. Weople keeps human judgment explicit. The agent might notice that Maya and Carlos could benefit from an introduction. The user still decides whether that introduction is appropriate. The same principle applies to timing. An intervention can be useful but mistimed, so the user can snooze it without rejecting the reasoning behind it. The challenge build keeps observed facts separate from inference. Northstar announcing a new facility is stored as an observed fact. The idea that the expansion may produce operational scaling pressure is stored as a hypothesis, with its own evidence and confidence. That lets the agent reason with uncertainty without turning it into fact. How I built it I kept the challenge version small and focused, rather than trying to build the entire future Weople product. I built the first working version with ChatGPT Sites . I used it to quickly build the interaction model, synthetic relationship state, Today view, People view, person details, policies, and the WebMCP tool surface. Once the application worked, I synced the project to GitHub for a standard source repository and version history. I then pulled the project down to my desktop and continued refining it locally. I used the Impeccable design skill in that pass to improve the visual design, hierarchy, spacing, typography, and overall presentation, while preserving the interaction model and WebMCP behavior. The final challenge application is deliberately lightweight. It uses deterministic synthetic data and local state rather than external email, calendar, or contact integrations. That let me focus the submission on the core question the challenge is testing: what becomes possible when a person and an agent share the same structured web application context? Challenges The most difficult part was not the relationship reasoning itself. It was understanding the boundary between the webpage and the browser environment executing the WebMCP tools. During testing, the Weople page registered its WebMCP tools correctly, and ChatGPT read context successfully. But write operations failed at first because ChatGPT sometimes opened a separate browser window. That new document did not contain the document.modelContext from the already-open Weople page. At one point the agent reasoned correctly about the Maya/Carlos opportunity and described the action it intended to take, but the actual Weople intervention was never written. That was a useful failure because it forced me to distinguish between: the model saying an action occurred and the WebMCP tool actually returning a successful result and changing application state. Once the browser was operating on the document that actually registered the Weople tools, the full read → reason → write loop worked, and the intervention appeared immediately in the live interface. What I learned The biggest lesson: WebMCP gets interesting when it exposes an application's semantics instead of recreating its buttons as tools. create_intervention is useful because it represents a meaningful Weople operation. The agent does not need to know which button to press, where a card is rendered, or how the DOM is structured. That changed how I think about the relationship between people, agents, and software. The web application does not have to become invisible when an agent appears. The person can continue using Weople visually while ChatGPT works through the same state semantically. The two interfaces become different projections of the same system. That's the experience I wanted this prototype to demonstrate. What's next The challenge version is a narrow vertical slice. The larger direction for Weople is to connect relationship context from sources like calendars, email, contacts, and personal knowledge. Relationship-specific reasoning, evidence, attention, and authority stay inside Weople. The goal is not to automate relationships. It is to augment human attention around them. Weople remembers. The agent notices. The human keeps judgment. title: Auricle
pitch: A climate dashboard that builds itself from your questions through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A climate dashboard that builds itself from your questions through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Data-rich websites make people do the mechanical work of understanding them: find the right chart, decode its visual grammar, hunt through tooltips, compare distant points, and repeat the process whenever the question changes. General-purpose agents can try to interpret screenshots, but pixels are an unreliable source for exact figures, units, and provenance. Exporting the data into another tool removes it from the page where its context and visual evidence live. This is especially costly for people who cannot rely on charts visually. A screen reader can traverse a table row by row, but a chart often collapses to “image.” The underlying problem is broader, though: conventional dashboards present answers chosen by their designers instead of letting each person interrogate the underlying evidence directly. Auricle opens with this gap in plain sight: 2,026 rows. Zero answers. Four real climate datasets are available as semantic tables, but no dashboard or on-page chatbot is present. Solution Auricle turns the webpage itself into an interviewable climate instrument. The page exposes WebMCP tools backed by its own data. A user asks through their browser agent; the agent calls the page's tools; Auricle computes an exact, source-attributed answer and mirrors the result into the shared page. Ask “Show me warming over time” and the page creates a NASA temperature chart. That action also registers the chart's five-tool family at runtime. Ask “When was the hottest year?” and Auricle answers +1.28 °C in 2024 while highlighting the point in gold. Ask “Play the century as sound” and it sonifies 146 years as a rising tone with a peak cue. Ask for warming stripes and the same data appears in a second, queryable form. The result is not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard. The browser agent supplies the conversation; the site supplies authoritative tools, data, visual state, speech-ready answers, and sonification. Every chart on the screen exists because somebody asked for it. Why This Matters Auricle demonstrates a new interaction model for the agentic web: people and agents compose and interrogate a live dashboard together without exporting data or guessing at pixels. The page remains the source of truth, the human directs the inquiry, and everyone in the session shares one evolving surface. For blind and low-vision users, page-owned tools can replace pixel interpretation with exact, source-backed spoken answers and sonification. For everyone else, the same system makes complex evidence faster to explore and easier to verify. Accessibility is therefore a demanding proof case for a broadly useful product—not the boundary of Auricle's audience. The reusable contribution is an agent-accessibility grammar: Orient the agent before asking it to act. Make the tool surface follow the user's focus. Return narratable answers with figures, units, and provenance. Mirror every agent action into the visible and accessible page state. Treat non-visual encodings such as sound as first-class capabilities. This pattern can extend beyond climate data to finance, health, public policy, and any data-rich site where fixed dashboards or visual-only answers limit exploration. Key Features Dashboard by conversation: the initial publication has no charts; create_view commissions each requested view. Dynamic WebMCP surface: five global tools exist at boot, while dataset-specific families register, change with focus, and unregister when their final view is removed—21 tools across the complete experience. Exact page-owned answers: queries run against baked NASA, Our World in Data, and NOAA data, with figure, unit, and source in every narrated return. Shared visual evidence: tool calls create views, highlight points and ranges, and leave a provenance footnote on the page. Accessible HTML foundation: semantic landmarks, real data tables, chart labels, keyboard-operable controls, reduced-motion support, and a visually hidden aria-live answer log. Sonification: time series become a roughly three-second pitch sweep with a distinct peak cue. Nine visualization forms: line, area, warming stripes, vertical and horizontal bars, share bars, scatter, live, and stat views. Self-describing experience: describe_screen tells a newly arrived agent what is present, focused, available, and possible next. Architecture Auricle is a static Vite + React + TypeScript application deployed on Vercel with no backend. Source datasets are fetched by a keyless script and baked into JSON, so the production experience does not depend on runtime data APIs. A framework-agnostic registry wraps each internal tool definition into the WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool shape. Five orientation and workspace tools register at page load. When create_view commissions a dataset, an AbortController-scoped family registers for that dataset; focus changes replace the active family, and removing the last view aborts it. The simulated live CO₂ view re-registers its family on each bounded tick so its tool description reflects current session state. Agent calls share one execution path: validate the input, run the page-owned handler, return speech-ready text, emit a mirror event to every relevant view, and append the answer to both the visible provenance trail and hidden aria-live region. Charts are hand-rolled SVG. Known Limitations Accessibility is an important beneficiary and proof case, not a claim that Auricle has completed user validation. The experience was built by sighted developers and has not yet been tested with blind or low-vision users. ChatGPT's built-in browser with Site Tools was the AI agent tested end to end: it discovered Auricle's five global tools, invoked create_view to draw the warming curve, observed five temperature tools register dynamically, and invoked temp-anomaly_describe_trend, whose exact answer Auricle mirrored visibly into the page. Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled and the Model Context Tool Inspector was used only as developer tooling for protocol-level inspection, not as another AI agent. The Mauna Loa “live” movement is a clearly labeled bounded simulation seeded from the latest baked NOAA weekly mean; it is not presented as a real-time NOAA stream. Sonification and warming stripes have established prior art. Auricle's contribution is combining them with exact, queryable WebMCP operations under a reusable agent-interaction and accessibility grammar. title: Runbook Zero: Incident Command for the Agentic Web
pitch: Runbook Zero turns any WebMCP site into a shared incident workspace where agents diagnose and stage exact actions while humans keep approval authority.
about_excerpt: Runbook Zero turns any WebMCP site into a shared incident workspace where agents diagnose and stage exact actions while humans keep approval authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 01 Runbook Zero Incident Command 02 Checkout Dependency Topology 03 Live Telemetry Evidence 04 Agent Evidence Trail 05 Low Risk Mitigation Comparison 06 Exact Change Awaiting Human 07 Capability Firewall Locked 08 Human Approval Unlocks Apply 09 Verified Deterministic Recovery 10 Generalized Incident Pack Launcher 11 Payment Queue Incident 12 Same Contracts New Incident 13 Catalog Cache Stampede 14 Live Site Evidence Graph 15 Approval Bound Action Receipt Inspiration Incident response still forces humans to translate between dashboards, browser consoles, agents, runbooks, and change controls while an outage is unfolding. An agent can investigate quickly, but giving it broad action authority makes the human approval step vague or performative. We wanted the browser itself to expose a precise operational contract: enough authority for an agent to gather evidence and stage an exact response, but no authority to approve its own consequential action. Runbook Zero is my answer. It treats WebMCP as a state-aware incident control plane and keeps the product interface as the shared source of truth for both the operator and the agent. What it does Runbook Zero is an installable incident product for the website an operator is actually using. The Codex plugin begins read only, inspects bounded evidence from the selected site, inventories its WebMCP capabilities, and derives an issue specific component, dependency, user flow, telemetry, change, and evidence graph. The generated Incident Pack opens in the Runbook Zero workbench, where real document.modelContext tools let an agent inspect services, trace paths, query signals, record a hypothesis, compare mitigations, and stage one exact action. Every tool call updates and focuses the same topology, telemetry, evidence, mitigation, provenance, and capability interface the human sees. The visible Capability Firewall shows active agent capabilities, unavailable consequential capabilities, application phase, and authority state. apply_approved_mitigation is not registered before approval. The agent has no approval tool. A human must review the exact target, diff, risk, reversibility, assumptions, incident, and seed, then click the visible approval control. Only after that click does apply appear, narrowed to the exact approved mitigation. It disappears immediately after use. For a live target, Runbook Zero releases an origin-, tool-, and input bound receipt that Codex carries back to the target site. If no matching action exists, it produces an honest operator handoff instead of pretending automation happened. The product also includes three polished deterministic packs—checkout pool regression ( INC-042 ), payment queue backlog ( INC-117 ), and catalog cache stampede ( INC-203 )—plus safe local JSON import. They all run through the same domain and WebMCP contracts. The canonical pack makes the judging flow reproducible the installed plugin proves Runbook Zero is not limited to a premade walkthrough. How we built it The workbench uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, a guarded state machine, and a validated Incident Pack v1 schema. Thirteen page defined WebMCP contracts are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . The active subset is derived from incident phase, the current pack, approval state, and execution mode; stale registrations are cancelled with AbortController whenever that state changes. The repository hosted Codex plugin defines a conservative Site Capture v2 contract. It treats page text, tool descriptions, and tool results as untrusted evidence, rejects browser secrets and invalid cross references, and deterministically builds a graph and provisional diagnosis from the evidence actually observed. Live action receipts bind the incident, seed, origin, target tool, and exact JSON input. Post action evidence must still satisfy the pack's recovery thresholds before an incident can resolve. We validate the product with 17 Vitest files / 69 tests covering domain commands, state transitions, pack validation, dynamic registration, stale tools, the approval invariant, imported-pack failures, deterministic reset, and UI behavior. Four Playwright regression journeys cover reset-to-resolved, multi-pack behavior, keyboard and viewport usability, and live-site receipts. Real local, deployed in-app-browser, installed-plugin, and Chrome WebMCP evidence is recorded separately from the test-only browser harness. The public AGPL-3.0 app is deployed on ChatGPT Sites. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making human authority a runtime property not a disabled button. Rejecting an early apply call was not enough, the consequential tool had to be completely absent from discovery until the exact staged object had visible human approval, and old handles had to become stale as soon as state changed. The second challenge was cross origin honesty. Runbook Zero cannot claim that its page silently changed an unrelated website. We separated approval bound release from target site execution and verification, with an operator handoff fallback when the site exposes no applicable action. The third challenge was escaping a scenario specific demo without sacrificing a deterministic judging path. Generalizing the schema, UI, tool inputs, graph layout, thresholds, and recovery engine. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is the product's control plane. The same thirteen tool contracts operate against bundled, imported, and evidence derived live site incidents. The agent and human share one synchronized operational interface with explicit Agent, Human, System, and Change provenance. Pre-approval application is impossible through the registered WebMCP surface. Approval itself is human only. The Capability Firewall makes the transition from locked apply to exact approved apply visually obvious. New issues produce new evidence graphs instead of replaying a fixed demo. Live actions use exact origin/tool/input receipts and an honest handoff fallback. The canonical workflow resets deterministically and resolves through fixed recovery frames. The public app, source, AGPL-3.0 license, installable Codex plugin, tests, and judging evidence are reproducible from the repository. What we learned WebMCP capability discovery can also be policy. The safest consequential tool is not one that merely promises to reject unsafe input. It is a tool that does not exist until the surrounding human-visible state makes its use valid. We also learned that agent legibility matters as much as agent capability. When tool calls update the interface already in front of the operator, the human can see what the agent inspected, why it formed a hypothesis, what exact change it staged, and which authority boundary remains. Finally evidence topology is a far stronger bridge from demo to product than a library of hardcoded incident scripts. What's next for Runbook Zero Next we will validate more real sites, add capture adapters for richer browser and observability evidence, and expand the portable policy and receipt model. Production integrations will follow only where they can preserve the same boundary: read only observation, evidence backed diagnosis, exact staging, visible human approval, origin bound execution, independent verification, and auditable closure. title: House Design Tool
pitch: A 3D home designer that allows humans and agents to collaborate on a proejct. WebMCP gives agents 21 tools on the live house design, while a shared rulebook keeps every wall and walkway legal.
about_excerpt: A 3D home designer that allows humans and agents to collaborate on a proejct. WebMCP gives agents 21 tools on the live house design, while a shared rulebook keeps every wall and walkway legal. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every AI design tool today works like a vending machine: you describe what you want in a chat box, and a finished result drops out. That's backwards for spatial work. Nobody designs a home by describing it. They nudge a wall, stand in the kitchen, drag the sofa two feet, and look . We wanted the agent in the room with you, not on the other side of a chat log. WebMCP made that possible: if the page itself exposes its live state as tools, the human and the agent can finally work on the same object at the same time. What it does WebMCP Home Design is a 3D floorplan editor that registers 21 tools on document.modelContext . A human picks a shell (floors, then a template per floor), reshapes rooms, and furnishes by dragging, rotating, and resizing, while an agent in the browser reads the same live design and edits it through tools: placing furniture, moving walls, cutting doors, batching twenty edits in one call, even proposing three alternative layouts that ghost over the plan for the human to compare and apply. A simplified residential constraint engine (13 rules: door widths, bedroom egress, kitchen aisles, toilet clearances, furniture facing walls) referees both parties identically: every edit returns what changed and what it broke. Designs autosave locally, export as JSON, and travel as share links with the whole compressed design in the URL fragment. No server, no accounts. How we built it TypeScript end to end. The domain layer models rooms, shared walls, openings, and furniture in plan inches, with pure operations (clone in, result out) that both the UI and the agent tools call: one rulebook, two doors in. React Three Fiber renders the scene: procedural canvas-painted textures with bump and roughness maps, parametric furniture built from primitives (a resized sofa grows a third cushion), dollhouse-cut walls overhead and full walls in a street-view-style walkthrough. Zustand holds per-floor state with undo history; Zod schemas define tool inputs and compile to the JSON Schemas agents see. Everything is generated in code, with no model files and no fetched assets, so the app works fully offline. Challenges we ran into The hardest problems were about shared control. Coincident walls desynchronized until we rebuilt the model around one wall per partition. Agent calls serialize at roughly a second each in the browser, which pushed us to design apply_edits for single-round-trip furnishing. Grid snapping silently moved agent placements until every operation learned to echo where things actually landed. And a long tail of 3D truths: coplanar surfaces z-fight into flicker, room polygons run along wall centerlines so furniture sank 3 inches into walls, and an agent with no orientation guidance will happily face a wardrobe into a wall, which became both a smarter placement default and a new validation rule. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop genuinely works both ways. An agent can validate a plan, fix a too-narrow door, furnish a bedroom, and then walk the human through the result with the camera; a human can drag a sofa and the agent's next get_layout reflects it. We're proud that refusals are as useful as successes (every rejected edit explains what would break and suggests a fix the grid can actually produce) and that 267 tests pin the whole thing down, from constraint rules to camera math to the persistence format. What we learned Tools-on-the-page is a different discipline from tools-on-a-server. The agent needs what a colleague needs: honest echoes of what actually happened, actionable refusals, bounds included in summaries so it doesn't ask twice, and documentation precise enough to reason about (our rotation docs went from "0 faces the bottom" to a full compass after watching agents guess wrong). We also learned that the referee matters more than either player: the constraint engine is what turns two editors sharing one document from chaos into collaboration. What's next for House Design Tool Furniture variants: extending propose_variants beyond wall moves so an agent can ghost three complete room arrangements, pre-validated, for the human to pick from. Stacked multi-floor 3D with stairs and alignment rules. Real collaboration transport (two humans plus an agent on one design). And a richer catalog with materials, lighting fixtures, and cost estimates, so the conversation can become "make it nicer for under $3,000." title: Physical AI WebMCP Command Center
pitch: An Agent-Native Control Layer for Autonomous Warehouses.
about_excerpt: An Agent-Native Control Layer for Autonomous Warehouses. Like Comment Story Updates AGV-03 completes the approved mission after safely stopping at N07 and replanning around the blocked aisle. Live WebMCP trace showing every tool call, result, run ID, timestamp, and measured latency. Production Hero E2E verified: 7/7 WebMCP tools, ordered flow PASS, mission completed, and final metrics captured. Inspiration Warehouse software is usually designed for humans clicking through multiple screens. Browser agents can interact with those interfaces, but they must infer operational meaning from pixels and DOM structure. We wanted the web itself to expose a safe, typed contract shared by humans, AI agents, and autonomous machines. What it does Physical AI WebMCP Command Center is an agent-native warehouse control layer built around a deterministic digital twin. A user gives one intent: move pallet P-104 from INBOUND-01 to RACK-A12. Through seven WebMCP tools, the Agent observes warehouse state, inspects the pallet, plans a safe route, selects AGV-03, and creates an approval-gated proposal. A human must approve before physical movement begins. During execution, AGV-03 encounters a blocked aisle at N07, stops safely, replans through N08 and N11, and completes the mission. The safety engine validates destination, occupancy, vehicle availability, battery reserve, route safety, approval state, communication heartbeat (SAFE-11), and traffic reservations (SAFE-12). Every WebMCP call, result, and measured latency is displayed in the interface. The observable workflow is: OBSERVE → PLAN → VALIDATE → APPROVE → EXECUTE → RECOVER How we built it The application uses React and TypeScript and runs on a public HTTPS deployment. A shared deterministic state engine powers both the manual UI and WebMCP interface. Dijkstra routing produces the 41.6 m primary route and the 49.4 m recovery route. The simulator controls AGV movement, fault injection, safe stopping, replanning, resuming, and mission completion. Exactly seven WebMCP tools are registered with strict JSON Schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, and production discovery. Runtime instrumentation measures planner stages, tool latency, route length, approvals, replans, mission success, and Human vs Agent performance. Challenges The main challenge was preserving a trustworthy boundary between AI intent and physical execution. Planning must never start a mission. Creating a proposal must never imply approval. An unapproved mission cannot move. A route blockage must stop the AGV before replanning. Communication timeouts and conflicting traffic reservations must deterministically prevent unsafe movement. We also ensured that all displayed traces and metrics come from real runtime events rather than scripted presentation data. Accomplishments Seven discoverable WebMCP tools with strict schemas Human approval that cannot be bypassed by an Agent tool Deterministic Dijkstra planning and blockage recovery SAFE-11 communication-timeout enforcement SAFE-12 traffic-reservation conflict prevention Visible WebMCP and planning traces with real latency Complete reset of missions, proposals, traces, metrics, timers, and faults Human vs Agent benchmark using the same operational task Public HTTPS deployment with a verified 7/7 Agent E2E run No account, API key, database, broker, or physical hardware required What we learned Agent-native UX is not about removing human control. The strongest design separates responsibilities: The model expresses intent. WebMCP defines how it asks. Deterministic software decides what is allowed. A human authorizes high-impact action. The physical system executes. What's next The same WebMCP interface could be connected to real fleet-management systems. Approved missions could be translated into VDA5050, MQTT, PLC, or vendor API commands while retaining deterministic safety policies, audit traces, and human authorization. title: careercrew
pitch: CareerCrew uses AI and WebMCP to find best-fit jobs, tailor evidence-based resumes, and assist applications while candidates approve every submission and stay in control
about_excerpt: CareerCrew uses AI and WebMCP to find best-fit jobs, tailor evidence-based resumes, and assist applications while candidates approve every submission and stay in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job searching is often repetitive, fragmented, and stressful. Candidates move between career pages, compare job descriptions, rewrite resumes, prepare for interviews, and repeatedly enter the same information. Existing automation tools may save time, but they can also recommend irrelevant roles, invent resume content, or submit applications without enough candidate oversight. We created CareerCrew to offer useful automation without taking control away from the candidate. Our goal was to build a trustworthy career assistant that uses WebMCP to connect AI agents with structured web actions while keeping every important decision transparent and candidate-approved. What it does CareerCrew supports the job-application journey from resume review to guarded application assistance. Candidates can upload a PDF, DOCX, or TXT resume. CareerCrew extracts their skills, experience, contact information, and suitable career tracks for review. It then evaluates available jobs using an explainable 0–100 fit score and recommends the strongest qualifying role from each company. For a selected role, CareerCrew prepares an application packet using only evidence-backed, candidate-approved experience. It also creates cited interview-preparation plans covering technical questions, coding, system design, and behavioral interviews. CareerCrew exposes structured WebMCP tools for working with candidate profiles, campaigns, job matches, and application questions, approvals, and interview plans. After receiving explicit approval, its Chrome companion can preview and fill verified information into supported Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby application forms. It pauses whenever a mandatory question needs candidate input and never guesses sensitive answers such as salary expectations, work authorization, relocation, or notice period. How we built it We designed CareerCrew as a modular full-stack platform: Next.js, React and TypeScript power the candidate dashboard. FastAPI, Python and Pydantic provide the backend workflows and validation. WebMCP exposes nine structured tools through the web interface. Auth.js provides configurable Google authentication. PDF and DOCX libraries process uploaded resumes. A Manifest V3 Chrome companion supports guarded ATS form assistance. One-time, origin-bound application codes connect approved CareerCrew data with the browser companion. Vitest, Testing Library and Pytest verify the frontend, extension, and API. Synthetic Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby portals allow us to demonstrate and test the workflow safely. The hackathon version uses clearly labelled demonstration jobs and ATS pages, so we do not represent demo actions as real applications. ## Challenges we ran into One major challenge was balancing automation with candidate control. Automatically filling and submitting forms sounds convenient,but sensitive questions cannot be answered safely without the candidate. We designed explicit approval boundaries and pause states instead of allowing the system to guess. Another challenge was supporting different ATS structures. Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby organise their forms differently, so the browser companion needed separate adapters and careful field detection. We also needed to keep resume tailor-trustworthy. CareerCrew links generated resume content to approved evidence so that stronger wording does not become fabricated experience. Finally, we had to design WebMCP tools that were useful to AI agents while remaining narrow, predictable, and safe for sensitive actions. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CareerCrew is more than a static concept—it is a tested, end-to-end local vertical slice. It can process resumes, build a candidate profile, explain job-fit scores, shortlist roles, prepare evidence-based application content, generate cited interview plans, request approval, and securely hand verified information to a browser companion. We successfully integrated nine WebMCP tools and demonstrated the guarded workflow across synthetic Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby portals. Most importantly, CareerCrew does not sacrifice trust for automation. It never fabricates qualifications, treats a fit score as hiring probability, or assumes that clicking a button means an application was successfully submitted. What we learned We learned that responsible automation is not about automating every possible step. It is about knowing which actions can be automated safely and where human judgement is essential. WebMCP showed us how structured tools can make interactions between AI agents and web applications more reliable than coordinate-based browser automation. We also learned that explainability matters in career technology. Candidates should understand why a role was recommended, where resume claims came from, what information will be entered, and what action the system intends to take. Building synthetic ATS portals was another important lesson. They allowed us to test realistic workflows without risking accidental submissions or interacting with real employers. ## What's next for CareerCrew Our next step is to turn the hackathon prototype into a production-ready candidate platform. We plan to add: Live role discovery from official company career pages Job freshness and source verification Durable encrypted data storage Model-assisted resume tailoring with evidence controls Production-quality resume and cover-letter generation Additional ATS adapters Stronger audit trails and submission confirmation Cloud deployment and monitoring Candidate feedback loops for improving recommendations Calendar, email, and interview-tracking integrations Our long-term vision is for CareerCrew to become a trusted career command centre: one place where candidates can discover opportunities, prepare credible applications, practise for interviews, and move through their job search with confidence—powered by AI and WebMCP, but always controlled by the candidate. title: Mermail
pitch: Email for your AI: a WebMCP-native inbox where agents and people can safely search, read, compose, send, and organize mail together.
about_excerpt: Email for your AI: a WebMCP-native inbox where agents and people can safely search, read, compose, send, and organize mail together. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Email is one of the web’s most useful coordination layers, but most inboxes were designed only for people clicking through screens. AI agents often need a separate integration, broad account access, or brittle pixel automation. Mermail starts with a different premise: it is not AI for your email; it is email for your AI. Each agent can have a private inbox while its human keeps a visible, familiar mail interface. WebMCP turns that interface into a native collaboration surface. What it does In a WebMCP-enabled browser, Mermail exposes tools that match the active page. On the public site, an agent can check service status, inspect pricing, and start signup. In an authenticated workspace it can list and open mailboxes. Inside a mailbox it can list and search mail, read one clean-scanned message, open the visible composer, send/reply/forward with human confirmation, change read state, move messages, and confirm trash or permanent deletion. This lets a person ask an agent to find a thread, inspect a safe message, prepare a reply, or organize an inbox without handing it an invisible, open-ended automation channel. Why WebMCP fits Email combines private data, untrusted external content, and consequential actions. Raw browser automation is brittle and risky here. WebMCP gives Mermail a small, typed capability surface tied to the current page and authenticated workspace. The agent handles search and repetitive navigation; the person stays in the same interface and approves sending or deletion. Public tools appear on the landing page, workspace tools on the mailbox list, and message tools only inside an active mailbox. How we built it Mermail uses the standards-track document.modelContext.registerTool() API in Next.js and React. The shared registration layer: validates every input with strict Zod JSON schemas gates tools with off , read , and full rollout modes aborts tools when the page lifecycle ends bounds result sizes and marks email-derived output as untrusted uses the authenticated API and current mailbox state records registration/execution telemetry without message content leaves unsupported browsers unchanged Read tools request bounded, agent-safe projections. Bodies are returned only for clean-scanned mail and are truncated. Send, reply, forward, trash, and permanent-delete tools reuse visible Mermail confirmation UI. Sends use an idempotency key and an “outcome unknown” recovery path to discourage duplicates after interruption. What we added during the challenge Mermail existed before the submission period. We have extended it with WebMCP across the public landing page, authenticated workspace home, and active mailbox. The work added contextual tool catalogs, lifecycle-aware registration, strict validation, bounded outputs, confirmations, telemetry, deployment configuration, and focused browser/security tests. We verified the live deployment in a WebMCP-enabled in-app browser: public status and pricing tools executed successfully, authenticated mailbox discovery succeeded, and the active mailbox registered its complete 11-tool catalog. Challenges we faced The hard part was making every tool safe enough for email. Incoming messages are untrusted, React rerenders can create stale registrations, interrupted sends need special recovery, and destructive actions need stronger confirmation than navigation. We addressed those cases with strict schemas, bounded projections, clean-scan requirements, lifecycle abort signals, stable catalogs, high-impact action locks, visible confirmations, and cancellation tests. What we learned WebMCP works best as a progressive enhancement to a product people already understand. The strongest tools are contextual and narrow, and the safest agent experience combines typed capabilities with visible human checkpoints. What’s next We plan to add judge-friendly demo data, richer thread-level tools, clearer indicators of available WebMCP capabilities, and more end-to-end evals for prompt injection and cancellation races. title: Haggle
pitch: The first bike store where your AI haggles the price with our AI — and the deal becomes a real discount code at a real Shopify checkout.
about_excerpt: The first bike store where your AI haggles the price with our AI — and the deal becomes a real discount code at a real Shopify checkout. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Price negotiation died when commerce moved online — it needed a human on both ends. WebMCP removes exactly that constraint: the storefront exposes a negotiation protocol as tools, the browser's agent represents the buyer, and the human keeps the final say. We wanted to build the first store where "can you do better on the price?" is something your agent just… does — and the timing is right: when agents do the shopping, merchants get squeezed into pure price comparison, and a sanctioned negotiation channel with a hard ceiling is their controlled answer. What it does Your agent → negotiation → real deal → real Shopify discount code → checkout. That is the whole loop, and it runs live today on Bikepoint, a Shopify store with a real e-bike catalog. Claude speaks. The engine decides every price. The floor cannot be negotiated away — the seller never knows anything the engine didn't decide, so there is nothing to jailbreak. Try it. One script line in the theme registers five WebMCP tools ( list_negotiable_products , start_negotiation , make_offer , get_negotiation_state , accept_deal ) on every page of the store; on a product page they default to that product. The agent trades offers in NOK with the server-side AI seller over up to six rounds. Accept, and the server mints a single-use discount code scoped to that product, valid 48 hours — worthless to coupon sites, redeemed in the normal checkout. Shopify's own storefront WebMCP tools ( update_cart , proceed_to_checkout , …) are live on the same pages — Shopify's webmcp_adapter feature-detects the very same document.modelContext surface, verified on the live store. So the full journey is agentic with zero coordination: negotiate with our tools, cart and check out with Shopify's. A small widget shows the human the negotiation in real time; to everyone else the store looks like a completely normal bike shop. An actual negotiation from the live store, verbatim: Buyer's agent: offers 12 000 kr for the Scultura Endurance 300 (listed 18 999 kr) Seller: «Nesten! Denne går sjelden under 18350 kr — men da er den din.» Buyer's agent: counters at 17 500 kr Seller: «Da har vi en avtale! 17500 kr for Scultura Endurance 300 — godt forhandlet. Bruk rabattkoden i kassen.» → a real HAGGLE-… code, applied at checkout at the negotiated price. Why would a merchant ever allow haggling? Because negotiation is controlled price discrimination — the oldest trick in retail, finally automatable: Capture price-sensitive buyers without a storewide sale. The list price keeps its integrity; only buyers who negotiate get below it, and never below the merchant's ceiling ( MAX_DISCOUNT_PCT , 10 % here). "Everyone just gets 10 %"? No. Lazy bids close well above the floor, and even a perfectly played negotiation bottoms out at the seller's final offer — a step above a floor that is never crossed. The deal can't leak. Single-use, product-scoped, 48-hour expiry ( discountCodeBasicCreate ). Only one buyer can ever redeem it. Who it's for: high-ticket Shopify categories with real margins and a haggling culture — bikes, furniture, jewelry, appliances, refurbished electronics. Installation is one script line on any Online Store 2.0 theme, invisible to non-agent visitors. Prior art is one-way or human-gated: eBay's Best Offer waits on a human, coupon plugins are static. Haggle is an instant, two-way protocol between two AIs on the merchant's own store. How we built it Server: a zero-dependency Node 20 service on Cloud Run. The price floor exists only inside a deterministic engine — never in a prompt, never on the client — and the tests hammer it: never breached, never leaked. Seller's voice, never in charge: Claude phrases the replies (a charming Norwegian bike dealer) when a key is set; a deterministic Norwegian template voice otherwise. Either way the voice only phrases — any reply that doesn't quote the engine's price is discarded. Storefront: one <script> line in the theme registers the tools on document.modelContext (with the navigator.modelContext fallback) and talks to the server. Tested like an agent: a Playwright suite shims the WebMCP runtime, captures the registered tools and plays the buyer through full negotiations — in CI on every push to main and on every PR. The live store loads this same storefront source file, pinned by commit on a CDN. Challenges we ran into Letting an LLM speak for the seller without ever letting it touch a number. WebMCP is brand new — built against the spec, Chrome's enable-webmcp-testing flag and ChatGPT's in-app browser, with a navigator.modelContext fallback for older builds. Real-store plumbing: custom-app tokens, scopes, and a theme with a broken product template to diagnose before the demo could run on genuine product pages. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop at the top is not a mock-up — it runs on a real store, and anyone can verify it. The whole negotiation surface is reproducible without accounts: MOCK_PRODUCTS=1 fixture mode, a standalone demo.html , a smoke script and an e2e suite judges can run. What we learned Tools beat chat for commerce: a protocol (offers, rounds, state, acceptance) gives agents something they can be genuinely good at, while the human keeps the decisions that matter. And WebMCP's page-level registration composes beautifully — our negotiation tools sat next to Shopify's native cart tools with zero coordination. What's next for Haggle Dynamic tool lifecycle (registering make_offer / accept_deal only while a negotiation is open, via AbortSignal unregistration), per-product and inventory-aware floors via metafields, bundle haggling ("throw in a helmet"), a merchant dashboard with negotiation analytics — and turning it on for a store that isn't behind a dev-store password. Try it (judges) Best path: ChatGPT's browser. Open https://bikepoint-no.myshopify.com (store password: haggle ), go to a product page such as /products/scultura-endurance-300 , and ask the agent: "This store lets you negotiate the price — use its tools to get me a better deal on this bike." The widget bottom-right shows the negotiation live. Accept a deal → apply the single-use code at checkout. Try to push the seller below its floor — it won't go. Chrome's chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing exposes the WebMCP surface so the tools register (console logs [haggle] WebMCP tools registered ), but stock Chrome ships no agent that drives them — pair the flag with a WebMCP-driving agent/extension, or use ChatGPT's browser for the full loop. Without any accounts: git clone https://github.com/noktohq/haggle && cd haggle/server npm test # engine test suite (price floor, rounds, leaks) MOCK_PRODUCTS=1 node src/index.js # fixture catalog on :8080 bash ../scripts/smoke.sh # black-box negotiation over HTTP cd ../e2e && npm ci && npx playwright test # plays the buyer's agent in Chromium Built With claude github-actions google-cloud-run javascript node.js playwright shopify webmcp Try it out bikepoint-no.myshopify.com github.com haggle-463490695016.europe-north1.run.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Founder and product owner. I came up with the concept, own and run the Bikepoint store and the Nokto infrastructure (Shopify, Google Cloud), set the direction, and did the manual store setup, testing and the final submission. Engineering was done in close collaboration with Claude Code as the coding agent, as described in the "AI tools" section. title: Grid — Spreadsheets with your agent
pitch: Co-edit a live spreadsheet with ChatGPT. WebMCP tools read ranges, set cells/formulas, sort, filter, chart, and highlight on the open grid — you see every change.
about_excerpt: Co-edit a live spreadsheet with ChatGPT. WebMCP tools read ranges, set cells/formulas, sort, filter, chart, and highlight on the open grid — you see every change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most “AI for spreadsheets” still lives in a chat sidebar or a separate Sheets API. You describe a budget; you get a table pasted back into the thread — not co-editing the grid you’re staring at. Google Sheets has Gemini-style help and backend MCP connectors, but the live sheets.google.com page is not exposing WebMCP tools on the open workbook. That gap is the point of the challenge: shared client state . Grid was inspired by that white space — and by Flavio’s note that spreadsheets are strong WebMCP cases because the open page holds state a remote API may not. What if ChatGPT and a human shared one workbook, with the agent writing cells, formulas, sorts, charts, and highlights you watch appear live? What it does Grid is an agent-native shared spreadsheet: Co-edit a seeded “Move budget — London” workbook toward a £4k total Read and write ranges, set formulas ( =SUM , arithmetic), sort and filter rows Highlight cells, add/remove a simple chart, insert rows/cols, export CSV Full human UI (formula bar, selection, editable cells) that works with WebMCP idle 17 WebMCP site tools on the same Zustand store as your clicks Agent tools panel + activity feed; ?demo=1 (optional delay / delayMs ) for judges and screencasts You steer in plain English in ChatGPT; Grid’s tools update the open grid in real time. Side effects like export_csv , clear_highlights , and remove_chart are annotated so confirmation policies can apply. How we built it Vite + React 19 + TypeScript SPA ( base: '/grid-webmcp/' ) Zustand as the single source of truth for the React UI and every WebMCP execute handler WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext fallback), feature-detected on the top-level page Lightweight formula evaluation, SVG chart panel, filter/highlight overlays MIT-licensed, client-only, no backend or secrets — GitHub Pages Built with Codex Core tools: get_workbook_state , get_range , set_cells , set_formula , clear_range , select_range , sort_range , filter_rows , clear_filter , highlight_cells , clear_highlights , add_chart , remove_chart , insert_rows , insert_cols , export_csv , list_activity . Challenges we ran into Same-state collaboration — agent tools and keyboard edits must never drift. Both paths go through one store. Formulas without a full engine — enough SUM + arithmetic for a credible budget demo, without shipping Excel. Read vs write vs side effect — inspection tools stay read-only; clears, chart removal, and CSV export are explicit side effects. Demo without a live agent — ?demo=1 replays the happy path for screencasts while real tools still register for ChatGPT’s in-app browser. Staying distinct — orthogonal to Nest (flats), Frame (canvas), Brief (evidence), and Redline (propose ≠ commit). Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete co-edit loop on one grid: fill → formula → sort → chart → highlight → export Non-trivial WebMCP surface (17 tools), not a single toy cell writer Human-first UI that stays usable if WebMCP is missing A fifth submission that targets a category often confused with “Sheets already does AI” — and shows the difference is tools on the open page What we learned WebMCP’s superpower is co-presence. Spreadsheets prove it cleanly: when set_formula runs, you watch the contingency cell resolve; when add_chart runs, the bar appears beside the sheet. That shared visual ground is harder to fake with a headless Sheets API MCP — and it’s exactly what Grid is for. What's next for Grid — Spreadsheets with your agent Richer formula surface (IF, VLOOKUP-class helpers) and named ranges Multi-sheet workbooks and freeze panes Conditional formatting tools the agent can propose and you confirm Presence cursors when multiple humans join the same workbook Deeper ChatGPT desktop testing with confirmation UX on destructive tools Built With codex Try it out omercelik.github.io Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Serdar Murat ÇELİK Omer Celik Abdulhamit Mabocoglu Like Share this project: Updates Omer Celik started this project — Sep 02, 2026 07:27 PM EDT

title: AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk
pitch: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents. Like Comment Story Updates AI Governance Watch turns source-backed AI governance research into a shared briefing workspace for people and browser agents. Inspiration AI governance information is scattered across legislation, agency announcements, standards, procurement records, civil-rights proceedings, and technical guidance. Government leaders and policy professionals often need a concise briefing, but the distinctions behind that briefing matter. A proposal is not an enacted law. A publication date may differ from the underlying event date. An official announcement is not proof of an outcome. A general AI summary can easily blur those boundaries. We built AI Governance Watch to explore a more trustworthy model. The website remains the authority for its research and actions, while a browser agent helps the user search, verify, compare, and organize the information. What it does AI Governance Watch is a public, standalone WebMCP Briefing Desk built around a dated governance snapshot and a 62-entry Source Ledger. The application exposes four focused WebMCP tools: search_updates searches the locally bundled governance report using text and structured filters. get_source_record retrieves an exact Source Ledger entry by its registered identifier. compare_updates compares developments while preserving their dates, jurisdictions, statuses, confidence labels, and sources. build_briefing assembles selected records into a visible, session-only briefing for human review. A user can ask a browser agent to find developments relevant to a government leader, verify the underlying sources, compare the most important records, and construct a briefing focused on implementation, procurement, or public accountability. The resulting briefing appears directly in the application. The human can review, reorder, remove, or clear its contents before relying on it. This is a strong use case for WebMCP because traditional browser agents must interpret layouts, cards, filters, and buttons to determine what an application can do. That approach can be fragile when a page contains legally or operationally significant distinctions. WebMCP allows AI Governance Watch to expose its real domain functions as structured tools. The agent receives validated parameters, stable record identifiers, bounded outputs, and explicit fields for status, confidence, jurisdiction, event date, publication date, and source. How we built it The project uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . The four tools register only on the public /webmcp route. No tools register on the application’s unlock page or protected monitor routes. Each tool has a strict JSON Schema and repeats validation at runtime. Every registration promise is awaited before the interface reports that the tools are available. An AbortController manages the registration lifecycle and removes the registrations when the React component unmounts, preventing duplicate tools during remounts. The three research tools are read-only. The briefing tool changes only visible session-level React state. It does not write to a database, publish content, send messages, download files, or contact an external service. All tool results are returned as valid, bounded JSON strings. A single JSON.parse() exposes the top-level ok field and the applicable results, source record, comparison items, or briefing details. The implementation uses the application’s locally bundled August 22, 2026 report and Source Ledger without adding a crawler, external AI provider, or autonomous publishing system. AI Governance Watch treats source-derived material as untrusted content and labels every WebMCP tool accordingly. The implementation includes strict validation, same-origin exposure, read-only annotations, bounded outputs, exact identifiers, visible and reversible state, registration cleanup, and no database or network writes. The standalone route includes dated-snapshot and independence disclosures. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by, or published by the Maryland Responsible AI Council, the State of Maryland, or any government body. If WebMCP is unavailable, the human interface continues to function and explains how to use a supported browser. Existing project disclosure The base Maryland AI Governance Monitor was created on August 22, 2026. Verified pre-challenge baseline commit: c5543d31d7cfc9bd4492bc539112c8801bada8b9 The WebMCP tools, standalone Briefing Desk, shared human-agent state, validation, tests, documentation, and public challenge interface were added during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. Final deployed challenge implementation: 310114de0dfcc426b19f9f2b438b9e7c54dbd487 Public standalone repository commit: 95b584f512cf27ca1ef9a3244f0121626f7a1799 Only the WebMCP extension and human-agent briefing workflow added during the challenge period are presented as challenge work. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was enabling useful agent action without weakening the information boundaries that make a governance monitor trustworthy. Search results needed to remain compact while preserving their status, confidence, source, jurisdiction, and two distinct date fields. The state-changing tool also needed to create meaningful collaboration without producing a hidden or irreversible external side effect. We also needed to separate the challenge project from the broader credential-protected Maryland monitor. The final /webmcp route is publicly accessible and uses a dedicated AI Governance Watch shell, while every existing monitor route remains protected. The resulting design keeps the agent workflow deterministic, inspectable, reversible, and under human control. Accomplishments that we're proud of Converted a human-first research interface into a genuine agent surface. Exposed a complete research-to-briefing workflow through four focused tools. Preserved exact sources, dates, statuses, and confidence labels. Created shared application state between the browser agent and human reviewer. Made the challenge desk publicly accessible without exposing the protected monitor. Demonstrated practical human-agent collaboration beyond a technical proof of concept. Added security annotations, runtime validation, output limits, failure handling, and lifecycle cleanup. Required no new backend, database, crawler, or external AI service. Published a clean standalone repository with no credentials, runtime secrets, authentication implementation, or unrelated application code. Verified all four tools in the live production application using Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. Confirmed that build_briefing creates visible state that a human can reorder, remove, clear, and reset on reload. Documented the exact pre-challenge baseline and challenge-period extension. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes an application’s real domain capabilities instead of turning every button into a tool. Four carefully designed functions were enough to let an agent complete a meaningful governance research workflow while keeping the website responsible for its evidence, validation, and state. We also learned that human-agent collaboration does not require unlimited autonomy. A narrow, visible, and reversible action can provide significant value while preserving trust. The project demonstrated that a website can remain the authority for its data and actions while giving agents a structured, safer way to assist the person using it. What's next for AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk Future versions could add versioned governance snapshots, user-approved exports, role-specific briefing formats, change detection between reports, claim-level evidence tracing, and additional vetted records. A private editorial pipeline could monitor an approved source registry, identify candidate developments, and route them for human verification before they enter a published snapshot. Any live ingestion, persistent storage, customer-specific workspace, or external action would require separate security, privacy, and editorial review. title: PlanOnIt
pitch: PlanOnIt gives a WebMCP agent real tools to plan your evening out — film, transport, dinner — while you keep the final approval.
about_excerpt: PlanOnIt gives a WebMCP agent real tools to plan your evening out — film, transport, dinner — while you keep the final approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a small, concrete domain to actually test what WebMCP makes possible, instead of a demo that just claims an agent did something. Planning a night out — a film, then dinner after — is a real multi-constraint problem: the showtime fixes the cinema, the cinema fixes the route, the route decides how much time is really left before the table, and every one of those choices moves the total cost. It's exactly the kind of thing an agent is good at grinding through and a person is good at approving. Most "agentic" demos I'd seen were either a chat box bolted onto a UI it couldn't see, or an agent with unchecked authority to just click "book." I wanted the version where the agent gets real capabilities and the person still holds the only button that matters. What it does PlanOnIt plans a real evening out in Dhaka — a film, the trip across the city, and dinner after — with an AI agent doing the tedious cross-referencing through 13 WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. The agent can search restaurants and showtimes, build a plan, check feasibility, calculate cost, and repair a plan a human edit just broke. It can never approve or reserve anything — that stays a real click in the UI, every time. Once approved, reservation is a genuine sandboxed transaction: a compare-and-swap against shared inventory, idempotent on retry, and it fails closed on conflict instead of quietly double-booking. How we built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite on the frontend, Zod for runtime validation, deployed as a static build to Vercel. The core decision was to build one domain layer ( src/domain.ts ) that both the human UI and the WebMCP tools call into — the same solver, the same nine feasibility checks, the same versioned mutations — so there's never a "friendly explanation for the person" that can quietly drift from "the raw check the agent gets." Every mutation carries an expectedVersion ; a stale write fails loudly with STALE_PLAN_VERSION instead of silently overwriting someone else's edit, whether that edit came from a human or another agent call. Same-origin tabs stay in sync through a Web Locks-backed compare-and-swap. Inventory sits inside a rolling two-week window computed off the real clock, so the demo never goes stale no matter when a judge opens it. Challenges we ran into The one I'm least proud of, and gladdest I caught before submitting: late in the build I found that a human could never manually pick a transport option — every click failed with "Transport option does not belong to the selected venue route." The agent's tools worked fine, and so did the auto-repair path, which made it easy to miss. It turned out the manual UI was resolving the cinema-to-restaurant route with the two location IDs swapped, and since each direction generates its own distinct set of transport-option IDs, the buttons on screen were always offering IDs from the wrong route object. It only ever broke the human path — a good reminder that "the agent's tools work" and "the manual UI works" are two separate claims, and testing one doesn't verify the other. I added a regression test that reproduces the exact failure so it can't come back silently. Building a reservation that's an actual transaction, not just a returned success string, was its own challenge: idempotency keys are bound to the reservation's content fingerprint, not just a request ID, so a retry after a dropped connection can't accidentally create a second booking, and a replayed or forged confirmation can't be pointed at a different reservation. And a last-minute one that had nothing to do with code: my original LICENSE restricted commercial use without permission, which meant it wasn't actually an open-source license, even though I'd always intended it to be. Caught and fixed to MIT before submission — "open source" has to be literally detectable, not just intended. Accomplishments that we're proud of 198 automated tests plus 21 real-browser Playwright tests, covering adversarial input, concurrency, the full reservation lifecycle, and idempotency — not just the happy path. The evaluation-symmetry property: the UI's "why isn't this plan valid yet" and the agent's validate_plan tool result are always the same function call against the same state. There's no second copy of the business logic that could quietly disagree with the first. Approval isn't gated by a permission check the agent could theoretically satisfy — it's architecturally absent from the tool surface. No WebMCP tool touches approval at all. Shipping with no login requirement, on purpose. It would have been easy to bolt on accounts to look more "complete," but this build doesn't actually need cross-device sync to do its job, so I didn't fake it. What we learned That "the agent works" has to be tested completely separately from "the human path works" — they share code, but a single reversed argument can break only one of them, silently. That documentation drifts fast: numbers like "12 tools" or "eight checks" written once during development go stale the moment the code moves on, and are worth re-deriving from the running code rather than trusting memory. And that the strongest trust story for an agentic feature isn't a more polite prompt — it's an architectural boundary the agent literally cannot cross, like approval never being expressed as a tool at all. What's next for PlanOnIt A real server-authoritative reservation boundary. The extension point already exists ( RemoteReservationAuthority in src/authority.ts ), but no concrete server ships in this build — a public browser bundle can't hold a shared bearer secret without a real per-user session, and I'd rather ship nothing than ship authentication theater. Real inventory behind the restaurants, cinemas, and routes, in place of the Dhaka sandbox data. A repair flow that explains the alternatives it considered and rejected, not just the plan it landed on.
