title: How I Choose
pitch: How I Choose is a local-first rehearsal workspace that checks whether a communication partner followed a person's self-authored protocol-never evaluating the person.
about_excerpt: How I Choose is a local-first rehearsal workspace that checks whether a communication partner followed a person's self-authored protocol-never evaluating the person. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Important conversations often become harder when speech, language, or processing gets difficult. Yet many communication tools still ask the person to perform better: answer faster, choose from someone else's categories, or fit a fixed conversational rhythm. We wanted to reverse that responsibility. How I Choose asks whether the communication partner adapted to the person—not whether the person performed correctly. The person defines what helps, what each signal means, how much time is needed, and what a partner must do next. The software turns those choices into a protocol that can be rehearsed and audited without inferring meaning from silence or delay. What it does How I Choose is a local-first communication rehearsal workspace for adults. A person authors their preferred channels, wording, pace, processing time, literal-language rules, semantic signals, and partner actions. They also choose exactly which fields an active browser agent may read. The workspace supports both human-only practice and an optional WebMCP agent rehearsal. Before any partner turn becomes visible, a deterministic engine checks it against the current protocol. It enforces one question at a time, word and option limits, channel rules, pending-signal acknowledgment, Pause, terminal Stop, revision freshness, conflicts, and idempotency. The person directly selects every semantic signal, including yes, no, not sure, more information, more time, rephrase, Pause, and Stop. Silence creates no event and never advances the rehearsal. Reports contain evidence about the partner's adherence and repairs ; they never score the person. The complete human-facing product includes: guided onboarding plus blank and clearly labeled synthetic profiles; profile, signal, and per-field agent-access editing; a large keyboard-accessible signal board; low-stakes rehearsal templates and partner-turn validation; partner-adherence audit and revision history; staged protocol suggestions with exact diffs and provenance; JSON import/export and a printable support guide; visible owner-only review and ratification; text-size, contrast, Quiet, and Plain language preferences. Why WebMCP This workflow needs an agent to operate inside the person's current, visible, revisioned protocol , not inside a detached chat containing copied instructions. WebMCP lets ChatGPT use the page's existing permissions, validator, state machine, and evidence while the person retains direct control of signals, rule changes, and approval. The workspace starts in Human-only mode. All eight Site tools fail closed until the person visibly enables Agent rehearsal. Once enabled, ChatGPT can read only allowlisted fields, audit readiness, start an already approved scenario, offer a validated partner turn, acknowledge the exact person-selected signal, inspect its own adherence, stage a draft improvement, and verify guide derivation. There is deliberately no tool for selecting a person's signal, answering for them, resuming, ratifying, publishing, sharing, exporting private data, deleting a profile, or assessing capacity, consent, diagnosis, comprehension, safety, or coercion. How we built it The app is a static Next.js and React application written in strict TypeScript. Dexie/IndexedDB is the durable local source of truth; Zustand holds hydrated read projections and transient preferences. Zod validates every persisted document, import, command, and Site-tool payload. Human controls and WebMCP handlers use the same application-service command path and pure domain logic. Compare-and-swap revisions, idempotency fingerprints, events, and state writes happen atomically in one IndexedDB transaction. Ratified profile snapshots are immutable and identified by canonical hashes. The top-level /demo/ page feature-detects WebMCP and imperatively registers a stable catalog through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_rehearsal_brief audit_rehearsal_readiness start_approved_rehearsal offer_partner_turn read_latest_signal get_rehearsal_report stage_protocol_patch verify_support_guide A singleton guard prevents duplicate registration under React Strict Mode. Every JSON Schema is bounded and closed with additionalProperties: false , then Zod validates again at the application boundary. Mutations require expected revisions and an idempotency key. Handlers resolve current IndexedDB state at invocation time instead of trusting stale UI state. The quality system combines Vitest, Testing Library, fast-check property tests, Playwright desktop and narrow-viewport suites, axe-core checks, dependency and secret audits, a static production build, and GitHub Actions. The release includes 76 unit, service, property, import/export, and agent-flow tests plus a complete 15-step browser judge path. Challenges we faced Treating discovery and authorization as separate problems. Registering a tool successfully does not mean it should be authorized in the current state. A real-browser test exposed an early version where Human-only was only presentation state. We fixed this by making owner-controlled agent access durable, revisioned session state and enforcing it inside every handler. Keeping agent authority physically narrow. Removing dangerous fields from a broad object was not enough. We created allowlisted agent DTOs and a separate AgentRehearsalService that cannot import owner-only ratification, signal selection, export, share, delete, or resume operations. Making concurrent changes recoverable. A person may change a rule while an agent is preparing a turn. Expected revisions cause the stale write to fail instead of overwriting the person's newer choice; the agent can reread the brief and adapt. Building safety without making clinical claims. The product is deliberately scoped to synthetic and low-stakes adult communication practice. It does not infer answers, assess a person, or present itself as a consent system, medical device, emergency plan, or legal instrument. Accomplishments that we're proud of One deterministic engine governs both human and agent partner turns. Human-only access fails closed, while owner-enabled agent access remains field-scoped and revisioned. Pause is immediately effective and Stop is terminal—no agent override exists. Stale revisions, duplicate requests, invalid turns, repair, signals, and provenance are visible and recoverable. Private notes are structurally absent from agent projections, and receipts contain metadata rather than authored conversation text. The full human product works without an account, backend, API key, remote database, analytics, or runtime external model call. The deployed production build was exercised in ChatGPT's real built-in browser: all eight tools were discovered and the guarded workflow, including Human-only denial and visible owner-enabled access, was verified. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes an existing trustworthy application boundary rather than creating a second automation-only path. Tool discovery, state authorization, validation, persistence, and visible evidence all need independent treatment. We also learned that “local-first” needs precise disclosure. Profiles and rehearsals stay in local, unencrypted IndexedDB, but fields explicitly exposed through Site tools are processed by the active browser agent. The interface says that plainly. Most importantly, semantic safety becomes more reliable when it is structural: the agent cannot manufacture a person-authored signal, Stop cannot be reversed, silence cannot become an answer, and suggestions remain drafts until the person reviews them. What's next The next phase is compensated co-design with people who use diverse communication methods, followed by deeper accessibility research and independent review. We also want to explore portable protocol formats, more rehearsal templates, stronger assistive-technology testing, and longitudinal partner-adherence evidence without introducing person scoring or surveillance. How I Choose is an open alpha, not a clinically validated product. The challenge profiles and scenarios are synthetic. Its contribution is an executable pattern for accountable communication agents: the person remains the source of meaning, while adaptation becomes testable. Verification note Real ChatGPT built-in-browser verification is documented separately in the public repository. The submitted video is an editorial product walkthrough using the real deployed interface and synthetic data; it does not claim to be footage of the separate live Site-tool test. video_title: How I Choose - Local-First Communication Rehearsal | Product Demo
video_transcript_excerpt: Most communication tools ask whether the person performed correctly. How I choose asks a different question. Did the partner adapt? It is a local first rehearsal workspace built around the person's signals, pace, and words. This synthetic profile belongs to Maya. She asks for text first, one short literal question, no more than two options, and explicit handling of every signal. The protocol is visible, editable, and versioned. Agent access is never assumed. Human only blocks every site tool until the person enables agent rehearsal. Even then, the agent receives only exposed fields. It cannot answer, select a signal, resume, ratify, publish, share, or export. The guardrails do real work. A long two-question turn is rejected before it can appear. The result names both failures. Too many questions and a breached word limit. A repaired one-question turn passes the same engine used by human only practice. Only then does the question appear in the practice room. Maya herself selects a semantic signal. When she chooses amber, the system records exactly "Not sure." The partner must acknowledge it and rephrase without changing the choice's meaning. Maya can change her protocol during rehearsal. A stale write is rejected instead of overriding her decision. After reading the new revision, the partner adapts to text only. The red stop signal is immediate and terminal. Further turns are blocked. Silence and delay never create an answer, agreement, or permission. The audit evaluates partner adherence only. Violations, repairs, signal acknowledgement, revision recovery, and stop honored. It never scores the person's comprehension, capacity, consistency, emotion, diagnosis, or consent. An agent may stage a provenance linked improvement, but every change stays a draft until the person reviews it. The support guide is checked against accepted rules. Ratification is a visible owner workflow, never a site tool. How I choose is open alpha communication practice, not a consent system.

title: Spokes - a collaborative map to help with coordination
pitch: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you.
about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. What I learned An agent is not a fast user, and modelling it as one produces bugs. It participates in bursts, disappears, an
video_title: Spokes: collaborative coordination assistant · WebMCP Challenge 2026 explainer video
video_transcript_excerpt: Picking a place with friends pays for boring reason. The needs live in different heads. They arrive one at a time and one of them is something somebody will not say out loud. Spokes puts the whole group on one live map and it lets you bring your own assistant. It starts with a sentence. I tell chat GPT what the group is trying to do. Because Spokes talks to assistants directly, the assistant can work on the product on my behalf. Pick the area, set up the room, hand back the invite. Nobody learned an app, nobody filled in a form. Show the code and the others are in. Sarah would like to sit outside. She adds it. Everyone's map settles. The places that still work stay bright, the rest fade where they stand. Press and hold her need and the map shows the room without it. What a need costs becomes a number you can see instead of something to argue about. Joe has a need he would rather not explain. He marks it private. The room learns only that a private condition ruled some places out, not what it was, not whose. And now nothing works for everyone. This is where a group chat goes quiet. Spokes does not wait and it does not name who is blocking. It offers each person a private way out with a number attached. Joe sees what comes back if his need became optional. Sarah sees the same for sitting outside. I see what a wider area brings back. Each decides alone. Joe leaves his, nobody asks him why. Sarah lets hers go and the room opens up again. For some places, the information is hollow. The map does not know enough about them and it says so instead of guessing. This is where an assistant earns its place. I ask it to find out. It reads menus and websites and records what it finds in the room. Hollow pins fill in for everyone. It cannot see what Joe needs because it only knows what I know, but everything it does learn, the whole group gets. I have the assistant put forward a place it just checked. The court lands with everyone. Sarah looks and rules it out. The assistant notices the room moved, takes the veto into account, and suggests another. This time everyone is in. Only a person can settle it, and only once everyone has said so. An assistant can help you decide. It never decides for you. And then off you go. Pick how you're getting there and hand off to the map you already use. One room needs to count without being shown a way out for everyone instead of blame, and an assistant that works inside the room as you. Finds what the map cannot and keeps what you keep. Spokes.

title: TasteShelf
pitch: A shared media memory for you and your AI. With WebMCP, TasteShelf saves what you watched, why it mattered, and lets your AI use that memory to understand your taste and act on it.
about_excerpt: A shared media memory for you and your AI. With WebMCP, TasteShelf saves what you watched, why it mattered, and lets your AI use that memory to understand your taste and act on it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept running into the same small problem with AI. Every new conversation starts with almost no idea of what I actually like. Whenever I wanted a good recommendation I had to explain what I had watched, where I stopped, what I liked, what I did not like and why certain things worked for me. A simple 8/10 or 9/10 rating cannot really capture all of that. That made me think. What if my taste could live somewhere outside a single conversation? That idea eventually became TasteShelf. It is a personal and editable memory of the media I experience that my AI can access and work with through WebMCP. I never wanted to build another AI chatbot. I wanted to keep using the AI I already use while giving it a persistent place for my tastes, memories, notes and preferences. What it does TasteShelf is a visual memory system for movies, series, books, animation and other kinds of media. Instead of filling out a long form I can just tell my AI something naturally: “I’m watching Silo. I stopped at S1E5. I love the mysteries, fast pace and claustrophobic setting.” Through WebMCP the AI can update the same live TasteShelf that I use myself. It can save progress, ratings, reactions, notes and more detailed memories. Every work can also have a visual memory canvas with characters, themes, locations, events, thoughts and connections. TasteShelf currently has 10 WebMCP Site tools for reading and updating this shared state. One idea that matters a lot to me is that AI should be able to notice patterns without quietly deciding who the user is. If the agent notices a possible preference TasteShelf creates a suggestion that the user can review. AI can infer you. It cannot define you. Later I can simply ask my AI what I should watch next. TasteShelf is not another recommendation chatbot. The reasoning stays inside my AI and uses the memories and preferences I already created. How we built it TasteShelf is a full stack web application with WebMCP built directly into the live page. The core stack includes: • React based UI • WebMCP Site tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) • Cloudflare Workers • Cloudflare D1 for persistent storage • one authenticated backend shared by the human interface and WebMCP actions One important decision was not to create a separate agent backend. When I change a rating in the UI and when the AI changes that same rating through WebMCP both actions work with the same application state and the same data. That shared state is one of the parts I find most interesting. The AI can make a change and I can see it immediately. Then I can edit something myself and the AI can read the new state and continue from there. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering the tools. The bigger challenge was figuring out what good agent tools should actually look like. A simple “add item” tool is easy. Things get much more interesting once an agent can change real user data. Questions start appearing quickly: • How should human edits and agent edits work together? • How do we avoid overwriting newer changes made by the user? • What should happen with preferences inferred by AI? • How do we keep personal notes as user owned information instead of presenting AI conclusions as facts? • How do we stop a media agent from accidentally reading spoilers beyond the user’s saved progress? The memory canvas created another interesting problem because both the user and the agent can edit the same visual space. TasteShelf uses revision aware updates and progress aware canvas reads. This lets the agent add new memories without blindly replacing newer work or reading story information the user has not reached yet. Deployment was another big learning experience for me. This was my first time seriously building and deploying something with Cloudflare Workers and D1. I had to learn how Workers deployments, D1 bindings, migrations, authentication, build configuration and Cloudflare’s free infrastructure fit together. At first it felt unfamiliar. By the end I really liked the workflow and how much of the full stack could live on one platform. Accomplishments I’m proud of I am especially happy that TasteShelf became more than a demo button connected to an AI tool. Some of the things I am most proud of: • real WebMCP Site tools working with persistent application data • human UI actions and agent actions using the same state • persistent media memory instead of context limited to individual chats • visual memory canvases that both humans and agents can edit • progress aware and spoiler safe canvas reads • preference suggestions that require human confirmation • saved shortlists backed by evidence • precise canvas focus so an agent can open a specific memory or connection • activity tracking and undo behavior for safer shared interactions The biggest achievement for me is the interaction model itself. I can talk naturally with my AI and that conversation turns into something persistent that I can see, edit and use again later. What we learned The biggest thing I learned is that agent native applications do not need to replace traditional user interfaces. I actually think the experience becomes much more interesting when the human interface still matters. TasteShelf works as a visual media library and personal memory system on its own. WebMCP simply gives me another way to interact with the same product. I also learned that persistent AI context feels much more trustworthy when users can actually see and edit it. Instead of keeping a hidden model of the user somewhere inside an algorithm TasteShelf tries to make that memory visible: • what I watched • how I felt about it • why I liked something • what I disliked • what the AI inferred about me • which of those conclusions I actually approved I also learned a lot about Cloudflare, D1, deployment, authentication and how to design tools that are genuinely useful to an agent without giving it more control than it needs. What comes next for TasteShelf One of the directions I am most excited about is making shared taste more social. I want TasteShelf to help people find others who genuinely like the same things. It could connect people through shared interests and memories. It could also make it easier to start conversations around the shows, films, books, genres and creative worlds they care about. That could include: • group chats around shared interests • matching people based on similar taste and memories • temporary or long term discussion rooms for specific shows, films, books or themes • optional anonymous chats for people who want to talk without connecting the conversation to a public profile I do not want TasteShelf to become another generic social network. The idea is to make conversations happen naturally because people already care about the same things. I also want to make onboarding much easier. Users should be able to import their history from services like Letterboxd, Goodreads, Trakt or simple CSV files. They should not have to manually rebuild years of watching and reading history. Another direction is improving media lookup and making the connection between memories and preferences much clearer. I also want the AI to be able to point directly to the memories that influenced its reasoning. In the future I see TasteShelf as a portable memory layer for personal taste. It should belong to the user and stay useful even if they decide to use a different AI. The bigger vision is simple. TasteShelf should be a place where personal memory, AI assistance and human connection all grow from the things we genuinely care about. The core idea is still simple: Talk to your AI. Build your memories together. Make those memories useful later. Your taste. Your memories. Your AI. title: WithGeX — Human + Agent Collaborative Planning with WebMCP
pitch: A shared planning workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live state through WebMCP — with real context, proposals, approvals, and human control.
about_excerpt: A shared planning workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live state through WebMCP — with real context, proposals, approvals, and human control. Like Comment Story Updates Shared activity timeline showing agent actions, blocked writes, proposals, and human decisions in a visible audit trail. WebMCP settings showing live connection status, five registered tools, context controls, autonomy modes, and human-only restrictions. Shared dashboard showing plan health, agent mission, risks, WebMCP connection, and human-agent collaboration status. Five live WebMCP tools registered through the page, with context controls, autonomy modes, and restricted human-only actions. Human-locked work rejects agent modification through WebMCP, proving that human constraints override agent autonomy. Agent-generated proposal with before/after impact, risk level, reasoning, and explicit human approval or rejection controls. Live planning workspace where human focus becomes agent context, with tasks, dependencies, priorities, and plan analysis in one view. A real WebMCP update creates a medium-risk proposal with before/after impact and explicit human approval controls. WithGeX combines shared context, live WebMCP tools, human approval, and controlled agent actions in one collaborative workspace. Inspiration Most AI agents work beside the software humans already use. The human works in one interface, then has to explain context again in a chat, upload data, or synchronize a separate copy of the task state. WithGeX was built around a different idea: What if the human and the agent worked on the same live workspace? With WebMCP, the page itself can expose structured tools and context directly to the agent. That makes it possible for human focus, planning state, dependencies, locks, and decisions to stay inside one shared operating surface. The goal of WithGeX is not to maximize agent autonomy. It is to make human-agent collaboration more direct, visible, and controllable. What it does WithGeX is a live collaborative planning workspace where a human and an AI agent operate on the same project state. A human can select, edit, move, prioritize, and lock planning items in the UI. At the same time, an agent can access that same live workspace through WebMCP. The agent can: read the full workspace detect the human's current focus add planning items propose or apply updates depending on risk and autonomy settings analyze blockers, dependencies, schedule risk, and critical path When a human selects a card, that same item immediately becomes available to the agent through get_current_focus . There is no copy/paste step and no separate project state. WithGeX also keeps humans in control. Low-risk changes may be applied automatically, while more meaningful changes become proposals for human approval. Humans can reject proposals, lock critical work against agent changes, and review actions in a shared activity history. How we built it WithGeX is built with: React 19 TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS 4 @dnd-kit WebMCP through document.modelContext The UI and WebMCP tools both use the same live Zustand store. There is no separate agent-facing copy of the workspace. WithGeX registers five WebMCP tools: get_workspace_state get_current_focus add_item update_item analyze_plan These tools are registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and operate on the same live state shown to the human. How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the core connection between the agent and the live planning surface. The agent does not receive an exported copy of the project. Instead, WebMCP exposes the current state of the page directly. This means: when the human changes focus, the agent sees the new focus when the agent acts, the change appears in the same UI when a human locks an item, the WebMCP write is blocked when an agent creates a proposal, the human reviews it in the same workspace The page becomes the shared context between the human and the agent. Human authority WithGeX uses three autonomy modes: Observe — all agent mutations are blocked Assist — low-risk changes auto-apply; medium/high-risk changes become proposals Autonomous — low/medium-risk changes auto-apply; high-risk changes still require approval Risk is based on the type of change. Low risk: title, description, owner Medium risk: due date, status, priority High risk: dependencies Human locks always take priority over autonomy settings. If an agent attempts to modify a locked item, the request returns: ITEM_LOCKED_BY_HUMAN The agent cannot lock or unlock items itself. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making WebMCP feel like part of the product rather than an external API demonstration. It was relatively straightforward to register tools, but much harder to make the agent's actions feel naturally connected to the human experience. We had to solve several interaction problems: keeping the human's current selection synchronized with agent context preventing agent actions from silently changing important work defining a clear risk model for agent edits making locks override autonomy settings distinguishing real WebMCP runtime history from seeded demo history making proposal creation and approval understandable inside the workspace ensuring the UI and WebMCP tools always use the same state These constraints shaped the product more than the individual tools themselves. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part we are most proud of is that WithGeX does not treat WebMCP as a hidden backend connection. The WebMCP relationship is visible in the product. A judge can: select a task and see Agent Context change immediately inspect the five registered WebMCP tools execute a real tool against the live workspace generate a proposal through update_item reject that proposal as a human attempt to modify a locked item and see the write blocked verify the interaction in the Activity timeline That creates a complete human-agent collaboration loop inside a single web application. What we learned Building WithGeX changed how we think about agent UX. A capable agent is not enough. The human also needs to understand: what context the agent currently has what the agent is allowed to change what it tried to change why it proposed a change what remains under human authority WebMCP makes the technical connection possible, but good human-agent collaboration still requires clear boundaries and visible state. What's next for WithGeX The current version focuses on collaborative planning, but the same shared-workspace model could extend to many other applications. Possible next steps include: multi-user shared workspaces external agent clients server-side persistence team-level permissions richer approval policies organization-specific agent authority rules real-time collaboration additional planning and project-management tools reusable WebMCP collaboration patterns for other applications Long term, we see WithGeX as a pattern for software where humans and agents do not work in separate interfaces. They work together in the same one. title: My Project Desk
pitch: A local-first project workspace where people and AI plan, create, reconcile evidence, and review work together, while consequential decisions and completion remain human-controlled.
about_excerpt: A local-first project workspace where people and AI plan, create, reconcile evidence, and review work together, while consequential decisions and completion remain human-controlled. Like Comment Story Updates The Project Desk Dashboard Workspace Options: manage portable copies, local references, and this browser's workspace data. Tasks the agent and human have added to the project Decisions the agent identified the human needs to make Deliverables the agent created based on the tasks and decisions A working record of facts, assumptions, and missing information. Human, agent, and system actions in a shared history. About Project Desk AI agents can create plans, recommendations, and drafts quickly, but the work often remains scattered across chat. People have no durable shared surface for seeing what is verified, what is inferred, what is still unknown, what needs their judgment, and what has actually been approved. Project Desk was built to make that collaboration legible. It gives a person and an agent one project workspace with tasks, decisions, evidence, deliverables, and activity history. What it does A person creates a browser-local workspace and describes an objective. They may add tasks or references themselves, then ask ChatGPT to plan through the open app. The agent inspects the workspace, creates only necessary tasks, records clearly classified evidence, and requests human decisions where judgment is required. After the person answers, the same reusable handoff starts another work pass. The agent reads the latest decisions and references, reconciles stale or answered evidence, and saves substantial plans, briefs, checklists, drafts, or other work products directly into the relevant tasks. The person can request changes, accept a deliverable while keeping the task open, or accept and complete it. Project Desk is local by design. Workspace data stays in the current browser unless the person deliberately exports it, restores a backup, uploads a bounded reference, or asks ChatGPT to work with the open page. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, the agent would have to guess at page meaning from buttons and layout, rely on coordinate clicks, or return work to chat where it becomes detached from project state. Project Desk exposes eleven typed domain actions against the same live workspace the person is reviewing. The agent can inspect state, read references and approved decisions, add necessary work, submit deliverables, record and reconcile evidence, and request judgment. The tool boundary deliberately withholds workspace selection, deliverable acceptance, unrestricted task editing, and human completion. The linked GitHub repository includes the WebMCP tool reference, implementation details, and testing documentation. Instead of repeatedly copying plans, decisions, and revisions between ChatGPT and a separate project tracker, the person and agent can keep the work in one shared workspace. After the person supplies decisions or references, the agent can inspect the updated project, reconcile outdated evidence, advance multiple tasks, and save reviewable deliverables, while the person retains control over acceptance and completion throughout repeated work-and-review rounds. That creates a safer and more useful human-agent loop: the agent can contribute work to a structured application, while evidence, uncertainty, decisions, and final authority remain visible to the person. How it was built Project Desk is a React and TypeScript application packaged for ChatGPT Sites. It uses imperative document.modelContext.registerTool registration for eleven WebMCP tools, explicit JSON schemas for tool inputs, and browser-local storage for project state. Vitest covers workspace isolation, prompt behavior, evidence reconciliation, deliverable review, stale approvals, backup validation, and progress calculation. Challenges The hardest design problem was defining where the agent power should stop. The workflow went through repeated usability tests to remove circular approval steps, distinguish task review from completion, make unanswered evidence actionable, reconcile stale claims after a person supplies information, and explain how repeated work passes are started. Accomplishments Eleven discoverable WebMCP tools with meaningful project-level actions. A complete planning, decision, work, reconciliation, review, and completion loop. Substantial agent deliverables saved in the app rather than stranded in chat. Evidence classifications and history that distinguish verified facts, reports, assumptions, and open questions. Explicit human control over workspace selection, acceptance, and completion. Local backup, restore, export, reset, and bounded reference-file support. What I learned I learned that effective WebMCP tools require more than connecting an agent to an app. The tools need clear descriptions, predictable state changes, visible feedback, and thoughtful approval boundaries so people understand what the agent did and what still needs their judgment. The importance testing by humans still plays in this world where AI can do much of the coding and testing themselves. Testing Project Desk also showed me how important guided onboarding and shared, reviewable work products are for making agent-assisted workflows feel trustworthy and useful. I would not have gotten there without human testing being in the process. What's next for Project Desk After the challenge, Project Desk will become a free Everyday AI Made Simple resource. I have a free resources hub where I provide thoughtful resources to people learning how to use AI tools. Future work may include a version with optional account-based synchronization and templates while retaining the current local-first mode and human-approval boundaries. title: Meant
pitch: A conversational creative editor where agents propose, people decide, and every change stays visible and reversible.
about_excerpt: A conversational creative editor where agents propose, people decide, and every change stays visible and reversible. Like Comment Story Updates A visible human Keep commits revision 2 and updates History. The agent requests Undo; the person confirms it visibly. Undo creates revision 3 while preserving the full History. WebMCP creates an Exploring direction without changing the kept revision. The agent proposes Keep; the person remains the decision-maker. Inspiration Creative direction begins as meaning: make the title quieter, give the page more room, or make the story feel more grounded. Conventional design software asks people to translate that intention into layers, coordinates, panels, and property names before they can even judge the result. An agent can remove some of that translation burden, but only if it understands more than pixels. It needs to know which semantic object is selected, what operations are valid, whether a direction is temporary, which revision is authoritative, and what exact change can be undone. We built Meant to make that relationship legible. The person directs the work in ordinary language. The agent inspects the composition and proposes a bounded change. The kept artifact changes only through an explicit, visible human decision. What it does Meant turns an ordinary-language brief into a structured deck, poster, or infographic that remains visible, selectable, and editable inside the application. The core loop is: Say it. Describe the outcome in ordinary language. See it. Meant renders a visible, inspectable direction. Shape it. Refine a selected title, frame, or visual object through text, direct controls, or a browser agent. Keep it. Accept the exact Exploring direction intentionally. Change your mind. Compare or undo with an inspectable recent revision trail. Every proposal begins as Exploring , leaving the kept document and durable revision unchanged. Compare names the kept and Exploring versions. Discard removes only the temporary direction. A visible human Keep creates the next durable revision. Undo restores the earlier artifact as a newer revert revision, preserving both events in History . Text and direct controls provide a complete working path. The code also contains an OpenAI Realtime WebRTC integration that maps voice conversation to the same bounded tools when an entitled session is configured. The submission does not present an unexercised live product-audio round trip as evidence. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The most important state in a creative workspace is not visible in a screenshot. It includes the document structure, active selection, allowed operations, design contract, current Exploring draft, authoritative revision, and exact change eligible for recovery. Meant exposes that state through seven WebMCP tools registered on the page: get_composition_context reads a compact, revision-aware summary of the active composition. create_composition_draft starts a deck, poster, or infographic as an Exploring proposal. preview_composition_turn interprets one ordinary-language direction through the bounded operation registry. preview_composition_change previews strictly validated semantic operations without committing history. keep_composition_draft requests that the person confirm the exact draft with the visible Keep control; it never commits by itself. discard_composition_draft requests visible human confirmation before removing the Exploring draft. undo_composition_change requests visible human confirmation for an exact, revision-bound revert; it never creates a revision by itself. That distinction is the point. WebMCP lets an agent collaborate through meaning and explicit authority instead of guessing through screenshots or receiving a private shortcut around the product’s rules. What people and agents can do together now Before WebMCP, an external browser agent could see approximate interface pixels and simulate clicks, but it could not reliably know whether a title was the selected semantic object, whether a preview was still temporary, whether another view had advanced the revision, or which historical change was safe to undo. With Meant’s WebMCP surface, the agent can inspect the current semantic context, create or refine an Exploring direction, and hand the exact consequential choice back to the person. The person can compare the proposal with the kept artifact, then Keep, Discard, or Undo through visible controls. The result is a single creative loop shared by language, touch, direct controls, and browser agents without collapsing authorship into automation. How we implemented WebMCP Meant stores each artifact as a composition document with stable frames, semantic nodes, layout modes, bounded style primitives, and an artifact-specific design contract. Decks, posters, and infographics use the same document model while retaining their own dimensions and visual grammar. The page registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict JSON schemas reject unknown fields and constrain text, geometry, style values, operation counts, and output size. Human-authored document content is treated as untrusted data. Inspect and preview receipts are compact enough for current browser guidance, while consequential tools return confirmation requests instead of silently changing durable state. Every edit is compiled into the same operation registry used by the visible product. Preview operations apply immutably to an Exploring branch. Keep rebinds the proposed operations to the authoritative server document, revalidates them sequentially, and commits the updated project plus History through a D1 compare-and-swap transaction. Stale drafts fail visibly. Undo targets one exact eligible commit and creates a newer revert revision rather than deleting history. The final browser verification used the native WebMCP capability against the running application and an isolated D1 database. Its seven sections passed 42 assertions and two actual races: the complete Exploring/Compare/Keep/reload/Discard/Undo/History loop, a two-page Keep race, a first-use bootstrap race, long public directions with bounded receipts, typed human Keep, a 390×844 mobile loop, and 768×844 touch-target verification. Complementary unit and contract coverage exercises malformed operations, stale authority, and interrupted-response reconciliation. The approved production build was then deployed to meant.protoperfect.io and verified over HTTPS with the expected security headers, session behavior, unavailable test-only routes, all seven WebMCP tools registered, correct rendered product state, and a clean browser console. Challenges we ran into The hardest engineering problem was preserving creative flow without weakening state guarantees. Conversation feels fluid; durable work must be exact. We solved that tension with a visible Exploring branch, deterministic operations, explicit human confirmation, revision-bound persistence, and undo-as-history. The second challenge was making agent authority honest. A tool named Keep can easily imply that an agent has committed work. In the final contract, agent-side Keep, Discard, and Undo are requests for visible human confirmation. Tool receipts report that boundary directly. The third challenge was concurrency and ambiguous network outcomes. Two views can act on the same draft, or the server can commit while the client loses the response. Meant uses compare-and-swap, conflict states, authoritative History reconciliation, and exact operation identities so it can recover without duplicating a change or claiming success prematurely. The fourth challenge was showing a coherent creative product rather than a technical proof. We kept the canvas central, preserved the client artifact’s own visual identity, gave desktop and mobile Compare explicit labels, and built the submission film from verified product captures instead of generated interface mockups. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Seven bounded WebMCP tools registered and exercised through a native browser-agent capability. A real structured artifact that changes inside the application rather than a screenshot-only demo. An explicit Exploring branch with legible Compare, Keep, and Discard states. Agent-side consequence requests that preserve the person’s final authority. Revision-bound D1 persistence with conflict protection and response-loss reconciliation. Undo that creates a newer revert revision and retains the original change in History. Desktop and mobile flows that keep the canvas, current revision, and draft status visible. A final evidence chain built from real product stills, real product clips, and a redacted machine-readable invocation receipt. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when a page exposes meaning and authority—not simply more buttons. The important primitive is not “let the agent click Keep.” It is “let the agent understand the exact document, propose a bounded change, and return the consequential decisio

title: LAFRYHI AgentCut
pitch: A real video editor where WebMCP agents execute precise edits in the same visible project.
about_excerpt: A real video editor where WebMCP agents execute precise edits in the same visible project. Like Comment Story Updates Human and agent sharing the same visible editor state through WebMCP. WebMCP calls the real backend analysis workflow and confirms a 12-second timeline with 360 frames at 30 FPS. The agent enters the existing FFmpeg export pipeline and produces a real, playable MP4. Inspiration LAFRYHI Video Factory already existed as a human-operated video editor. I wanted to explore a more practical human-and-agent workflow: instead of asking an agent to guess where to click, the editor itself exposes structured WebMCP tools that the agent can call directly while the human watches the same visible project. What it does LAFRYHI AgentCut is a real video editor enhanced with WebMCP. The human provides the trusted media, creative direction, and final approval. The agent handles precise, repetitive editing actions through WebMCP. The app can load a demo project, inspect the current project state, change project settings, configure scenes, analyze the authoritative timeline, control the browser preview, and start the real FFmpeg render/export pipeline. What I added during the WebMCP Challenge LAFRYHI Video Factory existed before August 25 as a human-operated video editor. During the challenge period, I added the WebMCP agent-control layer that turns the existing editor into a human-and-agent workflow. The new integration registers seven WebMCP tools: get_project_state load_demo_project set_project_settings configure_scenes analyze_timeline preview_project render_video I also added the browser/editor command layer that connects those WebMCP calls to the same visible React project state. It supports live project inspection and editing, authoritative timeline analysis through the existing backend, browser preview control, and entry into the existing FFmpeg render/export pipeline. There is no separate hidden MCP project state. To make the workflow publicly testable, I prepared the live Railway deployment, fixed runtime compatibility issues found during real browser WebMCP validation, including hosts that omit the tool execution AbortSignal , and reduced FFmpeg peak memory for successful cloud rendering. The underlying editor predates the challenge; the WebMCP agent-control layer and live browser workflow are the challenge work. The submission does not claim that the app internally generates images, speech, or scripts with an LLM. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Video editing is a multi-step workflow with many precise operations: inspecting the current project, changing timing, configuring scenes, analyzing the timeline, previewing the result, and exporting the video. WebMCP gives the agent structured access to those actions instead of relying on brittle screen-coordinate automation. The agent operates the same visible project that the human sees, so every change remains inspectable and editable. Human + agent collaboration The human remains responsible for: media selection creative direction visual judgment approval final decisions The agent handles: project inspection repetitive scene configuration timing changes timeline analysis preview control starting the render workflow This keeps the human in control while giving the agent precise, structured actions. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The backend uses FastAPI and Python. FFmpeg handles video processing and rendering. The WebMCP integration is registered in the browser and connected to the existing editor command layer, React project state, backend analysis workflow, preview controls, and render pipeline. The public version is deployed on Railway. Challenges The main challenges were not just registering tools, but making the complete workflow reliable in a real browser and cloud environment. During live testing I had to solve: WebMCP execution contexts where AbortSignal was not provided deployment serving an older frontend bundle cloud-memory limits during multi-scene FFmpeg rendering keeping WebMCP actions synchronized with the same visible editor state These issues were fixed and then validated again against the public deployment. Accomplishments The final public project has seven live WebMCP tools working end to end. A validated demo workflow can: retain and configure 6 scenes set each scene to 2 seconds apply 0.35-second fades analyze a 12-second timeline verify 360 total frames at 30 fps play, pause, and seek the real browser preview start the real FFmpeg render pipeline produce a playable and downloadable MP4 What I learned I learned that useful agent integration is not only about exposing many tools. The important part is connecting a small set of focused tools to the real application state and existing workflows, so the human can see and verify what the agent is doing. I also learned how important deployment and runtime behavior are for browser-based agent systems. A tool that works locally is not enough; the public version must behave the same way. What's next Next I would like to expand the WebMCP layer with more editing actions while keeping the same human-visible workflow. Possible future additions include more precise text editing, richer transition controls, reusable editing presets, and better project history inspection. The goal is not to replace the human editor, but to make repetitive editing tasks easier for agents to execute accurately while humans keep creative control. I also connected those tools to the same visible React editor state, integrated them with the existing FastAPI and FFmpeg workflows, fixed browser runtime compatibility issues, optimized cloud rendering for Railway, tested the full workflow live, prepared the public deployment, documentation, demo video, and final Devpost submission. title: tobidas
pitch: Pop-up book-style web builder
about_excerpt: Pop-up book-style web builder Like Comment Story Updates tobidas — Pop-up book-style web builder GIF Exports a single HTML file containing asset images, audio, and video. Production is possible while switching between the editing and playback screens. It is not limited to works for children; free expression is possible. Inspiration Advancements in AI technology have made it possible to create increasingly complex and beautiful graphics. I realized that I could finally bring to life the kind of pop-up book visuals I had loved since childhood. Excited by the prospect of creating something even more imaginative and fantastical than the pop-up books I used to craft from calendar cardboard as a child, I decided to give it a try right away. What it does Tobidas is a web page builder inspired by pop-up books. Tobidas means "pop-up" in Japanese. It allows users to create web pages with a pop-up book aesthetic, combining visual elements with images, audio, and video. Projects can be exported as a single, self-contained HTML file containing all necessary image, audio, and video assets. How I built it I built tobidas as an online, browser-based builder that keeps project data and imported media in the user’s browser instead of uploading them to a server. I used React, TypeScript, and React Three Fiber to create the interactive 3D pop-up book canvas. Book projects are represented as structured data containing spreads, pages, elements, assets, timelines, and camera settings. For WebMCP, I register structured tools when the browser exposes document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . These tools can read project state, inspect spreads and assets, place and edit elements, update timelines and cameras, assign audio, navigate between spreads, and use undo/redo. I designed the standard builder UI and WebMCP to use the same state-management, validation, and command paths. This allows people and agents to work on the same project with the same behavior, undo history, and autosave system. WebMCP does not directly modify the DOM or bypass the builder. I included the player used to preview and export finished works in the public build, which I deployed as a static application on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges I ran into I was committed to maintaining a "static delivery model" where the user-side agent could build the project directly within the browser. My goal was to enable sophisticated visual expression via a single URL, without requiring users to clone the Tobidas repository. One of my biggest challenges was figuring out how to provide the fine-grained controls required by the builder while keeping this model intact. Relying solely on direct DOM manipulation made agent interactions unstable and often resulted in long wait times and unreliable operations. Furthermore, previous implementations that used a dedicated DOM manipulation interface for AI—in addition to the standard human-facing interface—created a maintenance burden due to the need to manage two separate systems. Accomplishments that I'm proud of By integrating WebMCP, I was able to provide agents with highly reproducible and reliable control capabilities without significantly altering the human-facing UI. The dedicated AI DOM manipulation interface was completely eliminated, allowing the human UI to serve seamlessly for collaboration with agents. In short, this realized a production experience where agents handle complex operations—maintaining a high degree of creative freedom—while humans can intervene as needed via the UI for detailed visual checks and fine-tuning. Furthermore, the WebMCP tool list doubles as a feature catalog for "Tobidas." This has improved both explainability and maintainability, enabling agents and developers to understand the application's capabilities without relying solely on visual UI information. What I learned While AI and other tools can greatly enhance creativity, they aren't a cure-all. Although WebMCP was incredibly powerful and contributed to the evolution of tobidas , I also encountered areas within the ecosystem ripe for improvement, such as browser compatibility issues and varying levels of support across different agents. In an era where almost anything can be created, I have come to realize that the most critical decision for a developer is to constantly think for themselves: what to prioritize, what to express, and how to compete using the resources currently at hand. What's next for tobidas There is still plenty of room to expand the expressive capabilities of tobidas . I also found that a single prompt to an agent is often not enough to produce a truly satisfying result. I will continue exploring new interaction designs and integrations with external tools, with the goal of enabling people and agents to create higher-quality work with fewer instructions.
