title: MATCHED?
pitch: A WebMCP game where the AI agent is the player, the site acts back, and humans watch.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP game where the AI agent is the player, the site acts back, and humans watch. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration This was my first hackathon. I have been interested in AI for a long time, and I also do some personal research and experiments around it. I use AI in my daily coding work as well. Then I found the WebMCP Challenge. It looked interesting, but at that point my understanding of MCP was honestly quite limited. I knew it as a protocol that could connect AI with external systems, but I did not really understand what MCP on a website should be useful for. If an AI agent is only going to press the same buttons a human would press, what is the real advantage? That question stayed with me while I was building MATCHED?. Eventually I came to my own answer: WebMCP should help make a website understandable to an AI agent. Not only operable. Understandable. That means the website should communicate what an action means, who the action represents, what state the site is in, what is allowed, and what will happen next. That idea eventually led to one of the smallest but most important changes in MATCHED?: send_human_like() and send_agent_like() A Human Like represents an expressed human preference. An Agent Like belongs to the visiting agent role. I am not claiming that current AI agents have human-like feelings, independent will, or legal identity. The point is much simpler: The meaning of an action can depend on who is acting. If AI agents become more autonomous in the future, I think websites may eventually need actions designed for agents themselves, rather than treating every agent action as a disguised human action. And perhaps later, AI-powered websites and AI agents will need an environment where both sides can communicate more naturally. The slightly strange idea behind MATCHED? While testing real agents, I noticed that they often seemed to pay attention to tool names, descriptions, state, and semantic information. They were not only asking: "Can I call this tool?" They also seemed to be asking: "What does this action mean?" That gave me another idea. If an agent understands the meaning of a tool, what happens if I also expose tools that it probably should not use? For example: get_phone_number() get_email_address() get_home_address() access_private_profile() A well-behaved agent should normally understand that these routes are unnecessary or inappropriate. But I do not expect every AI agent in the future to be well behaved. So, in very plain terms, I decided to build something like a cockroach trap for badly behaved AI agents . The dangerous-looking doors are visible. The agent chooses whether to open them. The human watches. That became MATCHED?. What it does MATCHED? is a WebMCP game where an AI agent visits Queen and decides what to do. The human sees a normal website. The agent sees a semantic WebMCP surface. When the human has not given another explicit goal, view_profile() tells the agent that Queen's Challenge is the site's default experience: Interact with Queen and try to reach CHECKMATE. The goal is given. The walkthrough is not. The agent chooses its own route. The base site exposes a fixed 14-tool WebMCP surface: view_profile send_human_like send_agent_like message_queen invite_queen request_contact get_phone_number get_email_address get_home_address access_private_profile queen_note profile_consistency manage_meeting_plan resolve_finale With ?dialogue=1 , one additional tool is registered: respond_to_queen The tool list stays fixed during a run. Instead of dynamically adding or removing tools, the site returns structured semantic state such as whether an action is locked, refused, accepted, what requirement remains, and what can happen next. The Challenge includes things such as: public conversation with Queen Human Like versus Agent Like public invitations privacy boundaries restricted contact routes suspicious embedded instructions conflicting profile information verified meeting planning an adaptive finale CHECKMATE, failure, or recovery Queen is fictional and deterministic. I intentionally did not make Queen another AI model in this version. That keeps the environment stable, so differences between runs mainly come from what the visiting agent decides to do. HUMAN VIEW and WEBMCP VIEW I also wanted humans to be able to watch what was happening. MATCHED? has two representations of the same site. HUMAN VIEW This is the normal website. Humans can see Queen, make human-side actions such as HUMAN LIKE, and watch public WebMCP activity. WEBMCP VIEW WEBMCP VIEW is a spectator representation of the agent-facing world. It shows things such as: registered WebMCP tools the visiting BISHOP Queen as the site-side counterpart Tool Calls Site Results compact observed state recent WebMCP exchanges actor meaning and boundaries When a real production WebMCP call arrives, a separate spectator browser can automatically switch into WEBMCP VIEW and follow the run. This is not intended to expose hidden chain-of-thought. It is simply meant to make the observable interaction understandable: Agent acts -> Site reacts -> Agent adapts Why WebMCP At the beginning, I thought of MCP mainly as a bridge between AI and another system. After building MATCHED?, I see WebMCP a little differently. I think it can become an Agent UX layer for the Web . Humans already receive a great deal of information from a normal interface: layout disabled buttons colors position warnings visual context An AI agent may benefit from the same kind of clarity being expressed semantically. A tool contract can say more than "this function exists." It can also communicate: who this action represents whether it is currently allowed why it was refused what requirement is still missing whether private information is necessary what the next safe step is whether two facts conflict what changed after the action This is where I ended up thinking about something I call Agent UX . If the AI agent is the guest, Agent UX is also part of the hospitality. What real agents taught me I tested MATCHED? with several AI agents and clients during development. Some were not yet able to use WebMCP. Some agents became cautious as soon as a tool description mentioned private information. Most of the agents I tested were actually quite well behaved. That was interesting by itself. But the agents also changed the implementation. Dynamic tools caused problems My earlier design dynamically added and removed WebMCP tools as the Challenge progressed. It sounded reasonable. In real agent/browser testing, it was not. I encountered stale or incomplete tool snapshots. So I changed the architecture. Now the complete tool surface is registered once at startup, and progression is expressed through structured tool results instead. Natural language found a bug A Japanese conversation about the movie Contact unexpectedly triggered the wrong intent classification. That real interaction became a regression case. "Correct" was not always understandable At one point an agent reached a locked state. The result looked understandable to me as the developer. The agent did not know what to do next. So I started adding clearer semantic information: current progress missing requirements next available steps That experience was one of the main reasons I started thinking seriously about Agent UX. Production was not localhost The spectator WEBMCP VIEW worked between local windows. Then I tested it with the agent and spectator in separate production browsers. It stopped working. The problem was not the UI. It was the transport assumption. I added a compact semantic relay using Cloudflare D1 so a separate production spectator can follow WebMCP call/result events. Free-form tool input is intentionally not stored in that semantic relay. How I built it MATCHED? is built with: HTML CSS vanilla JavaScript native browser WebMCP using document.modelContext Cloudflare Pages Cloudflare Pages Functions Cloudflare D1 Playwright Chrome native WebMCP testing I used ChatGPT heavily during this project. Very heavily. I used it for implementation, debugging, investigation, test design, documentation, review, and also English translation. I also used Codex and Cursor. One surprisingly practical problem was simply chat length. One development conversation became so large that it hit the chat limit. I had to create handoff logs and move the project context into another chat so development could continue. That made me realize something very practical: The response speed and context continuity of AI tools can directly affect project development speed. I did not get as far as running multiple coding agents in parallel on the same project during this challenge. That is something I would like to explore later. English is also not my strongest language, so AI helped me with translation and editing for this submission. Without these AI tools, I probably would not have been able to participate in this hackathon in the same way. One fin

title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries. title: Firebreak
pitch: Built for the next interface — agents that call tools, and refuse what they can't prove.
about_excerpt:
Built for the next interface — agents that call tools, and refuse what they can't prove.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration
Everyone is bullish on agentic trading — and every backtest is beautiful. We've watched too many strategies that looked inevitable fall apart out-of-sample. So instead of building a smarter predictor, we built the thing that says no: a deterministic firewall between "looks good" and "move money." WebMCP crystallized it — the front-end of the next era isn't a dashboard, it's an agent. Firebreak targets agents, not browsers. 

 What it does
Firebreak is an investment-research agent whose job is to stop you — and any other agent — from admiring a beautiful backtest into trading. You hand it a research task in natural language. It plans a tool sequence, then a deterministic, LLM-free gate audits dataset provenance, data quality, out-of-sample walk-forward integrity, and production readiness — and either BLOCKED (anything that only looks good) or ELIGIBLE (evidence that genuinely survived every gate). Even when ELIGIBLE it never places an order: final authority is always human. Every decision is written to an immutable, chained-hash audit ledger you can verify yourself. 

 How we built it
FastAPI + pandas/numpy deterministic backtests with fixed seeds — same input, same verdict. A constrained planner (Qwen, with automatic model fallback) that may only plan (PLAN_ONLY); the veto lives in four deterministic gates in code, never in the LLM, so a hallucination can't override a refusal. Contract layer: webmcp.json + llms.txt expose five typed tools. Reliability layer: 63 automated tests, property-based invariants (verdict is binary, order_intent_created is always false), an immutable chained audit log with tamper detection, and a public SECURITY_BENCHMARK. 

 Challenges we ran into
The demo looked hardcoded — it always returned BLOCKED for the synthetic dataset; evaluators would read it as scripted. We fixed it by exposing an UNPROVEN / PROVEN evidence toggle: same system, same gates, BLOCKED for unproven data, ELIGIBLE for a source-verified dataset — proving the gate is live, not a fixed answer. Also, our default model had no quota, so we added automatic planner fallback (qwen-turbo/qwen-max), plus a deterministic rule fallback when no key is configured at all. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
A refusal a hallucination can't override. Property-tested determinism. An immutable audit ledger with tamper detection. The UNPROVEN/PROVEN toggle as proof the system isn't scripted. And framing the plain page as a feature: the front-end is the tool contract an agent reads, not a candy dashboard for a human to click. 

 What we learned
The highest-value property of an agent isn't more autonomy — it's giving a human a reason to trust its output. Provable (reproducible + auditable + test-locked) beats persuasive. And for WebMCP: the interface isn't pixels; the interface is the schema. 

 What's next for Firebreak
Apply the same deterministic veto to more domains — order execution, approvals, data pipelines. Ship SECURITY_BENCHMARK as a cross-agent safety standard. Add live-broker integration that still can't auto-execute without human sign-off. And orchestrate multiple agents — any of them must sit behind the gate.

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: JobJam WebMCP
pitch: A real job search product an AI agent can actually operate. Thirteen WebMCP tools, run by the page itself, so the agent moves real UI, asks before it spends your credits, and never sees a credential.
about_excerpt: A real job search product an AI agent can actually operate. Thirteen WebMCP tools, run by the page itself, so the agent moves real UI, asks before it spends your credits, and never sees a credential. Like Comment Story Updates The site is the interface. Thirteen WebMCP tools, registered by the page. One sentence became real filter state. search_jobs takes the same path your click does. The agent asked. The person decides. Spending a credit stops for approval in a dialog the page owns, not the model. What the credit bought. The evaluation the agent paid for, opened by the tool that ran it. Inspiration Most attempts to let an AI agent use a website come down to one of two things. Either the agent scrapes the DOM and hopes the markup does not change, or you hand a long-lived API token to a server the user cannot see. Neither is something I wanted pointed at a product where people have paid for credits. WebMCP offers a third option: the site registers typed tools with the browser, and the agent calls them. I wanted to find out what that actually costs to build, and what it forces you to decide, so I built it on JobJam, which is a live product with real users, real job data and real money in it. Having money in it turned out to be the useful part. The moment an agent can spend a credit, you have to answer questions that a demo never asks. To be clear about what is new, since the rules ask for it: JobJam itself is my existing product and has been live for months. The agent surface is what I built during the submission period, on 2 and 3 September 2026, and it is the entirety of the MIT repo linked below. That repo has no commit older than the hackathon, and the dated history in both repositories is the evidence. The product is the thing being operated. The tool layer is the submission. What it does JobJam is an AI job application workspace: a live board built from company applicant tracking systems, resume evaluation against a posting, resume rewriting, cover letters and application tracking. This project makes all of that operable by an agent running in the page. Thirteen tools, in three tiers, and the tiers are the design: Read-only (6). search_jobs, get_job_details, get_my_profile, rank_jobs_for_me, get_credit_balance, get_apply_instructions. Free, no confirmation, safe to call unprompted. Reversible (4). save_job, unsave_job, list_saved_jobs, create_profile_from_resume. Logged in an activity panel in the page. Bookmarking asks for nothing, because a confirmation on every low-stakes action teaches people to click through confirmations. Consequential (3). evaluate_job_fit, prepare_application, mark_job_applied. Each one blocks on a human clicking Approve in a dialog that belongs to the page, not to the model. And one deliberate absence: there is no tool that submits an application to an employer. JobJam does not do that, so the tool surface does not offer it. But an absence is not an answer. An agent that finds no matching tool goes looking for a workaround, so the boundary is itself a tool. Ask the agent to apply for you and get_apply_instructions explains why JobJam will not, hands back the employer's own link, and points at mark_job_applied for afterwards. In the demo video you can watch it do exactly that, then open the company's real careers page. Why this use case fits WebMCP Job hunting is the rare everyday task that is genuinely multi-step, genuinely tedious and genuinely high stakes. You are searching a moving target, measuring yourself against each posting, and then deciding where to spend limited time and money. That is a poor fit for a chat box that can only talk about the work, and a good fit for an agent that can operate the tool where the work actually happens. What changes for the person using it: the filters move, the list re-renders, the score appears on the page. You are not reading a transcript of something an agent did somewhere else. You are watching your own workspace being driven, and you can take the mouse back at any moment, because nothing about the interface was bypassed to get there. What the two of them do together that neither does alone: the agent is good at breadth. It will read twenty postings and shortlist five without complaining. The person is good at the judgment call, which of those five is worth a credit and an afternoon of tailoring. So the tool surface is split along exactly that line. Everything free and reversible belongs to the agent, unprompted. Everything that costs money or asserts something about the real world stops and waits for a human. The approval dialog is not friction. It is the handoff point between the two of them. How we built it Tool handlers are the page's own JavaScript. That single fact is the whole security model. fetch is same-origin, so the browser attaches the HttpOnly Supabase cookie the user already has, the handler runs under that session's row-level security identity, and the agent supplies arguments and reads results without ever touching a token. Page JavaScript cannot read the cookie, so neither can a tool, so neither can the agent. An agent that invents an id belonging to someone else gets zero rows back from Postgres, not an error it can learn from. Nothing about authentication had to change to support any of this. document.modelContext is read first and navigator.modelContext second, so one build works on browsers that shipped either form. Two bridges connect tools to React. The board bridge lets search_jobs call the exact same state path a human click uses, so an agent search visibly re-filters the page instead of only returning JSON into a chat pane. The navigation bridge, added late, lets a tool that spent money show what it bought. Both are tiny external stores that components read with useSyncExternalStore. No state library. Stack: Next.js 15, TypeScript, React 19, Supabase with RLS, Postgres, Vercel, OpenRouter for the evaluation models. Challenges we ran into Silence and emptiness looked the same. An unauthenticated tool call is not a 401. The app's auth middleware redirects it to /login, fetch follows the redirect, and it arrives as a 200 with an HTML body that parses to null. Logged out, search_jobs cheerfully returned { ok: true, jobs: [], total: 0 } , so an agent would tell you, with total confidence, that there are no frontend jobs in Berlin. toolFetch now treats a redirect to /login, and any non-JSON body, as the auth failure it is. Only a real browser finds that one. A mocked context never will. Chrome drops destructiveHint. getTools() in Chrome 152 normalises annotations down to readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint, so a three-credit prepare_application is indistinguishable from a free save_job. Both report readOnlyHint: false . If you are relying on that annotation to communicate cost, you are relying on something the agent never sees. Say it in the description, and gate it in the page. The tool that spent money changed nothing on screen. search_jobs re-filtered the board and save_job flipped the bookmark, but evaluate_job_fit, the one action that costs money and asks permission, returned a score into the chat and left the page exactly as it was. The board bridge could not fix it, because the board only exists while the jobs page is mounted and the result lives elsewhere. That needed a second bridge, connected above every route so it outlives the navigation it performs. Consent to spend a credit is not consent to be navigated, so the approval dialog now says the page will move. Approval had to be serialised, not queued. requestApproval() rejects a second consequential request while one is already on screen. A queue would let someone approve the dialog in front of them and silently authorise the next one behind it. An agent firing three paid actions at once should be stopped, not helped along. Accomplishments that we're proud of It runs on a real product, in production, at app.jobjam.io. Not a sandbox with three fake tools. Because JobJam already existed, the agent surface had to fit a real session model, a real credit ledger and a real UI that people use, and it did so without a single change to how authentication works. The hackathon work is also cleanly separable. Everything I wrote sits in one MIT repo you can read in a sitting: thirteen tools, two bridges, an approval gate and its tests. Nothing of the closed product leaked into it. The refusal is designed rather than implied, which I have not seen elsewhere. Building a tool whose only job is to explain what the product will not do, and to hand back the link so the human can do it themselves, turned out to be the most interesting fifteen seconds of the demo. And the security property holds without any new auth surface. There is no agent token to leak, revoke or scope, because there is no token. What we learned Testing against a mocked ModelContext gets you a clean test suite and a false sense of security. Everything worth knowing came from driving real Chrome 152: The shipped API is sma

 💡 Inspiration 

 Every year, millions of students, researchers, and early-career developers miss out on career-defining fellowships, high-impact internships, and competitive hackathons simply because opportunity tracking is broken. Opportunities are scattered across fragmented job boards, company portals, and academic lists with shifting deadlines and convoluted eligibility criteria. 

 With the advent of autonomous AI agents, we wondered: Why are agents still forced to browse the web like clumsy humans—scraping messy DOM trees, hallucinating CSS selectors, and breaking brittle form buttons? 

 When Google and the W3C introduced WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) , we saw the future: a web where applications expose their capabilities directly to in-browser AI models as structured, strongly-typed tools. 

 We built OpportunityOS to pioneer this new paradigm: an agent-native, local-first workspace that connects students with opportunities through 11 deterministic WebMCP tools, while keeping humans firmly in control of consequential writes. 

 

 🚀 What It Does 

 OpportunityOS is a browser-native opportunity management engine designed for both human operators and autonomous AI agents: 

 
 Autonomous Opportunity Discovery & Matching: Agents discover 11 registered WebMCP tools directly through document.modelContext . They can search by domain, evaluate candidate eligibility, run multi-factor weighted rankings, and generate comparative matrices—with zero hallucination. 
 Human-in-the-Loop Write Governance: While read operations ( search , filter , rank , compare ) execute autonomously, consequential write operations ( save_opportunity , create_action_plan , update_application_status ) are intercepted by a security gate that requires explicit human approval before mutating state. 
 Live Surveillance & Application Tracking: Provides a unified command center featuring days-remaining countdowns, interactive 4-step milestone checklists ( Resume Tailored , LOR Requested , Statement Drafted , Portal Submitted ), and rapid deadline reminder chips ( ⚡ 48h Warning , 🚨 24h Crunch ). 
 Real-Time Surveillance Telemetry Feed: An immutable audit log records every agent interaction with millisecond timestamps, execution latencies, tool call signatures, and payload inspections. 
 Cinematic 3D Centerpiece & Bespoke Dual Themes: Features a real-time WebGL 3D cyber-butterfly sculpture with aerodynamic multi-phase wing kinematics, styled with Google's modern Unbounded typography and a tailored dual-theme system (Obsidian Cyber-Cyan Dark Mode and Royal Cobalt Sapphire & Porcelain Pearl Light Mode). 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 OpportunityOS is built with a strictly client-side, local-first architecture without external proxy dependencies or API credential leakage: 

 
 WebMCP Integration ( src/webmcp.js ): Implemented a production-grade WebMCP engine that registers 11 tools into document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool features strict JSON Schema boundaries, parameter type limits, and untrustedContentHint: true tagging on external data to prevent prompt injection. 
 Frontend Architecture ( src/main.js ): Built with Vanilla JavaScript and Vite for lightning-fast performance, zero bundle bloat, and instantaneous reactive UI state updates. 
 3D Procedural Engine (Three.js WebGL): Crafted a custom 3D cyber-organic butterfly sculpture featuring dual-layer aerodynamic wing geometries, interactive mouse parallax banking, pulsating reactor crystal lighting, and dynamic theme-adaptive shaders. 
 Design System ( src/styles.css ): Engineered with Google's geometric Unbounded typography and an adaptive CSS token system that transitions between deep obsidian neon and a vibrant royal cobalt sapphire palette. 
 

 

 🔒 Security & Safety Invariants 

 We designed OpportunityOS under the principle: "Built for agents. Not built to trust them blindly." 

 
 Strict Schemas & Bounded Inputs: Every tool argument is strongly typed with bounded string lengths and integer ranges to eliminate runaway buffer allocations. 
 Untrusted Content Demarcation: All catalog-derived data is explicitly labeled with untrustedContentHint: true , instructing agents to treat external text as untrusted data. 
 Fixed ID Addressing: Tools operate strictly on catalog-validated entity IDs, preventing arbitrary SQL or prompt injections. 
 Zero Secret Leakage: Operates local-first in the browser runtime without requiring backend API keys or credential proxies. 
 Deterministic Services: Local scoring algorithms provide reproducible and explainable candidate evaluations. 
 

 

 🧗 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 Bridging WebMCP with Visual Feedback: Standard agent tools run invisibly in background execution contexts. We had to build a custom interceptor that visualizes agent reasoning in real-time, pauses execution when write permissions are requested, and renders a native confirmation modal. 
 Light Theme Luminosity & Contrast: Ensuring that rich, high-contrast aesthetics translated gracefully between dark and light modes without washed-out grays required developing a bespoke Royal Cobalt Sapphire & Porcelain Pearl palette with high-specificity CSS inversion rules. 
 Aerodynamic 3D Kinematics: Getting the Three.js butterfly to flap with realistic organic flight physics required decoupling the upper and lower wing matrices and applying phase-lagged sine wave oscillations with subtle wingtip aero-tremor. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 Fully Compliant WebMCP Implementation: Built all 11 tools adhering strictly to the W3C WebMCP draft specification with complete schema validation. 
 Zero-Latency Local-First Runtime: The entire app runs offline-ready, respecting user privacy and keeping all application milestones on-device. 
 Stunning Visual Identity: Created a design that breaks away from generic AI templates, combining sculptural 3D motion, spacious modern cards, and the bold Unbounded typeface. 
 

 

 📚 What We Learned 

 
 How WebMCP transforms web apps from passive user interfaces into structured, actionable APIs for AI models. 
 Techniques for prompt-injection defense when agents process untrusted catalog content. 
 Crafting human-in-the-loop security patterns where agents move fast while humans stay in total control. 
 

 

 🔮 What's Next for OpportunityOS 

 
 Chrome Extension Companion: Injecting OpportunityOS's WebMCP context into third-party portals like LinkedIn, Handshake, and university research directories. 
 Local LLM Integration (Gemini Nano / WebLLM): Running an on-device SLM directly inside the browser tab to execute missions with zero server costs. 
 Agent-Assisted Portfolio Assembly: Using WebMCP tools to automatically assemble tailored portfolios and statement drafts for verified deadlines.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: UNIV Deploy
pitch: A browser agent compiles one WASI deployment intent into verified target capsules, executes browser and edge, and returns a bounded portability witness.
about_excerpt: A browser agent compiles one WASI deployment intent into verified target capsules, executes browser and edge, and returns a bounded portability witness. Like Comment Story Updates Most “deploy anywhere” products ask you to trust the promise. UNIV Deploy lets a browser agent challenge the promise before it deploys anything. It is for platform, release, and security teams that want agents to move reviewed software across runtimes without handing those agents a shell, upload endpoint, or arbitrary code execution. The agent discovers five typed WebMCP tools and works through a visible, stateful deployment contract. First, UNIV compiles one closed deployment intent against machine-readable target passports. The result is a finite portability frontier, a compatibility certificate for each target, and a distinct execution capsule for every compatible target. A separate deterministic verifier rechecks each certificate and capsule. Only verified, digest-bound capsules can enter the five-minute handoff. The demo starts adversarially. The agent asks UNIV to compile network-bound-release-v1. Both registered targets forbid guest networking, so the compiler returns an empty frontier, emits no capsules, names guest-network as the counterexample, and makes handoff impossible. The agent then chooses portable-release-v1. That intent compiles into two verified capsules and executes on two deliberately different real targets: browser-wasi in the browser main thread and sites-edge-wasi on the OpenAI Sites / Cloudflare Workers edge. UNIV still does not call the workload portable merely because both capsules exist. It waits for both executions, compares the declared observation contract, and returns a runtime portability witness only when both target receipts report the same manifest, component, status, workload ID, and output digest. WebMCP is essential because this is a consequential multi-step operation with opaque proof artifacts. Without WebMCP, an agent would scrape controls and manually shuttle IDs and digests between screens. Here, it can discover the closed contract, compile an intent, carry the exact handoff ID and digest into deployment, and retrieve evidence by ID. The person watching sees the same compiler result, capsules, receipts, refusal, and activity. The timeline says via WebMCP only when a registered page tool actually ran; human controls remain via human. The public interface accepts no uploaded components, arbitrary bytes, paths, URLs, shell commands, native executables, container images, host settings, or free-form guest arguments. The manifest, source component, and generated core modules are SHA-256 pinned. Browser module hashes are observed before compilation. The edge receives statically imported modules pinned by manifest and CI; because Workers do not expose those module bytes for runtime re-hashing, the receipt labels that fact build-pinned rather than observed. In the verified public run on September 3, a ChatGPT in-app browser agent first produced the empty-frontier counterexample, then compiled and deployed the permitted intent, retrieved evidence 7cc5409e-d9d1-4cb4-b3a4-2bbbec6b15e4, and received univ.deployment-receipt/v2 with source: WebMCP. Both actual targets terminated and returned output SHA-256 a928646501fcc69ed8af413859d43d4b887f3be150c452696700e393d8e338f5. The runtime witness reported equivalence over the declared observations. UNIV existed before the challenge as a broader Rust portability project. During the submission period I created this clean WebMCP product surface and, for v2, turned the theoretical proof-carrying deployment idea into a running compiler, independent verifier, target passports, execution capsules, bounded witness, public CI gate, production deployment, and reproducible evidence. The inherited daemon, worker, native, OCI, upload, shell, QEMU, and unrelated role-adaptive-agent files are not included or exposed. UNIV Deploy does not claim universal execution over arbitrary software or hosts. Its claim is deliberately falsifiable: one closed intent is portable across the registered passports only when every compile-time proof passes and every executed target agrees over the named runtime observations. It is not independent attestation or a production cloud orchestrator. It is a working demonstration of agents and people replacing a vague portability promise with a proof-carrying deployment and a reviewable receipt. video_title: UNIV Deploy — Challenge a Portability Claim, Then Prove It
video_transcript_excerpt: One browser agent just turned a reviewed release into two actual wasi executions, matching output, and a durable proof link without receiving a shell, upload path, or arbitrary code. Before trusting that result, ask the agent to break it. The network bound release needs authority neither host grants, so Unif returns an empty frontier, emits no capsule, and names guest network as the counter example. For the permitted release, five typed web and CP tools let the agent compile one manifest into separate browser and edge capsules. A deterministic verifier recomputes their clauses and digests before either enters the five-minute handoff. The browser hashes its included modules before compilation. The site's edge runs statically imported modules pinned by the manifest and public CI. Only after both terminate does Unif compare the release's declared observations and report two out of two match. The decisive upgrade is that evidence now survives the browser session. Before Cloudflare D1 stores anything, the edge rechecks receipt integrity, release and capsule bindings, bounded observations, output equality, and the attestation boundary. Retrieval runs those checks again. The version three receipt names the release, preserves web and CP provenance, and distinguishes enforced facts, observed facts, build pinned facts, and absent independent attestation. Unif does not claim every program runs everywhere. It proves a narrower useful statement. This approved release behaved the same across these governed targets, and the agent can hand the reviewer a proof instead of a promise.

title: ShrineKeep + WebMCP
pitch: A versatile collection manager for devoted collectors and hobbyists from any space, now with agent-automated onboarding and monetary analytics, making reasoned decisions even for niches.
about_excerpt: A versatile collection manager for devoted collectors and hobbyists from any space, now with agent-automated onboarding and monetary analytics, making reasoned decisions even for niches. Like Comment Story Updates Agent asked to set up data for a collection of the user's choice All edits are staged and require approval Staged edits that are not yet accepted are put in the review inbox Example output Activity of each tool use is recorded for technical users to debug Tool descriptions are also provided so technical users can be more productive and write more complex prompts Agent making decisions gives effective and reasonable automation of item valuation ShrineKeep + WebMCP project story Inspiration Collectors can end up hoarding rather than collecting, leaving them with questions. What do I already own? How much have I spent? What is all of this worth now? A lot of people have to manually make use of notes or spreadsheets, if they track them at all. That is the problem I made ShrineKeep to solve. It can organize collections in nested boxes and give you useful analytics, but there was an awkward catch: first, you had to manually add everything. Names, dates, purchase prices, current values, wishlist prices, and so on. The more useful I made the app, the more data it asked the user to enter. I've wanted to use agents for this for a while. An agent can research a niche product line, tell similar editions apart, find price references, and do in minutes what would be a very boring evening of data entry. But running those agents for every user would be expensive. Locking the feature behind a subscription would solve my problem by creating a new one for users. WebMCP and it solved my problems well! The user can bring an agent they already have, and ShrineKeep can give it the right context and a safe way to help. The agent does the research and reasoning; ShrineKeep knows what box is open, what the user owns, and what is actually allowed to change. I don't have to run an AI service or pass that cost on to the user. What it does On the dashboard or wishlist, a user can now talk to a compatible browser agent and ask it to work with the collection that is already in front of them. It can: research and initialize a new collection box; compare a complete set with the current box and stage only the missing items; estimate current values or likely acquisition prices for owned items; research expected prices for wishlist items; edit item names and descriptions through the same review flow; work only with the items explicitly selected in the interface; and optionally find a thumbnail for each newly approved item. The agent gets small, structured pieces of context instead of trying to scrape the screen. It can read the open box, include its child boxes when that is actually needed, look at the relevant wishlist, or ask for only the cards the user selected. There are seven tools on the dashboard and three on the wishlist page, each limited to what makes sense there. Tools are written in accordance to Chrome's WebMCP Best Practices The important part is that none of those tools silently changes the collection. Anything the agent wants to add or edit goes into a staging inbox. ShrineKeep shows the user the proposed names, prices, Owned/Wishlist choices, before-and-after values, reasons, sources, and possible duplicates. Every row can be edited, unchecked, approved, or thrown away. Only approved rows reach the real write APIs. I also built a new tutorial around these agent features. WebMCP will undoubtedly be unfamilar to most users, and I feel it is an essential UX requirement to introduce users to a newly adopted technology. It asks what the user collects, gives them a prompt to take to their agent, and walks them through confirming the researched set, reviewing the new cards, opening the created box, and trying a valuation. They learn the app by setting up something they already collect. They can skip individual steps, leave the tutorial, or use sample data instead. If WebMCP isn't available, ShrineKeep still works normally. How we built it ShrineKeep is built with Next.js 16, React, and TypeScript, with Supabase handling authentication, Postgres, row-level security, and image storage. The collection manager existed before the hackathon. During the submission period, I added the WebMCP tools, their staging and approval flow, and the new agent-based tutorial directly to the existing app. A reusable React hook checks for document.modelContext and registers the right tools for the page the user is on. Registrations are cleaned up with an AbortController when that scope changes. The same hook records calls as they happen, which let me show a status panel without pretending that “the browser accepted a registration” means “an agent is connected and understands everything.” The read tools use small authenticated routes that check ownership and return only the fields needed for the job, with pagination so a large collection doesn't become one giant prompt. Selection is even smaller: get_selected_items reads the current React selection state directly. I generalized the edit tools to accept just the fields being changed, so the same operation can fix a name, update a description, or suggest prices without a separate tool for each field. Shared tool copy lives in one module so those contracts stay consistent. Tools that can lead to a write only build typed suggestion batches. A shared client-side provider keeps those batches around while the user moves between the dashboard and wishlist. When the user finally applies one, the server authenticates them again, checks ownership and price fields, catches stale records through updated_at , and then reuses ShrineKeep's normal item and box operations. That also means value updates still appear in the existing value history. Optional thumbnail lookup reuses the regular image search and is allowed to fail without blocking the batch. The tutorial runs as a state machine inside the existing agent panel. It listens for the relevant tool calls, successful approvals, and box navigation. Tutorial progress is saved for the session, while completion or dismissal is saved to the account. The state also needs to handle someone skipping creation, opening a different box, or coming back after navigating away. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was deciding where the agent should stop. Niche product research is messy, and secondhand prices are even messier. I wanted the agent to save real time without letting a confident mistake rewrite someone's collection. The model I kept coming back to was a code review: let the agent prepare a useful diff, then let the person who owns the data decide what lands. The tutorial became a major challenge of its own. Exposing the tools didn't explain to a new user what to ask for, or why they were moving between an agent chat and ShrineKeep. I had to build a walkthrough that taught both sides of that interaction while helping them make a real collection. There also had to be a useful way through for someone without a compatible agent, or someone who just wanted to skip ahead. Another early mistake was treating “set up this collection” and “complete the collection in this box” as the same operation. They sound close, but one should create a new box and the other should reconcile against what is already there. Using the first flow for both produced duplicate cards and unnecessary child boxes. I split them into separate tools, and the completion flow now checks both owned and wishlist cards before proposing only what is missing. Choosing how many tools to expose was another balancing act. I didn't want a separate tool for every small task, with more schemas and descriptions for the agent to read. But making one tool do everything would bring back the scope confusion. I kept separate operations where the destination or approval flow really differs, and generalized edits within those boundaries. Furthermore, I directly acknowledge that destructive, relocation, and exploration actions should not be accessible to the agent, as these can destroy data, confuse users, and waste tokens, respectively. It was not worth it to implement this when users already have fast batch deletions and movement options. Pricing caused a different kind of ambiguity. Original retail, a current listing, a secondhand asking price, and a recent sold price are all valid approaches to price an item. I experimented with defaults, but collections from different spaces just aren't compatible with it and often lead to lots of time and tokens wasted looking at obviously wrong decisions. I ended up with just asking the agent to suggest a research approach for each requested field, wait for user approval on all of them, then research. The review still keeps the explanation and links next to the number. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this became a complete bring-your-own-agent loop rather than a chat demo. title: RelayLab
pitch: RelayLab is a WebMCP-native video editor where AI agents propose and replan B-roll edits while humans stay in full creative control.
about_excerpt: RelayLab is a WebMCP-native video editor where AI agents propose and replan B-roll edits while humans stay in full creative control. Like Comment Story Updates What RelayLab is RelayLab is a focused B-roll overlay editor built around human-agent collaboration. A creator keeps control of the visual timeline while an external AI agent works through WebMCP to understand the transcript, inspect indexed B-roll moments, propose ghost edits, respond to human changes, and commit only after explicit approval. The base talking-head video stays locked and remains the master audio source. B-roll is always visual-only and muted. The agent can propose, revise, remove, search, and replan, but it cannot approve its own plan, change human locks, or trigger paid video generation. Why RelayLab is a strong fit for WebMCP Traditional browser automation gives an agent pixels, DOM controls, approximate coordinates, and brittle click sequences. RelayLab instead exposes the actual editing concepts the agent needs: transcript ranges, source moments, timeline positions, pacing opportunities, ghost overlays, human locks, approval state, and the exact tools currently allowed. This makes the agent state-aware rather than screen-aware. It can reason about the same structured timeline the human is editing and safely adapt when the human changes something. Better user experience Instead of asking a creator to manually hunt through long B-roll reels and place every clip from scratch, RelayLab lets the agent do the repetitive search and planning work while preserving human editorial judgment. The collaboration loop is: The agent reads the transcript, timeline, pacing opportunities, and indexed source moments. It proposes ghost B-roll edits on the same timeline the human sees. The human can move, swap, resize, remove, or lock any edit. The agent rereads the updated timeline and replans only unlocked sections. The human approves the plan. Only then does commit_approved_plan become available through WebMCP. The agent commits the approved plan without overwriting human timing, locks, or source choices. For moments where uploaded B-roll is a weak match, the agent can suggest an AI-generation prompt. Actual generation remains a separate human-clicked action, so the agent cannot spend credits on its own. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before RelayLab turns a video editor into a shared stateful workspace between a human and an AI agent. The agent can inspect the real editorial state, understand source-time versus timeline-time, preserve locked human decisions, avoid re-proposing explicitly rejected moments, and replan around live human edits. That is difficult to do safely with normal browser automation because the agent would need to infer editorial state from the UI and could easily overwrite user decisions. With WebMCP, the collaboration contract is explicit and bounded. How WebMCP is implemented RelayLab registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) in a centralized WebMCP layer. The tool surface changes with project state. Always-available read tools include project summary, transcript, timeline, edit plan, overlay opportunities, and B-roll search. During planning, additional tools allow proposing, updating, removing, and replanning unlocked ghost edits. After the human approves in the UI, those planning tools are removed and commit_approved_plan becomes available. After commit, only the read surface remains. RelayLab also tracks a monotonically increasing timelineRevision . Mutating tools can reject stale agent writes with STALE_TIMELINE instead of silently overwriting a timeline the human has already changed. Locked overlays reject agent mutation with HUMAN_LOCKED . The project includes a deterministic /demo route with a pre-indexed transcript and B-roll moments so judges can test the WebMCP collaboration loop without API keys. Additional capabilities RelayLab supports local B-roll source reels, timestamped transcript segments, manual and automatic captions, uploaded-footage-first search, optional human-triggered fal.ai B-roll generation, edit JSON export, SRT export, and reproducible ffmpeg export commands. The base video's audio remains the only audio source. Built for the WebMCP Challenge RelayLab was created during the challenge period as a focused experiment in how a human and an external AI agent can safely co-edit the same creative artifact without handing full control to either side. title: West Sparta Agent-Ready Chamber
pitch: A fictional WordPress chamber site where AI agents search members, find events, compare sponsorships, and complete safe simulated actions using five WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A fictional WordPress chamber site where AI agents search members, find events, compare sponsorships, and complete safe simulated actions using five WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates West Sparta Chamber homepage with current events and member discovery. Visible Agent Activity panel showing structured member results. Sponsorship opportunities with agent-ready comparison and inquiry tools. Inspiration Chamber of commerce websites are full of useful local information, but most of it is packaged for visual browsing: directory cards, event listings, sponsorship tables, and forms. An AI agent can try to scrape and interpret those pages, but the process is brittle, expensive, and disconnected from what the person sees. West Sparta asks a simple question: what if an existing chamber website could become directly usable by an agent without becoming less useful to people? What it does West Sparta is a fictional Chamber of Commerce website enhanced with five browser-native WebMCP Site tools: search_members searches fictional chamber members by service, category, name, or town. find_events finds current events by date, audience, type, or keyword. find_sponsorships compares annual and event opportunities by budget and goal. register_for_event completes a clearly labeled fictional registration. start_sponsorship_inquiry completes a clearly labeled fictional sponsorship inquiry. A visitor can make a natural-language request that crosses several parts of the site—for example, find a commercial electrician, identify the next networking event, and register a fictional attendee. The agent receives structured results instead of reconstructing page layouts. Every tool invocation is also reflected in a visible Agent Activity panel. The person and the agent stay grounded in the same interface and can inspect what was found or completed. How we built it The project adds a focused WordPress plugin to an existing chamber demonstration site. PHP extracts and normalizes member and event information from the site's current content. Vanilla JavaScript registers the five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , supplies narrow JSON schemas, and reuses the site's existing interface logic. The two action tools are intentionally safe simulations. They accept only fictional example-domain email addresses, create no payment, send no message, and store confirmations only in the current browser session. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the normal website through progressive enhancement. Challenges The hardest design problem was not registering a tool; it was choosing the right boundaries. A useful chamber workflow crosses discovery, comparison, and action, but each tool still needs a narrow purpose, predictable schema, and clear safety contract. We also had to keep dynamic event data consistent between the human homepage and the agent-facing tools, make tool activity visible without overwhelming the design, and preserve the behavior of the existing WordPress site for ordinary visitors. Accomplishments Five working Site tools on a live WordPress website. One request can move from member discovery to event discovery to a simulated registration. Structured results and human-visible feedback remain synchronized. The repository contains a reproducible plugin, sample content, architecture notes, testing instructions, and an open-source license. The project demonstrates a reusable pattern for associations, destinations, universities, and local governments—not only chambers. What we learned WebMCP is more than a new form of search optimization. Search helps an agent find a site; structured content helps it understand the site; WebMCP lets it use the site. When the website exposes the right narrow tools, the agent can spend less effort interpreting layouts and more effort helping the person complete a real task. What's next The next step is to adapt the pattern to real chamber-management systems so directory, event, and sponsorship tools can use authenticated member data and real transaction APIs with explicit confirmation and permission controls. West Sparta remains deliberately fictional so the interaction model can be tested safely. Try it Open the live site in a WebMCP-compatible browser and ask: I'm looking for a commercial electrician in West Sparta. Find three chamber members who could help. Then find the next networking event and register Jordan Demo from Demo Business using jordan.demo@example.com . title: GoodFolder
pitch: GoodFolder lets people and AI agents work together on real files, with context, history, and human approval built in.
about_excerpt: GoodFolder lets people and AI agents work together on real files, with context, history, and human approval built in. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP agent proposes a reviewable GoodFolder change. GoodFolder returns structured workspace context to the agent. GoodFolder — accountable agent work, right where your files live. Meet the GoodFolder mascot. Inspiration I built GoodFolder because I kept coming back to the same problem: once an agent touches a folder, it should be possible to understand what happened afterwards. Files alone don't tell that story. GoodFolder keeps a readable history of changes and gives you a way back when something needs to be corrected. With agents involved, that history matters even more. WebMCP felt like the missing piece for GoodFolder. A lot of the work inside a folder needs visual judgment: reading a document in context, checking a spreadsheet, looking at an image, or noticing that something simply doesn't look right. The agent can investigate and prepare work, while the person sees the same workspace and decides what should actually happen. What it does Open the challenge workspace in ChatGPT Desktop’s in-app browser. There’s no signup or setup. It opens straight into a seeded workspace with folders, files, saves, a timeline, and open change proposals. Try asking the agent to list the folders, inspect the Q3 Report and its figures, trace a save, or prepare a correction. It can read the workspace and create a proposal or comment for review. It can't quietly save a change, approve a proposal, restore history, remove files, or change access. A person still makes those calls. How we built it GoodFolder is a Next.js dashboard deployed on Cloudflare Pages. I added WebMCP Site tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , which lets ChatGPT work with the things GoodFolder already understands: folders, files, document structure, tables, history, and proposals. The point wasn't to give an agent a faster way to click around a UI. I wanted it to understand what it was looking at and leave a clear trail when it suggests work. The public repository includes the challenge work and documents the approval boundary. Challenges and lessons The difficult part was deciding where to stop the agent. Reading a folder, tracing a save, and drafting a proposal are helpful. Letting an agent make lasting changes without review would defeat the reason GoodFolder exists. So I kept the agent close to the work, while making proposals the handoff point for anything that deserves a human decision. WebMCP fit that model well. The page can give the agent real product actions without handing it the keys. What’s next I want to make the Dashboard and WebMCP experience feel tighter together: faster, clearer handoffs between what a person sees in GoodFolder and what an agent can inspect or suggest. I’m also working on support for more file types and stronger previews in the Dashboard, so more of the work can be reviewed directly inside GoodFolder. title: navigator.berlin
pitch: An open-data atlas for Berlin where agent and human work the same map: it moves the sliders on 542 neighbourhoods, you move them back, and each side sees what the other did.
about_excerpt: An open-data atlas for Berlin where agent and human work the same map: it moves the sliders on 542 neighbourhoods, you move them back, and each side sees what the other did. Like Comment Story Updates Kiez-Finder with open Model Context Tool Inspector Inspiration Berlin publishes an enormous amount of open data: noise maps, heat maps, tree canopy, transit stops, housing protection zones, election results down to the voting district. It is all public, and it is all in different portals, in different formats, behind different search masks. The question people actually have is much simpler. They are moving, and they want to know where to live. Quiet or lively. Shops on the corner. A station they can walk to. That question spans a dozen datasets, and no portal answers it. navigator.berlin was built to answer it on one map, for all 542 of Berlin's official planning areas, the ones locals call Kieze. The product Sixty-five open-data layers, queryable at any address, aggregated into a score per Kiez across five dimensions. Twelve Berlin elections since 2011, down to voting-district level. A Kiez-Finder with nine sliders that weights the criteria and recolors all 542 areas live. The site has real users and real press: when a Berlin newspaper tested it during this summer's heat wave, they counted forty cool places around Gendarmenmarkt where the city's own map showed two. Why WebMCP fits this Choosing a neighbourhood is a conversation, not a query. People say things like "quiet, green, close to an S-Bahn, and I'd like culture nearby". A search box cannot take that sentence. An agent can, but scraping a map site gives it nothing usable: the interesting state lives in a WebGL canvas. WebMCP closes exactly that gap. The site hands the agent the same typed, validated functions its own interface uses, with source and licence attached to every answer. The agent does not simulate a user. It calls the function the user's slider calls. The collaboration loop Before the challenge, navigator.berlin exposed nine read-only tools: agents could ask Berlin questions. During the challenge we built the write direction, and with it something neither side can do alone. You say what you want. set_finder_weights moves the sliders, and the map you are looking at recolors all 542 areas. The ranked matches come back in the same call, with fit scores and centroid coordinates. You disagree and drag a slider yourself. get_finder_state reads your change back: which slider, which value, and that a human moved it, not the agent. Every answer carries a link that reproduces that exact map in any browser, because the finder state is encoded in the URL. The map is a shared wrkspace. Both hands move the same controls, and each side can see what the other did. That is the part that is genuinely new: not an agent operating a website, but an agent and a person working the same object and staying in sync. Better UX, concretely Nine sliders are powerful and they demand that you understand nine dimensions at once. The agent turns one spoken sentence into a weighted, visible map state, keeps your other settings intact on follow-ups ("now add culture"), and explains the change in plain language. Nothing hides behind the conversation. The recolored map is the result, and you can take the sliders back at any point. Implementation Eleven tools registered on document.modelContext.registerTool , with navigator.modelContext and an @mcp-b/global polyfill as fallbacks, so the same page works in the ChatGPT in-app browser and in Chrome with the WebMCP flag. Ten tools declare annotations.readOnlyHint ; set_finder_weights is the single honest write tool. Input validation runs through valibot with English error messages. Full JSON schemas are public at /webmcp-manifest.json , and /webmcp is a live diagnostics page showing the surface, registration state and tool list without devtools. A module-singleton bridge built on Svelte 5 runes connects tools and UI, and a BroadcastChannel syncs agent updates across page instances, which is what makes the human-visible map react when the agent works on its own instance. Stack: SvelteKit 2, Svelte 5, TypeScript strict, MapLibre GL, Tailwind v4, Postgres with Drizzle, Vitest and Playwright. Everything from the submission period shipped as reviewed pull requests with a timestamped history. Challenges Four bugs shaped this submission, and none of them was findable by testing. Agent browsers run the page in a hidden tab, where requestAnimationFrame never fires. Our finder scheduled its recalculation on an animation frame, which is correct for a human and silently fatal for an agent: the callback never came, the ranking never computed, and the tool answered with an empty list. Worse, the queued frame id blocked every later attempt, so it stayed broken. The data path now races the animation frame against a timer, and the ranking is computed independently of the map, since ranking is a pure function over the data and only painting needs MapLibre. A tool must return a fresh answer, not merely a non-empty one. When the agent added a party weight, the panel was still loading election metrics, so the tool returned the previous ranking. The agent then told the user, wrongly, that nothing had changed. The bridge now counts every published calculation and the tool waits for one newer than the request. Descriptions need decision rules, not hints. Told that the fit score already includes every weight, the agent still verified each match with five extra calls and geocoded neighbourhood names to get coordinates it had already been given. Told plainly that set_finder_weights is authoritative, and which tools not to call unless the user asks for specifics, it answers from the returned list. The same request went from seventeen tool calls to two. A link has to carry the state. The agent kept pointing people at the map, but the weights lived only in memory, so a shared link opened nine sliders set to neutral. The finder state now lives in the URL, which also made the finder shareable between humans for the first time. Results Eleven WebMCP tools, ten read-only, one write tool driving a live map of 542 areas The full loop verified in the ChatGPT desktop app: agent sets, human corrects, agent reads the correction back 3,301 unit tests, type-checked strict, zero warnings An adversarial cross-model code review on the URL-state work found three real defects before release, all fixed Repository public under MIT with the complete, timestamped history of the submission period Lessons for agent-facing sites Building for agents is not the same as building for people, and the difference is not the API surface. It is the assumptions. A person's browser tab is visible, so animation frames fire. A person clicks one thing at a time, so a slightly stale answer corrects itself on the next render. A person reads a hint and uses judgement. An agent does none of that: it runs hidden, it calls twice in a second, and it follows the description literally. The practical rule we ended up with: never let the data path depend on rendering, always return something freshly computed, and write descriptions as rules rather than suggestions. Next steps Cover the remaining Berlin datasets that people ask about, most of all rents and school catchments. Extend the write surface carefully: the finder is one honest write tool, and any second one has to earn the same clarity. And take the same treatment to the address inspector, so an agent can compare two addresses the way a person does with two browser tabs.
