title: Lumi
pitch: Build physical machines with an AI collaborator, not a black box simulator. Lumi gives humans and WebMCP agents one live 3D studio for evidence, safety checks, and simulation.
about_excerpt: Build physical machines with an AI collaborator, not a black box simulator. Lumi gives humans and WebMCP agents one live 3D studio for evidence, safety checks, and simulation. Like Comment Story Updates drone humanoid robot ai rover Inspiration A robot can look complete in a 3D viewer while its motors are underpowered, its battery is incompatible, or its wiring cannot work. Creating an attractive model is only part of the problem. Creating a machine whose parts, interfaces, and physics are supported by real evidence is another. We kept running into the gap between a product page and a simulation-ready component. Specifications are scattered across tables, descriptions, diagrams, and downloads. Important values are missing, units disagree, and copying everything manually makes it easy to lose track of where a number came from. We wanted the AI to remain involved after collecting that information. Instead of producing another isolated design, could it work beside the engineer, inspect the same project, and help build and test the actual machine? That question became Lumi. What it does Lumi is a browser-native hardware studio where people and AI agents build and simulate machines in the same live 3D workspace. You can import public product pages, inspect the resulting components, choose quantities, create an assembly, validate its wiring, and run deterministic physics experiments. Every value keeps its evidence status, so sourced measurements remain separate from provisional suggestions. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect the open project, load a rover, drone, or humanoid example, arrange selected components, confirm a topology, validate connections, control the 3D view, run simulations, and compare saved results. Both collaborators use the same project state. When an agent loads a rover, it appears in the Studio the person is already viewing. When it runs an experiment, the same timeline, telemetry, and findings become visible to both. Lumi can also turn a measured trajectory into a cinematic world visualization. The generated footage remains clearly labeled as imagined and never replaces MuJoCo’s measured result. WebMCP fits because the work depends on live page context: the available components, current design, readiness findings, selected experiment, simulation history, and hardware state. The agent can act on that context directly instead of maintaining a separate copy of the project. How we built it The central decision was to represent hardware as typed component evidence instead of free-form AI descriptions. Each component records its category, specifications, units, ports, geometry, capabilities, and provenance. Deterministic gates check power, signals, connections, geometry, and adapter readiness before a supported simulation can run. The Next.js, React, and TypeScript frontend contains the workflow controls, WebMCP integration, simulation timeline, evidence inspector, and Three.js workspace. React Three Fiber renders the component models and complete machine assemblies. A FastAPI and Pydantic backend manages projects, validates external data, builds supported topologies, and stores immutable simulation runs. MuJoCo produces the authoritative physics and telemetry. The Studio registers 22 task-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Human controls and agent tools call the same application actions, so there is no second agent-only workflow to keep synchronized. Tools are scoped to the current project state. A new workspace initially exposes inspection and import operations. Design tools appear after components exist, simulation tools appear after a confirmed design passes its checks, and hardware controls appear only when the required connection state exists. The underlying product-to-simulation prototype began under the development name Scrape2Sim. For the WebMCP Challenge, we added the browser-native collaboration layer, state-aware tool registration, visible WebMCP status, cancellation handling, shared agent and human state, tool-contract tests, and guarded hardware actions. Challenges we ran into The hardest failures were often successful actions applied at the wrong time. Registering every tool immediately would let an agent request operations whose prerequisites did not exist. We instead made tool availability follow the project’s capabilities, which required registration to update safely as components, designs, simulations, generated worlds, and hardware connections changed. Long-running actions introduced another challenge. Product collection, design generation, physics simulation, and world generation cannot be treated like instant button clicks. Tool calls needed cancellation signals and structured errors without leaving the visible Studio in a misleading state. The human interface and agent interface also had to remain aligned. If an agent loaded one project while the person saw another, the result could appear correct while operating on the wrong machine. Sharing the same action layer and visible state was essential. Adding a visible WebMCP status indicator uncovered a subtle recording issue: existing automation assumed the first status label always described the simulation. Once WebMCP had its own status, those selectors targeted the wrong label. We updated the capture flow to distinguish registration status from workflow status. Finally, we had to preserve the boundary between simulation and generated imagery. Cinematic footage can communicate an experiment beautifully, but it must never be presented as measured engineering evidence. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working shared engineering loop: inspect the Studio, invoke a registered WebMCP tool, see the project change immediately, and continue from the new state. An agent can call get_studio_state , load the evidence-backed rover with load_demo , and run a bounded MuJoCo experiment with run_simulation . The results appear in the same 3D workspace, telemetry panels, and timeline used by the person. We implemented 22 state-aware tools across component ingestion, design, wiring, simulation, generated device families, world visualization, and guarded rover hardware. We also built three deterministic demonstration families: a differential-drive rover, a measured FPV drone, and a servo humanoid. Unsupported projects remain honest editable assemblies instead of receiving invented physics. The latest verification passed the TypeScript check, WebMCP contract test, and production build. We also recorded the real WebMCP registration state and verified that a registered tool could load the rover through the live application. Most importantly, Lumi remains useful without an AI conversation. WebMCP adds another collaborator rather than replacing the engineer or the existing controls. What we learned A valid 3D model is not automatically a valid machine. Electrical compatibility, mechanical interfaces, evidence quality, and physical behavior need checks that visual generation alone cannot provide. We learned that good agent tools should describe meaningful goals rather than individual button presses. run_simulation is a stronger contract than asking an agent to locate and click a changing interface element. We also learned that tool availability can communicate product state. When an action is not safe or meaningful yet, hiding that tool gives the agent a clearer workflow than exposing it and returning avoidable errors. The strongest AI interaction was not an unconstrained design. It was a small, traceable action performed on the project already in front of the engineer, using the same validation rules and producing a visible result. What's next for Lumi Next comes broader evidence-backed component ingestion and more deterministic simulation families. We want users to move from unfamiliar product pages to trustworthy experiments with less manual cleanup. We also want stronger run comparison, improved calibration workflows, and clearer explanations of why a proposed machine is or is not ready to simulate. The physical rover workflow needs further validation across additional hardware configurations. Human confirmation and emergency-stop controls will remain mandatory for any action that can move a real machine. Finally, we plan to complete the transition from the Scrape2Sim development branding to Lumi across the public Studio, repository, documentation, and demonstration material. title: WebMCP Consent Layer
pitch: One React hook that gates risky AI tool calls behind human approval; with risk metadata, audit logging, and optional biometric verific. so agents handle the routine while humans approve what matters.
about_excerpt: One React hook that gates risky AI tool calls behind human approval; with risk metadata, audit logging, and optional biometric verific. so agents handle the routine while humans approve what matters. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP lets any website register tools that AI agents can discover and invoke. Some runtimes already gate risky calls behind their own native approval UIs — ChatGPT's built-in browser shows a "Site tools" review panel, and the MCP-B Agent Chrome extension has per-tool approval settings. But most WebMCP clients don't provide any consent mechanism at all: every registered tool runs silently, whether it's a read-only health check or an irreversible production rollback. This project closes that gap at the package level. It adds a consent and annotation layer to @mcp-b/react-webmcp that any site using WebMCP can adopt — one hook, one provider — without every site inventing its own approval flow from scratch. How it creates a better user experience The consent layer is deliberately selective. Every tool registration carries structured metadata — scope, reversibility, risk level — and only actions flagged as requiring approval actually interrupt the user with a consent card. Low-risk reads (fetching service health, listing deployments) execute immediately and are logged silently in the audit trail. When a high-risk call like rollbackDeployment fires, the consent card shows exactly what's at stake: which systems are affected, whether the action is reversible, and what the agent wants to do. The audit log records every tool call — approved, denied, or auto-approved — so users can review the full history of what an agent did, not just the decisions they were asked to make. Cross-tab attention cues (a favicon badge and title blink) ensure pending approvals aren't missed when the user is in a different tab. For irreversible, high-risk operations, an optional WebAuthn gate (Touch ID, Windows Hello, or a hardware key) raises the bar beyond a simple click. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Without a consent layer, site authors face a binary choice: either don't register destructive tools with WebMCP (safe but crippled), or register them and hope the runtime provides its own gate (flexible but risky on runtimes that don't). With useGuardedWebMCP, an agent can be handed genuinely powerful tools — rollbackDeployment, deleteUser, revokeAccess — with a human gating only the specific calls that matter. The agent handles the routine reads autonomously; the human approves or denies only the irreversible, high-impact actions. The result is collaborative agentic work where the human's attention is spent on the decisions that actually need judgment, not on rubber-stamping every API call. Brief implementation explanation The core mechanism is a React hook, useGuardedWebMCP, that wraps the existing useWebMCP from @mcp-b/react-webmcp — it composes rather than forks it. Each tool registration includes a ConsentMetadata object (scope, reversible, riskLevel, requiresApproval, optionally requireUserPresence). The hook maps this metadata to standard MCP ToolAnnotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint) via toMcpAnnotations(), so native runtimes that do have their own gates receive real behavioral hints. When requiresApproval is true and no native gate is detected, the call suspends in a framework-agnostic ConsentBroker, which manages a queue of pending requests, session preapproval for reversible tools, timeout/expiry, and decision event streams. The React layer (ConsentBrokerProvider, useConsentBroker, usePendingConsentRequests) lets any component render approval UI against the broker's state. The on-page card includes an isTrusted guard to reject script-dispatched synthetic clicks — a best-effort defense, not a tamper-proof boundary, which is why hasNativeConsentGate() exists as an escape hatch to defer to real browser/OS-level permission prompts where available. The upstream PR (link) adds only the hook, broker, types, annotations, WebAuthn presence verification, and tests to @mcp-b/react-webmcp — the demo app is a separate workspace member, not part of the package. title: Mandate
pitch: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents are locked out of nearly every high consequence system on earth. Not because they lack the capability, a model can read a payment queue and spot a duplicate or a sanctions hit faster than a person can, but because none of these systems has a way to grant an agent partial authority: enough to be useful, bounded enough to be safe, revocable the instant a human changes their mind. Today the choice is binary. Either the agent gets your credentials and can do everything you can do, or it gets nothing. Every bank, hospital, and factory picks nothing, and rationally so. WebMCP changes where that decision can live. Because tools are defined by the page itself, not by the model or its vendor, the site gets to decide what an agent may do, under what conditions, and for how long. Mandate is what that looks like on a bank's payment operations desk, where getting it wrong moves real money. What it does Mandate is a bank payment operations desk with an AI agent connected through WebMCP. The agent can investigate freely: read the queue, check a beneficiary, ask a partner screening bureau to recheck a sanctions match, but it cannot release a single payment on its own authority. To act, it has to negotiate. It calls propose_mandate , asking for what it needs, for example "up to 5,000 euros a payment, 50,000 total, SEPA only, verified beneficiaries only, for the next thirty minutes." That request shows up on the desk as a card a person can edit before agreeing: tighten the ceiling, shorten the clock, or refuse outright. The moment they grant it, the page re-registers its tool surface and a tool that did not exist a second earlier now does ( release_under_mandate , revoke_mandate ). The moment they revoke it, those tools vanish from the agent's list mid session. Three things fall out of that same property: A refusal is a conversation, not a 403. When the agent tries to release a payment it has no authority for, it gets back a plain English reason ("Segregation of duties: an agent cannot authorise a payment on its own authority") plus the two tools that would actually work, so it reroutes itself. The human sits inside the tool call, not notified after it. request_authorization returns a promise the page only resolves when a person clicks, so the agent is genuinely blocked and comes back with the real human answer. Nothing leaves the tab. All desk state is client side, so a bank could put real positions behind this and the agent would operate on data that never reaches a third party. What people and agents can do together that they could not before Until now an agent on a desk like this had two settings, and both are useless. Read only, in which case a person still makes every keystroke and the agent is a search box. Or the agent holds a human's credentials, in which case it can do everything that human can do and no bank will ever connect it. There was no way to express "you may do this much, for this long, and I can stop you." Three things happen on this desk that had nowhere to live before: An agent asks for authority in its own words, and a person edits the request before granting it. The agent proposes 5,000 euros a payment. Priya makes it 2,500 and grants that instead. The agent is told in its return value that its request was tightened, and works to the smaller number, leaving behind a 3,960 euro payment it would have been allowed to clear under its own proposal. Neither side had to anticipate the other in advance, which is what makes it a negotiation rather than a settings page. Two organisations settle one case without either handing over its data. The desk cannot see the bureau's watchlist. The bureau never sees the desk's payments. The agent asks the desk, the desk brokers the call across origins, and the answer comes back attributed to the bureau with an audit entry on both sides. That used to be a server to server integration with a contract behind it. Here it is one tool published to one named origin, and it works between two independent deployments. Authority ends mid conversation. A person clicks revoke and the tool the agent was about to reach for is gone from getTools() before its next call. Not a rejected request, and not a permission checked inside a handler: the capability itself stops existing while the session is still open. How it creates a better user experience For the person at the desk, the change is that they stop approving things one at a time and start setting a boundary once. Fifteen payments before a cut off used to be fifteen decisions. It becomes one decision about scope, after which the agent clears everything inside that scope and brings back everything outside it with the reason attached: above the ceiling you set, beneficiary not verified, sanctions match, wrong currency for that rail. Nothing is agreed to by accident either, because the ceiling, the budget, the rails, the beneficiary rule and the clock are all on screen and all editable before anyone clicks grant. For the agent, the change is that a refusal stops being a dead end. Every control answers in the shape a colleague would use: what is blocked, why, and what would work instead. So it reroutes itself instead of retrying the same call or inventing a workaround. And the desk keeps a permanent panel showing what the browser is actually holding, read live from getTools() rather than described in prose. Grant a mandate and the count moves from 18 to 20 on screen, in the same frame as the click. Revoke it and it drops back. Being able to see exactly what an agent may do at this moment is the thing you most want to know when you let one near your money, and it is normally the thing you cannot see at all. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This only works because WebMCP puts tool definitions in the page, computed from live state, instead of behind a static, server hosted tool list. A conventional MCP server hands a fixed set of tools to a client it cannot see. Mandate's tool surface is rebuilt and re-registered against an AbortSignal every time authority changes, so the mandate is real rather than cosmetic: tools do not exist until authority does, and they stop existing the instant it is withdrawn. That loop, an agent asking for authority, a human shaping it, and the tool surface itself changing as a result, is not possible outside a page hosted model. How we built it No backend, no database, no AI model of our own, no build step, and zero runtime dependencies. The visiting agent (Chrome with the WebMCP flag, or ChatGPT's in-app browser) brings the model; the page brings the tools and the governance. Twenty tools across five tiers, plus one published from a separate origin: Read tools with readOnlyHint: true (free rein: search payments, explain a hold, get exposure, pull the audit trail) Prepare tools that move no money (draft, amend, attach evidence) Consequential tools that block on a person ( request_authorization , release_payment , a declarative ask_the_desk form) Governance tools where the agent negotiates its own limits ( propose_mandate , get_mandate , undo_last_agent_action ) Mandate only tools that exist purely while authority is in force ( release_under_mandate , revoke_mandate ) The cross origin piece is Sentinel Screening Bureau, a genuinely separate deployment holding the sanctions watchlist. It never hands the list over. It publishes exactly one tool, scoped to origins it names: await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: 'recheck_beneficiary_screening', description: 'Re-run sanctions screening for one beneficiary.', inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }, { exposedTo: ['https://mandate-webmcp.vercel.app'] }); The desk embeds that origin with allow="tools" , discovers what it publishes with getTools({ fromOrigins }) , and brokers the call under its own governance, so the agent asks the desk and the desk answers with the bureau's decision plus an audit entry. Two organisations cooperating on one decision, neither handing over its data or its authority. The controls behind all of this (segregation of duties, four eyes approval, per role limits, sanctions screening, rail eligibility, duplicate detection, mandate scope) live in a pure, DOM free control engine covered by 34 tests that run on CI. Challenges we ran into Two spec behaviours we only found by testing against real Chrome, not by reading the explainer: executeTool takes a JSON string as its argument, not an object as the explainer shows, and it returns a JSON string too, which the explainer does not mention at all, so we had to handle both raw and serialised result shapes. We also learned the hard way that getTools({ fromOrigins }) is additive, not a filter: it returns your own tools plus the named origin's, so matching a partner's tool by name alone would have let a

title: My Calendar Planner
pitch: My Calendar Planner (MyCP) is an agent-native shared calendar and planning tool that resolves scheduling conflicts, finds available times, and accounts for user preferences when proposing times.
about_excerpt: My Calendar Planner (MyCP) is an agent-native shared calendar and planning tool that resolves scheduling conflicts, finds available times, and accounts for user preferences when proposing times. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Scheduling meetings with large teams can be a pain, even when everyone is available. When you need to account for different schedules, locations, time zones, focus time, or other factors, things can get unwieldy very quickly. Existing assistants often force people to choose between manually coordinating everything and granting broad write access. We wanted to show a better default: give the agent just enough structured context to help, then keep the final decision visible and human-owned. What it does MyCP is a seeded shared-calendar demo for a distributed launch team. A browser agent uses WebMCP tools to inspect narrowly scoped context, find one-time or weekly availability, and rank meeting options. A weekly proposal checks every requested occurrence against private busy time, protected focus blocks, work patterns, travel buffers, and time preferences without revealing why another person is unavailable. When one weekly check-in conflicts with the manager’s existing meeting, it can stage one bounded reschedule for that instance without moving the existing event. The same pattern works for time away: the agent can prepare one compact change-set draft containing a private absence, proposed cancellation of the manager’s owned meetings, and a transfer to an approved delegate. It cannot apply any of those changes or send notifications. The person reviews a before/after diff in the calendar, opens a confirmation dialog, and explicitly adds the event. That API path requires the reviewed draft revision, a five-minute one-time confirmation, and an idempotency key. Private events remain generic Busy blocks outside the owner’s access. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite for the calendar interface. A Cloudflare Worker for static assets, same-origin API routes, and the WebMCP headers. Cloudflare D1 for persistent seeded-demo state with revision-checked writes. Zod schemas shared at the command boundary. WebMCP imperative tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Vitest coverage for scheduling, redaction, draft lifecycle, confirmation, idempotency, and rate limits. WebMCP Usage MyCP registers fourteen intent-level tools rather than exposing DOM selectors or database access. get_calendar_context provides bounded calendar/team identifiers, while get_user_scheduling_profile reads a purpose-limited profile with meeting preferences, recurring focus blocks, and office/remote work patterns—never a home address, live location, or private events. propose_recurring_schedule validates one weekly local-time slot across 2–26 occurrences and can return no more than four explicit, reviewable exceptions. get_events_in_range and propose_time_away_changes return only active events the user owns, while create_time_away_change_set_draft can only stage—not apply—cancellations and approved-delegate transfers. Read tools are annotated as read-only. Tool outputs carrying calendar content are marked untrusted and limited to 1.4 KB of UTF-8 data; the adapter returns compact events and candidate slots, or a safe truncation response. commit_event is intentionally blocked so an agent cannot bypass the human confirmation flow. Challenges we ran into The key challenge was making the agent useful without making it overly powerful. We separated recommendation, draft creation, and final commit; applied server-side ownership and revision checks; and designed bounded result shapes that still give an agent enough information to continue safely. Persisting the deterministic demo across Worker isolates also required an explicit D1 persistence boundary rather than relying on in-memory state. Accomplishments that we're proud of From a design standpoint, it took some time to really hone in on what would make this tool useful. At first it was basically a scheduling assistant that didn't do much more than what Outlook can do now. However, once I started experimenting with recurring meetings that need occasional alterations, I realized that there are scenarios I run into all the time in real life that MyCP would actually help with. What we learned I mostly got a much better understanding of what could be possible with WebMCP and I'm already thinking of other ways to implement it in my day job. What's next for My Calendar Planner One area where this tool could be incredibly useful is with room management as well as meeting management. Bringing in systems to manage space bookings and maintenance in a large organization, like a university, could really help alleviate pain-points for scheduling that involve lots of difference factors. From a technical standpoint, we could add real authentication, provider OAuth, per-user notification preferences, RSVP-aware recurrence exceptions, delegate acceptance, outbound notifications, and a normalized D1 schema. Those additions would preserve the same visible-draft and explicit-confirmation boundaries. title: Advocate
pitch: When promises break, Advocate acts.
about_excerpt: When promises break, Advocate acts. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration A contract can tell you exactly what you are owed. That doesn't mean getting it is easy. When an obligation is missed, the person on the other side suddenly has another job: find the right clause, verify the breach, calculate the remedy, prepare the notice, submit the action, and keep enough evidence to prove what happened afterward. AI can already explain a contract. We wanted to see if the browser could do the harder part: turn the obligation into action. But that immediately created a second question. If an agent can take consequential actions on your behalf, where should its authority stop? That question became Advocate. We built Advocate to let an agent do the tedious work of investigating and preparing an enforcement action, while reserving the final consequential decision for the human. What it does Advocate is a browser-native WebMCP enforcement simulation. Our demo starts with a contract requiring an approved invoice to be settled within 15 calendar days. The invoice has remained unpaid for another 32 days, with $12,840 in principal at stake. From there, Advocate runs one complete workflow: Contract → Entitlement → Approval → Action → Receipt The website exposes four WebMCP tools: fetch_contract_clause(clause_id) Finds the controlling contractual obligation. compute_statutory_penalty(jurisdiction, delay_days, base_amount) Calculates the simulated entitlement from structured claim data. generate_enforceable_demand_notice(claim_payload) Prepares the action the agent intends to take. file_dispute_record(action_id, proof_hash) Executes the simulated filing after authorization. The first part can happen autonomously. Advocate can inspect the contract, determine the breach, calculate the claim, and prepare the next step without repeatedly interrupting the user. Then it stops. Immediately before notice generation and filing, Advocate requires explicit human authorization. That approval generates a SHA-256 proof tied to the exact execution intent, timestamp, and nonce. Only after that authorization can the filing continue. The completed run produces a receipt containing the action ID, filing timestamp, claim hash, authorization proof hash, statutory citation used by the simulation, ledger sequence, and final receipt hash. So Advocate doesn't end with: "The agent says it did it." It ends with a record of what the user approved and what the system executed. How we built it The most important technical decision was to build the workflow around WebMCP instead of browser automation. A traditional browser agent has to inspect a page, guess which DOM elements matter, click through the interface, and hope the website has not changed. With WebMCP, Advocate exposes the underlying capabilities directly as typed tools. Each of our four tools has a JSON schema defining exactly what the agent can provide and what operation the website will perform. We register those tools against the current document.modelContext WebMCP producer API, with a compatibility path for the earlier navigator.modelContext surface. We deliberately did not create one giant enforce_contract() tool. Splitting the workflow into four tools makes every transition visible: evidence → calculation → preparation → execution It also gives the website a natural place to apply authorization before the consequential operation. Every invocation feeds Advocate's telemetry stream with schema validation, typed inputs, execution state, outputs or errors, and latency. Human authorization The approval step is separate from the agent's reasoning. When the user approves the proposed enforcement action, Advocate creates a SHA-256 proof from the execution intent, timestamp, and nonce. That proof is carried into the filing step so the executed action can be associated with the authorization that permitted it. Replay protection Agent workflows retry. Networks fail. Tools can be called more than once. An agent may even repeat an operation while reasoning. For a consequential action, "just don't call it twice" is not a sufficient safety mechanism. file_dispute_record is therefore idempotent by action ID. Calling the same filing again does not create another record. Receipt After execution, Advocate generates a final receipt containing the important identifiers and hashes from the completed run and provides a downloadable PDF representation. Verification We added automated checks for syntax, WebMCP schemas and flow behavior, idempotency, and the production build. The application has no runtime package dependencies and is deployed over HTTPS on Vercel, giving WebMCP the secure browser context it requires. The result is intentionally small: 4 browser tools. 1 human authorization boundary. 1 consequential action. 1 inspectable receipt. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not getting WebMCP tools to execute. It was deciding where the agent must stop. If we asked for permission before every tool call, the agent would become little more than a complicated button sequence. If we let the agent continue through the filing step without interruption, the user would no longer meaningfully control the consequential action. The boundary we arrived at was: Preparation can be autonomous. Execution requires authority. That lets Advocate do the boring work while asking the human for a decision only when that decision actually matters. The second challenge was making approval specific enough to be useful. A boolean like approved = true tells us almost nothing. What was approved? Was it the same action that eventually executed? Could an old approval be reused? We therefore bind authorization to the execution intent, timestamp, and nonce and carry the resulting proof into the filing. The third challenge was retry safety. Web and agent workflows are not perfectly reliable, so we had to design the consequential tool assuming duplicate calls could happen. That led us to make filing idempotent by action ID rather than treating retries as an edge case. Finally, WebMCP itself is an emerging browser capability. We wanted the project to use the real producer model while remaining inspectable and testable during development, so we built a compatibility surface and a local runtime mirror alongside the canonical API. Accomplishments that we're proud of The thing we're most proud of is not any individual feature. It is that the entire loop works together. A single run can move from a contractual obligation, through four typed WebMCP operations, through an explicit human authorization boundary, into an idempotent filing, and finally into a receipt. We also made the normally invisible parts of an agent workflow visible. Judges and users can watch the tool name, schema validation, payload, latency, returned result, authorization point, and final receipt instead of having to trust a loading spinner. And WebMCP is not decorative in Advocate. If you removed WebMCP, you would have to redesign how the agent interacts with the application. That was one of our goals from the beginning: build something where WebMCP changes the product itself rather than simply appearing in the technology list. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is: A tool schema is not an authorization model. WebMCP can tell an agent what a website is capable of doing. It does not automatically answer whether the agent should be allowed to do it. For consequential workflows we found ourselves thinking about four separate questions: What can the agent do? What does the agent intend to do? What did the human authorize? What actually happened? Those sound similar, but they are different parts of the system. We also learned that human-in-the-loop does not have to mean human-in-every-step. The agent should be able to perform reversible investigation and preparation without constant confirmation. Human attention should be reserved for the boundary where authority actually changes hands. Finally, we learned that retries and observability are not boring implementation details once agents can act. A duplicated tool call or an invisible failure means something very different when the operation creates a real effect. What's next for Advocate Advocate today is a controlled enforcement simulation, not legal advice or a production dispute-filing service. The next meaningful step is not adding more AI. It is replacing the simulated boundaries with real ones. That means connecting WebMCP tools to authenticated account and dispute APIs, moving authorization and receipt storage to a trusted server-side environment, using independently maintained jurisdiction-specific rules, strengthening receipt verification, and adding durable identity and policy controls. We would also like to explore a reusable authorization pattern for consequential WebMCP actions so that the same idea could apply beyond contracts—to refunds, account changes, purchases, bookings, claims, and other actions where an agent can

title: EXPOSURE // INCIDENT ZERO
pitch: Governed AI incident response where ChatGPT investigates infrastructure through WebMCP, humans authorize consequential actions, and the agent executes remediation and verifies recovery.
about_excerpt: Governed AI incident response where ChatGPT investigates infrastructure through WebMCP, humans authorize consequential actions, and the agent executes remediation and verifies recovery. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Project Logo Inspiration Production incidents rarely fail in obvious ways. A database may appear overloaded even when the real cause is an application deployment several layers upstream. Engineers must correlate telemetry, logs, dependencies, changes, risk, and human constraints—often while customers are already affected. Exposure explores a better operating model: an infrastructure engineer and an AI agent working together inside the same live command environment. What it does Exposure is an agent-native operational intelligence system built around a simulated nine-node Enterprise Linux 9 production fleet. The featured scenario, Incident Zero , begins when a checkout platform develops severe latency and HTTP 502 errors. PostgreSQL appears to be failing, but the database is actually a downstream victim of a faulty application deployment. Using WebMCP, the agent can: Inspect fleet health Examine individual hosts and services Map infrastructure dependencies Query metrics and logs Review deployments and configuration changes Develop and test competing root-cause hypotheses Record human operational constraints Evaluate remediation options Request explicit human authorization Execute a simulated rolling rollback Verify recovery through measured evidence Generate an auditable incident record Why WebMCP WebMCP is the operating interface between Exposure and the AI agent. Instead of requiring ChatGPT to infer actions from page text or manipulate arbitrary UI controls, Exposure exposes explicit, governed incident-response tools with defined inputs, state transitions, safety constraints, and authorization boundaries. The agent can investigate the incident, register constraints, propose remediation, request authorization, execute an approved rolling rollback, and verify recovery. It deliberately cannot authorize its own consequential remediation. This creates a practical human-agent operating model: the AI can reason and act, while the human retains authority over consequential decisions. Human authority Exposure does not allow an agent to jump directly from suspicion to execution. The operator can establish a constraint such as: Do not restart PostgreSQL. That constraint becomes part of the operational state and blocks conflicting actions. When Exposure identifies the faulty checkout deployment, it proposes a rolling rollback and stops at an authorization gate. Only the human operator can approve the consequential action. Incident Zero The simulation models: One Nginx edge load balancer Two Nginx web servers Three checkout application servers One Redis cache server One PostgreSQL primary One PostgreSQL replica A faulty checkout release creates excessive database connections across the application tier. This causes database pressure, replication lag, web-tier timeouts, and customer-facing failures. The agent must distinguish root cause from downstream symptoms, compare remediation options, respect the operator’s constraints, and prove that recovery occurred. Product experience Exposure presents the incident through a cinematic operational interface: A living infrastructure topology Animated traffic and dependency paths Fleet telemetry Structured evidence Competing hypotheses Contradiction detection Risk assessment Human authorization gates Visible rollback progression Recovery verification A sealed decision trace Every visual transition communicates real application state rather than decorative animation. Technical approach Exposure uses TypeScript, React, Vite, structured JSON Schema inputs, and the WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool() API. A deterministic client-side incident engine controls fleet state, evidence, tool results, authorization, remediation, and recovery. The competition build requires no production credentials, external infrastructure, or paid APIs. The fleet is simulated, but its telemetry, Linux services, logs, dependencies, failure behavior, and remediation sequence are designed to remain technically credible. What comes next The challenge release focuses on one polished, deterministic incident. Future versions could connect Exposure to authenticated operational systems such as Prometheus, Grafana, Ansible, cloud platforms, service-management systems, and enterprise observability tools. Exposure’s objective is simple: expose what is happening, reveal why it is happening, control what happens next, and prove whether the action worked. Built With aiagents chatgpt cloudflare codex css enterprise json linux pages react schema svg typescript vite webmcp Try it out incidentzero.swarmaxis.ai github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built Exposure // Incident Zero end-to-end, combining my infrastructure engineering background with agent-native operational design. I developed the incident model, WebMCP tool architecture, human-authorization boundary, deterministic remediation workflow, and production experience. I also designed the scenario around a realistic failure pattern: distinguishing an overloaded PostgreSQL database from the upstream application deployment actually causing the incident. The goal was to demonstrate that AI can safely investigate and operate infrastructure while humans retain authority over consequential actions. Scott Steele Lead Automation Architect. Brings WebMCP to consumers and photographers to interact, create, and edit prints before they buy thee, in natural language or with agents.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 This project was inspired by my love for merging the bleeding edge of technology with issues I personally run into or know other's in my community that also have frustrations surrounding it. Commonly, people just want "that thing" to work, right now. WebMCP feels like the magical layer we've been missing! 

 What it does 

 Batch Relay allows you to visualize and edit prints, text and image nodes, before you "add to cart". You can also interactively say use "that" image and order "that" print, all in the background. It lets us have a sort of companion-like shopping experience0 This proof-of-concept demo, brings an agentic layer into the interface with WebMCP. Anything a human can do, an agent has access to. 

 How we built it 

 This project was built using Codex, ChatGPT, Vercel/Next.js, and a bit of other LLMs sprinkled in. I throughly tested it with the built-in ChatGPT web Browser as well as Nekuda's WebMCP workbench Chrome plugin. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Testing the interactions were a bit of a challenge. Sometime's the tools would break down, and would need new chat threads, be told how to proceed and such. Outside of that, it was clear Batch Relay's API needed some other stuff, so a bit of back and forth here! 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 With new technology, comes new challenges. As such, I'm personally proud of the special agent-human interactions I crafted, such as the live previews that show up in the lower left corner, asking a human to confirm or deny a change made by an agent. This also lets humans stay in-focus with their current task at hand. It's there when you need it with a gentle nudge, and gone when you don't. 

 You can also see what an agent is working on, in the lower right corner. Actions it takes will be presented here, so it's not a total "blackbox" experience! 

 What we learned 

 I honestly learned a lot, but most importantly, this challenge has shifted my product-thinking. Going forward I will lead with not only thinking about the user experience, the agentic experience, but also the human-agent layer. 

 What's next for Batch Relay WebMCP 

 A lot! We've already rolled some of this into our custom Templating Engine, as well as our Form builder. It's clear WebMCP is here to change how we interact with our browsers and the way we experience the web... How exciting! As such, I'm excited to keep building & exploring new ways to surface even more of the platform!

title: Relocates.io
pitch: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't.
about_excerpt: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We had one weekend of viewings, in a city none of us had lived in, and a spreadsheet. The question was simple and nothing could answer it: where can all four of us actually live? Property sites filter by price and bedroom count. But nobody is unhappy about a bedroom count. They're unhappy because the school run takes forty minutes, and because that got decided once, in a hurry, from three timezones away, and then paid for every morning for three years. So we guessed. Everybody guesses. It's a constraint satisfaction problem and it deserved a solver, so we wrote one. Every requirement becomes a comparison over a 250-metre grid of the real city: real schools from Google Places with their real ratings, real gyms, real parks, and real terrain, so a hill costs the minutes it actually costs. Where everyone's requirements overlap, a volume lights up over the photorealistic map. Then it goes to zero. Six honest requirements from four people usually don't fit in one city. Every tool we'd used treats that as a dead end. Empty list, try removing a filter. But "nowhere works" is genuinely useful information, as long as you also say which two requirements are fighting and how much one has to give. So the page tests dropping each requirement, then every pair, then sweeps the blocking thresholds to find the smallest concession that reopens the map. It draws both options at once, in the colours of the two people involved. That's the point where WebMCP stopped being a technology choice. The solver can tell you bending one limit reopens more ground than bending the other. It can't tell you that one of those limits is a bad knee and the other is a fourteen-year-old walking to school by herself. It can't know that the cheaper concession is the harder one to live with. Somebody has to say "hers is cheaper, but hers is the medical one" — and a slider is never going to say that. But it doesn't work from a server either. The agent offers two futures, the page draws both over the real city, and the person picks by looking at them. What's being compared is a shape on a map, not a number in a response. The state and the solver have to sit where the person's eyes already are. The loop runs both ways too, which is the part we didn't expect to matter as much as it does. People don't wait their turn. They drag a threshold while the agent is still talking, delete something, accept an option on their own. Those edits are real and they aren't the agent's. So the page logs who changed what and hands the agent everything a human did since its last turn. What it does Relocates.io finds the part of a city where everyone in a household gets what they need at the same time, draws it on a photorealistic 3D map, and when that region doesn't exist, tells you exactly which requirements collide and how far one has to move. You can describe your household to an agent or build it by hand. Both drive the same state. Pick a city. It builds a 250 m grid and loads the terrain. Add people, then their requirements. Not filters — requirements that belong to someone, each carrying their own reason in their own words. "She walks alone, it's her independence." "It's his knee, not a preference." That sentence matters later. Watch where they overlap. The intersection is contoured and extruded over the real buildings. The area in km² is the number on screen. When it hits zero, you get options, not an error. The page finds what's blocking, works out the smallest movement that reopens the map, and draws both candidate futures at once with the area each one buys. You choose. Click one and it resolves. Both numbers were already on screen — what the agent adds is which concession is cheaper, which is easier, and why those aren't the same. Then check a real listing. Paste an address, get pass or fail on every requirement with the margin, plus the nearest spots that would have worked. Or search homes restricted to inside the feasible region, so it can't return somewhere that fails one of your family. The 3D isn't decoration. If you can't fly out for a third viewing, the two things you most need to see are what a street looks like and how steep it is, and a flat map shows neither. Walking times run through Tobler's hiking function over real elevation, so a kilometre uphill costs about 40% more than a flat one. The hill you can see is the hill that makes the school walk eleven minutes instead of seven. Same dataset drives the picture and the arithmetic. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Google Maps Platform, WebMCP. About 4,600 lines. No server, no database, no API routes. Browser tab ├── Grid 250 m lattice over the search area ├── Layers one Float32Array per question — walk time, commute, grade ├── Solver masks · marching squares · diagnosis · relaxation sweep ├── Map3D photorealistic tiles + pooled extruded volumes ├── WebMCP 18 tools on document.modelContext └── Cache IndexedDB — a city is learned once Everything runs in the browser through the Maps JS SDK and caches locally. Nothing about the household leaves the page. That started as a constraint and turned out to be the reason the whole thing works: an agent can reach into live state and get an answer in the same tick. Places and Elevation are real. Commute times are modelled from distance and mode rather than routed, and we say so on screen. We skipped the Routes API on purpose. Real routed commutes meant thousands of billed matrix elements per origin and several seconds of latency on every threshold change, which would have killed the thing that makes the sweep feel like an instrument. Two functions carry the project. diagnose.ts answers why there's nowhere to live. With a dozen requirements over a few thousand cells there's no need to be clever, so it tests every leave-one-out combination, then every pair if none of those work. Exhaustive and exact. frontier.ts answers how far a requirement has to bend, sweeping its threshold across the grid for the smallest movement that opens any cell, then the area gained at every step after. It returns a curve, not a point, so the agent can describe what a concession costs. Both measure off the grid. Neither estimates. That's the whole technical claim, so it lives in the code rather than in a paragraph. The map uses Map3DElement with regions as extruded Polygon3DElement volumes and drawsOccludedSegments on, so buildings never hide the answer. Those are DOM nodes, not batched geometry, so they're pooled at startup and mutated in place. Three things about the tools mattered more than the rest. Descriptions say when to call something, not just what it does: "call this whenever the area is 0, before telling the user anything." Every requirement carries a required rationale field. And get_state returns humanChanges , so the agent finds out what a person did while it wasn't looking. Challenges we ran into deck.gl doesn't work over photorealistic tiles. The obvious stack was a dead end. Overlays float above the terrain instead of sitting on it. We dropped deck.gl for native Polygon3DElement , which Google renders against the same terrain as the tiles. Found it with a throwaway HTML file before writing any real code, which saved a day. Google has no ratings for schools. Gyms, parks and supermarkets all return them. Secondary schools returned zero out of eight. Our "4★ or better" filter emptied the pool, so every school requirement became permanently unsatisfiable and the map went permanently blank. Saying "nowhere qualifies" would have been a lie with a straight face, so the filter now drops itself, says so in a banner, and reports the caveat to the agent. Nobody agrees where WebMCP lives. Drafts disagree on navigator.modelContext versus document.modelContext . We built against navigator , and an agent looking at the live page told us exactly what that produces: "exposes WebMCP capability, but currently provides no WebMCP tools." It now checks document first, awaits each registration, and tears down with AbortSignal . Photorealistic tiles take no style array. No saturation: -100 , so the grey-out when there's no answer had to be a CSS filter on the container. It greys the regions too, but during a conflict there are no regions to keep coloured, so that worked out. The numbers sit in an unfiltered layer above. Cutting things. Routes API, air quality, saved sessions, multi-city. All had to go to keep one sequence working reliably: requirements, conflict, two futures, a choice. Accomplishments that we're proud of The empty state is the product. Treating "nowhere works" as the interesting case is the idea everything is built around, and it held up against real data from a real city. Every number is real. Every km² and every minute comes off the grid. The agent is told never to state a figure it didn't get from a tool, and the tools are shaped so it never nee
video_title: Relocates.io
video_transcript_excerpt: Finding a place for a family usually means juggling dozens of open tabs, trying to guess where everyone's daily life actually intersects. Relocates.io solves this geometrically. We input a family of four relocating to San Francisco. David commuting to Google, Sarah, Leah, and 8-year-old Tom. The agent parses the household and registers the profiles directly into client state. Now we define their daily mobility constraints. David needs transit within 30 minutes. Leah needs a 15-minute walk to high school. Tom needs 10 minutes to primary school, plus a nearby gym and park. The browser intersects these travel boundaries on device, 29.38 square kilometers across five candidate zones. Now the hard constraint. Sarah has an injured knee. Any pedestrian incline over a 6% grade is physically out of the question. That medical requirement is treated as non-negotiable, factoring San Francisco's elevation profiles into the pedestrian routes. >> The viable terrain immediately collapses by more than half down to 13.44 square kilometers. Hills eliminate most of the city. Instead of negotiating back and forth in chat, I open the drawer and adjust the sliders myself, granting Tom 17 minutes and tightening the park to six. Web MCP immediately detects my manual edits and synchronizes the agent state. The polygon updates dynamically to 11.88 square kilometers, highlighting five qualifying neighborhoods, including the Presidio. We drop straight into 3D terrain to verify street inclines before signing a lease. Compromise isn't an argument anymore. It's just geometry.

title: Meshful
pitch: Learn anything and make it stick. Your AI agent prepares the material and grades answers in your own words, while Meshful schedules each concept for the right time.
about_excerpt: Learn anything and make it stick. Your AI agent prepares the material and grades answers in your own words, while Meshful schedules each concept for the right time. Like Comment Story Updates How Meshful was Born A study system should test your memory, not your patience. Spaced repetition works, but using it can feel like building the course before taking it. You start by deciding what matters and how to organize ideas you do not understand yet. Then you grade yourself. You might reveal the answer before trying to recall it, think “Oh, I knew that!” only after seeing it, or explain the right idea in different words and still doubt yourself. Meshful removes deck setup and self-grading, but you still do the work that makes learning stick. An agent prepares the material and evaluates your answers while you recall each idea, explain it in your own words, and learn from honest feedback. Meshful schedules every review, tracks your progress, shows what comes next, and brings each idea back when it is time to try again. What Meshful does Meshful turns that burden into one clear study loop. Choose a course from the Deck Library or ask an agent to build a custom deck on your topic. For custom decks, the agent draws on its own knowledge and runs Meshful's validator to catch missing definitions, duplicate cards, and broken prerequisite links. The validator checks the deck's structure. It cannot verify every fact. Once the deck is ready, all you have to do is click Study and give each term your best attempt. Study shows you one term without its definition. You explain it in your own words in chat. The agent checks your answer against the card's built-in rubric and rates your recall as Again, Hard, Good, or Easy. Through WebMCP, it sends the grade to Meshful, which saves it and updates your FSRS schedule. Meshful reveals the definition while the agent explains what you got right or missed. Then the next term appears. The agent handles judgment and teaching, so the experience can improve as models improve. The site owns the decks, review history, schedule, progress, and interface. Choose a Deck Library course or have an agent build a custom deck ↓ Click Study ↓ Give your best answer in your own words ↓ The agent grades your recall and sends the grade to Meshful ↓ Meshful saves the grade and updates your FSRS schedule ↓ See the definition and get feedback ↓ Move to the next useful idea ↺ Finish today's reviews or continue with eligible new material Due reviews come first. When they are done, Meshful continues with eligible new material. Ideas you miss return sooner. Strong answers earn longer gaps. As you earn Good or Easy on prerequisite ideas, later ideas open. You move toward mastery without leaving older knowledge behind. How I built Meshful I started with the study loop and worked backward: what must the agent understand, and what must the site make exact? One shared deck model. Every course uses the same structure, whether it comes from the Deck Library or an agent. Each card stores a term, a hidden definition, a grading rubric, and links to the ideas that should come first. This gives learners one consistent study experience instead of a different format for every subject. A learning map, not a pile. The prerequisite links form a map of how the ideas fit together. That map decides which new cards are ready to appear. It solves a different problem from the memory schedule: prerequisites control what you are ready to learn, while FSRS controls when you should review it. FSRS sets the pace. Meshful gives each grade to FSRS, which updates when the card should return. Missed ideas come back sooner, strong answers earn longer gaps, and reviews that are due come before new material. WebMCP closes the loop. The agent reads the active card and its rubric, understands the learner's own words, chooses a grade, and explains the gap. It sends one grade to Meshful through WebMCP. The site checks the active session and card, records one review, runs FSRS once, and moves forward once. WebMCP lets the agent work with the same study state the learner sees while Meshful remains the source of truth. Challenges I ran into 1. Keeping the agent flexible without letting study state drift The problem. Agents are good at understanding the different ways people explain an idea, and that judgment should improve as models improve. A study site has a different job. It must know exactly which card is active, save one grade, update the schedule once, and show the right next step. If those roles blur, a retry or model mistake could create duplicate reviews or conflicting progress. The solution. I split the work at a clear boundary. The agent reads the learner's answer, applies the rubric, explains what was missing, and proposes a grade. Meshful validates and commits every exact change through WebMCP. Why it works. The learning record stays deterministic while the intelligence can keep improving. The boundary leaves room to trade speed for deeper reasoning as agent models improve, without changing the rules of the deck, schedule, or progress. 2. Making generated decks and grading trustworthy The problem. A deck can look complete while hiding a weak definition, a broken prerequisite, or a rubric that grades normal wording unfairly. Free-form grading is just as difficult. A correct answer may use different words, while a confident answer may still miss the key idea. Structural checks alone cannot prove that the content is right or that the grader is fair. The solution. I used deterministic validation to catch missing fields, duplicate cards, and broken references. Then I built small benchmarks with synthetic learner answers that ranged from wrong to partly right to correct in different words. I compared each grade with a frozen reference judgment, reviewed the feedback for mistakes, changed the instructions, and ran the same cases again. Why it works. The validator tests the deck's structure, while the benchmark tests the judgment built on top of it. The current benchmark is small, so it does not yet prove broad accuracy. It does give me a repeatable way to improve performance as I add more subjects, answer styles, and models. Why Meshful matters Meshful matters to me because it turns curiosity into a study system I can act on. A new subject can begin with an honest attempt, useful feedback, and a clear next review instead of hours of setup and uncertain self-grading. As the Deck Library grows and agents improve, the same trusted loop can support more subjects and stronger feedback. Meshful is more than a demo. It is a foundation for making serious study easier to begin, continue, and measure honestly. What's next for Meshful I see two main paths for Meshful. A broader Deck Library. I want to add law, medicine, history, and more advanced courses in the subjects already covered. This would save more people from having to build every deck themselves. I also want to explore deck publishing, so people can easily share what they make while keeping the source and quality of each deck clear. Practice beyond terms. I want to move from recall into questions and problems. Math and coding are learned by doing. The agent could review a solution, explain where the reasoning or code went wrong, and bring back focused practice later. The hard part is adapting an FSRS-like schedule to work with many valid paths and several skills at once. Rather than repeat one problem, Meshful could schedule a problem type and create a fresh version each time. This would bring the same loop of practice, feedback, and well-timed review to richer challenges. title: CoCanvas
pitch: Chat is a bad place to move a box. You write the brief. A WebMCP agent draws on the same board. If the draft is a mess, undo it. No screenshot guessing.
about_excerpt: Chat is a bad place to move a box. You write the brief. A WebMCP agent draws on the same board. If the draft is a mess, undo it. No screenshot guessing. Like Comment Story Updates Astra from the announcement. Drawn on this board. Payment skipped. The page finds it. Try it. Link in the description. Inspiration When I try to map a product flow with an agent, the work happens in chat. I ask it to add payment between address and success. It returns a paragraph, or a table of labels. I still rebuild the diagram by hand. Exporting a PNG is not a better contract. The model infers from pixels, and I cannot undo a node. I wanted the brief and the board in the same tab, and I wanted the agent to edit that board the way I do. WebMCP is how I tried that. What it does CoCanvas is a product-flow canvas that stays in the browser. You write a brief. You and an agent add nodes, arrows, and pins to the same document. There is no account and no server. The board is stored in localStorage . Connect an agent and it receives 25 tools on that store. It can draft from the brief, connect two element ids, run a review owned by the page, and pin a note on a real node. Every change is tagged You or Agent. Undo reverts the last turn. Find the gap is the short path. The page sets a grocery-checkout brief, draws cart, address, and success, and omits payment. review_canvas reports the gap and pins it on Success. You add Payment in the UI and export a PNG. Astra from the source is the longer ChatGPT prompt. It opens the GPT-6 Astra announcement and draws a product map: a hub, four children, score bars for figures that appear on the page, and pins on what is still rolling out. If the tab has no host, the header reads Not connected. The Agent panel still runs the same tools. Once a host is connected, tool results can enter its context, and writes stay undoable either way. How I built it The tools run in the page, against the same store the UI writes to. The tools register on document.modelContext after the store loads, then navigator.modelContext , then window.modelContext . ChatGPT injects the host after first paint, so registration retries. The Agent panel uses a private polyfill that does not occupy document.modelContext , which leaves room for a late host. Availability follows board state. draft_from_brief and review_canvas require a brief. connect_elements requires two nodes. Each tool has its own AbortController . When a tool leaves the gate, that signal aborts and the host removes it. review_canvas is application code. It reads the brief, the nodes, and the connectors. It reports a missing step, an unlabeled shape, an arrow between siblings that already hang from a hub, and an arrow attached to a score bar. await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "review_canvas", description: "Page-owned review of the live board against the brief.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: () => { const report = reviewCanvas(store()); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(report, null, 2) }] }; }, }); Challenges I ran into The agent kept producing layouts that did not read as a diagram: a table of labels, a row of colored cards, a hub stretched across the page so every arrow could stay vertical, then a side arrow from API into Rollout that appeared to pass through the box. Those constraints now live on the page: arrows bend from a compact hub, sibling links and score-bar links are rejected, and review reports them when they slip in. Site tools failed the same way they did on Glassbook. The Microsoft Store build of ChatGPT desktop left document.modelContext undefined. The installer from the ChatGPT website worked. The connect guide now names GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra, and notes that Luna and Light do not expose site tools. What I'm proud of The Astra board is what I wanted out of this. It comes from the announcement, and it stays a map I can still edit. Find the gap is simpler, and it is the clearest proof. The page catches the missing step, pins it on the success node, and I add Payment in the UI without leaving the board. What I learned If the page does not own the review, the model will accept a table of labels as a finished board. If the last turn cannot be undone, it is hard to let the agent draft. The pin on Success did more useful work than another write tool. What's next for CoCanvas Too much of the diagram guidance still lives in the prompt. I want more of it enforced by the tools. Sharing is not built. localStorage covers one tab, which is enough for a demo and not enough for a workshop.
