title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: PawPilot
pitch: PawPilot is a WebMCP-powered pet-care agent that turns natural language into action
about_excerpt: PawPilot is a WebMCP-powered pet-care agent that turns natural language into action Like Comment Story Updates PawPilot — Project Story Try the live agent demo Live agent demo: https://agent-6a965dc9f0937d545273e692--pawpilot-webmcp.netlify.app This is the agent-facing PawPilot deployment used for the demo experience. The underlying WebMCP capabilities, server-side validation, human approval boundary, and persisted care-plan workflow remain part of the PawPilot application. What inspired me PawPilot started with a simple question: What if talking to a pet-care website could feel as natural as talking to an assistant? Pet care is full of information—profiles, routines, products, services, and care plans—but people are still expected to click through pages and menus to make something happen. I wanted to see what would happen if the website could actually understand what an agent needs to do. So I built PawPilot around my dog Dojo and started turning a normal pet-care website into something an agent could actually work with. That became my experiment with the agentic web: PawPilot. Why WebMCP matters to me WebMCP changes the interaction model from People → Pages → Buttons toward People → Agents → Capabilities. That idea really clicked for me. Instead of an agent having to guess what a website can do by looking at text and buttons, PawPilot explicitly tells the agent what capabilities are available. PawPilot exposes six structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext: get_pet_profile get_daily_needs find_pet_services find_pet_products save_care_plan list_care_plans The result is a website that can participate in an agent conversation instead of just waiting for a person to navigate it. What people and agents can do together A person can simply ask: “Build Dojo a care plan for today.” From there, the agent can use PawPilot's structured capabilities to retrieve Dojo's profile, understand his daily needs, find relevant services or products, and prepare a proposed care plan. But I didn't want “agentic” to mean “the agent gets to do whatever it wants.” The important boundary is the write operation. PawPilot does not allow the OpenAI agent to silently save a care plan. The person gets to see what is being proposed and explicitly chooses Confirm & Save. Only then does the server issue a short-lived approval token tied to that exact pet and exact plan before accepting the database write. So the collaboration loop becomes: User request → Agent discovers capabilities → Agent prepares action → Human reviews → Human approves → Server verifies → Action is saved That separation between what an agent can discover, what it can execute, and what a human must authorize became one of the most important parts of PawPilot for me. I didn't stop at the website — I built a Safari WebMCP Bridge While I was building PawPilot, I ran into another question: what happens when the browser experience around WebMCP isn't there yet? Instead of treating that as a reason to stop, I built a PawPilot WebMCP Bridge Safari Web Extension alongside the application. This part matters because I wasn't trying to fake native WebMCP support. The extension is deliberately a browser-side inspection, compatibility, and testing layer. PawPilot's own WebMCP registration and server-side authorization remain the source of truth. The extension can detect native WebMCP through document.modelContext, discover tools with getTools(), and, when the runtime supports it, invoke executeTool(). It also treats write-capable tools differently and requires explicit confirmation before executing them. I gave the extension its own little developer workspace too: an in-page PawPilot WebMCP Console, a Safari-friendly popup dashboard, live tool and toolchange monitoring, runtime and Permissions Policy diagnostics, background event history, and structured report export. I also ran into one of those very real browser problems that doesn't show up in a clean architecture diagram. Safari/WebKit was giving me a WebKitBlobResource failure around report downloads. I changed the exporter to use a data: URL instead of Blob URLs and URL.createObjectURL(). That made the export path Safari-safe and taught me something I probably wouldn't have learned by only testing in one browser. The extension is kept separate under safari-extension/ specifically so it can inspect PawPilot without modifying the existing WebMCP registration. That separation was intentional: the bridge can tell me what the browser actually supports instead of pretending native support exists when it doesn't. And then PawPilot needed somewhere to remember what happened I also didn't want the care-plan part of the demo to be a fake screen that only looked like it saved something. PawPilot uses a Netlify-hosted database with Drizzle migrations to persist care plans. The application has a database migration for the care_plans data, and the server-side tool layer performs the validation and persistence after the approval boundary has been satisfied. That gives the demo a complete path from agent request to real application state: WebMCP capability → validated operation → human approval → authorized server write → persisted care plan That was important to me because I wanted the “action” in agentic web to actually mean something. The agent isn't just generating text about a care plan; PawPilot can turn that approved plan into saved application state. How I built it PawPilot is a Next.js application deployed on Netlify with a browser-native WebMCP layer. The WebMCP client registers the six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(), including descriptions, JSON input schemas, read/write annotations, and executable handlers. Tool execution is routed through the application's server-side validation layer rather than trusting browser-provided parameters. The OpenAI interaction layer uses the same centralized tool catalog for its agent-facing read capabilities, while save_care_plan remains UI-controlled. This keeps the WebMCP surface and application implementation aligned instead of creating a separate set of business rules for every integration. The Safari WebMCP Bridge lives separately under safari-extension/ so it can inspect PawPilot without modifying the application's existing WebMCP registration. Its content script handles discovery, diagnostics, events, and controlled execution; the popup provides the developer-facing controls; and the background script keeps bridge event history. The care-plan persistence path uses the Netlify database and Drizzle migration already in the project. The database write remains behind the same server-side approval and validation boundary as the rest of the application. Browser testing: real WebMCP calls I tested PawPilot with WebMCP enabled in Microsoft Edge and Google Chrome. I didn't want to stop at seeing a WebMCP object on the page. The six tools were exposed through document.modelContext, discovered with getTools(), and actually invoked through executeTool() against live PawPilot implementations. The Safari extension gives me another way to inspect that capability surface and see what the browser/runtime is actually exposing. That distinction matters: PawPilot isn't just an HTTP API with “WebMCP” written on top of it. The website exposes structured capabilities through the WebMCP surface, and those capabilities connect to real application behavior and persisted state. Challenges WebMCP is an emerging standard, which meant I had to learn while building. Browser support and developer tooling are still evolving, and testing exposed differences between environments. I ended up separating several things that are easy to blur together: The website registering its capabilities The browser exposing those capabilities The agent discovering and using them The server validating and executing the underlying operation The database persisting the approved result The human deciding whether a consequential action should actually happen Building the Safari Bridge made that separation even clearer. A browser tool shouldn't quietly pretend that native support exists. It should tell you what is really happening and give you useful diagnostics when it doesn't. Safety and trust PawPilot is a demo of controlled agentic action, not autonomous pet-care decision making. Read operations can be performed through structured tools. A care-plan write requires explicit human confirmation and a server-generated approval challenge tied to the exact proposed payload. Approval tokens are short-lived and single-use within the active server instance. The demo does not claim user identity or authentication. The approval mechanism is an action-authorization boundary for this demo, not an identity system. I wanted that distinction to be clear rather than hiding it behind impressive-sounding AI language. title: Clunk
pitch: A game-asset shop where a person and their agent use one screen: the agent pulls the capsule machine, shops by measured facts, drives the 3D viewer and creates assets via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A game-asset shop where a person and their agent use one screen: the agent pulls the capsule machine, shops by measured facts, drives the 3D viewer and creates assets via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Indie game developers spend hours in asset stores guessing: is this model actually game-ready? How many triangles, how many materials, does it have a walk clip, will it pass my engine's budget? Store pages show renders, not measurements. And an AI agent helping a developer cannot use a normal store at all: it cannot see the 3D viewer, cannot pull a lever, cannot verify a file before recommending it. What Clunk is Clunk is a small marketplace of real, measured game assets (3D models, sprite sheets, tileable textures) plus a studio that builds new ones. Every listing carries facts that were measured from the file bytes: polygons, materials, bounding size, animation clips, file size, a game-ready score. The front page is a physical capsule machine: pick a theme, pull the lever, a capsule drops, open it, and a real asset from the catalogue is yours. Why WebMCP fits Clunk's data already lives on the page: the catalogue, the measured facts, the 3D viewer's controls, the machine's state. WebMCP lets us hand exactly those controls to the agent that is sitting next to the human, without a separate API key, without scraping, and without the agent leaving the page the human is looking at. The human watches the machine; the agent pulls the lever. The human sees the model; the agent flips it to wireframe and plays the walk clip to check for foot sliding. Both act on one shared surface. What humans and agents can do together (that they could not before) Shop by measurement, not by render. "Find me a character with a walk clip" — the agent searches the catalogue facts and opens the product; the human sees the 3D viewer update live. Inspect together. The agent switches the viewer to wireframe, toggles grid, shadows and autorotate, plays a named clip, and runs the pivot test; the human judges what they see. Draw a capsule. The agent sets the theme and pulls the lever; the page scrolls the human to the reveal; the agent reads the drawn asset's facts and explains the grade (S/A/B/C) from the same rule the page prints. Create. On the studio page an agent can start a generation from a template with the human's prompt and return the stored file's facts. Verify a file. On the inspector page an agent can hand the page a URL; the page measures the file in the browser and returns score, blockers and warnings. The tools (23, all registered from the page itself) Everywhere: clunk_search_assets , clunk_asset_facts , clunk_navigate , clunk_site_map , clunk_connection_check , clunk_product_capabilities Capsule machine (home): gacha_state , gacha_list_themes , gacha_set_theme , gacha_pull , gacha_open , gacha_again , gacha_claim Product page (while the 3D viewer is mounted): viewer_set , viewer_play_clip , viewer_stop , viewer_pivot_test , viewer_state , asset_download_link Studio (signed in): studio_templates , studio_create , studio_my_generations Inspector (signed in): inspect_url Every tool name, description and schema is in English; human-facing strings come back in English with Korean _ko twins, because the site itself is Korean. Implementation Tools are registered with navigator.modelContext.registerTool() (falling back to document.modelContext ) from a small typed layer ( app/webmcp/register.ts ). Global tools are mounted in the site layout; page tools (gacha, viewer, studio, inspector) register on mount and unregister on unmount through an AbortSignal, so an agent only sees tools that can actually act on the current page. Every tool returns plain JSON. Every number is read from the same source the page renders (the catalogue API and per-file facts measured by Clunk's inspector). Nothing is invented. Tools drive the real UI: pulling the lever runs the same state machine as a human pull, scrolls the film so the human sees it, and waits for the capsule/result stage before returning. /webmcp lists the live tool set on the current page (from the registration status event), the schemas, and step-by-step testing instructions for Chrome and the ChatGPT in-app browser. Stack: React 19 on Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2; Three.js for the machine and viewer. Code is MIT-licensed; the asset files carry separate terms (ASSETS-LICENSE.md). Testing See https://clunk.games/webmcp . No account is needed for search, facts, the machine, the viewer and navigation. Studio and inspector tools need a free sign-in (Google or GitHub); signing up grants 25 credits, no card. Challenges The hardest part was keeping the agent honest: every number a tool returns had to come from the same measured facts the page renders, and page tools had to appear and disappear with the surface they act on, so the agent never sees a lever it cannot pull. title: Vast
pitch: A real-time collaborative canvas that gives AI agents the same tools a human uses not screenshots, not clicks, the actual API.
about_excerpt: A real-time collaborative canvas that gives AI agents the same tools a human uses not screenshots, not clicks, the actual API. Like Comment Story Updates vast Inspiration Every "AI edits your app" demo we'd seen worked the same way: an LLM either writes DOM-manipulation code and hopes it doesn't break something, or a browser-automation layer clicks around pretending to be a mouse. Neither one actually knows what a "connector" or a "frame" means in the app it's touching it's reverse-engineering intent from pixels. We'd already built Vast as a from-scratch realtime canvas rooms, shapes, live cursors, a shared undo stack as its own project, no AI involved. When WebMCP landed, the fit was obvious: Vast is already multiplayer. Every edit already goes through a typed, named function (create_element, align_elements, undo_action) over the same Socket.IO connection every guest uses. Making an agent a participant didn't mean bolting on a special "AI mode" it meant registering those exact functions as tools and letting an agent join the room like any other guest. What it does How we built it The base —Vite/React/TypeScript/Canvas2D client, Node/Express/Socket.IO server in a layered architecture, Postgres for shape state and an event log came together first, over about five days, ~14,000 lines. WebMCP went in afterward in a single focused push, under one rule: no separate agent path. Every tool calls the exact same socket events a human edit fires. Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of One code path, not two an agent literally cannot do anything the UI itself couldn't. Undo/redo that's genuinely shared between human and agent, cascades and all. A believable peer, not a gimmick the agent gets a name, color, and cursor because the server has no privileged notion of "human" to begin with. Real, deployable output via export_html, not just a screenshot of a session. Native-first: proving out where WebMCP is headed, not propping up an API that doesn't exist yet. What we learned What's next for Vast More tools under the same rule grouping, z-order, true component instances. Multi-agent rooms, to stress-test the undo stack with more than one agent peer at once. Giving the agent read access to why something was drawn (nearby notes, replay history), not just current state. Scoped tool permissions once the server has real auth, without breaking the no-separate-path guarantee. Following WebMCP beyond Chrome as other runtimes adopt document.modelContext. title: Loadshed
pitch: A page's own cut list for agents.
about_excerpt: A page's own cut list for agents. Like Comment Story Updates Measured result: a 320 ms frame hitch cuts Crowd from 480 to 48 while Live trace and Mixer stay protected. Before pressure: the agent-set 100 ms promise and second protected element agree with the visible receipts. Guardrail: Loadshed refuses to pin the last measured-relief step while the responsiveness promise is active. Pressure alone is not enough: at 100% Crowd load, Loadshed waits for a real frame-hitch signal. After the hitch: Crowd drops to 48, protected controls keep working, and the receipt records why. Same runtime, different page: Sale protects Hold my size while cutting aisle shimmer from 480 to 48. When a page gets slow, who decides what survives? A live show desk, a checkout on a mid-range phone, a control room dashboard: each one already has a private answer. Somebody hand-tuned what degrades first. An agent looking at the DOM cannot see that answer, so it either guesses or does nothing. Every latency-sensitive page already has this cut list. Loadshed makes it explicit, agent-readable, and auditable. Loadshed lets the page publish the answer. The page declares a click-latency ceiling, the element that must stay useful, and an ordered ladder of work it is willing to drop. It registers six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , so an agent can inspect the promise, negotiate the ceiling, protect a second element, apply or reverse one bounded cut, and read a receipt for everything that happened. On the deployed Desk, a person drags crowd load to maximum and clicks once. The page measures a long frame of about 320 ms, drops the crowd layer from 480 items to 48, and leaves the live trace and mixer untouched. The agent set that contract, and the receipt names the frame signal, the caller, and the click that proved it. Turn the promise off and everything comes back. The honest part: the runtime rejects agent-injected clicks as evidence, refuses cuts on protected or pinned work, and fails closed when the browser has no frame-hitch signal. The Sale page proves the same runtime protects a different task, Hold my size, without knowing the Desk's DOM. No build, no backend, MIT licensed, 50 Node tests. about_excerpt: Give an AI agent access to a live whiteboard. It discovers 32 WebMCP tools and uses them to build visual diagrams in real time, directly on the canvas, right before your eyes. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI diagram tools work in batches. You give a prompt, wait, and get a static result. I wanted something more interactive: a whiteboard where a person and an AI agent can work together in real time. WebMCP made this possible by allowing the website to expose tools through document.modelContext , which an AI agent can discover and use without a plugin or API key. What it does Whiteboard Live is a live whiteboard with 32 WebMCP tools . An AI agent can discover these tools and build diagrams directly on the canvas while you watch. It supports: Text, shapes, sticky notes, illustrations, icons, equations, code blocks, sketches, and connectors Live step-by-step drawing instead of batch rendering Human and AI working on the same canvas Light, Dark, Sepia, and Blackboard themes Voice input and typed prompts Up to 20 levels of undo How I built it The app uses React + SVG . SVG is used for connectors and strokes, while regular DOM elements handle draggable and resizable content. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . When an agent calls a tool, the canvas updates immediately with a reveal animation. For visuals, I use a four-level fallback system: Local SVG illustrations Iconify for icons AI-generated SVGs using Minimax for unknown concepts Emoji as a final fallback Generated assets are cached so they can be reused. The apply_visual_scene tool also has an automatic layout engine. The agent only decides what should be shown, while the layout engine handles the positions. It supports layouts such as horizontal processes, radial diagrams, hierarchies, comparisons, timelines, two-column layouts, and architectures. The app also includes a WebMCP polyfill, so it can work in regular browsers through the built-in prompt input. Challenges The main challenges were making batch operations safe, finding visuals quickly, supporting browsers without WebMCP, and keeping the AI from having to calculate pixel coordinates. For batch operations, the canvas state is saved before changes and automatically restored if something fails. For visuals, the fallback system makes sure every concept gets something useful without blocking the agent. The polyfill allows the same experience in browsers that do not support WebMCP. The semantic layout system handles positioning so the agent can focus on the content instead of coordinates. What I learned WebMCP creates a different way for humans and AI to work together. The AI can discover website tools and interact directly with the page instead of just returning an answer. The biggest insight for me was the shared canvas. The AI can build something, the human can edit it, and the AI can continue from the updated canvas. It feels less like using an AI tool and more like working with an AI teammate . title: Volt
pitch: Plan EV road trips with an AI agent that compares routes, finds better chargers, and updates a shared itinerary while you inspect the map.
about_excerpt:
Plan EV road trips with an AI agent that compares routes, finds better chargers, and updates a shared itinerary while you inspect the map.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 EV route planning is a chain of tradeoffs: vehicle range, starting charge, arrival reserve, charging speed, detour time, price, and whether a stop has the amenities a driver needs. Traditional route planners make people manipulate those constraints one control at a time. Agents can help, but only if they can understand and safely update the same itinerary the driver is reviewing. 

 Volt explores a more collaborative model. The human stays grounded in a visual map, while an agent works through structured WebMCP tools that expose the route-planning decisions directly. 

 What it does 

 Volt is an interactive, charger-aware EV trip planner. Drivers can: 

 
 Select an EV profile and starting battery level. 
 Set a minimum arrival reserve. 
 Prefer charging stops near coffee, food, and restrooms. 
 Compare fastest, balanced, and comfort-focused route strategies. 
 Inspect charging power, estimated availability, price, amenities, and stop duration. 
 See every route or charging-stop change reflected immediately on the shared map. 
 

 The demo uses a Los Angeles to San Francisco corridor with realistic sample station data and four supported EV profiles. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Route planning is stateful and visual. The agent needs to know what the traveler currently sees and prefers, while the traveler needs to inspect every recommendation before relying on it. WebMCP lets Volt expose narrow, typed actions from the live page instead of forcing an agent to guess through UI controls. 

 The site registers seven JavaScript WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_trip_context reads the current vehicle, preferences, route, and stops. 
 list_vehicle_profiles lists supported EV profiles and range data. 
 find_chargers filters corridor chargers by power and amenity. 
 compare_route_options returns three complete route strategies. 
 create_trip_plan creates a route and updates the visible map. 
 set_trip_preferences changes the vehicle, reserve, or amenity preference. 
 replace_charging_stop replaces one stop in the visible itinerary. 
 

 Read tools return enough structured state to explain a recommendation. Write tools reuse the same React state and planning logic as the human interface, so agent actions and manual actions stay synchronized. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 A traveler can ask, “Keep me above 25% at every stop and find chargers with coffee.” The agent can inspect the current vehicle and route, search the charger set, update the reserve preference, compare alternatives, and apply the selected plan. The traveler immediately sees the resulting stops, duration, charging cost, and arrival battery on the map. 

 Without structured site tools, this would require brittle clicking, scraping labels, and reconstructing hidden application state. Volt gives the agent explicit operations while preserving a clear human review surface. 

 How it was built 

 
 React 19 and TypeScript for shared planner state and interactions. 
 Vinext and Vite for the application and Cloudflare-compatible build. 
 OpenAI Sites for public hosting. 
 Shadcn/Base UI components and Lucide icons for accessible controls. 
 WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool on the top-level page. 
 A fully client-side demo dataset, so judges need no credentials or API keys. 
 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing tool boundaries that were substantial without becoming overly broad. Route comparison and charger search are read operations, while applying a plan or replacing a stop changes the shared interface state. Each tool therefore has a narrow schema, a clear description, and a result that makes the action verifiable. 

 Another challenge was making agent actions visible. Volt includes a live activity card, charger detail cards, route-mode controls, and an itinerary summary so the human can always see what changed. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Seven working WebMCP tools with both read and write workflows. 
 One shared state model for manual interactions and agent actions. 
 Three coherent route strategies and six charger locations. 
 Responsive, accessible map and planner controls. 
 A complete public experience that requires no account or API key. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most useful when the interface is already good for people. The tools should not replace the product; they should expose its meaningful operations so the agent and human can collaborate on the same artifact. 

 We also learned that tool results should include verification data. Returning the applied route, selected stops, and updated preferences lets the agent explain the result and lets the interface confirm it visually. 

 What's next 

 
 Connect live charger availability and pricing providers. 
 Add nationwide routing and elevation-aware energy estimates. 
 Support saved vehicle profiles and road-trip collections. 
 Add weather, towing, and seasonal range adjustments. 
 Introduce opt-in live vehicle data adapters while keeping every external action reviewable.

title: Asympta World
pitch: Asympta World is a living AI world where people, businesses, and agents coordinate, trade, communicate, and complete real-world tasks together.\n
about_excerpt:
Asympta World is a living AI world where people, businesses, and agents coordinate, trade, communicate, and complete real-world tasks together.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but most of them still live inside isolated chat windows. 

 They can reason, search, plan, and use tools, yet the real world is not a single tool. A simple goal such as “prepare dinner for tonight” can involve understanding a person's preferences, finding nearby businesses, checking availability, purchasing goods, coordinating delivery, and adapting when something changes. 

 At the same time, businesses have their own agents, resources, schedules, inventory, and constraints. 

 We imagined a different interface for this future: 

 What if AI agents existed inside a shared world where people, businesses, services, and other agents could coordinate directly? 

 That became Asympta World . 

 Instead of showing AI as a sequence of hidden API calls, Asympta World turns agent activity into a visible, spatial, living system. You can watch agents move through the world, communicate, discover services, coordinate tasks, exchange information, and complete real-world workflows. 

 The inspiration is simple: 

 
 AI should not only answer. It should be able to participate. 
 

 

 What it does 

 Asympta World is a living AI world where people, businesses, and autonomous agents coordinate, communicate, trade, and complete real-world tasks together. 

 The interface is built around an explorable world map. 

 A person can give an agent a goal. The agent then begins moving through the world and interacting with the entities required to complete it. 

 For example, a task may involve: 

 
 understanding the user's intent, 
 discovering relevant businesses or services, 
 communicating requirements, 
 checking resources or availability, 
 coordinating multiple participants, 
 performing actions, 
 adapting when conditions change, 
 and returning the completed result to the user. 
 

 The important difference is that Asympta World models both sides of an interaction . 

 A restaurant is not simply an API endpoint. Its side of the world may have its own agent coordinating orders, ingredients, preparation, scheduling, communication, and delivery. 

 A supplier may interact with the restaurant. 

 A delivery service may interact with both. 

 The user's agent coordinates across all of them. 

 This creates something closer to a miniature digital economy than a traditional chatbot. 

 Asympta World also makes autonomous activity understandable: 

 
 agents visibly move toward relevant locations, 
 task progress reflects estimated completion time, 
 the camera can automatically follow active work, 
 agent status and communication can be observed, 
 scheduled tasks can exist inside the same world, 
 Auto Explore allows agents to discover useful next actions, 
 active parts of the map react visually when work is happening, 
 and the interface supports multiple languages across both UI and agent context. 
 

 The goal is to make autonomous systems feel observable, understandable, and alive instead of invisible. 

 

 How we built it 

 Asympta World is built as an interactive web application with a simulation and coordination layer underneath the visual world. 

 The world 

 The map acts as the primary interface rather than a traditional dashboard. 

 It is designed as a large, zoomable environment where agents, businesses, resources, and activity can exist spatially. 

 We developed a lightweight visual system that can display many active entities while keeping movement smooth and the interface readable. 

 The simulation engine 

 Underneath the map is a world simulation representing: 

 
 agents, 
 people, 
 businesses, 
 resources, 
 tasks, 
 workflows, 
 locations, 
 events, 
 and relationships. 
 

 Rather than hard-coding every interaction as an animation, the simulation maintains world state and lets the interface reflect what is actually happening. 

 This allows agents to move, exchange information, react to events, and participate in multi-step processes. 

 Agent workflows 

 Tasks are represented as sequences of coordinated actions. 

 An agent can transition through states such as discovery, travel, communication, negotiation, execution, waiting, and completion. 

 The visual world reflects those states. 

 We also built estimated workflow timing so that progress follows the expected duration of the underlying task rather than an arbitrary animation percentage. 

 Business-side simulation 

 One of the most important architectural decisions was to simulate more than the user's agent. 

 Businesses and services can participate as active entities in a workflow. 

 This lets us demonstrate agent-to-business, business-to-supplier, and multi-party coordination rather than treating every external service as a passive database lookup. 

 WebMCP and tool interaction 

 Asympta World is designed around the idea that agents should interact with capabilities exposed by the web instead of requiring every website to be manually rewritten into a custom integration. 

 WebMCP provides an important building block for this model: websites can expose structured capabilities that agents can discover and use. 

 Asympta World explores what happens when those capabilities exist inside a shared spatial coordination layer. 

 Instead of thinking: 

 User → Agent → Website 

 we started thinking in terms of: 

 Person ↔ Agent ↔ Business Agent ↔ Services ↔ Other Agents 

 with the world itself providing the context connecting them. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making an agent feel like it actually exists in the world 

 It is easy to place an agent icon on a map. It is much harder to make the agent's movement correspond meaningfully to what the system is actually doing. 

 We had to connect task state, destination selection, animation, camera movement, and progress so that they behave as one system. 

 Showing complex activity without overwhelming the user 

 A real workflow can involve many simultaneous actions. 

 Displaying everything creates visual noise. Hiding everything makes the world feel fake. 

 We experimented with temporary activity indicators, contextual agent status, dialogue bubbles, fading map activity, automatic camera following, and progressive disclosure to find a better balance. 

 Modeling the supply side 

 Many agent demonstrations stop once an order is sent. 

 But the interesting part often begins after that. 

 A business may need to confirm inventory, prepare materials, coordinate staff, request something from a supplier, schedule fulfillment, and arrange delivery. 

 Representing these processes forced us to think about the world as a network of interacting systems instead of a single user's workflow. 

 Performance 

 A living world means many moving objects, effects, state transitions, and UI updates. 

 We repeatedly had to reduce unnecessary rendering work, control how much context was displayed at once, and make activity effects temporary rather than permanently accumulating. 

 The principle became: 

 
 The world can become more complex without rendering cost growing at the same rate. 
 

 Localization 

 Another unexpected challenge was keeping language changes consistent across a live simulation. 

 Static interface text is straightforward to translate. Dynamic agent statuses, workflow messages, task descriptions, and rapidly changing state are more difficult. 

 We had to treat language as part of the world state rather than merely translating the surrounding UI. 

 Designing something that feels like a product 

 It was easy for an agent simulation to start looking like a debugging dashboard. 

 We deliberately kept returning to the question: 

 Would somebody actually want to explore and use this? 

 That pushed us toward a calmer map interface, fewer permanent controls, contextual information, smoother motion, and a visual language closer to a real product than a developer demo. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is that Asympta World became more than an animation of an AI agent. 

 It became a working model of a different way to think about agent interfaces. 

 We are particularly proud that: 

 
 agents visibly move through the environment as tasks pro

title: Streaming Lens — streaming market data, agent-native
pitch: Market research on streaming — micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, sports rights. Free WebMCP tools tell an agent what the paid data covers and how fresh it is, without returning a value.
about_excerpt: Market research on streaming — micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, sports rights. Free WebMCP tools tell an agent what the paid data covers and how fresh it is, without returning a value. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We already sell streaming-market research: 17,470 sourced datapoints on micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, the creator economy and sports rights, behind a paid MCP server with 194 tools. So the WebMCP question was never "what demo could we build" — it was sharper and more uncomfortable: what does a paywalled B2B product do when the visitor is an agent? Today, agents scrape sites like ours. They read the marketing pages, miss the data entirely, and invent the numbers. Blocking them is not an answer either: an agent that leaves with nothing never comes back, and never buys. Giving the data away ends the business. WebMCP allows a fourth option, and that is the whole submission: describe the asset precisely, withhold its substance, and always say where the substance lives. What it does Every page of lens.streaming-radar.com — 49 of them — registers tools on document.modelContext . Seven, all free, no key, no account, and no flag for the visitor to enable: we serve a first-party Chrome origin-trial token in <head> . ask_site — returns the page sections that answer a question, with canonical URLs. search_intelligence_archive — searches the published newsletter editions and analyses. check_data_coverage — the one that carries the idea. Ask about any company, country or topic and it returns how many sourced datapoints we hold, which report silos they sit in, which countries and years they cover, the confidence mix, when the most recent one was updated, and one sample datapoint — metric name, unit, source, confidence — with its value withheld . Asked about ReelShort: 408 datapoints, across five silos, 2022 to 2028, the most recent updated this week. get_market_signals — the live monitoring feed; it also re-renders the visible feed on the page. estimate_streaming_pnl — drives the on-page P&L calculator and returns the model output. Registered on /calculator only: a tool with no valid target is a broken contract. request_report_teaser — the conversion step. Requires an explicit consent argument and fills the page's own email gate, so the human sees what the agent did. browse_reports — the catalogue. Then the boundary itself. Until this week, a paid tool called without entitlement answered Authentication required — three words, a dead end. Now the JSON-RPC error carries error.data : what the silo holds (5,306 datapoints, 51 countries, 2004 to 2033 on our vertical-drama silo), one sample with its value withheld, the URLs to buy or authenticate, and the exact instruction to replay the call with a key. The refusal proves possession instead of ending the conversation. The same computation answers the free tool and the refusal, because they answer the same question and must answer identically. How we built it The site is static HTML with no bundler and no package.json , so the SDK is vendored as a pinned ESM asset and the module graph is injected by the site's page producer , never edited page by page. Tools are side-effect-free ES modules, registered once per document, unregistered on pagehide . The tools never reimplement the page. request_report_teaser calls the site's own email-gate API through a small public seam; estimate_streaming_pnl moves the calculator's real controls and lets the page compute; get_market_signals reads the same endpoint the visible feed reads. One behaviour, one implementation, whether a human or an agent triggers it. Agent traffic is measured server-side with a cookieless beacon — no cookie, no identifier, nothing to consent to — because GA4 only loads after a cookie banner and an agent never clicks Accept. Without it, agent traffic would be strictly invisible. Challenges we ran into A cache header that silently ate a release. Two new tools worked on the origin and reached no browser. Cloudflare Pages does not let a more specific _headers rule override a broader one — it concatenates them: max-age=31536000, immutable, public, max-age=300, must-revalidate . Browsers keep the first directive, so the modules stayed immutable for a year. The fix was to move the whole graph out of the /js/ prefix; there is no negation and no override. Short acronyms matching inside words. Our coverage counter used ILIKE '%ott%' and returned 109 rows; word-bounded, 78. Twenty-eight percent phantom matches in a number we use as a commercial argument. The same bug in our signal matcher had been filing Ridley Scott stories into the sports silo — ott inside Scott , mma inside summary . Both are bounded now, with regression tests. Bilingual pages. Our HTML carries French and English in the same DOM, hidden by CSS. In a detached document no CSS applies, so the first version of ask_site handed agents both languages glued together: "En brefTL;DR". A surface that switches off in silence. Without a valid origin-trial token, document.modelContext simply does not exist and the SDK no-ops — no error anywhere. Our pipeline health check now reads the token off the deployed page, decodes its expiry, and goes red fourteen days before. Accomplishments that we're proud of It is not a demo. It is a production B2B product, the surface is measured, and the independent webmcp.com directory grades the implementation A . 1,404 tests green, including three whose only job is to prove no datapoint value can escape through the free surface. What we learned An agent-native paywall is not a wall with an API. It is a boundary that explains itself. Publish the shape, withhold the substance, always say where the substance lives — everything else follows. What's next for Streaming Lens An agent-reachable checkout, so the handoff completes without a human copying a key. And per-call payment at the edge: our MCP already runs on Cloudflare, and a 402 with a machine-readable price is the same envelope we just built, with an amount attached. title: Mission Center WebMCP — Human in Command
pitch: A browser-native mission control where agents inspect tasks, verify evidence, and propose actions while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A browser-native mission control where agents inspect tasks, verify evidence, and propose actions while humans retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates What I built Mission Center WebMCP is a browser-native mission control where agents can inspect tasks, trace dependencies, verify evidence, and propose safe next moves while humans remain the only authority who can approve lifecycle changes. Why WebMCP matters Mission Center already treats task state, evidence, handoffs, and verification as explicit, reviewable concepts. WebMCP makes those semantics available directly to browser agents instead of forcing them to infer meaning from pixels or DOM structure. The tools share the same live in-page state, evidence model, proposal queue, human approval UI, and audit trail as the person viewing the mission control. Human and agent collaboration The judge journey asks an agent to find the task in Review, inspect whether its evidence is current, and propose the safest next lifecycle move. The agent discovers WMC-103, checks its passing evidence, and proposes Review → Done. The task remains in Review and a pending proposal appears. A human then reviews the proposal and clicks Revalidate & approve. Mission Center rechecks the task revision and completion evidence before moving the task to Done. The agent has no approval tool and cannot silently change lifecycle truth. Agent calls, proposals, and human decisions remain separate and auditable. How it was implemented The app is a static HTML/CSS/ES module site with zero backend and zero API keys. It registers eight imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, keeps validated state in browser storage, exposes proposal-only agent mutations, and enforces a human evidence/revision gate. The repository includes deterministic Node tests, verification scripts, and a GitHub Pages deployment workflow. Prior work disclosure This competition edition is derived from the existing MIT-licensed Codex Mission Center project. The frozen upstream baseline is documented in UPSTREAM_BASELINE.md. Browser WebMCP support, agent tools, proposal workflow, judge UX, and the static deployment are the challenge work. title: Con-Sche — a construction schedule an agent can operate
pitch: An agent reads the float on a live construction schedule and moves the work — through WebMCP, without the schedule ever leaving the browser.
about_excerpt: An agent reads the float on a live construction schedule and moves the work — through WebMCP, without the schedule ever leaving the browser. Like Comment Story Updates Con-Sche — Construction schedules that agents can actually operate Live app: https://hackathon-con-sche.pages.dev/ Repository: https://github.com/tatelog/Hackathon-Con-sche (AGPL-3.0) Open the link and a real schedule is already loaded. No sign-up, no sample to pick, nothing to configure — the WebMCP tools are registered and ready to call. What it is Con-Sche is a browser-based editor for ADM network schedules — the arrow-diagram form of critical path scheduling that construction sites in Japan still run on. A single project holds hundreds of activities linked by dependencies. Move one activity and the effect ripples through the whole network. It runs entirely in the browser. Schedule data is stored locally in IndexedDB (via Dexie.js) and is never sent to a server. With WebMCP, an agent sitting next to the user can read that schedule and change it — without the data ever leaving the page. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 1. The data cannot leave the browser. A construction schedule is one of the most sensitive documents a contractor owns. It exposes delivery dates, subcontractor assignments, and — by implication — cost structure. Firms will not upload it to a third-party server so that an assistant can read it. A conventional MCP server would require exactly that: ship the data out, process it remotely, ship the result back. WebMCP removes the requirement. The tools run inside the page, against state already in the user's browser. Nothing is transmitted. The privacy constraint that blocks AI adoption in this industry simply does not apply. 2. The computation is already local. Con-Sche calculates CPM (ES/EF/LS/LF, total float, free float, critical path) on the client. When an agent shifts an activity, the recalculation happens immediately, in the same process. The agent asks a question and gets an answer grounded in a real solver — not an approximation, and not a round trip. 3. The data model was already structured for this. This is the part we want to be clear about: Con-Sche was not retrofitted with an API wrapper. It was built as a local-first application with an explicit activity/event graph, because that is the correct way to model an ADM schedule. When WebMCP arrived, exposing that graph took seven tool definitions — not a rewrite. An app designed to keep its own state coherent turns out to be an app an agent can operate. How it creates a better user experience Network schedules are read by specialists. To move one activity in a GUI you must know which arrow to grab, how far it may travel, and what it will drag with it. Total float — the number of days an activity can slip without delaying the project — is computed but not obvious. Most site staff never see it. With an agent in the loop, that knowledge becomes conversational: "How many days can I delay the 3F concrete pour?" "What work is scheduled for today?" "Push the steel erection back three days and tell me what it hits." The agent reads float, checks the allowed range, applies the change, and reports the new project duration. The user does not need to know the vocabulary of CPM to benefit from it. Every change an agent makes goes through the same undo stack as a human edit. The user stays in control of their own document. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before: interpreting a network schedule was tacit knowledge held by experienced schedulers. "The drywall is running late — can we absorb it?" was answered by a person who could hold the network in their head, or by nobody. Now: the question is answered against the actual graph, in the browser, in one turn. In the demo the agent looks up the drywall activity, reads its total float — zero, it sits on the critical path — and says plainly that any delay there moves the completion date. Told the work will take four more days, it updates the duration; CPM recalculates and the project goes from 97 days to 101. One undo puts it back, because the agent writes through the same history stack a person does. Concretely, an agent working with Con-Sche can: Summarise an entire schedule including full CPM results ( get_schedule ) Report how far one activity can move in each direction, and what it would affect ( get_activity ) Change a duration and return the recalculated project duration, so a delay reported on site becomes a new completion date in one turn ( update_activity_duration ) Shift an activity within its allowed range ( shift_activity ) Detect circular dependencies and orphaned event nodes ( validate_schedule ) Answer "what work is happening today?" ( get_activities_on_date ) Find activities by name, zone, or floor ( find_activities ) This is not a chatbot describing a picture of a schedule. It is an agent holding the same object the user is holding. How we implemented WebMCP Registration is feature-detected and non-invasive: export function registerConScheTools(): void { if (typeof document === 'undefined') return const modelContext = document.modelContext if (!modelContext || typeof modelContext.registerTool !== 'function') return for (const tool of ALL_TOOLS) { try { void modelContext.registerTool(withTelemetry(tool)) } catch (e) { console.warn(`[webmcp] tool registration failed: ${tool.name}`, e) } } } On a browser without WebMCP, nothing happens and ordinary users see no change. A failure to register one tool cannot take down the others or the app itself. Design decisions worth naming: Tools read and write the in-page schedule store only. They operate on the Zustand store backed by local IndexedDB. No schedule content is sent anywhere. This is enforced by the shape of the code, not by policy. Mutating tools are undoable. update_activity_duration writes through the same history stack as a manual edit, so a single undo reverses what the agent did. The demo ends on exactly that. Tools return structured, bounded results. get_activity reports the legal shift range and the affected chain, so the agent can reason before acting rather than guessing and retrying. Telemetry records the tool name only. A separate Cloudflare Worker + D1 logs who called which tool and when — never schedule data. This is the metering layer for future paid tiers, and it was built so that usage can be billed without the operator ever seeing a customer's schedule. Stack: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Konva.js (canvas rendering), Zustand (state), Dexie.js (IndexedDB), Tailwind CSS. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages, with Cloudflare Workers + D1 behind the telemetry endpoint. Prior work vs. work during the Hackathon Con-Sche existed before this Hackathon and is a shipped product. Per the rules, here is the split. Before the Submission Period (as of 2026-08-07): The Con-Sche ADM editor, CPM solver, and local-first storage model (IndexedDB) All seven WebMCP tools ( src/webmcp/ ), committed 2026-08-07 The usage-telemetry endpoint ( workers/api/src/webmcpEvent.ts ) During the Submission Period (2026-08-25 – 2026-09-03): Relicensed to AGPL-3.0 so the source is genuinely open Split this open build out of the hosted product into its own repository, and removed the landing page, the sign-up gate, the usage telemetry and the commercial pathways. The scheduling engine and the WebMCP layer are untouched Translated the entire interface to English — roughly 900 strings, down to the messages the tools themselves return to an agent Added a real sample schedule that loads on first visit: an 18-storey office building in fit-out, with exterior, interior, services and site works running in parallel, a genuine critical path, and activities that carry float. Judges and agents start on something worth asking questions about instead of a blank canvas Submission materials and demonstration video We are entering an existing application rather than a new one. What we are putting forward is not "we added WebMCP in ten days" but "we had spent months building an app whose state an agent could safely operate, and WebMCP was the interface it had been waiting for." What we learned The most useful realisation was not a technical one. It was that WebMCP changes who has to supply the AI. Construction firms in Japan are not short of AI. Their staff already have an assistant open. What has been missing is a way for the software they work in to be operated by the assistant they already have and already trust. Until now the answer was for every vendor to embed a model in their own product, and carry the cost, the support burden and the privacy problem that comes with it. WebMCP lets us stop doing that. We publish the tools; the customer brings the agent. For a small vendor selling into a conservative industry, that is a different economic proposition entirely — and it is why we think WebMCP matters specifically for construction software, not just generally. title: PayablePilot
pitch: A browser agent prepares the invoice review. A person makes the payment decision.
about_excerpt:
A browser agent prepares the invoice review. A person makes the payment decision.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The exact $200 invoice hold and its supporting evidence. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent can stage a draft. A person confirms or dismisses it. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The exact $200 invoice hold and its supporting evidence. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent can stage a draft. A person confirms or dismisses it. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 PayablePilot already had a clear safety boundary: the agent could finish routine
work, but a person had to decide what happened to an invoice exception. WebMCP
made it possible to carry that same boundary into the browser. The agent no
longer needs to infer state from a dense dashboard or click the same buttons as
the reviewer. 

 What it does 

 The page exposes two WebMCP tools. review_payables_queue returns the current
run, source document IDs, exact price variance, allowed actions, and decision
status. stage_invoice_resolution puts one permitted choice into a visible
Agent Draft. It cannot confirm the draft, release a payment, or contact the
supplier. 

 The included run has two fictional invoice packets. One clears. PP-2086 stops
because eight units were invoiced at $119 instead of the $94 purchase-order
rate. The deterministic difference is $200. An agent can read that evidence and
stage the credit-and-hold option. A person still checks the evidence and either
confirms or dismisses the draft. 

 How I built it 

 The live page is a React and TypeScript app. It registers two tools with
 document.modelContext.registerTool() , uses strict JSON Schema inputs, and
returns concise JSON. The review tool carries the read-only annotation. The
staging tool updates visible page state but has no code path to record a final
decision. An AbortController unregisters both tools with the component
lifecycle. 

 The queue facts live in one typed module shared by the tools and tests. The test
suite independently checks the $200 calculation, the pending human-confirmation
status, and rejection of actions outside the two visible choices. 

 Challenges 

 The hard part was making the browser tool useful without quietly widening the
agent's authority. A tool that clicked the final button would have been easy to
demo and wrong for the product. I split the flow at the decision boundary: the
agent can prepare the review, while the final click stays with the person who is
accountable for the payment. 

 I also had to treat the existing project honestly. PayablePilot predates this
challenge, so the repository documents exactly what was added after August 25
and the dated commits isolate the WebMCP work. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Both tools are detected and callable on the public page in ChatGPT's in-app browser. 
 The live staging call produces the same visible Agent Draft shown in the demo. 
 No agent tool can approve an exception or send anything to a supplier. 
 All 17 tests pass, including three focused WebMCP boundary tests. 
 

 What I learned 

 The most useful browser tools are often smaller than the interface around them.
Two narrow tools were enough here. One reports exact state. One prepares a
reversible draft. Keeping those jobs separate made the agent easier to guide and
the safety boundary easier to verify. 

 What's next 

 The next step is connecting the same tools to a real authenticated review queue.
The browser contract would stay narrow, while the server would add organization
policies, duplicate-invoice checks, reviewer identity, and a durable audit log. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 Invoice review is a poor place for an agent to guess from button text. The page
contains a purchase order, invoice, receipt, arithmetic, and a hard approval
boundary. WebMCP gives the agent a small, typed contract for reading that state
and putting one allowed choice in front of the reviewer. 

 The agent does not scrape the page, calculate the difference, invent an action,
or click through a payment decision. PayablePilot returns the exact $200.00
variance from deterministic application data. The write-capable tool can only
stage one of the two choices already present in the interface. It cannot confirm
either choice. 

 Work added during the challenge 

 PayablePilot existed before The WebMCP Challenge. The WebMCP implementation,
visible agent draft, safety boundary, tests, and this documentation were added
after the submission period began on August 25, 2026. Git history provides the
dated record required for a pre-existing project.

title: ClawRoom
pitch: Git for agent work. Everyone brings their own agent, every agent gets its own computer, and a room can borrow tools from any API or MCP server once a person approves. Every tool call is a commit.
about_excerpt: Git for agent work. Everyone brings their own agent, every agent gets its own computer, and a room can borrow tools from any API or MCP server once a person approves. Every tool call is a commit. Like Comment Story Updates The manager's first screen. One action waiting, and the card carries the words it would ship, not just a title. Approving is the whole loop. A member's console into their own Linux computer. The same computer_run tool the agent uses, so the room gets one line and never the output. Computers in this room: counts per member, never contents. And a signal, because Ella's agent has failed four commands in a row. A person approved an OpenAPI document and four tools appeared in every browser in the room at once. 7 to 11, with nothing else moving. Codex, from somebody's own terminal, parked. This project did not stage this one: a real run, read out of the room it happened in. Connect your own agent. The claude and codex commands, printed inside the room with that room's link already in them. This is not a support problem. The same export check failed across three different tickets. That is a bug, not a queue. The ablation, live on the site. The model called publish in all sixteen trials. With the engine, 0 of 8 shipped. Without it, 8 of 8. Every tool called through executeTool with no agent involved. 23 of 23, in a clean Chrome with no flags. Ten test a claim, not a function. The front door. One click opens a demo room as Cara the manager, and a second window as Ella, one of your team. No signup, no flags. Live, one click, no signup and no flags: https://clawroom.thankywal-bkk.workers.dev Film (2:53): https://youtu.be/c9gOER5Djeo ClawRoom is git for agent work. A shared room where everyone brings their own AI agent, every agent gets a Linux computer of its own, every tool call lands in a log the whole room reads like a commit, and nothing irreversible ships until a person approves it. Press Open the demo room . Two windows open: you as Cara, the manager, and Ella, one of your team. Ella's agent has already drafted twice, run a script on its own machine, and asked to publish. That request is sitting in your window with the actual words in it, waiting for you. The smaller case, which is the one that is true today A room is for a team, and a team where everybody brings an agent is a near future rather than a present one. The version that is true on an ordinary Tuesday is smaller: one person running more than one agent at once. Anybody with Claude Code and Codex both installed already does it, and already has the problem: two terminals, two histories, no shared record, and the only thing stopping either of them from doing something irreversible is that you happen to be watching. Same product, not a different mode. Each agent gets a seat with its own name, its own computer, and one log you read. Both bridges started within a second of each other against one room, and this is what a third window, which neither agent could write to, recorded: Claude local list_posts read the board, 3 posts Codex local list_posts read the board, 3 posts Claude commit publish asked to publish "Launch announcement" to blog Codex commit publish asked to publish "Launch announcement" to blog Claude local check_approval checked apv_ir7e Codex local check_approval checked apv_d6hq The lines interleave because both were working in the same second, and the names are still right, because the server stamps the sender from the socket rather than believing the envelope. Two agents asked to publish the same item and got two separate handles. Neither shipped. Two decisions were waiting on a person at the end of it, which is the point of the smaller case: you can leave two agents running and come back to a queue of decisions rather than a pile of published work you did not ask for. --away "<task>" is the same thing on a machine you are not watching. An agent can work all night. It cannot ship anything all night. Why WebMCP, and not a server Because the tools have to live in the page. Each person's agent runs in their own browser with their own private context. A server-side MCP integration funnels everyone's drafts through one process, which is the exact arrangement this is trying to avoid. WebMCP puts the tool surface inside the document, so the private half of somebody's work never has to leave their machine to take part in shared work. Remove WebMCP and this is not a worse version of itself, it is a different product. The surface is also live, and that turns out to be the best thing in here. Registration is per tool under its own AbortController , because the API has no unregisterTool() . So when a person approves a new tool source, four tools appear in everyone's browser at once and nothing else moves: measured going 21 to 25 with no dip, where a whole-surface rebuild used to drop to zero in between. That is a self test case now, and it asserts the delta rather than the total: four named tools added, none lost, read back out of getTools() . ontoolchange is what tells a long-lived client, and the MCP bridge listens on it. Three tiers, and the tier is not a permission level It is a statement about where the payload lives. work stays in the member's browser. The room gets one line: "drafted variant 3 of the launch announcement". Never the variant. share puts something on the board. That is the moment a thing stops being yours. commit does nothing at all until a person approves. Enforcement is by construction, not by asking nicely: the engine wraps every tool before registering it, and hands the unapproved pass of a commit-tier tool a put() that throws. A room author cannot forget the rule. Commit-tier calls do not block the agent. The call returns a receipt with a handle, the approval becomes an object in shared state, and the agent carries on or polls. The API as shipped has no user-confirmation mechanism (measured: ModelContext exposes only registerTool , getTools , executeTool and ontoolchange ), and holding the execute promise open for minutes would time out and occupy the page's surface while it waited. That is our proposal for the gap, and it went to the spec group. No agent can approve, and the person approving reads the thing itself: the card carries the headline, the words, and the arguments. "The room sees the work, not the people" is about never capturing somebody's conversation. It was never about hiding the artefact from the person asked to ship it. An approver who cannot read what they are approving is a rubber stamp, which is the failure this design exists to avoid. A computer for every agent The moment a member's agent walks into a room it gets a Linux sandbox: a shell, /workspace , Python and Node, one per person per room, asleep when idle. Built on Cloudflare Sandbox. The point is not that agents can run code. It is where the code runs and who gets to see: Ella local computer_run ran `python3 analyse.py` (exit 0, 14 lines out) Ella local computer_write_file wrote report.md (2311 bytes) Ella shared computer_share_file shared report.md to the board (2311 characters) The first two lines are what the manager sees. The third is the agent choosing, through a tool whose description says exactly that, to make one file public. It is a real machine: computer_serve keeps a server running, computer_share_page puts what it shows on the board, computer_browse reads a public page through Browser Rendering, computer_snapshot and computer_restore keep the workspace. And the person has a console into the same machine through the same computer_run tool, so a person and their agent share one computer and one log. The manager gets counts per member, never contents, and a signal when somebody has failed three commands in a row. Tools the room borrowed Point a room at an OpenAPI document or a remote MCP server and its operations become tools for everyone, tiered by the same rules. Reads are work, writes are share, and anything that sounds irreversible is commit and waits for a person. What makes it safe to offer is that add_tool_source is itself commit tier. An agent can propose a source and nothing registers. A person approves, and in that instant every browser in the room has the tools. Two URLs that work today: https://clawroom.thankywal-bkk.workers.dev/api/demo/openapi.json a fixture with a refund in it https://mcp.deepwiki.com/mcp a real MCP server, no key Point it at an ordinary page that registers its own WebMCP tools and the room says it found them and cannot call them. A tool surface belongs to a document, and getTools({ fromOrigins }) is not implemented. Saying so beats pretending. Bring your own agent, or your own model claude mcp add clawroom -- node scripts/clawroom-mcp.mjs "<member link>" codex mcp add clawroom -- node scripts/clawroom-mcp.mjs "<member link>" The bridge holds no tools.
