title: KnownGate
pitch: The food verification layer for people's agents: state your family's rules and KnownGate rules products, menus, and plans against read-and-dated evidence. Four verdicts. Never "safe."
about_excerpt: The food verification layer for people's agents: state your family's rules and KnownGate rules products, menus, and plans against read-and-dated evidence. Four verdicts. Never "safe." Like Comment Story Updates A ruled answer: source and date attached Some lines can never be dropped We measured the difference the page makes The famous chain, answered honestly A refusal is an answer The agent works in the open The page speaks to agents natively. Why we built it People ask AI what they can eat, and a wrong answer has a cost. We asked GPT-5.2 directly, no tools: can a milk-allergic child have this chicken broth? It answered that it could not say: "the label is the only way to confirm," and asked us to photograph the pack. The model is right. Someone has to have read the label, and the web gives an agent no place where that reading lives. KnownGate is that place: the verification layer for people's agents. What it does Tell it your household's rules in plain words: "milk allergy, and keep sodium under 200 mg per serving." It turns them into typed rules you can see, then rules a product, a whole restaurant menu, or a week of meals against evidence: printed nutrition panels and published allergen charts, each with its source and the date we read it. Four verdicts can come back, and two of them are honest ways of saying "we don't know." The word "safe" never appears. Unknown counts as no. Nothing is stored unless you ask for a record, and a saved record is a permanent dated page you can hand to a school or a kitchen. We measured the difference the page makes On 2 Sept 2026 we ran one question three ways: "milk allergy, sodium under 200 mg per serving, Kroger 99% Fat Free Chicken Broth." Asked directly via the OpenAI API (gpt-5.2, no tools): no verdict in 9.7 seconds. "The label is the only way to confirm." A browser agent (Claude in Chrome) driving our human page with no tools: the correct conflict (780 mg, dated) in 1 minute 21 seconds and 6 counted actions, zero wrong turns, because the page is built to be legible to agents even without tools. Through the page's own engine, the same calls our WebMCP tools expose: the same correct verdict in 2 calls, under 5 seconds (median of three runs). One product, one question, single runs, not a benchmark suite. But the shape is the finding: the page supplies the trust; the tools supply the determinism. Why WebMCP fits this use case Food is the domain where an agent must not answer from training data, because a wrong answer carries liability. WebMCP lets the page hold the authority: knowngate.com registers its checking engine as tools on the page via document.modelContext (check an item, check a venue, check a plan, parse a premise). An agent that lands on the site calls the site's own engine instead of scraping it, and the human watches every call on a live step list on the same screen. We call the pattern the page as authority : the agent proposes, the page rules on evidence, and the human owns the premise. What people and agents can now do together An agent can rule a whole menu in one turn: 84 items at one chain, 72 conflicts, 12 that need one named kitchen question, plus a cross-contact caveat the site forbids any agent to omit, relayed word for word. It can save a dated record page a parent shares onward. It can answer for a famous chain honestly: In-N-Out returns 7 milk conflicts from the chain's own chart and "couldn't verify" where the chart is silent, never a clear the chart cannot support. And where there is no evidence at all, it refuses. That refusal is the part everyone else leaves out. How we built it Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel; Supabase Postgres holding a production evidence corpus: 67,791 products, 711,900 shelf records, 446,371 nutrition panels, 12 chains with 7,022 dishes ruled, measured 2 Sept 2026 and growing daily (current figures are published on the site's refusals page, along with how often we refuse). We also mapped 54,909 California venues so real places resolve; venues without evidence refuse honestly, and on our first recovery trial all 400 sampled venues resolved to a real place, 91% with a menu source. The same engine is exposed three ways: WebMCP tools on the page, an MCP server at mcp.knowngate.com, and plain REST with a free key. Agents without tool access get DOM-path directions published on every page, with stable element ids and a strict relay rule for must-not-omit lines. The MCP server is published in the official MCP Registry as com.knowngate/verify, DNS-verified to our domain Challenges we faced The hardest bugs only exist where agents live: document.modelContext exists only in agentic browsers, so our tool-registration crash never reproduced in a normal one. Reading evidence honestly was its own fight: In-N-Out's allergen chart draws its answers as red dots, vector graphics invisible to every text-extraction tool, and we had to render the page the way a person sees it before we could ingest a row. And we ingested that 12th chain 24 hours before this deadline: its one-sided chart structurally cannot prove an item clear, and the engine returned zero clears from it, exactly as the standard requires. The safety property held under deadline pressure, which is the only time it matters. What we learned A page that can say "couldn't verify" is worth more than one that always answers. Everything in our video runs on production; the rules of what counts as proof are published at knowngate.com/standard. The question we started with was whether an agent can be trusted about food. The answer we found is that trust doesn't live in the agent. It lives in what the page gives the agent to stand on. title: Study Map
pitch: Learn anything as a map you and ChatGPT draw together.
about_excerpt: Learn anything as a map you and ChatGPT draw together. Like Comment Story Updates Live: https://hungson175.github.io/study-map/ · Code: https://github.com/hungson175/study-map I study most days, and I build software one small piece at a time. I want to learn the same way. Mind maps that arrive finished have never worked for me. NotebookLM is good, but a complete map is someone else's map: I read it once and keep nothing. I want one that opens only where I got curious and ends up holding my own notes, so next time I can just glance at it. So Study Map does not fill everything in at once. The page's guide tells the agent to draw a few nodes and stop. I select a node, pin a question, and only that branch grows. Working together. WebMCP is what makes this simple. The page hands the agent what it needs as tools: the map, my selection, my open questions. It draws and it researches; I drag, rewrite, delete and write in my own notes. It can also refuse, when there is no room beside a node, rather than write over my work. Same canvas, both of us, no screenshots in between. Built. An MIT retrofit of Excalidraw. The page registers 17 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The one that took by far the most work is how_to_use : read-only, recomputed from the live canvas, it is the page teaching the agent how to run this kind of session — a few nodes, then stop and wait for the person, then grow only what they asked about. That guideline is really the product. The other sixteen tools just carry it out. The demo is me using Study Map to learn WebMCP itself. title: GeneVault- AI check DNA File without ever seeing it
pitch: GeneVault uses zero-knowledge Groth16 zk-SNARKs to prove genetic drug contraindications in-browser. Clinical safety for AI agents, zero exposure for your raw DNA.
about_excerpt: GeneVault uses zero-knowledge Groth16 zk-SNARKs to prove genetic drug contraindications in-browser. Clinical safety for AI agents, zero exposure for your raw DNA. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Imagine an AI medical assistant wants to prescribe you a common blood thinner — Plavix. But for about 30% of people, genetics prevent the drug from working, which can lead to fatal blood clots. So the AI asks: "Just upload your full DNA sequence so I can check." And there's the trap. You should never paste your private genetic code into an AI model or a cloud server — once your DNA leaks, it's leaked forever. You can change a stolen password; you cannot change your genome. We started GeneVault the moment we realized the technology to break this deadlock already existed in the browser. WebMCP lets a website advertise real, callable tools to any AI agent. Zero-knowledge proofs let you prove a statement about secret data without revealing the data. Put them together and the answer to "upload your DNA" becomes: "No — but I'll prove the conclusion to you mathematically, right here on my device." That reframing — the browser as the trust boundary between a patient and any AI model — is the entire project. And here is the part that keeps us up at night (in a good way): this deadlock is not a medical problem. It is the structural problem of the AI era. An AI HR tool that wants your therapy history. A tax agent that wants your bank statements. A hiring agent that wants your face. In every case the model's context window is treated as the place where private data goes to be processed — and leaked. GeneVault is our answer, demonstrated end-to-end on the highest-stakes dataset we could find: the human genome. If the pattern survives DNA, it survives anywhere. What it does GeneVault turns a browser tab into a privacy-hardened pharmacogenomics workstation that any WebMCP-capable AI agent can operate — without ever receiving a single letter of DNA. Parses real raw genetic files fully client-side. Drop in a 23andMe / AncestryDNA / VCF export and GeneVault scans 643,000+ positions in a single pass, entirely in local memory. Nothing is uploaded — there is no server to upload to . Advertises 12 live tools to any AI agent through document.modelContext.registerTool — file parsing, marker listing, drug-safety checks, alternative-therapy recommendations, proof generation/verification, and even 3D protein manipulation. The agent discovers them on its own; we never prompt-inject instructions. Answers the question that matters: "Can I safely take this drug?" — for CPIC Level A pairs like Plavix/CYP2C19, Warfarin/CYP2C9+VKORC1, Simvastatin/SLCO1B1, Codeine/CYP2D6, 5-FU/DPYD, Abacavir/HLA-B and more. Backs every risky verdict with a real Groth16 zero-knowledge proof generated on-device in ~4.4 seconds. The agent receives a verified pass/fail — not your genotype. Keeps the human in charge. Every tool call from an external agent hits a consent gate (Allow once / Allow all session / Deny). Deny returns denied_by_patient and nothing is released. Every call lands in an on-page audit ledger. Visualizes the science. A built-in 3D viewer loads real protein structures (e.g. CYP2C19, PDB 4GQS). Every safety verdict now auto-renders its target enzyme in the viewport — and the agent can dock a drug into the catalytic pocket, zoom, highlight, and pin clinical annotations — live, from a chat prompt. The bigger picture: a pattern, not just a product. Everything above is shipped and working for pharmacogenomics — but the architecture itself is domain-agnostic by construction, and it has exactly three reusable layers: The tool boundary (WebMCP). The website advertises capabilities to any agent via document.modelContext.registerTool ; the agent never gets raw data access, only tool calls with typed schemas. The consent gate (human-in-the-loop). Every tool execution passes through a human decision point that cannot be prompt-injected around, with machine-readable denial ( denied_by_patient ). The zero-knowledge release. Verdicts leave the device only as Groth16 proofs — mathematical conclusions with zero source data. Swap "genome" for credentials, finances, or imaging and the same three layers hold. The genome demo is our proof that the pattern is real, not theoretical. How we built it The WebMCP layer. Each capability is registered in the standard form — document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) — and verified via getTools() with AbortController cleanup. Tool descriptions are written for agents , not humans: the discovery quality of the demo comes entirely from those description strings. For non-WebMCP browsers we ship an honestly-labeled local fallback, so judges on any browser still see the full pipeline. The zero-knowledge layer. The core claim — "this patient's CYP2C19 diplotype belongs to the poor-metabolizer set" — is compiled into a Circom circuit (8,845 constraints on the bn128 curve): Poseidon-hashed Merkle membership with depth $k = 16$, an EdDSA curator signature, and a single-use nullifier, all verified inside the SNARK: $$ \text{Verify}_{vk}(\pi_a, \pi_b, \pi_c;\; \text{root},\, \text{claim},\, \text{nullifier}) \Rightarrow 1 $$ Secrets are derived at parse time from the patient's actual file — never hardcoded: $$ s = \text{sha256}(\text{gene} \,|\, \text{genotypes} \,|\, \text{salt}) $$ $$ \text{nullifier} = \text{Poseidon}(s, \text{nonce}) $$ The nullifier makes every proof single-use, so a leaked proof can't be replayed by an attacker — double-spend protection, but for DNA claims. Groth16 proving runs in-browser via snarkjs (~4.4 s for witness + proof). Because witnesses are generated from the real file, a false phenotype fails witness generation — we ship a "Forgery Audit" button so anyone can watch the circuit refuse a forged claim in real time. The trust UX. A consent wrapper intercepts every execute() . External agent calls block until a human decides; the 3D viewport, HUD, and audit ledger visualize what the agent is doing as it does it. One click runs a built-in "Full Agent Demo" where the AI self-asks six questions and executes the full pipeline — our insurance policy for any demo environment. Challenges we ran into Two parse paths, one engine. Our file-upload and inline-text parsers initially kept separate state, so the ZK engine would report "not ready" after one path but not the other. We only caught it through end-to-end agent testing — the fix was unifying both paths into a single claim-tree build. Lesson: in agent-driven apps, every entry point must reach the same invariants. Making Groth16 feel instant. A ~4.4-second proving pause is an eternity in a demo. We restructured the UI so the wait is part of the show — the HUD narrates witness generation, proving, and verification step by step, turning dead time into credibility. Blocking an agent with a human. Agents expect fast async answers; our consent gate intentionally makes them wait for a human click. Wiring that without deadlocking the tool promise — and returning a machine-readable denied_by_patient the agent can respect — took several iterations. The honesty tax. SNP arrays can't see CYP2D6 copy-number variants, HLA alleles beyond our panel, or UGT1A1. We could have hidden those gaps; instead every limitation is stated in-UI, in tool responses, and in the README. It cost us "it does everything" bravado and bought us something better: judges believing everything else we claim. Accomplishments that we're proud of Nothing is mocked. Real Groth16 proofs, independent on-device verification, replay rejection, forged-claim rejection — all running in a browser tab with zero backend. Our automated suite passes 32/32 end-to-end (parse → phenotype → secrets → Merkle trees → prove → verify → replay-reject → forgery-reject). A real agent really did it. In our final integration test, a WebMCP-connected AI discovered all tools unprompted and executed the full chain — parse a genuine 643,163-position genome, assess Plavix, recommend an alternative, generate and verify a Groth16 proof — without ever receiving the genome. We made refusal a feature. Watching the circuit reject a forged phenotype, or an agent accept denied_by_patient , communicates our values better than any slide. What we learned With WebMCP, descriptions are the API. Agents choose tools based almost entirely on description quality. Writing for the model — not the user — was the highest-leverage engineering we did. Client-side ZK is production-plausible today. Seconds, not minutes, on commodity laptops, with snarkjs and careful circuit design. The "too slow for the browser" excuse expired. Policy belongs at the tool boundary, not the prompt. Prompt-level safety evaporates with a clever prompt; a consent gate inside execute() cannot be talked around. This, we think, is a pattern every WebMCP app should copy. Design for the agent's blind spots. In one real integration session an agent did everything we asked

title: dug
pitch: Live DNS, TLS and mail diagnostics where your agent’s tool call renders on the page. It picks the lookups, you read the evidence. 27 WebMCP tools, one of which can’t exist on a server.
about_excerpt: Live DNS, TLS and mail diagnostics where your agent’s tool call renders on the page. It picks the lookups, you read the evidence. 27 WebMCP tools, one of which can’t exist on a server. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I asked a model why mail from a domain was going to spam. Got back a confident, detailed, completely stale answer. Which makes sense. Its weights hold the DNS and certificate state of whenever training stopped, and all of that changes without telling anyone. Giving an agent live lookups fixes half the problem. Here’s the half nobody talks about: when the agent runs six lookups and gives you a paragraph, you’re trusting the paragraph. You never see the SPF include tree that blew past ten lookups. The evidence existed for a second inside a context window and then it was gone. What it does dug is a command-driven terminal for domain and network diagnostics. One question per command, live, no key and no signup. DNS across six resolvers, TLS chains, RDAP registration, SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment, ASN and routing, plus a family of commands for how readable a site is to crawlers and agents. The full list is at https://dug.sh/llms.txt , generated from the same registry the app runs on, so it’s never out of date. Every command is registered as a WebMCP tool on document.modelContext. When an agent in the page calls one, the answer doesn’t go only to the agent. It renders on the page, as the same screen you’d have got by typing the command yourself. The tool I cared about most is the one that isn’t a command. dug_investigate takes a question, a target, and a list of commands the agent wrote itself: dug_investigate({ question: "why is mail from this domain going to spam", target: "acme.com", steps: ["MAIL acme.com", "SPF acme.com", "DIG acme.com MX", "RDAP acme.com"] }) It runs them in order and files every screen under the question, each one showing up as it arrives. You end up reading a case file instead of a summary. The header says “planned by your agent”, so you know which half of the room asked. Why WebMCP and not only MCP Because dug_investigate can’t exist on a remote MCP server. I shipped one so you can check. /mcp serves the same commands over Streamable HTTP. An agent there runs the same four lookups and gets the same four payloads. What it can’t do is leave them anywhere a person is looking. An investigation’s output is a page, and there’s nothing at the other end of an HTTP response to render onto. So don’t take my word for it. Call it over /mcp, you get JSON. Call it in the page, somebody watches the case get built. There’s a second reason that matters more than it sounds. Every tool is annotated readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint, because every answer here is built out of whatever some third-party nameserver or registry returned. A TXT record is attacker-controlled text. The page knows that. A scraper guessing at the DOM doesn’t. How it makes the thing better to use Typing “why mail acme.com” means knowing there’s a topic called “mail”. That’s exactly what you don’t know when you’ve got the problem. You know the symptom. I kept the keyword form for people without an agent, and the page says outright that it’s the worse path. Then I gave the prompt its own planner: type the sentence and dug asks a model to pick the lookups, and the case is headed “planned by dug” so it never pretends an agent was there. With a real agent you say “our invoices are landing in spam” and it plans through dug_investigate itself. Either way you didn’t learn a grammar, and you still get the evidence instead of somebody’s opinion about the evidence. What people and agents can do together now Read the same thing at the same time. That’s it. I think it’s new here. Before, an agent using a diagnostics API ate the output privately, and whatever you learned came through its summary. Scraping the UI is worse: the agent guesses at a DOM it doesn’t understand, and the site has no way to tell it a DKIM record is untrusted input. With dug, the tool call and the thing a human looks at are the same event. The agent gets structured payloads to reason over. You get a few thousand pixels of evidence to argue with it about. When it tells you SPF is fine, the include tree is sitting right there and you can see it at ten of ten lookups, one CNAME from breaking. There’s also a loop this challenge made possible, which I didn’t expect to build. WEBMCP checks whether some other site is wired for agents: the Origin-Agent-Cluster header native WebMCP needs, whether the page’s scripts reference the API, the remote MCP surface. It’s careful about what it can’t know. Tools register at runtime, so nothing fetched from outside a browser can list them, and the screen has a frame titled “what this cannot see” that says so. A checker printing a tool count off a curl would be making it up. How I built it WebMCP lives in lib/webmcp.ts, written against the current spec, not the February draft. That distinction cost me a day. Entry point is document.modelContext. navigator.modelContext is read as a fallback only, since it’s a deprecated alias as of Chrome 150. Registration is registerTool(tool, { signal }), one tool at a time, with a single AbortController for the whole set. provideContext got pulled from the spec because it replaces the entire list in one call, which on a page where two scripts register tools isn’t cooperation, it’s a takeover. Every response sends Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1. Without it Chromium disables the API and nothing you register works at all, which is a fun hour to spend. @mcp-b/global installs the API where the browser hasn’t shipped it yet. One command registry generates the tools, and the REST routes, the OpenAPI document and the MCP server all read the same registry, so the four surfaces can’t drift into describing different tools. A parity test fails the build if they do. Errors are made for agents too. A refusal is a 400 with a code the caller can branch on, and it says what would have worked: ask the DNS endpoint for a record type it doesn’t know and the hint lists the ones it does; send a command to an endpoint that doesn’t serve it and the hint names the ones that do. The plain-text form that curl and the MCP bridge get prints every block the page shows, and strips any control characters a page title or a TXT record might carry, so a hostile record can’t rewrite a terminal or slip an escape sequence to a model. Backend is Go on Vercel functions. The dialer validates every outbound destination right before connect, so a lookup can’t be aimed at private or loopback space, and it judges IPv4 wrapped in IPv6 by the address inside rather than the wrapper. What I learned Static analysis can’t see a WebMCP tool set. Obvious in hindsight, and it ended up changing the product. Building WEBMCP as a checker forced me to get precise about the difference between “this page’s scripts reference the API”, which you can observe, and “an agent is connected”, which nobody can observe from anywhere. The page never claims the second one, because nothing it could call would know. Things that were on the “next” list until yesterday A fleet in one case. dug_investigate takes a targets list, and a step written as MAIL {target} runs once per domain, in order, under one heading. WHY mail a.com b.com does the same from the prompt, and so does the planner: type “is mail set up right for a.com and b.com” and dug files one case for both. An agent asked about three domains files one case, not three. The server card as an MCP resource. SEP-1649 recommends it, so a client that’s already connected can read mcp://server-card.json and validate the tool set without a second fetch to .well-known. Both come from one builder, so they can’t disagree. Two more built-in investigations for people without an agent: “is this site down for everyone or only for me” and “is this domain’s registration and delegation healthy”. The whole point still stands, though: an agent doesn’t need me to write them. What’s next Whatever the judges break. Try it Live: https://dug.sh Code: https://github.com/zaidmukaddam/dug (MIT) Remote MCP: https://dug.sh/mcp Server card: https://dug.sh/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json For agents: https://dug.sh/llms.txt For judges: open https://dug.sh in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing turned on. Then ask your agent something like “why would mail from github.com go to spam?” or “is vercel.com readable by agents?”. No signup, no key, nothing to install. In an ordinary browser the tools register and nothing is listening, and the page tells you that instead of pretending otherwise. title: Sodium by Result
pitch: Sodium is the PostHog for WebMCP tools. It turns your app’s features into WebMCP tools so agents can discover and use them directly along with signed deployments and advanced tool analytics.
about_excerpt: Sodium is the PostHog for WebMCP tools. It turns your app’s features into WebMCP tools so agents can discover and use them directly along with signed deployments and advanced tool analytics. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Run npx sodiumtools init , and Sodium inspects the application’s routes, forms, client actions, and same-origin APIs. It then generates a typed sodium.json tool contract, any required browser-safe handlers, and a framework-native SDK integration. Developers review the changes and run npx sodiumtools deploy to validate, publish, and sign an immutable contract that agents can use to interact with the site. All tool execution happens inside the customer’s application. Sodium is the analytics layer that records what happens at the tool level and gives users a dashboard displaying useful information such as: Tool calls Success and failure rates Confirmation denials Registration failures P95 execution latency Activity by tool and day Answer-engine referrals How we built it Sodium is a pnpm and Turborepo monorepo with four main parts: A Next.js control plane for authentication, projects, deployments, analytics, and CLI authorization A CLI for initialization, validation, deployment, and live diagnostics A shared specification package for schemas, compilation, risk rules, and deployment receipts A local browser SDK for tool execution, WebMCP registration, and telemetry Supabase as the database which stores projects, immutable deployments, hashed CLI credentials, and usage events. Challenges Understanding the best DX We launched our first version , in which users added the Sodium GitHub app to their repositories and Sodium generated a PR that added the tools and analytics. Based on the feedbacks we received from x.com/saviomartin/status/2093780571638149523 , we revamped Sodium within two days , publishing our CLI and moving to a framework-agnostic approach so that even people with private GitHub repositories could fully trust and use Sodium. Generating and managing tools accurately A coding agent can misunderstand an application or invent behavior that does not exist. That’s why we decided to build sodium.json , which serves as a one-stop destination for everything and is much easier for users to manage from a DX point of view. What we learned WebMCP is an inevitable technology that will create a world in which agents use the web more than humans do. Staying at the forefront of the latest technologies will help businesses flourish faster. title: Consensus
pitch: Human + AI decision workspace powered by WebMCP, where agents research, score, flag conflicts, and propose rankings while humans retain final control.
about_excerpt: Human + AI decision workspace powered by WebMCP, where agents research, score, flag conflicts, and propose rankings while humans retain final control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration - AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of researching, analyzing, and making recommendations, but important decisions still require human judgment. We wanted to build a workspace where humans and AI could work together on the same decision instead of the AI simply giving a final answer. Consensus was inspired by the idea of making AI an active collaborator while keeping humans in control of important decisions. What it does - Consensus is a shared decision and research workspace for human + AI collaboration. In Decision Mode, AI agents can use WebMCP tools to read the board, add options, score options, flag conflicts, resolve flags, and propose rankings. Humans can independently score options, review AI reasoning, dispute evaluations, and lock the final decision. Consensus also includes Research Mode for extracting claims, checking evidence, identifying contradictions, and building citation relationships. All important actions are persisted and can be reviewed through activity history and provenance. How we built it - The frontend is built with React and Vite, with WebMCP integrated through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The backend uses FastAPI and is deployed on Google Cloud Run. Firestore stores shared board state, evaluations, flags, and activity history. Vertex AI with Gemini 2.5 Flash provides AI-assisted analysis. The WebMCP tools connect to the same real backend operations used by the application, so agent actions update persistent state rather than a simulated demo. Challenges we ran into - A major challenge was deciding what AI agents should be allowed to do and what should remain under human control. We wanted the agent to be useful without allowing it to silently make consequential decisions. We also had to make WebMCP tool registration reliable as the application changed between different modes and states. Finally, connecting the React frontend, FastAPI backend, Firestore, Vertex AI, and WebMCP into one working deployed application required careful coordination. Accomplishments that we're proud of - We are proud that Consensus is a real deployed WebMCP application with persistent state, rather than just a prototype or mock demonstration. The live application exposes six Decision-mode WebMCP tools that can interact with the shared workspace. We are especially proud of the human-agent boundary: agents can investigate, evaluate, flag issues, and recommend actions, while humans retain control over scoring, overrides, and locking the final decision. Our backend verification tests also pass checks for persistence, provenance, conflict handling, evaluation history, overrides, and locking. What we learned - We learned that WebMCP becomes much more powerful when tools operate on real shared application state. We also learned that human-AI collaboration is not only about giving agents more capabilities. It is equally important to define the actions they should not control. Building Consensus also taught us how browser-native agent tools can work together with a persistent cloud backend and an AI reasoning layer. What's next for Consensus - Next, we want to expand Consensus into more complex collaborative workflows. We plan to explore multi-agent debate, stronger evidence and citation verification, configurable decision rubrics, richer provenance, and approval workflows with different levels of human confirmation. Our long-term goal is to create a workspace where humans and AI agents can work together on complex decisions while keeping the reasoning, evidence, actions, and final authority visible and auditable. title: Solaris — agent-native solar sizing lab
pitch: A home solar sizing lab where the agent doesn't fill in your form it searches. One WebMCP tool call evaluates 2,000 configurations in 40ms, in the browser, against the same state your sliders write to
about_excerpt: A home solar sizing lab where the agent doesn't fill in your form it searches. One WebMCP tool call evaluates 2,000 configurations in 40ms, in the browser, against the same state your sliders write to Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it## Inspiration I looked through the WebMCP demos that already exist — hotel booking, sports storefronts, restaurant reservations, movie tickets — and noticed they mostly share the same shape: The agent searches, filters, fills, and submits. It does what a person could already do, only faster. I wanted to build the other thing: a web app where the agent has a capability the interface fundamentally cannot offer. Sizing a home solar system turned out to be the perfect problem. A solar system is a three-way trade-off between panels, battery, and inverter. The best configuration depends on how all three interact, along with electricity usage and tariffs. There are thousands of sensible combinations. A person moving sliders can explore one configuration at a time. An agent can search the entire design space. That difference is the project. What Solaris Does Solaris is a browser-based solar and battery simulator that lets humans explore systems manually — while giving AI agents the ability to search the design space computationally. You can use Solaris normally: Adjust solar panels Adjust battery capacity Adjust inverter size Change daily energy consumption Run simulations See annual generation, grid dependence, cost, and payback But you can also ask for an outcome instead of a configuration: "I use about 14 kWh a day, mostly evenings. Find me the cheapest setup over ten years that keeps me at least 80% off the grid." The agent can call grid_search . Instead of moving sliders one by one, it evaluates roughly 2,000 possible configurations in about 40 milliseconds , ranks them against the requested objective and constraints, and returns the best trade-offs. Solaris then visualizes the search: Every configuration the agent evaluated The trade-off frontier The best options at different budgets The selected configuration The agent can then apply the winning configuration, and the sliders visibly move on screen. Why This Is WebMCP The most important part of Solaris is that grid_search has no meaningful UI equivalent. A slider can represent one value. A button can trigger one operation. But grid_search takes: Parameter ranges An optimization objective Constraints A requested result size …and evaluates thousands of possible combinations. There is no sensible "Search 2,000 configurations" button for a human to use interactively. The agent isn't simply operating the existing interface. It has gained a new computational capability through the web page. That is what I wanted to explore with WebMCP. The browser is the computational environment Solaris runs entirely in the browser. There is no backend, no external simulation service, and no separate MCP server holding the model state. The simulator and the WebMCP tools operate on the same client-side state. So if a human changes the battery slider halfway through an agent conversation, the agent can call get_state and immediately see the new configuration. The browser supplies the model and compute. The agent supplies the search strategy. WebMCP connects the two. What Humans and Agents Can Do Together Solaris enables interactions that are difficult to express through a traditional UI. 1. Ask for outcomes instead of settings Instead of figuring out which slider values to use, a person can describe the result they want. "Keep me at least 80% off-grid while minimizing my 10-year cost." The agent searches the design space and shows the resulting trade-offs. 2. Explore the agent's reasoning space Solaris doesn't only return the winner. It visualizes the configurations the agent explored, allowing the human to see the shape of the optimization problem and the alternatives that were rejected. The result becomes something the human can inspect rather than a black-box recommendation. 3. Human changes become agent context A user can manually change the system after an agent recommendation and ask: "Was that a good idea?" The agent reads the current browser state and can compare it against the previous configuration. 4. Expensive computation requires human approval Searches over more than 200 configurations trigger an approval dialog that tells the user how much computation will be performed. The user can approve or decline the operation. A refusal is returned to the agent as structured tool output, allowing it to respond intelligently rather than treating the action as an error. How I Built It Solaris is a self-contained HTML application with no backend, build step, or external dependencies. The simulation model is deterministic JavaScript. It models: Hourly solar generation across 8,760 hours A daylight generation profile Monthly peak-sun-hour scaling Inverter clipping Battery charging and round-trip efficiency Battery discharge Grid imports Energy exports Annual costs and payback There are two simulation fidelities. simulateFull runs all 8,760 hours and powers the detailed UI. simulateFast uses twelve representative days scaled to a year and powers parameter sweeps. The two agree within 0.1% on annual generation. WebMCP Tools Solaris exposes nine tools through document.modelContext : get_model_spec get_state set_params run sweep grid_search pin_run compare_runs explain_state The most important is grid_search . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "grid_search", description: "Search several parameters together and return the best configurations found.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { ranges: { type: "object" }, objective: { type: "string", enum: [ "min_annual_cost", "min_payback", "min_total_cost_10yr", "max_self_sufficiency" ] }, constraints: { type: "object" }, topN: { type: "integer" } }, required: ["ranges"] }, execute: async (input) => { // Build grid → request approval when necessary // → evaluate → rank → return compact results } }); Every tool call is wrapped with telemetry before registration, allowing the interface to display the tool name, arguments, duration, and number of simulations performed. Large searches run in chunks with a progress indicator so the browser remains responsive. Results are also returned compactly — top configurations plus aggregates rather than thousands of raw rows. Challenges Getting the economics right My first cost assumptions made the optimization landscape almost useless. The default configuration already achieved roughly 99% self-sufficiency, meaning grid_search could evaluate thousands of configurations only to discover that the starting point was already nearly optimal. I brute-forced the search space, found the optimum sitting on a slider boundary, and retuned the tariffs and component costs. The optimum moved into the interior of the search space. That made the optimization meaningful. Teaching the agent when to use each tool My first tool descriptions simply explained what each function did. That produced timid behavior. The agent would sometimes use a one-parameter sweep when the user's question required a joint search. The solution wasn't more code. It was better tool descriptions. I explicitly described when each tool should be preferred , and made it clear that grid_search exists specifically for questions that cannot be answered efficiently by manipulating individual controls. That changed the agent's behavior dramatically. Approval without approval fatigue Putting a confirmation dialog in front of every operation would train users to blindly click through it. Instead, Solaris only requires approval once a search exceeds 200 configurations. The dialog shows the number of configurations and the estimated computation rather than presenting a vague "Are you sure?" What I Learned The most interesting discovery came from the agent itself. The cheapest configuration deliberately undersized the inverter, producing a DC:AC ratio of around 1.6 . It accepted some midday clipping because the clipped energy would only export at ₹1.50, while additional inverter capacity cost ₹7,000 per kW. I didn't explicitly encode that conclusion. It emerged from the search. That was the moment the idea clicked for me: The interesting result wasn't sitting in the UI waiting to be clicked. And it wasn't something I had manually programmed the agent to say. It emerged from giving the agent the ability to explore a space that would be impractical for a human to explore manually. What's Next Solaris is one example of a broader pattern. Many useful problems aren't about finding a single value. They're about exploring a frontier . The same architecture could apply to: Financial scenario planning Staffing and queue optimization Logistics Engineering tolerances Resource allocation Energy systems Capacity planning Wherever a browser can hold a model, WebMCP can potentially give an agent the ability to describe

 Inspiration 

 Most browser agents still have to inspect a page, infer what controls mean, and simulate clicks. That approach is fragile, and it gives the web application very little control over how its capabilities are exposed to an AI agent. 

 At the same time, giving an agent unrestricted permission to change real application state creates another problem: useful autonomy can quickly become unsafe autonomy. 

 ActGeX explores a different contract between humans, agents, and web applications: 

 AI agents should be able to analyze, recommend, and act — while humans remain in control of consequential changes. 

 Personal finance is our demonstration environment because it makes that trust boundary easy to understand. An agent can safely analyze spending, but changing a real financial goal should remain a human decision. 

 

 What it does 

 ActGeX is a WebMCP-native financial workspace where a human and an AI agent operate on the same live application state. 

 The application exposes eight typed WebMCP capabilities: 

 
 query_transactions 
 get_category_summary 
 compare_spending_periods 
 flag_unusual_spending 
 recommend_budget_goal 
 simulate_budget_change 
 set_budget_goal 
 export_report 
 

 These tools support a complete agent workflow rather than isolated tool calls. 

 ActGeX's Agent Mission can: 

 
 read transaction data 
 summarize spending 
 compare periods 
 detect unusual spending 
 recommend a budget goal 
 simulate its financial impact 
 present the proposed change to the human 
 apply it only after explicit approval 
 

 For example, the agent can identify that Dining spending increased, recommend a new target, and simulate how that target would affect monthly savings. 

 But the recommendation itself does not silently change the application. 

 When set_budget_goal is requested, ActGeX opens a Human Approval Required dialog showing the proposed change and its Before/After impact. 

 Only after the human explicitly approves does the real application state change. 

 The agent recommends. The human decides. 

 

 How we built it 

 ActGeX exposes application capabilities through WebMCP using: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool has: 

 
 a stable semantic tool name 
 a clear description 
 typed input parameters 
 validation 
 execution logic connected to real application state 
 

 The application is built with: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 Zustand 
 DuckDB-Wasm 
 WebMCP 
 

 The human UI and WebMCP tools operate on shared application state. 

 There is no separate agent-facing copy of the financial workspace. 

 ActGeX also exposes an Agent Financial Context so the agent-visible context is understandable from the human interface itself. 

 The workspace includes dedicated sections for: 

 
 Overview 
 Agent Mission 
 Tools 
 Shared State 
 Approvals 
 Executions 
 Agents 
 Settings 
 

 Shared State makes the live financial data visible as the common state used by both the human and the agent. 

 Approvals surfaces human-owned budget goals and recent approval/rejection decisions. 

 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent often has to reason about visual controls or DOM structure and simulate user interaction. 

 ActGeX changes that model. 

 Instead of asking the agent to locate the correct button or infer the meaning of a UI element, the application exposes semantic capabilities directly. 

 The agent calls capabilities, not pixels. 

 That improves reliability, but more importantly, it lets the application define its own trust boundary. 

 ActGeX can explicitly decide: 

 
 what the agent may read 
 what the agent may analyze 
 what can be simulated safely 
 what requires human authorization before mutation 
 

 WebMCP therefore becomes more than an automation interface. It becomes part of the application's permission and collaboration model. 

 

 Human + Agent collaboration 

 ActGeX is designed around a shared financial state. 

 The human sees the same transactions, budgets, summaries, recommendations, and decisions that the agent operates on. 

 The core interaction loop is: 

 Shared State → Agent Analysis → Recommendation → Simulation → Human Approval → State Change → Activity History 

 This is visible directly in the product. 

 The Agent Mission shows the agent's analysis sequence. 

 The Recommendation explains: 

 
 What should change 
 Why the agent recommends it 
 What impact the change may have 
 

 The Approval dialog shows the Before/After financial effect. 

 The Activity Timeline records agent executions and human decisions. 

 The goal is not invisible automation. 

 The goal is visible collaboration with explicit authority boundaries . 

 

 Human authority 

 ActGeX provides human control over agent behavior. 

 The application supports Observe and Assist authority modes. 

 In Observe mode, the agent can inspect and analyze financial state without making consequential changes. 

 In Assist mode, the agent can perform analysis and prepare recommendations, while consequential state changes still pass through the human approval boundary. 

 The most important example is set_budget_goal . 

 The agent may request the change, but it cannot silently commit it. 

 The user sees the recommendation and simulated impact before choosing whether to approve or reject it. 

 This makes human authority part of the application workflow rather than an external safety policy.

title: RockFoundry
pitch: RockFoundry turns rough app ideas into structured product drafts and interactive design previews through WebMCP-powered site tools inside ChatGPT
about_excerpt: RockFoundry turns rough app ideas into structured product drafts and interactive design previews through WebMCP-powered site tools inside ChatGPT Like 1 Comment Story Updates Logo Thumbnail Home Design Generate 1 Design Generate 2 Inspiration Coding agents are getting very good at writing code, but they still need clear product context before they can build the right thing. I built RockFoundry to bridge that gap: turn a rough product idea into structured product decisions, documents, and an interactive design before implementation starts. For this challenge, I extended RockFoundry with WebMCP so ChatGPT can operate the product workspace directly from the browser. What it does RockFoundry turns a simple idea into a structured product workspace. From ChatGPT, WebMCP site tools can: start a new RockFoundry product inspect the current product state generate a Product Draft refine product decisions generate an interactive Design Preview The Product Draft includes six connected artifacts: BRD PRD ERD User Flows Screen Map Design Brief The same product context is then used to generate a multi-screen interactive prototype. How I built it RockFoundry is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Prisma, SQLite, and Docker. WebMCP tools are registered directly by the RockFoundry web interface using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The tools are page-scoped: the homepage exposes a tool for starting a product, while an active project exposes tools for inspection, drafting, refinement, and design generation. The WebMCP layer reuses RockFoundry's existing APIs and product workflows instead of duplicating business logic. Challenges The biggest challenge was making an AI workflow feel fast and reliable. Product documents originally required several long-running sequential AI calls. I changed the generation flow to use bounded parallel batches. Design generation was also too slow, so the initial preview now uses a deterministic design specification and one focused AI prototype-generation call. Another challenge was tool routing. Generic tool names could collide with other agent capabilities, so the WebMCP tools were namespaced specifically for RockFoundry. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when tools represent real product actions instead of generic browser automation. Giving the agent access to the same live product state as the user makes the interaction feel much more like collaboration than automation. What's next Next I want RockFoundry to produce an even stronger handoff for coding agents, so a product can move from idea → product specification → design → implementation with less context loss. title: dabdabdab
pitch: Try on makeup virtually with your AI makeup artist
about_excerpt: Try on makeup virtually with your AI makeup artist Like Comment Story Updates What is it dabdabdab is a browser-based virtual makeup studio that turns a WebMCP-compatible AI assistant into a live makeup artist. People can try individual makeup products or complete looks on their own face in real time. They can ask an agent to analyze their coloring, create or refine a look, and find matching products with purchase links. The app is privacy focused. Face tracking, makeup rendering, and color analysis all run locally in the browser. Its WebMCP tools return only current makeup settings and aggregate color estimates, never camera frames, screenshots, face landmarks, or facial geometry. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Choosing makeup combines two types of interaction. Natural language is best for intent, such as “give me a ’90s supermodel look,” “try on CHANEL Rouge Coco in Mademoiselle,” or “create a Burning Man look that suits my coloring.” However, the user is not limited to imprecise interactions like “less red,” “even less red,” or “no, a bluer red.” Direct controls add the option for precise adjustments, such as selecting an exact shade or finish. WebMCP lets both interactions happen in one shared experience. The agent can read the current studio state, apply coordinated changes, and see the user's manual adjustments. The user can move between conversation and page controls without restating the look or losing progress. WebMCP is especially well suited to maintaining user privacy because the tools run directly in the webpage. A regular MCP integration would require a separate MCP server and requests to that server. With WebMCP, the page can give the agent useful makeup settings and color estimates while all image processing and the live camera feed stay on the user’s device. How WebMCP improves the user experience Online beauty shoppers often move between inspiration, tutorials, product pages, and a bathroom mirror, with no reliable way to see whether the result will suit them. dabdabdab connects those steps. This lets them try a look BEFORE buying. A user can describe a look, see it on their face in seconds, adjust any detail, and ask for matching products. Users can also ask to see specific products like “MAC lipstick Ruby Woo,” and the agent will research it and apply a matching color. Actions taken by the agent update the visible controls, so every change is clear and editable. The product is also usable without an agent as a complete virtual makeup studio. It includes a demo mode with a model if the user prefers to not opt-in to live camera mode. What people and agents can do together The agent contributes style knowledge, coordination across six makeup categories, and product research. The user contributes personal taste and visual judgment. The site analyzes the user’s skin, eye, and hair colors on the device and shares only the resulting color profile with the agent. If an estimate is wrong, the user can correct it quickly and easily in the interface. For example, a user can ask, “Create a ’90s supermodel look that suits my coloring.” The agent reads the studio state, requests an on-device color analysis, and applies six coordinated layers. The user can then change the lipstick manually, ask the agent to soften the eyes to match, and shop the final look. Because the agent reads the same state that the controls update, neither participant loses the other’s changes. Together, they can turn an idea (extreme glam look), occasion (summer festival), or reference (Sabrina Carpenter's pink stage makeup), try it on, refine it through chat or direct controls, and find products with links for the final result. Before WebMCP, an assistant could describe a look but could not inspect the active layers, apply the look to a live preview, or stay synchronized with the user's edits. How we implemented WebMCP The site registers eight tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_makeup_state analyze_coloring get_appearance_profile apply_makeup apply_full_makeup_look undo_last_makeup_change clear_makeup show_product_matches Each tool has a strict JSON schema and calls the same in-browser application logic as the visible controls. Human edits and agent actions therefore share one state and undo history. The handlers enforce studio readiness, validate camera and demo source selection, reject unsupported styles and duplicate categories, and validate every input before changing the preview. State-reading tools are marked read-only, while product results are marked as untrusted content and accepted only when they match an active layer. A complete multi-layer look is applied atomically and recorded as one action. If any layer fails, the previous look is restored. The color-analysis tools also warn the agent that the tools return only aggregate colors and that by the user granting the website camera access, the user is not granting the agent permission to access raw camera data. MediaPipe tracks the face and analyzes skin, eye, and hair color locally. We use WebGL shaders to render six makeup categories onto the live video in real time. WebMCP connects the agent directly to that browser-based system without requiring a separate MCP server or backend API for the core try-on experience. Together, these tools let the agent understand what the user is seeing, safely change the live preview, and keep the page controls in sync so the user can take over at any time. title: Decision Workspace
pitch: An adaptive WebMCP workspace where agents ask one question at a time, expose trade-offs, and help people reach transparent, grounded decisions.
about_excerpt: An adaptive WebMCP workspace where agents ask one question at a time, expose trade-offs, and help people reach transparent, grounded decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Important decisions often get buried in long AI chats. Criteria drift, assumptions disappear, and it becomes hard to tell why a recommendation changed. We wanted a shared workspace where a person can see the decision model evolve instead of receiving an opaque answer. What we built Decision Workspace is a local-first decision canvas for humans and browser agents. It keeps options, weighted criteria, score-and-confidence assessments, evidence, uncertainties, constraints, and recommendations in one inspectable state. The app exposes workflow-level WebMCP tools through navigator.modelContext. An agent can read the current workspace, ask one high-value interview question at a time, process an answer atomically, apply only grounded mappings, and adapt the next question to the new context. Free-text or uncertain answers remain explicitly unresolved instead of being forced into a score. Users can explore temporary what-if scenarios without changing saved state. When the model is sufficiently grounded, the agent can create a readiness-checked Decision Brief with the leading option, drivers, remaining unknowns, and next verification action. The person remains in control of the final decision. How we built it We built the UI with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The canonical decision store is shared by the UI and the WebMCP adapter, so tool writes are immediately visible in the page and persisted locally on the device. Revision-aware writes and explicit question lifecycle states keep the interview consistent and auditable. Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was designing a small, coherent tool surface instead of exposing every UI control. We learned that an agent workflow needs explicit state reads, deterministic mapping policies, uncertainty preservation, non-destructive scenarios, and readiness gating. WebMCP works best when the browser page is the shared source of truth and the agent changes it through semantic workflow actions. title: Packedup
pitch: Plan together, travel better. \nDrop a code, vote as a group, get an itinerary everyone actually wants.
about_excerpt:
Plan together, travel better. 
Drop a code, vote as a group, get an itinerary everyone actually wants.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every time I travel with friends, the same thing happens: someone drops
five hotel options and a dozen restaurant links into WhatsApp, everyone
votes with thumbs-up reactions scattered across different messages, and a
day later nobody can remember what actually won. The votes get buried
under new messages, there's no single place to look back at what was
decided, and by the time we land, half the group doesn't even have a
day-by-day plan — just a chat log full of half-finished decisions. 

 I wanted a place built specifically for that moment: drop in the options,
let everyone vote, lock in a winner, and have it turn into an itinerary
automatically — instead of relying on a chat app never designed for
decision-making in the first place 

 What it does 

 PackedUp is group trip planning built around three boards — Stay, Eat, and Visit. Anyone with a 7-character invite code joins as a guest and drops in a suggestion — a hotel, a restaurant, a hike — for the group to vote on, up or down, in real time. The trip's creator finalizes a winner on each board, and those winners flow straight into a day-by-day itinerary — no re-typing, no digging through chat history to remember what won. 

 No sign-up is required to participate. A guest is identified by a session token stored locally, so joining a trip takes a name and a code, not a password — the whole reason WhatsApp felt easier than "download an app" in the first place, minus the part where votes get lost. 

 The newest layer is agent support: PackedUp exposes create_trip, get_trip_board_info, and add_recommended_suggestion as WebMCP tools — an emerging browser standard (document.modelContext) that lets an AI agent fill in the trip form or drop a recommended restaurant onto a board on a user's behalf, the same way a person would from the UI. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js 14 (App Router) for both the UI and the API — Route Handlers sit between the client and Supabase. 

 
 Supabase (Postgres) for data, with row-level security enabled on every table. Guest writes go through a service-role client scoped strictly to server-side route handlers, since a guest has no auth.uid() for RLS to key off of. 
 Zustand, persisted to localStorage, holds the guest session (member_id, trip_id, session_token) across visits. 
 TanStack Query manages server state — trip details, suggestions, members — with short polling intervals standing in for full realtime where it wasn't worth the complexity yet. 
 Framer Motion for the transitions between states (voting, finalizing, empty boards). 
 WebMCP, via the use-webmcp-tool React hook, registers tools directly on the page components where the corresponding UI action lives — create_trip on the landing and create pages, the suggestion tools on the board page — so a tool only exists while its page is actually mounted. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting from "WhatsApp thread full of forgotten votes" to an actual finalized itinerary in three clicks — join with a code, vote, finalize — without ever asking a single friend to make an account. Getting real-time-feeling voting working with plain polling instead of reaching for a heavier realtime setup before it was needed. And shipping WebMCP support early enough to be one of the first trip-planning tools an AI agent can actually operate, not just read. 

 What we learned 

 That an emerging standard is still an emerging standard — WebMCP is real, shipping behind flags and origin trials, but building against it means designing for graceful absence: useWebMCP reports supported: false in any browser without the API, and the app has to be just as usable without an agent in the loop as with one. We also learned, the hard way, that the fastest debugging step for a "healthy app, broken deploy" is checking whether the database itself is still awake. 

 What's next for Packedup 

 Real Supabase Realtime subscriptions in place of polling, an actual MCP server (not just WebMCP) so agents like Codex or Claude Desktop can drive trip creation without a browser tab open, and per-day budget estimates rolled into the itinerary so the group knows the damage before they land.

title: Unitwatch
pitch: A public web bench for crashed systemd units. Humans paste systemctl status. Agents call the same generators via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A public web bench for crashed systemd units. Humans paste systemctl status. Agents call the same generators via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Operators already paste systemctl status dumps into chat. Unitwatch makes those generators first-class page tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The human UI and the agent share one workspace. This is not MCP-over-HTTP. 

 What it does 

 Unitwatch is a public web bench for crashed systemd units. A human pastes systemctl status or a journal snippet. An agent calls the same generators as WebMCP tools. Both see the same proposed files: a restart drop-in, a TCP watchdog timer, and a rollback. 

 Nothing SSHes. Nothing emails. Nothing is installed on a host. The page only writes files onto itself. 

 Tools: parse_systemd_status, propose_restart_dropin, propose_watchdog_timer, propose_rollback, propose_hardening_plan, get_workspace. 

 How we built it 

 Built with JavaScript on Cloudflare Workers, exposing the same generator functions to the page UI and to agents via WebMCP (document.modelContext.registerTool). Try it: open the live URL in the ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Prompt: Parse the sample unit, then propose a restart drop-in and a TCP watchdog on 8080. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Keeping one set of generators authoritative for both the human UI and the agent tools, and keeping the bench strictly read-only with respect to real hosts. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 One workspace shared by human and agent, with no host access, no SSH, and no email. 

 What we learned 

 Page-native tools via WebMCP are a better fit than MCP-over-HTTP when the human UI and the agent should share state. 

 What's next for Unitwatch 

 More generators, richer journal parsing, and broader unit-type coverage. 

 MIT license is on the GitHub About page.

title: Callingly WebMCP - AI Sales Reps for Local Businesses
pitch: Need an emergency plumber? With the Callingly WebMCP script installed on their site, Joe’s Plumbing can have your agent call and get a plumber on the phone with you in seconds.
about_excerpt: Need an emergency plumber? With the Callingly WebMCP script installed on their site, Joe’s Plumbing can have your agent call and get a plumber on the phone with you in seconds. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every local business website has the same dead end: a visitor that needs immediate help, and a contact form that answers in "1-2 business days". The visitor wants to talk to someone, right now. An AI agent browsing that page hits the same wall. It can read the pricing and summarize the docs, but the moment its user says "I just need to talk to a human about this", the best it can do is fill in the form and hope. We build a phone system for a living, so we already had the missing piece - a live view of who is on shift and who is mid-call, and the ability to ring them. What we had no way to do was hand that to an agent standing on a customer's website. WebMCP is exactly that missing handle. What it does One script tag on any website registers two WebMCP tools: Tool What it does callingly-check-sales-availability Read-only. Is the business open right now, is a sales rep actually free (not on another call, past their cooldown), when is the next opening, and are call requests being accepted at all. callingly-request-sales-call Asks Callingly to call the visitor on the number the agent passes, and to connect them to the company. What happens on the second one is the part worth watching. Callingly's AI sales rep calls the visitor within seconds and starts qualifying - and at the same time it dials the company's reps in parallel. The moment a human picks up, the AI hands the caller over: "Ok great, let me get you on the line with one of our specialists." No hold music, no callback queue, and no dead air while the humans are being rung. So the agent can negotiate the timing of a human conversation : "They're free now, want me to get someone on the line?" / "Nobody until 9am Tuesday - shall I have them call you then?" That is not a lookup and it is not a booking link. It is a live check against who is on shift, who is mid-call, and what the team's calling hours are, turned into an offer the agent can actually make good on. A contact form cannot have that conversation. A scheduling widget offers slots without knowing whether anyone is at their desk. A chatbot can promise a callback with no authority to cause one. Concretely: a visitor asks an agent about a burst pipe at 8:47pm. Seconds later their phone rings, an AI rep is asking what's wrong, and by the time they've finished describing it a plumber is on the line - instead of a form submission someone reads on Monday. This is not a mock. The dialer, the routing rules, the availability logic and the reps are Callingly's production system, the same one paying customers use. The demo places real phone calls. How we built it webmcp.js is a dependency-free ES5 IIFE, 516 lines, no build step. It: registers both tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , falling back to navigator.modelContext for older origin-trial builds; polls for the model context rather than assuming one at load; unregisters through an AbortController , since WebMCP has no unregisterTool ; returns MCP content results and uses isError for refusals, so the agent gets a sentence it can act on rather than an exception; ships annotations: { readOnlyHint: true } on the availability tool and an inputSchema on both - required by ChatGPT's implementation; exposes the same functions on window.callingly , so ordinary page code, or an extension that doesn't speak WebMCP yet, can call them. Server-side is two public endpoints keyed by a webhook integration's slug: GET /embed/v1/{key}/availability and POST /embed/v1/{key}/calls . Accepted calls go into the same queued pipeline every webhook lead goes through - routing rules, de-duplication, then dialling - so the endpoint answers 202 rather than pretending to know which rep will pick up. Challenges we ran into Registration is not fire-and-forget. Agent browsers install document.modelContext at wildly different points. A context can arrive long after load, be replaced after you have already registered against it, or accept a tool and then reject it after your retry window has closed. Our own debug console lied to us - twice. It reported "no WebMCP in this browser" for every failure, including causes it had never checked. Then, once it did report honestly, it turned out ChatGPT hands out a model context whose registerTool cannot be replaced: our instrumentation's assignment failed silently, nothing reached our wrapper, and the console concluded registration had failed while both tools were in fact live. It now reads the snippet's own state instead of trusting its own instrumentation, and names which of four distinct causes it actually found. You have to convince ChatGPT to use the WebMCP when its on the site, it doesn't check for it automatically. We assume that in the future this will be the first thing that it checks for. Accomplishments that we're proud of The integration really is one line, and the before/after pair in the repo is a one-line diff - nothing else on the plumber's page changes. The contact form still promises 1-2 business days, because the human path is not what this replaces. It is wired to production, not a demo backend. And the failure paths got as much care as the happy one: outside calling hours the agent gets a real next-opening time and can offer it, rather than a dead end. What we learned WebMCP's is a very young technology and working with it is tricky the same way as working with any new tech, its not fully supported, people don't know what it is, even the AI agents themselves have to be coerced into using it. But it has a ton of potential, particularly in our space. In the future, AI agents will be doing the shopping around for consumers and our customers (the consumer businesses) will need to have AI sales reps of their own to deal with the AI agent shoppers. What's next More actions. The backend already schedules callbacks for a named time, so "have them call me at 9am Tuesday" is a natural third tool - right now the agent can only ask for a call now. Ship it to customers. The snippet is MIT and the endpoints are live, so any Callingly account can paste it on their own site today. title: GitWand Agent
pitch: A WebMCP-powered Git Merge Room where agents resolve deterministic conflicts and humans decide the ambiguous ones.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered Git Merge Room where agents resolve deterministic conflicts and humans decide the ambiguous ones.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Agents are useful when they can act directly on Git problems, but they become fragile when they have to guess through a UI or pretend every conflict is machine-solvable. GitWand started from a boundary-first idea: resolve what is objectively deterministic, surface what is ambiguous, and keep the human in control of the decision. 

 What it does 

 GitWand Agent turns a Git conflict into a shared Merge Room for humans and agents. The page exposes three WebMCP tools: resolve_conflict , parse_git_error , and list_cases . Deterministic hunks are settled automatically; genuinely ambiguous ones are filed for the human to choose; and the agent can read the room back to resume work once a decision is made. 

 How we built it 

 We registered the tools directly on the page and wired the UI around live case state. The same browser tab that the agent sees also shows the Merge Room, so the result is visible in real time. The implementation keeps the resolution logic narrow and explicit: no guessing, no hidden side effects, and no tool that can silently pick a side for you. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was resisting the temptation to make the agent do too much. Git conflicts often mix deterministic edits with real intent decisions, so the product had to make that boundary obvious. Another challenge was designing list_cases so the agent can return after a human decision and continue without losing context. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native software works best when it is precise about what the machine can and cannot decide. WebMCP is a good fit because it lets a website define exactly how an agent should interact with it, instead of forcing the agent to infer the UI. 

 What's next 

 More conflict patterns, richer case history, and tighter integration with real repository workflows.
