title: Data Airlock
pitch: Clean sensitive datasets with AI agents—without uploading raw data. WebMCP enables local analysis, human-approved cleaning, capability-gap detection, and safe tool evolution.
about_excerpt: Clean sensitive datasets with AI agents—without uploading raw data. WebMCP enables local analysis, human-approved cleaning, capability-gap detection, and safe tool evolution. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are extremely useful for understanding and cleaning data, but there is a fundamental problem with sensitive datasets: normally, the agent needs access to the data itself. Data Airlock explores a different model: An agent can work on a dataset it can never read. The raw file stays on the user's device and is processed locally in the browser. The agent receives only bounded, pseudonymized and aggregate evidence through WebMCP. What it does Data Airlock is a local-first environment for analyzing and cleaning JSONL and CSV datasets with an AI agent while keeping raw records outside the agent boundary. A user can ask ChatGPT to analyze a dataset in natural language. Data Airlock performs the actual work locally and exposes safe WebMCP tools that let the agent: inspect aggregate dataset profiles and quality findings; identify affected pseudonymous fields without revealing their original values; prepare cleaning actions; run a real local second-pass simulation; inspect aggregate simulation impact; detect structural patterns that are not covered by any active capability; create or evolve capabilities with Forge; evaluate candidates locally using aggregate coverage, specificity, overlap and stability metrics; retrieve the open-source source code of cleaning tools when needed; access an interactive Data Airlock guide. The included production demo is a real 500 MiB dataset processed by the same local engine used for user files. Human authority by design The agent can analyze, reason, propose and simulate, but it cannot approve a destructive operation on behalf of the user. The cleaning lifecycle is deliberately: PROPOSE → SIMULATE → HUMAN APPROVAL → EXECUTE Human approval happens independently in the Data Airlock UI. Changing an approved plan invalidates that approval and requires a new simulation and review. This separates two different security boundaries: data access and execution authority . Capability Gap Scan and Forge A fixed set of tools cannot anticipate every structure that may appear in real-world data. Data Airlock therefore includes a local Capability Gap Scanner . It recognizes broad structural families such as date/time formats, locale-dependent numbers, identifiers, encoded tokens, network formats, structured text, Unicode/script mixtures, length distributions and other patterns. If a field contains meaningful structure that no active capability explains, the agent can receive safe aggregate evidence about that gap without seeing the values that caused it. The agent can then use Forge to create a new capability or evolve a related existing one. Before adoption, candidates go through bounded validation and can be evaluated locally against the gap. The agent receives only aggregate metrics such as structural coverage, specificity, overlap and stability. The principle is: The agent can expand its capabilities, not its access to your data. Why WebMCP WebMCP is what makes the architecture possible. Instead of building a separate agent backend or uploading the dataset to an API, the website exposes a controlled set of capabilities directly to the agent. The browser owns the dataset and computation. WebMCP provides the agent with a narrow semantic interface containing only the information it actually needs. This means the agent can participate in a useful end-to-end workflow while the raw dataset remains local. Data Airlock currently exposes read-only analysis and guidance tools, controlled plan-management tools, Forge, and a dynamically gated execution capability that exists only after real human approval. Privacy boundary The agent never receives raw dataset records or original field values through the Data Airlock WebMCP tools. It can receive things such as: aggregate counts; finding categories; pseudonymous field IDs such as field_003 ; cleaning-plan metadata; aggregate simulation impact; aggregate capability-gap evidence; aggregate candidate-evaluation metrics; safe receipts and state; open-source tool source code. The application requires no backend, no account and no API key for local dataset processing. Building it Data Airlock is built in TypeScript and React and runs entirely in the browser. Large datasets are processed using automatic Web Workers. JSONL and CSV are streamed through the local processing pipeline, and output can be written using browser-local storage / file capabilities depending on the environment. The WebMCP layer is intentionally separated from the raw-data engine. Agent-visible results are projected through bounded privacy-safe representations before leaving the local runtime. The production deployment is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges The hardest part was not detecting data-quality problems. It was preserving a meaningful agent experience while keeping a strict capability boundary. We had to make sure that: raw values never leaked through normal results, errors or edge cases; the agent could not manufacture human approval; stale approvals could not be replayed after a plan changed; WebMCP registrations remained safe across browser-host lifecycle changes; large files stayed practical without moving processing to a backend; Forge could evolve functionality without becoming an arbitrary-code escape hatch; capability discovery produced useful evidence without exposing examples from the dataset. We also built extensive deterministic, privacy, lifecycle and end-to-end tests around those boundaries. What we learned The most interesting lesson was that hiding raw data does not have to make an agent useless. If the local application exposes the right abstractions, an agent can still reason about counts, structural families, impact, coverage and state transitions. That led to the third principle behind Data Airlock: Airlock does not only hide data from the agent — it gives the agent enough safe evidence to know when it still does not know how to handle something. What's next The same architecture can extend beyond dataset cleaning. The broader idea is a capability-oriented interface where agents can work with sensitive local information through safe evidence and constrained actions rather than unrestricted access to the underlying data. Data Airlock is one demonstration of that model. I designed and built Data Airlock end-to-end, including the local dataset engine, WebMCP tool surface, privacy boundary, human-approval workflow, Capability Gap Scanner, Forge capability evolution, testing, and deployment. title: Sprintfy
pitch: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan.
about_excerpt: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Live: https://sprintfy.vercel.app — no account needed to see the whole idea. Open it in the ChatGPT desktop app, in ChatGPT mode : its built-in browser exposes WebMCP on its own, so the tools register with no flag and no extension. Desktop Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing works too, as does Chrome with the ChatGPT extension. One caveat: Codex mode in that same desktop app does not expose WebMCP , so the tools stay dormant there and the page will honestly say so — same app, two modes, two answers. Ask your agent for start_guided_demo , or press "Show me a demo", and you land in a real workspace with a proposal already waiting in the review panel and six tools live. Inspiration Every "agent-ready" app I looked at exposed the same shape of tool: create_task , update_task , delete_task . The model writes straight to the database. That is fine until the model is confidently wrong about your sprint plan, and then you are doing archaeology on a project board, trying to work out what it touched and in what order. Project planning is exactly the wrong domain for blind writes. A plan is an argument about sequencing and effort — it is the thing a lead is paid to have an opinion about. Handing that to an agent as unsupervised INSERTs gets you a plan nobody trusts and everybody re-checks, which is more work than writing it by hand. So I wanted to find out whether WebMCP could carry something other than commands. Can a tool call ask a question and wait for a human's answer? If it can, the agent stops being a thing you supervise and becomes a thing you argue with. What it does Sprintfy is a sprint planner — requirements, sprints, tasks, hour estimates — that exposes its workspace to agents over WebMCP. No agent tool writes to the plan. The loop has three moves: 1. The agent reads the room. get_project_context returns the plan and what the human is currently looking at: active view, selected sprint, status filter, which proposal is open. The agent plans into a context, not a vacuum. 2. The agent proposes a diff. Every write tool authors a change set — an ordered list of operations stored as JSON, rendered in the review panel as a real diff: additions in green, field-level changes as before → after, removals struck through. Nothing has touched the domain tables. An agent can propose a sprint and the twelve tasks inside it as one unit, using local ref ids that resolve to real primary keys only at apply time. 3. The human decides, and the agent hears the answer. apply_pending_changes opens the diff and blocks — the tool call's promise stays open while the person reads it. Approve applies the whole change set in a single Postgres transaction and the tool resolves with what landed. Reject resolves with the reason they typed, delivered back to the agent as the tool result. You do not start from an empty board either. You hand Sprintfy the thing you already have — a backlog note, a PRD as .md , .txt , .pdf or .docx , or a few paragraphs typed in — and it returns a plan sequenced by risk rather than by comfort. A real Turkish brief produced 8 requirements, 4 sprints and 38 tasks in 56 seconds, in Turkish, with the database migration ranked critical and placed first. Sprintfy's own planner is held to the same rule. It does not write the plan either: it authors a change set marked source: "planner" that lands in the same review panel, behind the same gate. How we built it Next.js (App Router) and React on Vercel, Supabase for Postgres, Auth and Realtime, and WebMCP for the agent surface. The architecture is one idea repeated: the write path is a data structure, not a function call. Tools append operations to a change_sets row. A single PL/pgSQL function, apply_change_set , applies them atomically and resolves ref placeholders to real ids as it goes. It is declared security invoker , so row-level security still guards every insert it performs — an agent cannot use it to reach another user's project. On the WebMCP side: Surface detection. The API moved during the spec's life and shipping browsers do not agree yet, so one adapter registers against document.modelContext.registerTool , navigator.modelContext.registerTool , or navigator.modelContext.provideContext , whichever exists, and the header badge reports which one it found. Page-scoped tool sets. Four tools before you sign in, six inside a project. The surface changes as the human navigates. Cancellation is honoured. The AbortSignal passed to apply_pending_changes releases the approval wait, so an agent that walks away does not leave the page stuck on a modal. Tools never throw at the browser. Failures come back as text an agent can recover from, including "these task ids don't exist in this project, call get_project_context again." Planning uses a strict JSON schema derived from the same Zod schema that backs the propose_plan tool — one schema, two authors, so a plan from the model and a plan from an agent are the same shape. Challenges we ran into Tool calls do not wait for React. Two bugs had the same root: an agent could not always see the proposal it had just written, and focus moved the human's view without get_project_context reporting it. A tool call can land before React has committed state, so reading a render closure returns the past. Tools now read from a ref that is written before the state, never from a closure. Both cases became eval scenarios so they cannot come back. Registering the same tool twice. Navigating between pages left the previous page's registration alive and the browser rejected the new one as a duplicate. Fixed with a module-level registry where claiming a name synchronously releases the previous holder. A machine asking a question and getting an HTML redirect. An unauthenticated POST to the planning endpoint was redirected to the sign-in page; Next then read the multipart body as a server action and answered 404. In an app whose premise is that machines are first-class callers, that was the wrong answer to give one. API routes now reply in JSON. The date picker that could not be used. The month grid was absolutely positioned inside a modal that clips its own corners and scrolls its body, so it was sliced off a few pixels below the field. It renders into a portal now, in viewport coordinates, flipping above the field when there is no room below. Knowing where WebMCP actually exists. Support is not a property of an application, it turns out — it is a property of a surface inside it. The ChatGPT desktop app has two modes, and only one of them exposes the API: in ChatGPT mode the built-in browser hands the page document.modelContext with no flag and no extension, while in Codex mode the built-in browser does not, so the same URL in the same application registers six tools or none depending on which mode you are in. I spent a while concluding the tools were broken before realising I had been testing in the wrong half of one app. That is why the page never assumes. It probes each surface, reports which one it found, and — when it finds none — still works and still explains itself, in its own voice, to a person who came in through an ordinary browser. Faking things. An early version showed timed loading stages — "Reading the brief", "Sequencing by risk" — while the model call ran. They were theatre, in a product whose entire argument is that you should not have to take an agent's word for anything. They were replaced with the true elapsed seconds. Accomplishments that we're proud of The blocking approval gate. Turning a WebMCP tool call from a command into a request is the part that is hard to fake, and it means the agent can be genuinely useful — proposing whole plans rather than timid one-row edits — without ever being trusted with the write. The evals. /evals.js runs seven scenarios against the actual ToolDescriptor objects the page registered, on the live site, from the console, with no account. Seven of seven pass in production. They assert the invariants rather than the happy path: a proposal writes zero rows; a rejection arrives as the tool's return value; approval applies a sprint and its tasks in one transaction with refs resolved; hallucinated ids are refused outright rather than half-applied. And the fact that Sprintfy's own planner goes through its own gate. A product arguing for review does not get to exempt its author. What we learned That a tool result is a channel back to the human , not just a status code. Once you treat it that way, "the agent asked and I said no, here's why" becomes a normal part of the protocol rather than something bolted on top. That the reviewable-proposal pattern belongs in the page, not in the model. The site knows what a legitimate change to itself looks like, so the site should render the diff and hold the gate. Any agent — any model, any vendor — inherits that

title: Ribband
pitch: Source-backed personal decisions for shopping, gifts, dates, vacations, and project staffing.
about_excerpt: Source-backed personal decisions for shopping, gifts, dates, vacations, and project staffing. Like Comment Story Updates Ribband: About Inspiration Most recommendation tools begin with a category and a search box. People rarely make decisions that way. A good vacation can echo a childhood memory. A good gift depends on who it is for, what they already love, and the occasion. A good date balances two people and avoids repeating what they have already done. A project crew needs the right roles, credentials, equipment, location, and schedule. At the same time, most of the web is designed to be seen, not understood by an agent. Important facts are buried inside presentation markup, forcing agents to infer controls and reconstruct evidence out of sight of the person who asked for help. Ribband explores a clearer contract for the next era of surfing the web: let an agent understand the personal context a person deliberately shares, move quickly across explicitly authorized sources, preserve the evidence, and keep consequential actions with the person. The name nods to the Blue Riband, the historic distinction associated with speed records on Atlantic passenger crossings. What it does Ribband is an open-source, source-backed personal decision agent for five everyday needs: Shopping: compare products for yourself using goals, preferences, exclusions, existing items, and a budget. Gifts: recommend options using the recipient's age, interests, occasion, deadline, dislikes, and whatever else the shopper chooses to provide. Dates: balance two people's interests, constraints, prior activities, and desired mood across low-cost, balanced, and special-occasion ideas. Vacations: turn visited places, fond memories, desired novelty, dates, party size, and budget into value, balanced, and signature packages containing lodging, transportation, dining, and activities. Project staffing: assemble eligible laborers, technicians, and creatives by role, credential, equipment, geography, schedule, and quote mode while surfacing coverage gaps instead of inventing a match. A person can begin with a sparse goal and budget or share richer context. One read-only plan_decision WebMCP tool routes an explicit vertical through a fixed deterministic strategy and returns a DecisionEnvelope containing the selected strategy, exact context projection, evidence state, ranked options, tradeoffs, price range, revision linkage, and available next actions. General shopping is self-directed; gifts add recipient and occasion context rather than disguising every purchase as a gift. Ribband also preserves its original evidence workspace. Ten WebMCP tools let an agent list and select allowlisted origins, search and rank Offers, inspect product pages as stripped Markdown plus structured data, compare products, build a grounded brief, assemble a planning-only activity itinerary, and stage a purchase review. Both surfaces use the same normalized Offer protocol and the same visible workspace as the person. The agent can prepare, explain, and revise a decision. It cannot silently buy, book, contact a provider, request a quote, sign a contract, or save personal memory. Purchase handoff, provider-source opening, and memory approval remain separate visible human controls. How I built it Ribband is a TypeScript application running on Cloudflare Workers. The primary Worker serves the human workspace, same-origin APIs, security controls, diagnostics, and WebMCP handlers. A separate controlled public Worker serves original goods and service fixtures over live HTTPS. Every source adapter compiles into one Offer graph. Product feeds and page JSON-LD reconcile price, availability, condition, shipping, and returns. Service Offers add provider, location, duration, price basis, party limits, published windows, cancellation terms, credentials, service radius, and itinerary or staffing eligibility. Decision fields preserve canonical source links and are labeled verified , single-source , or conflict . The unified orchestrator projects only the context needed by the chosen vertical. Hard exclusions are applied before scoring. Deterministic strategies then expose their factors, reasons, tradeoffs, unknown costs, and source state rather than hiding the ranking inside an opaque model response. Revisions resubmit the complete visible context and link to the prior page-memory decision id; the Worker stores neither request. Vacation packages combine lodging, transportation, dining, and activities with category totals, contingency, and explicit unknown costs. Staffing plans combine controlled provider Offers, fail closed on missing roles or unverified geography, and require a second human review showing the destination and transmitted information before a provider source can open. Trust boundary Ribband never accepts an arbitrary upstream URL. Every upstream request must use HTTPS, match an exact authorized hostname and path, remain within byte and time limits, and reject off-origin or out-of-scope redirects. Each origin has a validated authorization manifest describing capabilities, response limits, freshness policy, and review date. Expired origins fail closed before an upstream request is made. The current controlled catalog intentionally demonstrates guitars rather than claiming arbitrary retail coverage. The controlled service directory contains 20 original fixtures: 5 activities, 1 wellness service, 1 home service, 3 lodging Offers, 2 dining Offers, 2 transportation Offers, and 6 professional services. These fixtures prove the data contract, provenance, planning, and action boundaries; they do not claim live inventory, measured travel time, reservations, messages, contracts, orders, or payments. Date and vacation outcomes can create a tentative memory proposal, but only a visible human approval can save the exact reviewed fact in that browser. Saved facts remain unselected until the person chooses them for a later decision, and the person can correct or delete them. There are no cookies, analytics identifiers, hidden profile reads, or hidden approval paths. Challenges and learning The central challenge was making personalization genuinely useful without turning personal context into invisible surveillance or giving the agent irreversible authority. Extending one Offer protocol from products into dates, vacations, and staffing also required separating facts that can be normalized from actions that remain specific to a vertical. The strongest lesson was that an agent interface should expose more than tools. Trust improves when the person can see the context used, authorization, source state, ranking factors, uncertainty, conflicts, activity, and the exact point where automation stops. A safe refusal is part of the product: Ribband should stop when evidence is stale, contradictory, out of scope, or insufficient. Current verification The deployed release passes strict TypeScript checking, 217 automated tests across 28 test files, eight running-Worker release checks, deployment dry runs for both Cloudflare Workers, and 30 production checks. Browser acceptance exercises all five strategies through WebMCP, the complete outcome-memory consent cycle, eligible and ineligible staffing source review, the homepage entry point, and a 390-pixel mobile layout with no horizontal overflow or console errors. title: Amaphupho WebMCP
pitch: Culturally grounded African dream insight that AI agents can safely invoke on the open web.
about_excerpt: Culturally grounded African dream insight that AI agents can safely invoke on the open web. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP agent completing a task live: toast confirms an interpretation ran and saved to the journal, real production UI. Landing page, dark mode: crescent moon hero and the "Sangoma AI Dream Interpretation" headline. Landing page, light mode: same hero, warm parchment palette. Dream Interpreter, dark mode: "The Sangoma is listening," the core tool guests can use without signing in. Dream Interpreter, light mode: same input flow, daytime theme. Dream Symbol Glossary, dark mode: the A-Z African dream symbol reference, one of the WebMCP-exposed tools. Dream Symbol Glossary, light mode: same glossary, light theme. Sangoma Circle, dark mode: the shared dreams community feed. Sangoma Circle, light mode: same feed, light theme. Inspiration Amaphupho started from a simple problem: general purpose AI can be useful for reflection, but it should not automatically become the authority on every cultural domain. Dream interpretation is deeply contextual, and African dream traditions carry meanings that are often flattened, generalised, or completely missed by mainstream AI systems. I built Amaphupho as a culturally grounded African dream interpretation platform, drawing on Southern African traditions including Zulu, Xhosa, and Sotho perspectives. When the WebMCP Challenge launched, it introduced a new way for me to think about how a specialist website like Amaphupho could work with general purpose AI agents. The idea that shaped the project was: The agent knows the person through their conversation. Amaphupho knows the specialist cultural domain. WebMCP lets them work together. Instead of an agent scraping the site, guessing how the interface works, or reproducing Amaphupho's cultural knowledge inside another model, I can explicitly expose the capabilities I want an agent to use. What it does Amaphupho WebMCP exposes three structured tools to compatible AI agents. search_dream_symbols allows an agent to search Amaphupho's African dream symbol glossary. It is public, read only, and does not consume a user credit. interpret_dream allows a signed in user to ask their agent to interpret a dream using Amaphupho. The tool uses the same production interpretation path as the normal application, so the existing authentication, credit, rate limit, and journal persistence rules still apply. search_dream_journal allows a signed in user to search their own private dream history through an agent. It is read only and explicitly restricted to the currently authenticated Supabase user. A typical interaction could be: A user asks their agent what a snake means in Amaphupho's cultural glossary. The agent calls Amaphupho's public symbol tool. The user shares a complete dream and asks Amaphupho to interpret it. The interpretation is generated through the existing production service and saved to the user's private journal. Later, the user can ask their agent to find recurring themes in their own dream history. The website still works normally in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How I built it I implemented the WebMCP extension in TypeScript using the WebMCP imperative API. Amaphupho registers tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool() I gave each tool a clear name, description, input schema, annotations, and execution function. The main architectural decision I made was to avoid creating a separate "agent backend". The interpret_dream tool calls the existing Amaphupho production interpretation service. That means agent initiated interpretations use the same authentication checks, credit accounting, rate limiting, Gemini integration, and Supabase persistence as interpretations started through the normal user interface. The symbol search tool reads from Amaphupho's curated cultural symbol data and returns structured results. The private journal tool queries Supabase using the currently authenticated session and explicitly filters results by that user's ID. I designed the integration as progressive enhancement. If WebMCP is not available in the browser, Amaphupho continues to operate as a normal web application. I also added Playwright browser tests, conversational eval cases, tool annotations, provenance documentation, GitHub Actions verification, and automated checks for repository formatting requirements. The live application is hosted through Netlify and served from Amaphupho's own domain at https://www.amaphupho.co.za . Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was deciding what not to expose. It would have been easy for me to create a broad agent endpoint that could perform many application actions, but that would also create a much larger privacy and security surface. Instead, I deliberately kept the WebMCP layer small. The public cultural search tool does not require authentication. Dream interpretation requires authentication and has a real side effect because it consumes a credit and saves an entry. Journal search requires authentication but remains strictly read only. Another challenge was making agent initiated behaviour match the existing product instead of creating a parallel implementation. Reusing the production interpretation service meant dealing carefully with sessions, credits, rate limits, failures, and journal persistence. Amaphupho also existed before the challenge, so another important challenge was making the new work independently reviewable. I therefore documented the pre WebMCP boundary and the new WebMCP extension separately in the public challenge repository. Finally, private dream journals contain personal information, so I designed the journal tool so that an agent can never provide an arbitrary user ID or search another person's data. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that the WebMCP integration is running inside a real production application rather than a standalone demonstration. I designed the three tools with different access and side effect boundaries that match what they actually do. Agent initiated dream interpretation reuses Amaphupho's existing production path instead of bypassing product rules. Private journal access is scoped to the authenticated user and remains read only. The site still works normally without WebMCP support. I also added automated browser verification and eval cases rather than relying only on manual demonstrations. Most importantly, I think the integration demonstrates a model where a general purpose agent does not need to own every specialist capability. Amaphupho remains responsible for its cultural knowledge, its user data, and its application rules, while the agent provides the conversational interface. What I learned The biggest lesson I learned was that building for agents is not mainly about exposing more functionality. It is about exposing the right functionality with clear boundaries. Tool names and descriptions matter because the agent needs to understand when a capability should be used. Input schemas matter because they make the interaction predictable. Annotations matter because read only actions should be distinguishable from actions with side effects. Authentication boundaries matter because an agent should not gain broader access simply because it is acting on behalf of a user. I also learned that WebMCP can create a useful relationship between general purpose agents and specialist websites. A general purpose agent can retain conversational context and understand what the user is trying to achieve, while a specialist service can remain authoritative for its own domain. That feels more sustainable to me than requiring every agent to replicate every specialist service internally. What's next for Amaphupho WebMCP The next step I want to explore is deeper longitudinal dream analysis with explicit user control. A user could ask Amaphupho to identify recurring themes across a selected period of their journal, compare repeated symbols, or explore how certain themes have changed over time. I also want to expand multilingual support across English, isiZulu, and Sesotho so users can interact with both the agent and Amaphupho in the language that is most meaningful to them. Future WebMCP tools could support richer cultural symbol exploration and guided reflection without exposing unrestricted access to private journal data. More broadly, I see Amaphupho as an example of how culturally specific and specialist web applications can participate in the agentic web while remaining responsible for their own knowledge, permissions, and user trust. title: Tessera
pitch: AI builds a dashboard in a minute, then next month's data arrives and you start over. Tessera stores dashboards, exposes them through WebMCP, and refreshes them without losing your edits.
about_excerpt: AI builds a dashboard in a minute, then next month's data arrives and you start over. Tessera stores dashboards, exposes them through WebMCP, and refreshes them without losing your edits. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Problem AI can generate a dashboard in a minute. The harder problem starts when that dashboard has to survive real work: someone moves a chart, changes the visual language, adds a hand-built analysis — and then next month's workbook arrives with renamed columns, new rows, and a business definition that may have quietly changed. Most generated dashboards end as outputs. Maintaining one means editing markup, rewriting a large JSON document, or asking a model to regenerate the artifact and hoping the human's changes survive. Over a few reporting cycles, maintenance costs as much as rebuilding. Solution Tessera is a visual analytics workspace for recurring operational reporting. Source workbooks, cleaned analytical tables, reusable transformation recipes, dashboard editions, data bindings, provenance, layout, and styling are all durable application objects, not rendered output. The person uses the visual interface. An external agent uses Tessera through WebMCP. Both paths resolve to the same typed command layer and the same project state. If the agent creates a chart, the person can drag and restyle it. If the person builds a visualization by hand, the agent encounters it as part of the same dashboard on the next refresh. If the person leaves an empty tile with a written brief, the agent can find it and build into that exact spot. When a new reporting period arrives, Tessera applies the saved recipe to the new source and creates a new edition of the existing dashboard. Layout, presentation, illustrations, and manual work persist; values and period-specific commentary change; earlier months remain intact behind a month selector. When a source change is genuinely ambiguous — a facility that stopped reporting a metric, a column that didn't exist last month — Tessera raises a Decision Needed instead of guessing. A person resolves it, hands the work back, and the interrupted workflow continues. Why This Matters Operations, finance, and analytics teams don't need another disposable chart generator. They need reporting artifacts that outlive the conversation that created them. WebMCP fits because Tessera is an application with many structured, composable operations: inspect a source, outline regions, map columns, create a clean table, save a recipe, add a dashboard block, bind a metric, style an exact element, inspect the result. Exposing those native operations gives an agent a reliable application to operate rather than a page of buttons to guess through or a generated artifact to rewrite. The result is one artifact with two operators. Agent work compounds across reporting periods, while business judgment and final approval stay with the person responsible for the report. How We Used AI In the product, AI stays outside Tessera. A connected browser agent discovers Tessera's WebMCP tools, inspects the active workspace, and calls validated operations to prepare data and compose or maintain dashboards. Tessera does not embed a chatbot, does not maintain a second agent-only state model, and does not accept arbitrary generated markup. The one exception is illustration: from a plain-language request, the external agent can generate a graphic and place it through Tessera as a recolorable illustration block in the product's house style, still part of the dashboard like any other object. AI tools were also used during development to review the architecture, refine the monthly workflow, diagnose interaction issues, improve accessibility, and exercise the product end to end. Every generated change went through the same build, lint, and automated test suite used for the final release. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the working product into a submission-ready release. It reviewed the repository and WebMCP surface, implemented and tested polish across the warehouse and dashboard studio, checked manual and agent parity, performed live browser verification, and ran the full release quality gate. Key Features A complete monthly data workflow: upload, source inspection, multi-region outlining, field mapping, decision capture, clean-draft review, and approval. Persistent recipes that carry learned structure and column mappings into later reporting periods. Dashboard month editions behind a single month selector — layout, styling, illustrations, and hand-built blocks preserved while bound values refresh; prior months never overwritten. Decision Needed: human-only gates for ambiguous source changes and for monthly approval, with a resumable handoff back to the agent. Draft markers: empty tiles with a written brief that the agent discovers and builds into, at the position the person chose. One-click provenance from a dashboard metric to its cleaned table and on to the source workbook. A 12-column canvas with drag, resize, stacking, undo, redo, presentation kits, and per-block inspectors. KPI, text, table, illustration, bar, line, donut, gauge, scatter, heatmap, treemap, and Sankey blocks. Visible WebMCP connection status and named operation activity — no embedded assistant. Per-visitor hosted workspaces, plus optional local folder mirroring to readable project, dashboard, and dataset files. Architecture Tessera is a React and TypeScript application backed by a validated command bus. Manual controls and WebMCP tool calls execute the same command definitions, so validation, persistence, live synchronization, and undo history cannot drift between the two interfaces. The browser registers seven native WebMCP tools: four high-value direct tools plus a three-tool catalog, schema, and execution gateway. The gateway exposes 64 agent-facing operations while keeping the browser's native tool budget small. Every input is checked against its JSON schema at the boundary. Mutations return an updated dashboard or project snapshot so an agent can verify its work without extra calls. Read-only and untrusted-content annotations follow the current WebMCP contract. Two judgment and approval operations are intentionally withheld from the agent catalog and remain available only in the human interface. Hosted state uses revision-aware persistence, isolated per visitor. Uploads are stored separately and scoped to the same workspace. The local server mirrors the same API, and an optional folder connection writes readable project JSON and source files to a location the user chooses. title: Bizgrid
pitch: Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for African sellers. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart without scraping the UI
about_excerpt: Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for African sellers. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart without scraping the UI Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Starting an online business in Africa is still harder than it should be. Many small businesses rely on social media because building an e-commerce website requires technical skills, time, and money. Existing platforms often expect merchants to understand themes, hosting, product management, and website design before they can even make their first sale. We asked a simple question: What if building an online store was as easy as describing your business to an AI? That idea became Bizgrid, this an AI-powered commerce platform that lets anyone create, customise, and launch a professional online store through natural conversation. What it does Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for sellers and SME's. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart ,without scraping the UI. Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Bizgrid is an AI-first commerce platform for African sellers: dozens of independent merchants each run their own storefront, with their own catalog, inventory, prices, and Paystack checkout, all hosted on one platform. That shape many sellers, one marketplace is exactly where WebMCP shines, because commerce is fundamentally structured data. Stores, products, prices, stock levels, variant options, and carts all have well-defined schemas. WebMCP's tool model lets us expose that structure directly, instead of forcing an agent to reverse-engineer it. Before WebMCP, an agent trying to shop on Bizgrid would have to scrape HTML fragile, slow, and blind to the rules that matter. It wouldn't reliably know whether a product is in stock, how many units can be purchased, what currency the merchant prices in, or which variant options are required. It certainly couldn't know that a "cart" on Bizgrid is scoped to a specific merchant, and that putting an item in the wrong cart means paying the wrong seller. Those are business-critical rules, not UI details. With WebMCP, we encode them once, as typed tool contracts: every tool response carries a store_slug, every add_to_cart validates stock, purchase limits, and variant options against the merchant's real data before writing. The agent can no longer guess wrong about who gets the money the platform itself enforces correctness. There's also a natural symmetry in our product story: Bizgrid merchants already run their shops with an AI assistant on WhatsApp. WebMCP completes the loop on the buyer side. Merchants sell through an agent; now buyers shop through an agent, too with Bizgrid as the structured layer that connects them. How it creates a better user experience Imagine a shopper in Lagos who wants a vitamin C serum under ₦20,000. The old way: they'd discover Bizgrid stores one at a time, open each storefront in a new tab, search each shop's catalog separately, compare prices by hand, and repeat the whole ritual for every product. The new way: they open ChatGPT (or any WebMCP-capable browser) on the Bizgrid homepage and say one sentence: "Find me a vitamin C serum under ₦20,000." The agent calls search_products with budget_max, gets back structured results from every published store at once — name, store, price, currency, stock status, and a direct product link and presents a ranked comparison. The shopper says "add the one from GlowSkin to my cart," and the agent calls add_to_cart with the correct store_slug, where the platform validates stock and variants and writes to that merchant's cart. The shopper then clicks one checkout link and pays normally with Paystack. What makes this a better experience, not just a different one: the human stays in the familiar, trusted flow the same storefront cart and checkout they already know while everything upstream (search, comparison, decision fatigue) becomes conversational. And because tools are typed, the agent quotes real prices in the right currency, never hallucinates a product, and never sends a shopper to a checkout that doesn't contain what they asked for. Discovery becomes instant; trust stays human. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before The genuinely new capability here is platform-wide shopping with a human-held checkout. Before WebMCP, an agent could only operate inside one website at a time, scraping one storefront's HTML. Cross-store comparison meant running one agent per tab, and adding to a cart meant custom per-merchant integrations that no small African seller could afford. There was no way for an agent to say "search all of Bizgrid" the marketplace existed in the URL structure, not in any machine-readable interface. WebMCP collapses that. A single tool layer registered on the platform homepage exposes every published store, every product, and every cart as first-class, callable operations. One agent can search across merchants, compare, negotiate the shopper's preferences, and fill the correct seller's cart then hand the same browser cart to a human for the final, money-moving step. That handoff is the heart of it: a division of labor that didn't exist before. The agent does what machines are good at exhaustive search, structured comparison, remembering constraints, enforcing rules. The human does what humans insist on reviewing, confirming, and paying with the checkout they trust. Agent discovers and carts; human reviews and pays. That collaboration was impossible with scraping, and it's exactly the human-agent partnership WebMCP exists to enable. How we implemented WebMCP We extended Bizgrid's Next.js frontend with a WebMCP tool layer, all client-side, no agent-specific integrations: Registration: src/lib/webmcp/bootstrap.ts polls for document.modelContext (up to 120 animation frames, so registration works even if the WebMCP runtime initializes after page load), registers all tools through registerTool, dispatches a toolchange event so agents re-discover them, dedupes via a single bootstrap promise (protecting against React Strict Mode double-invocations), and cleans up on pagehide. An app-wide provider (src/components/webmcp/platform-webmcp-provider.tsx) plus an instrumentation hook register the tools on every page, early. The seven tools (src/lib/webmcp/platform-tools.ts) — list_stores, list_catalog, get_store_info, search_products, get_product, add_to_cart, get_cart — each with a JSON Schema inputSchema, descriptions written to guide agent tool selection (e.g., "prefer search_products when the shopper has a specific query"), and readOnlyHint annotations so agents can reason about side effects. Data layer — tools call Bizgrid's existing catalog APIs (store listing, full catalog with pagination, search with budget filters, per-product lookup), so agents get live, real prices and stock, never static HTML. Shared cart, shared checkout — add_to_cart writes to the same per-store localStorage cart keys the storefronts already use (src/lib/webmcp/platform-cart.ts), with validation of stock, purchase limits, and variant options (src/lib/webmcp/shared.ts). Every response includes cart_url and checkout_url, so the human opens the exact checkout the agent filled. Agents and humans share one cart and one trusted Paystack flow nothing is simulated or sandboxed. No server changes required because everything is structured client-side on top of existing APIs, the entire WebMCP surface ships with the normal frontend bundle, live at https://www.bizgrid.shop today. title: TLDW | Too Long Didn't Watch
pitch: For those who want to Cut Through The Noise to Get to The Signal in their YouTube videos.
about_excerpt: For those who want to Cut Through The Noise to Get to The Signal in their YouTube videos. Like Comment Story Updates Step 1 Processing Result Icon Inspiration In a world of AI there is too much noise, this is a simple tool to leverage that very same AI to help cut through the noise to get to the signal of your YouTube videos. What it does TLDW is one web page where you paste a YouTube link and gets the captions, with the moment each line was said. An AI agent opening the page finds two WebMCP tools instead of buttons: get_transcript(url) hands it the captions as timestamped segments, and render_explainer(slides, url) draws whatever the agent wrote back onto the page, every timestamp a link that opens the video at that second, then reads it aloud. The thinking runs on the visitor's own ChatGPT plan, in their own session. How its built Built entirely with AI, Both tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool, with navigator.modelContext as a fallback for older builds, each with a JSON schema an agent can read. Errors are returned, never thrown, so a failure arrives as a result the agent can act on. Every fetch has three outcomes, not two: ok, not_measured with a reason, or a structured error, because a tool that cannot tell a failed measurement from a real zero will report the first as the second. Captions come from a transcript API first with a direct fetch behind it, held in memory for ten minutes and never written down. The page is served by a Cloudflare Worker. Read-aloud uses the browser's own voices by default with a voice picker; one opt-in experimental entry renders a natural voice on our server and streams it back. An agent whose browser has no WebMCP yet can paste the same slides into a Render box on the page and get the identical result. It was built from nothing in one evening, live on stream, by a fleet of AI bodies run by one human, with two independent reviews on every change. Challenges We (Myself and my AI Team) only had ~8 total hours for this as that's when I found out about the competition, then immediately started live streaming the start to finish. We had about ~3 hours of prep while waiting for the reset then 5 hours to build. The spec moved while we built: our first registration was on navigator.modelContext only, and Chrome's stable build binds document.modelContext, so the tools registered and nobody could see them. YouTube refuses caption fetches from a server, so the free path failed silently until we made refusal a first-class result and put a transcript API in front of it. Agents that fetched the captions then answered in chat instead of drawing on the page, until the tool text put the obligation before the data. And the browser's speech queue armed from the speak call rather than from what was drawn, so a slide with the wrong shape left a full explainer on screen and nothing to play. Each one was found by a second reader, not by the author. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got it done 40mins past the buzzer but fortunately there was a 12 hour extension, so we polished the video and made minor edits to the description etc (also generated by AI) The tool work on a free ChatGPT account, the desktop app's built-in browser, and with one sentence: explain this video and render it on the page. The page registers two tools, the agent calls them, the explainer appears with timestamps that jump into the YouTube video if you want to watch a particular segment in full, and it also comes with a reads aloud bar with play back controls and voice selection that uses your browser supported voices and 2 x experimental neural voices. The public repository has one clean history, one identity, and passed a whole-history scan by a stranger before it went public. What we learned The hard part was restraint. Every instinct said add a summarizer, add a model, add a key, and each one would have made it slower, costlier. The second lesson was the error surface: an agent is not a human staring at a stack trace, it reads your failure and decides what to do next, so a tool that throws ends the conversation and a tool that returns a readable error lets the agent try something sensible. The third was the voices, Chrome free supports free neural style voices as well as system voices, the ChatGPT browser uses only the free system voice. We are experimenting with some neural voices but the render time is slower, there could be an option to use something like Elevenlabs but then that would mean have to charge a fee for the service or run ad's on the page. It would be good if the ChatGPT could somehow enable support for the Chrome voices as those are pretty good. What's next for TLDW | Too Long Didn't Watch This is TLDW v1 .v2 & v3 will be better. I didn't want to create something that Notebook LM already does so keeping it video focused is the lane I'll stay in for now. v2 would be more generating more interactive lessons / explainers with interactive kinetic elements maybe a quiz at the end and then perhaps v3 would be the ability to generate a Summarized Explainer Video about the video on the fly. and then later another version of the product for teachers that uses the same logic and flow to help produce lesson plans and explainers on the fly for all students at all levels with all styles of learning requirements. title: Cascade
pitch: A shared decision canvas where people and agents map hidden assumptions, stress-test plans against real world shocks, and turn uncertainty into resilient action.
about_excerpt: A shared decision canvas where people and agents map hidden assumptions, stress-test plans against real world shocks, and turn uncertainty into resilient action. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When working on an app launch, we found ourselves sending planning docs back and forth between us and our agents. That was very problematic. We wanted to move beyond asking an AI, “What could go wrong?” and getting another list to read. What if the agent could work inside the plan itself, connecting assumptions, exploring consequences, and proposing alternatives that a person could inspect and challenge? That became Cascade: a shared decision canvas for people and their agents. What it does Cascade turns a consequential plan into a connected map of objectives, assumptions, dependencies, constraints, risks, and outcomes. Our demo starts with a product launch: six weeks, 500 teams, and a $12,000 budget. What happens if billing arrives three weeks late? An agent can create a separate what-if branch, apply the disruption, and trace modeled downstream effects. It can then stage possible responses, such as launching a free beta first. The human can inspect the map, drag cards with their connections following, compare scenarios, and accept or reject proposed factors and relationships. Applying a shock is allowed inside a what-if branch; proposed mitigations remain drafts awaiting review. Promoting a branch is a human action. Product launch is the starter. Cascade also includes a community tool-lending scenario and a blank workspace for other plans. Why WebMCP Cascade is built around a shared working surface, not a separate chat transcript. WebMCP lets the agent read and act on the structured model behind the page. Tool actions update the same interface the person is watching: branches appear, shocks enter the map, and proposals arrive for review. This makes an otherwise awkward workflow practical: the agent explores alternatives inside the live application while the person retains an inspectable record of the model and controls which proposals are accepted. There is no need to copy the plan into a chat and manually translate the answer back into a diagram. How we built it Cascade uses TypeScript and React, with a Next.js-style App Router implemented through vinext on Vite. React Flow provides the draggable node-and-edge canvas. Custom CSS and a Tailwind CSS build pipeline support the visual design. The app registers 11 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). They cover reading the workspace, staging factors and relationships, creating branches, applying shocks, proposing mitigations, running stress tests, and comparing or explaining results. Tools use structured schemas and bounded inputs. Version checks on scenario-editing tools help reject stale writes when a person and an agent are working on the same model. Draft revision is limited to unlocked draft factors. A local TypeScript engine propagates shocks through accepted relationships to produce deterministic sensitivity metrics and impact paths. Its outputs are modeling aids. Vitest tests cover stable metrics, shock propagation, draft exclusion from cost and schedule totals, and graph layout. The workspace is stored in browser localStorage and can be exported as JSON. The app does not need its own AI API key; a connected agent uses the page's tools. That agent still receives the workspace data exposed through those tools. Cascade is hosted on ChatGPT Sites with a Cloudflare Workers-compatible build, with source code on GitHub under the MIT license. Challenges we ran into One challenge was making the graph behave like a genuine working surface: cards needed to move freely while their connections stayed anchored. Another was separating exploration from commitment. An agent needs room to test a disruption without silently rewriting the baseline, and people need a clear distinction between proposed and accepted changes. Rehearsing the demo exposed a subtler problem: an agent created a scenario whose description mentioned a delay, but did not actually apply the delay to the model. That reinforced an important lesson: a success message is not proof of a state change. Reliable collaboration needs outcome verification, not just well-described tools. Accomplishments we're proud of We built a working shared canvas where agent actions become visible, reviewable changes rather than suggestions trapped in a conversation. The same decision model supports both the product-launch and community examples, and the app remains usable by a person when WebMCP is unavailable. Most importantly, human review is part of the interaction itself: proposals, locks, scenario branches, and promotion controls make the collaboration boundary visible. What we learned Agent-native design is as much about accountability as capability. Giving an agent tools is only the beginning; the application must make its actions understandable and checkable. We also learned to distinguish a useful model from a confident-looking number. Cascade's purpose is to expose assumptions and explore consequences, not claim certainty about the future. What's next Stronger end-to-end evaluations that verify actual model changes after agent actions. More explicit feedback when a scenario has been created but no disruption has been applied. Improved mitigation-effect modeling, uncertainty handling, and explanation of score contributions. Shared team workspaces with durable persistence. Evidence links and richer review history for the assumptions behind a decision. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about.
